This dance is not only a display of incredible athleticism but also a rite of passage. It is traditionally performed during ceremonies and festivals, showcasing strength, agility, and stamina. FLASHBACK: Who Founded or Co-founded Bilpam Base/General Headquarters?

By James Gatdet Dak Lampuar

This is not a tricky question. It is also not a personalized pride or arrogance or brag either. This is an honest piece of our national history! 

My article, as you will read it, is simply about setting the record straight and to serve as a history lesson for those who did NOT know the history of Bilpam.

History is important, and particularly when it is correctly and honestly recorded --- no matter how insignificant it may look. 

When told factually in all its pieces and then knitted together, it serves its rightful purpose for generations to come.

Yes, history is scientific, and it is supposed to be recorded as it naturally flows without doctoring it. 

Once history telling or recording is tempered with or manipulated, it becomes a disinformation and deception, thus misleading. 

But do we really tell our country´s history factually and truthfully, or do we, or some of us, selectively tell either facts or lies, depending on what we tell and who tells it? 

Do some of us get caught up in the heat of the moment with excitement and get tempted to tell a lie as part of our history, and even try to suppress the truthful ones?

Our nation's history --- as the people of South Sudan --- must be recorded factually and truthfully as it deserves, lest it confuses our current and future generations. 

If manipulated, it would obviously risk turning into mostly exaggerated, if not falsified, contests for undeserved credits. Thus, losing the true purpose for which history is intended to educationally serve and preserve.

I have introduced my article with those seemingly strange comments and questions because I have seen and heard people trying to falsify a piece of our national history. 

Some people, for whatever reason, may not appreciate this factual historical revelation. However, what matters most is that they read this article and know the truth.

I am very much aware that there are individuals or groups of individuals who always want to politically manipulate almost everything, and have no desire whatsoever to admit facts and truths. They wrongly think that politics is about lying in trying to advance yourself or your group. They even politicize social interactions and communication among individuals and communities. This is "politikac." 

Right. There are those who claim credits for particular things prepared by others, and in this case, which I am very well versed with, or being an active participant in. Claiming a credit for something good that you did NOT do is dishonesty, and not good! 

And this brings me to my topical article of today, which is 'Bilpam.' 

QUESTION: When, how and who established Bilpam, which currently proudly carries the historic and historical name of our national army`s General Headquarters in the capital city, Juba? 

Even if the original Bilpam's territory is no longer where our national army's General Headquarters is physically located today, the historic and historical roles it played in our final liberation struggles for independence, and its name shall continue to be remembered and honoured in the history of South Sudan.   

Before I proceed, I kindly ask the readers to receive my rejoinder as an informative and educative piece of history as far as our national history of liberation struggle is concerned. I am NOT trying to brag or exhibit pride or arrogance. 

I am NOT inviting contest or envy or jealousy either --- as the subsequent paragraphs below may be perceived to have suggested. Just setting the record straight on this important fraction of journey in our history in the subsequent liberation struggles on the road to INDEPENDENCE of South Sudan.

Having stated that, and being a journalist and insider, I am trying to educate others who may not know how Bilpam or its name we use today came about, etc. And after all, who can tell your history better than yourself as a participant. We  may be doing a disservice to ourselves if we do not tell our own stories and history. I therefore encourage each and everyone of us to present their stories, but factually. Writing a book is a plus.

So let me repeat the question: What do the people of South Sudan know about how and when and where the 'historical' Bilpam --- which our current military General Headquarters in Juba is named after --- was founded and established. And who founded or co-founded it?

Below is a brief factual and truthful history of how Bilpam was founded as the main base or headquarters for subsequent liberation movements since late 1975, from its previous status as an abandoned Nuer community village due to the threat against cattle by wild animals, such as roaming lions, etc. 

Nota bene! First, it was politically/militarily established officially by Anya-Anya Two movement and inhabited in 1976, and then taken over by SPLA/SPLM or SPLM/SPLA in 1983.

In a nutshell, it was the late General Benson Kuany Latjor and my humble and Christian father, Elder John Dak Lampuar, who --- after the Akobo mutiny in 1975 --- selected and laid the foundation of Bilpam with their own hands. It was established for the first time as the main base or General Headquarters for the Anya-Nya Two liberation movement (officially) from 1976, and later on taken over by the SPLA/SPLM in 1983 --- after forcefully dislodging Anya Anya Two from it. 

Here is a summary of the background story below:

When the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972 was partially abrogated by the former regime in Sudan under the leadership of President Jaafar Mohamed Nimeiri, several South(ern) Sudanese officers stationed in Akobo town --- of the present-day Jonglei state ---mutinied. 

They were led by the late Benson Kuany Latjor and decided to match out in protest towards Ethiopia in 1975. Benson Kuany (aka Vincent) had a rank of 1st lieutenant in the Sudanese Army at the time of the mutiny.

After reaching Ethiopia in Itang town and subsequently meeting former Ethiopian authorities from Gambela region, they were --- after a long wait --- finally welcomed to be assisted by the former Derg regime of President Mengistu Haile Mariam. 

The Ethiopian authorities then directed them to find a suitable site for their base around the area of Puldeng villages --- near the Ethiopian border with South Sudan.

Thanks to the people of Ethiopia who have been always welcoming our people to their country with their usual hospitality.

The would-be co-founders of the Anya-Nya Two movement were specifically directed to meet my father, Elder John Dak Lampuar, who was/is the church leader in that area, to host and guide them on the selection of a site for a base. 

Our village or Bilpam is also about six kilometers from Baro/Sobat river, where a small town called Makuach (Behrane Selam) was located. This is where I did my first two years of primary school.

Elder John Dak welcomed the four officers, namely, Benson Kuany Latjor, Michael Waat Latjor, James Tap Liah, and Bol Kur. While the first three officers were from the Nuer ethnic group of Unity state, Bol Kur was from the Shilluk ethnic group.

Elder Gordon Koang Chuol would join them at a later date and deputize Benson Kuany Latjor.

Elder John Dak told them about two possible sites to choose from as a base: Bilpam and Chotkuach!

However, Elder John Dak also strongly recommended Bilpam to them because it is a beautiful hilly site, with dense forests and a lot of coconut trees and many other types of trees with eatable fruits. It also has a river around it for easy access to water and fishing. 

Bilpam also had many kinds of eatable wild animals living inside its vast forests, while it had no human inhabitants at that time. It was about two kilometres from our beautiful village or church, just separated by the river.

After spending a night in our house, Elder John in the following morning took the officers to see Bilpam site, which, as mentioned above, was just a few kilometres away from his church and the surrounding villages. 

When they arrived, Benson Kuany and his colleagues liked the site, and did not bother to see the other site, Chotkuach..

Benson Kuany asked my dad as the host and Christian spiritual leader in the area to symbolically cut and clear the first grass and shrubs and put a mark on a big tree in the center of Bilpam --- in a ceremonial manner --- and to bless it with a prayer.  And hence officiated the founding of Bilpam as their headquarters. 

My father did exactly that by praying and cutting the grass and hitting a big tree with a panga (machete). From that moment Bilpam was declared established or founded as the main base for the renewed liberation struggle! 

But it took another time for the officers with their forces to physically establish themselves in Bilpam from 1976.

After officiating the establishment of Bilpam, the officers went back to Itang. Itang is an Ethiopian town which later on became the Africa's biggest refugee camp in the mid1980s and located about 15 kilometres east of Bilpam. 

It took the officers sometime to prepare before they could begin to build their houses or barracks in Bilpam.

Benson Kuany then brought about 50 of his men from Itang who cleared the bushes of Bilpam and gradually began to erect houses and their barracks around 1976, until 1983 when the SPLM/SPLA took over the base. 

Anya Nya Two forces, while in Bilpam, did not engage in significant, if any, military operations against the Sudanese government. Their military operations were limited.They were always saying they had been waiting for other South(ern) Sudanese to join them in Bilpam so that military operations could seriously kick off in the fight for independence of South(ern) Sudan.

Elder Gordon Koang Chuol----who later became the acting leader of Anya-Nya Two in the long absence of Benson Kuany in Gambela----and Paulino Matip Nhial, plus many other leaders, joined the Anya-Nya Two leadership after Bilpam was already founded or marked. 

But uncle Paulino Matip left Bilpam after he fell out with Gordon Koang. He went back to the present-day Unity state and established his own force.

Gordon Koang Chuol was the acting Anya-Nya Two leader whom the SPLM/SPLA dislodged from Bilpam in 1983. 

In brief, this is how Bilpam was founded since mid 1975!

For about 8 years, Elder John Dak Lampuar continued to support the Anya-Nya Two leaders, with all he could possibly provide --- being material, moral and spiritual support.

Also, many of the people he taught and groomed in his church --- which he established in 1974 in Nyigol (Bilpam) --- have now become either ordained Pastors, Elders, Deaconesses, Evangelists and Choirs as well as faithful members of the Christian church in South Sudan, Ethiopia, United States of America, etc.

Other elders including the late Elijah Yong Kier and Moses Bichiok Reath, etc., also played different roles, mainly in Itang.

WHAT HAPPENED NEXT?

Then Bor and Ayod mutinies occurred in 1983. Dr. John Garang de Mabior, Kerubino Kwanyin Bol, Akuot Atem, Samuel Gai Tut, William Nyuon Bany, Salva Kiir Mayardit, Lokurnyang Lado, Abdalla Chuol, etc., came to Ethiopia, particularly to Itang and Gambella, subsequently arriving at different times.

Their top, or let me say, senior leaders such as Akuot Atem, Gai Tut, John Garang, Salva Kiir, etc., were taken to Addis Ababa to meet the Ethiopian top leadership. They were promised assistance confidentially. This was coordinated by uncle Thokwath Pal, who was the chief of security in Gambella of Illubabor region.

Then power struggle and ideological differences emerged between them with Akuot and Gai and Abdalla, etc., on one hand, and Garang and Kerubino and Nyuon and Kiir, etc., on the other.

Dr. Garang won the support of Colonel Mengistu Haile Mariam, a socialist President of Ethiopia at the time. 

Dr. Garang, being a smart thinker, cleverly inserted the political and ideological slogans of Colonel Mengistu in what would become the SPLM/SPLA manifesto in order to win his support. 

Slogans such as 'New Sudan' as similar to the 'New Ethiopia' of Mengistu, or 'united socialist Sudan' as similar to the 'united socialist Ethiopia' of Mengistu, were all floated and dangled in the face of Colonel Mengistu. 

After the fall of Mengistu's regime in 1991, Garang later changed it to 'secular democratic united Sudan.'

Words of President Mengistu such as 'reactionaries' in reference to separatist Eritrea's fighting for independence from the rest of Ethiopia, was also mimicked by Dr. Garang and equally used to refer to Anya Nya Two separatists in Sudan as 'reactionaries', etc.

Also President Mengistu's insults, which allegedly described Eritrea's separatists as 'sellouts' or bloody 'traders' called 'negade' in Amharic language, also became 'nyegat' by SPLA/SPLM --- in a twisted pronunciation from the Amharic word 'negade' ---  in reference to Anya Nya Two separatists fighting for independence of South Sudan, etc.

Their ideas became twin or identical ideas. After all, also the two were not only military officers, but also Colonels in ranks. It was like a perfect match which would guarantee future relations between Sudan and Ethiopia. After all, President Mengistu wanted to see President Nimieri of Sudan overthrown as a revenge for supporting Ethiopian rebel fighters.

So Mengistu helped the group led by Dr. Garang to dislodge forcefully or militarily Anya Nya Two from Bilpam, including Akuot Atem, Gai Tut, etc., from Itang. 

Also, luckily, the SPLA/SPLM emerged during an era of a heightened cold war between the United States of America and the former Soviet Union and its allies, including Cuba. Thus, military assistance began to flow in big quantities and categories to the Movement from and through these communist and socialist powers. This is with the hope of capturing the state power in the Sudan and turning the country into a socialist state.

After the capture of Bilpam from Anya Nya Two, which I personally witnessed in 1983, we could see both William Nyuon and Kerubino Kwanyin, touring or inspecting our village (Linglaat) and Bilpam, searching for the wounded Anya Nya Two soldiers in hiding. 

They collected them and summarily executed them by firing squad. All of them, except one wounded man from Bentiu, called Muolpiny, who by God's grace was not seen during the execution of his colleagues. 

William Nyuon later spotted him while hiding inside a Luak (byre). But he spared his life by refusing to also execute him after his colleagues, calling him a lucky man. 

My father then asked William Nyuon to give the wounded man to him and nurse him in the church. Willian Nyuon agreed. 

The man stayed in our home, got healed and became a very good preacher in the church for nearly two years. My father even gave him a cow from the dowry of my elder sister's marriage in 1984. Then he went back to Bentiu, or present-day Unity State.

When the SPLM/SPLA took over Bilpam in 1983, under the leadership of Dr. John Garang de Mabior, and confirmed it as their General Headquarters, my dad and our village chief, continued to support the new liberation movement. 

Despite SPLA being violent from the onset, to me the SPLA looked more organized than the Anya Nya Two, even during its initial formation in 1983.

Elder John continued to support the administration of Bilpam at the time, under the late uncle Chagai Atem Biar. He was supporting them with all the material, spiritual and moral support he could mobilize. He helped in realizing harmonious coexistence between the liberation army and the communities around Bilpam. 

INTERLUDE:

Dr. Garang continued to present himself as a unionist against separatists. He was on record boasting that he fired his first bullet in 1983 against his fellow South(ern) Sudanese separatists. 

Throughout his life as the leader of the Movement, he would sometimes try to justify his unionist ideology as a 'fish-feed with a hook' (bait) to lure in fighters from the other marginalized parts of the Sudan and use them to fight the war against the center. 

However, what was not clear was whether he was truly a unionist against independence of South Sudan or not. Would Dr. Garang have had seriously pursued self-determination without others pushing for it --- whether through the Nasir Declaration or shaky or water-testing Khartoum Peace Agreement (KPA) of 1997 signed by Dr. Riek Machar Teny-Dhurgon, which was based on the right of self-determination --- or without the copied and pasted self-determination clause to the consolidated Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) of 2005 --- worked out by both leaders?

And another mystery which was not clear was the question of at which stage, if any, should Dr. Garang on his own decide to revert to pursuing independence of South Sudan ---if it was truly at the back of his mind --- or jump out of the united Sudan fish-feed with a hook agenda. 

And what if the fish entangled the hook around a firm object under a deep sea, eat its feed, but never allow the hook to come back to the surface of the water again with the desired result?

Or what if Dr. Garang could be trapped and blackmailed by the equally shrewd colleagues of the North or from the other marginalized peripheries of the Sudan ---- whom he lured in to fight with him --- but never wanted him to talk about independence of South Sudan, as the aspiration of his South Sudanese people?

Did he have an exit strategy in that ideological trap, without the KPA or CPA, apart from getting fighters from the peripheries of the Sudan to help force the center to accept a secular united  Sudan --- temporary it may be --- before another military coup re-introduces  'Sharia laws' in a united Sudan, and so the merry-go-around? 

Even Eritrea was allowed by the regional powers to talk of jumping out, and it actually jumped out of the union in Ethiopia in 1993. 

Or was Dr. Garang fine with a united Sudan as its First Vice President, secular or not, but relatively peaceful Sudan, that may never allow independence of South Sudan to be realized?

As goes the frog tale, when was the frog ready to jump out of the deceptive lukewarm, then boiling water trap before it could exhaust its body's adjustments and resistance capabilities in the speedily progressing very hot water, before the frog could unfortunately get too exhausted and collapse as it failed to jump out of the deceptive lukewarm and hot water? 

Those were some of the unanswered questions, or which answers were not clear.

SUMMARY

And back to Anya Nya Two and the founding of Bilpam. Some of the Anya-Nya Two leaders present whose names I have mentioned above --- or were among the 50 men during the founding of Bilpam --- include uncle James Tap Liah. 

Actually, I met one of the former Anya Nya Two officers in Juba and he reminded me again about the whole thing. 

I also met another founding member in Khartoum in January, 2019. He even still remembered the colour of the bull which my father gave to them for feeding during the establishment of Bilpam ----surprisingly after nearly 50 years of that event. He was so excited!

But someone asked, "Did you recently meet some of the top co-founders of Bilpam to give you more information in case you want to write a book?"

Yes, but not very recent!

From 1994-1999, I was in USA, same city, with uncle James Tap Liah, who is one of the co-founders of Bilpam, and who himself mutinied from the Sudanese army in Akobo in 1975 with the late uncle Benson Kuany. He also used to tell me stories about how Bilpam was founded, similar to the stories I heard from my father or I personally witnessed. 

He also came back to Juba and got reinstated in the army at the rank of Brigadier General and was put in charge of Administration and Finance for a Brigade stationed in Jonglei state before the December 2013 crisis.

I also personally met late General Benson Kuany Latjor in Juba around year 2005. He was so excited learning that I am the eldest son of Elder John Dak Lampuar. Although we did not have much conversations due to rush, he was so appreciative.

I also met late General Paulino Matip Nhial --- when he was the Deputy C-in-C of SPLA, at his residence in Juba, about two years before he passed on. "Your father is a great man," he told me, if I correctly remember his first comment.

They all called me "Gat Damaar" when I met the three of them separately, which in the Nuer language literally means 'Son Of My Brother' (nephew).

May their great souls rest in eternal peace!

I am collecting more information from many different sources too before writing a book.

Any one with vital factual and verifiable information to contribute to my upcoming book can contact me via messenger or WhatsApp.

Thanks to all in advance.

My father, Elder John, was very passionate about the liberation of South Sudan. Since I was an adolescent, I would from time to time hear him in our homestead chatting with any visiting Anya-Nya Two leader, including Benson Kuany Latjor and Gordon Koang Chuol, etc. 

Because my dad moved his family to Malakal --- the then regional capital of Upper Nile --- after the Addis Ababa Agreement was signed in 1972, he saw by himself the oppression inflicted on South(ern) Sudanese people inside Malakal town. 

He hence saw the need for a total liberation of the people of South(ern) Sudan to gain freedom or independence. This made him to wholeheartedly support any liberation movement fighting for the rights of our people after we returned from Malakal town.

Currently, and unfortunately, our people and leaders talk of Bilpam, and have even established modern army General Headquarters in the capital, Juba, in its memory, but are shying away from acknowledging or talking about how it was originally established and who founded or co-founded it, and its contribution to the liberation struggle, etc.. 

What do we tell our children and grandchildren about the origin of this historical Bilpam---which they keep hearing its name? Are they being taught about this piece of history in school?

Bilpam is a compound word, which literally means 'Rocky hill or Hill side.' 

When the name is translated from Nuer language to English, 'Bil' means 'Hill' and 'Pam' means 'Rock', or even mountain. 

Some people spell its name as 'Bilpham' or 'Bilpaam'  by unnecessarily adding either 'h' or another 'a' to its name.

For those who knew Bil-pam or Rocky-hill, it is on hilly ground, with a beautiful scenery.

In addition to being the foundational layer of the historical Bilpam we all talk of, Elder John----like many others---was also generous to the two subsequent movements. He is wise, humble and peaceful Christian church spiritual leader. 

He had been contributing some of his own family cattle and grain for feedings in Bilpam, and ensuring harmony between the community and liberation fighters through the church he established in 1974 in Nyigol/Puldeng (Bilpam area) after his return from Malakal town.

Again, a true history is scientific and important! Anyone interested in the basics I have provided above can then research its details. 

Majority of our people unfortunately do not know the history of Bilpam simply because political and military leaders in Juba do not educate people about it for whatever reason. Not even taught in history books in schools. I previously blackmailed myself not to write about it for many years, thinking that 'some people' may think I was being arrogant with pride, etc. But history is history and should be told. After all, history points to particular people. 

And I encourage all of us to share our history and stories. We should not wait for Western writers to write our history books for us as previously the tradition. Let us write them, ourselves, but factually.

I believe that God chose and assigned Elder John Dak Lampuar for that task to select that particular piece of land --- which became an important historical center for the liberation and freedom of his people --- at that particular time in our history. 

Thanks to all the community chiefs and elders of Nyigol and Puldeng who endorsed his decision nearly 50 years ago!

Today, while a very elderly person in his mid 80s, he doesn't mind whether people acknowledge his past contributions or not. He knows that God does it and will do it in many ways. He just wants to see the house we have called South Sudan to be put in order.

He is so humble, loving and caring!

"It is my SPLM," he once said, while talking to me on the phone when I was politically imprisoned in Juba and he predicted my release.

Of course, he met and had a brief conversation with Dr. Riek Machar Teny-Dhurgon in the year 2001 in Pagak, Upper Nile state. This is shortly before Dr. Machar signed the Nairobi Merger Agreement with the late Dr. John Garang on the 6th January, 2002, which also led to the signing of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) on the 9th January, 2005. 

He also met many other current leaders in 1980s in Bilpam.

He is so delighted and thankful to God for he has seen the birth of South Sudan as an independent nation, and he continues to pray for a sustainable peace and prosperity in the young nation.

Let us record our history that occurred on the long road to INDEPENDENCE scientifically with all its significant historical pieces knitted together.

Tell our children and grandchildren about the history of Bilpam General Headquarters! They hear its name a lot but hardly know how it all began.

Some of our smarter South Sudanese do not run short of tough questions to try to challenge historical facts. 

One interesting question or challenge in response to my story on Bilpam asks: "If another site was chosen rather than Bilpam as a bush time capital or headquarters, would it not have made a successful General headquarters also for the Movement?"

The answer is, yes. Any site, if suitable and welcoming, would have become our bush time capital and would have made it to history instead of Bilpam. 

But, luckily and strategically, Bilpam was the one chosen for both Anya Nya Two and SPLM/SPLA. May be like Torit or Owinykibul during the Anya Nya One history.

So the question is like asking, what if we chose another site rather than Juba as our national capital, would it not have worked out? Of course, it would have worked out as long as the site was also suitable and welcoming. 

But, again luckily, Juba was the one chosen or confirmed as the capital by the High Executive Council (HEC) of uncle Abel Alier and uncle Joseph Lagu, etc., as well as in the Government of Southern Sudan (GoSS) and currently in the Republic of South Sudan (RSS). 

Even if we left Juba and moved to another far territory, and whether we continued to call that new territory Juba or not, this would not have erased from history the fact that Juba is/was once our national capital city.

And so the same situation applies to Bilpam.

Cheers!

Appeal for the Return to Service of Hon. Gatwech Peter Kulang: Unmatched Humanitarian Leader and Peace Ambassador

Your Excellency,
We, the citizens of South Sudan, the most vulnerable among us, including war-disabled persons, widows, orphans, and returnees, write with deep respect and conviction to humbly request the return to service of Hon. Gatwech Peter Kulang. His unmatched thirty years of humanitarian experience and lifelong commitment to peace make him indispensable to South Sudan at this critical juncture. Our nation urgently needs a seasoned humanitarian expert to strengthen the delivery of humanitarian services, renegotiate with international organizations, and champion the safe return and resettlement of refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs).
Proven Humanitarian Leadership
Hon. Gatwech Peter Kulang’s humanitarian journey began during Operation Lifeline Sudan in Lokichoggio, where he earned trust through responsibility and consistent delivery. During the historic referendum of 2011, he successfully led the repatriation of thousands of South Sudanese citizens from Khartoum, ensuring their participation in the vote that birthed our nation.
His dedication was recognized when Your Excellency appointed him Undersecretary of the Ministry of Humanitarian and Disaster Management. In that role, he mobilized resources with unmatched expertise, securing thousands of tons of food from the People’s Republic of China, the Royal Family of Kingdom of Saudi Arabia department of humanitarian, and support from USAID, the UK, Germany, Norway, Australia, and other international partners.
Later, as Chairperson of the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC), Hon. Gatwech directly delivered relief to the most vulnerable, war-disabled citizens, widows, orphans, and IDPs, through the First Lady’s organization, Mama Mary Ayan. Even when major donors such as the United States suspended funding, he continued to initiate projects and attract support from UNHCR, UNDP, UNMISS (Department of RRR), UNOCHA, IOM, and European organizations. His ability to draft credible proposals, negotiate with donors, and ensure precise implementation of activities is a rare skill that sets him apart. In humanitarian work, many can serve, but few can design, fund, and deliver projects with such integrity and precision.
Champion of Refugee Return
Today, millions of South Sudanese remain in refugee camps across Kakuma, Uganda, Ethiopia, Sudan, Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo, and even as far as Malaysia. Hon. Gatwech’s expertise and international networks uniquely position him to return to humanitarian service and lead efforts to mobilize donors from Europe, America, China, and the Arab world to secure support for their dignified return and resettlement. His credibility with donors and fluency in humanitarian “language” make him the right person to serve in the RRC or the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs, restoring hope to our displaced citizens, war veterans, widows, and orphans.
Ambassador of Peace
Beyond humanitarian service, Hon. Gatwech has been a tireless peace ambassador. He supported youth in organizing peace conferences in Nasir (2022), Maiwut (2023), and Ulang (2024), as well as in Juba and Unity State, fostering reconciliation and unity among the next generation.
His peace legacy is rooted in the sacrifices of his late father, Elder Peter Kulang Chuol, who welcomed SPLM/A officers with love and resources during the liberation struggle in Bilpam. Inspired by his father’s last words “Be ambassadors of peace in South Sudan” Hon. Gatwech has lived a life of service, embodying humanity and peace.
Courage in Leadership
Recently, when Your Excellency appointed the youngest governor in South Sudan, many doubted his ability to bring peace. Hon. Gatwech was the first to volunteer his support, guided by your words that South Sudan will not return to war. His courage and loyalty enabled the governor to be received in Ulang and Nasir Counties—an unprecedented achievement that demonstrated his ability to translate presidential vision into reality.
A Call to Service
Your Excellency, South Sudan stands at a crossroads. The country needs Hon. Gatwech Peter Kulang’s unmatched humanitarian expertise, his trusted documentation, and his ability to mobilize resources globally. He is not only a humanitarian servant but also a peace ambassador whose deeds have consistently advanced your vision for a peaceful and prosperous South Sudan.
His return to service will ensure that refugees come home, IDPs are resettled, and international confidence in our humanitarian operations is restored.
We need him. South Sudan needs him. Humanity and peace need him.
Respectfully submitted,
Citizen of South Sudan

The Kakwa people, a Nilotic group in East Africa ( South Sudan, Uganda, DRC), have origins linked to migrations from the Nile region (Kakwa city) and tradition of fierce warriors nicknamed "biters," with stories pointing to ancestor Yeki settling in Koboko and his descendants adopting the name.
They are agro-pastoralists known for distinct culture, language (Kutuk Na Kakwa), and historical connection to Bari, mundari, and other Nilotic groups, living across boarders and evolving diverse custom.

ORINGINS AND MIGRATIONS:

• Nile valley: oral tradition suggest origins near the city of Kakwa on the Nile, migrating south through south Sudan into Uganda and DRC.

• Yeki tradition: An ancestor named Yeki migrated from korobi hill (Sudan) to Uganda's Koboko area, fathering sons, one nicknamed "biter" (Kakwan ji), leading to the name.

• Kooi tradition: Another beliefs says they were fierce fighters called Kooi, Who called themselves Kakwa (biters) due to their strong attacks.

• Luo incursions: Around the 16 century, luo expansion pushed Kakwa ancestors west across the Nile.

CULTURE & IDENTITY 

•Group Affiliation: part of the larger karo people, related to Bari, Kuku, mundari, and pojulu.

• Language: Speak Kutuk Na Kakwa, an eastern Nilotic language.

• Meaning of Kakwa: Can mean "biters," "rebels,'' or "harsh,'' reflecting their warrior past and identity.

•Key figures: Famous for figures like former Ugandan president Idi Amin Dada.

•Modern presence: Live across boarder regions with Uganda, south Sudan, and Democratic republic of congo (DRC), leading to some cultural variations .

- Rooted in Bari: pojulu are descendants of Bari-speaking ancestors, sharing origins in the Kidepo Valley.

- Forced Migration: push south and west by the Toposa, leading to migrations and dispersions.

- Splitting from Bari: They eventually broke away from the main Bari group, crossing the Nile to settle in their current lands before the colonial era.

Location & Livelihood:

• Homeland: primarily in Lanya county, CES, south Sudan, with communities in juba and yei.

• Economy: mixed farming (Maize, sorghum) and livestock (Cattle, goats).

Know Murle People,

Murle, most of whom live in Pibor County, specifically the Lotilla Murle, on the floodplains, while the Mountain Murle or Ngalam reside on the Boma plateau. The Murle believe they either originated from a place called ‘Jen’, further east, beyond Maji, in the Omo River region of Ethiopia, or consider themselves part of a larger group that migrated from a settlement atop Didinga Mountain, now on the border with Uganda. This origin story involves a legendary dispute over a pot of gazelle soup, a tale vivid in the minds of most Murle.

According to it, one day on Didinga Mountain, hunters caught nothing but an oribi, a type of small gazelle. On their return, they boiled their meat into soup and ate it, leaving none for others. An argument ensued, dividing clans and leading to the departure of the muur-lill, or Murle - the people who descended from the mountain to the valley. The Tenet and Longarim (or Larim) People, also known as the Boya, left simultaneously. This split is believed to have occurred around 1750, possibly during a famine caused by drought. 

The close linguistic relation of Murle to Didinga and Boya lends credence to this story.
The Murle’s political system is marked by ‘Drum Chiefs,’ or ‘red Chiefs,’ who oversee four ‘drum-ships,’ referring to guardianship of sacred drums. The pronouncements of these ‘red Chiefs’ are held in the highest regard, their spiritual powers being paramount. 

Murle culture revolves around cattle, which are bred, used as dowry for marriage, consumed as meat, and whose blood and milk are valued. They sleep on cow hides, sing songs about cattle captured in battles or raids, and perform sacrifices of bulls at major social events to invoke ancestral spirits and provide food for guests and relatives. 

Their vocabulary includes many cattle-related terms, covering colours, horn shapes, and various stages of growth for cows, calves, bulls, and oxen; every young man receives an ox from his father or uncle, along with a ‘bull’s name,’ and spends hours singing to it. 
Marriage, or kaavdhet, emphasises respecting parents-in-law; when a young man wishes to marry, he relies on relatives to provide cattle for the dowry, which is divided among her kin. 
The Murle refer to relatives as ‘people who have cattle between them,’ or atenoc. 

Every five or six years, families undertake a pilgrimage to a sacred site along the Nyandit River, where they make offerings to ‘Nyandit.’ With a strong awareness of spirits, they do not sharply differentiate between religious and secular life, often linking God with the importance of origin, particularly the migration from their ancestral lands. 

Anything unexplained, like a rainbow, they regard as ‘one of God’s things.’ The Murle also adorn themselves with scars and drawings of animals and birds, and wear various beads. 

They engage in fishing and hunting, demonstrating skill in stalking game, and on the Boma plateau, where rainfall is abundant, they cultivate maize, sorghum, sesame, tobacco, and coffee.

Gambella Must Avoid Importing the Unnecessary Dinka Nuer Ethnic Competition That South Sudanese Elites Historically Manipulated for Power

Response to Post Made by Pam Chuol Joack
By OPARA ACHIMO

The article by Pam Chuol Joack raises important issues, but many of its claims require clarification based on scientific evidence, constitutional law, and internationally recognized conservation practices not ethnic interpretations or political assumptions.

First, the Anywaa Biosphere Reserve (ABR) is part of UNESCO’s Man and Biosphere (MAB) framework. Under global standards such as the Lima Action Plan (2016–2025), biosphere reserves are designated according to ecological factors watersheds, biodiversity, and habitat conservation not ethnic borders. The claim that the ABR was expanded to appropriate Nuer or Majang land does not align with the scientific methodology used worldwide for ecosystem zoning.

Second, the Ethiopian Constitution states that land is publicly owned (Art. 40(3)) and obligates the state to protect the environment (Art. 44 & 92). Creating or expanding a biosphere reserve does not erase ethnic territories, take ownership from communities, or displace lawful residents. Biosphere zoning—core, buffer, and transition zones allows continued community activities such as settlement, farming, and grazing. Therefore, allegations of territorial “takeover” do not fit with the legal nature of conservation areas.

Third, national law requires public participation before adjusting protected areas, including under the Environmental Impact Assessment Proclamation No. 299/2002. If any community—Nuer, Majang, or Anywaa—feels consultation was insufficient, the proper response is legal review, environmental audit, or federal inquiry, not ethnic framing.

It is also important to reject the narrative that political power in Gambella is structured to benefit one ethnic group over another. Ethiopia’s governance system relies on shared institutions, councils, and constitutional representation—not simple demographic majority. Claims of engineered ethnic dominance require verifiable evidence.

Scholarship such as Shadows on the Grass and John Markakis’s Resource Conflict in the Horn of Africa emphasizes that protected landscapes across East Africa serve ecological and community needs, not ethnic agendas. These works show that conservation succeeds when local populations cooperate under scientific guidelines.

Furthermore, Gambella must avoid importing the unnecessary ethnic competition seen between Dinka and Nuer in South Sudan, where political elites have historically manipulated identity for power. That destructive pattern should not be replicated in Ethiopia. Environmental policy must remain technical, lawful, and inclusive—not another arena for external ethnic rivalries.

Finally, any legitimate concerns about boundaries, grazing access, or environmental management should be addressed through peaceful mechanisms: participatory mapping, regional hearings, environmental assessments, and federal oversight. All communities of Gambella Anywaa, Majang, Opo, and Komo depend on the same ecosystems and share responsibility to protect them.

In conclusion, the Anywaa Biosphere Reserve is an environmental conservation initiative, not a tool of ethnic or political domination. Gambella’s stability will be strengthened through evidence-based dialogue, legal due process, and the rejection of imported ethnic divisions—not through alarmist narratives.

A measles outbreak has been reported among Sudanese refugees arriving in the Abyei  Administrative Area, the area’s health minister said while warning that years without vaccinations are putting thousands of children at risk.

Speaking during a panel discussion organised by medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in Juba on Wednesday, Dr Ayom Korchek said a large influx of people fleeing Sudan’s war, now in its third year, has overwhelmed health services in northern Abyei, where most refugees are settling.

Many of the children arriving have never been vaccinated, he said, creating conditions ripe for rapid disease transmission.

“There is an outbreak of diseases, especially among these refugees,” he said, adding that measles cases have surged in recent weeks.

According to Dr Korchek, national health authorities have begun releasing vaccines to support an emergency response, with a wider immunisation campaign expected soon.

He said the area had previously battled a cholera outbreak traced to population movements from the north, and now faces additional threats.

The minister also reported a rising number of hepatitis E cases, describing the situation as “killing our people.” He attributed the spread to severe water shortages and the absence of partners working on water, sanitation, and hygiene in the area.

He said Abyei’s drug supplies are no longer sufficient because humanitarian and government partners still allocate medicines based on outdated population figures. Since conflict erupted in Sudan, he noted, many South Sudanese returnees and Sudanese refugees have settled in Abyei, straining already limited services.

“Some have been integrated into the community, and some are in the northern part, and they are sharing health services with us,” he said.

Insecurity has further complicated the health response. The minister said health facilities in several locations were forced to close months ago due to violence, while recent fighting in Sudanese border towns such as Babanusa led to an influx of gunshot casualties into Abyei.

Although the situation has calmed in recent days, movement restrictions imposed by UNISFA peacekeepers continue to hinder supervision and support visits to affected health facilities, he added.

Despite the challenges, the minister said the overall security situation in Abyei has slightly improved and that authorities are working with national and local partners to curb the disease outbreaks.

“We presented our situation at the summit to reflect what we are facing in Abyei,” Korchek said. “We hope the national health services will continue supporting us as we respond to these crises.”

December 15, 2013, violence erupted in Juba, South Sudan, which quickly led to the systematic mass killing and ethnic cleansing of the Nuer people by Dinka-led government forces and militias. While the events are widely described as a massacre and ethnic cleansing by human rights organizations and the African Union, the term 'genocide' is used by Nuer community members, activists, and some scholars. 

Key Details of the Events 
Trigger: The violence began as a political power struggle between President Salva Kiir (ethnic Dinka) and his sacked Vice President Riek Machar (ethnic Nuer). Kiir accused Machar of an attempted coup, a claim later dismissed as a fabrication by an African Union inquiry. 
Perpetrators & Victims: Soldiers loyal to Kiir, primarily from the Dinka ethnic group, went house-to-house, using identity cards to target and kill Nuer civilians. The violence was systematic and organized, reportedly coordinated by high-ranking military officials. 
Death Toll & Atrocities: Estimates of the Nuer killed in Juba within the first few days range from over 20,000 to more than 47,000. Atrocities included mass killings, mass burials, burning of corpses, and targeting civilians in their homes, churches, and even UN compounds. 
Consequences: The Juba massacre marked the beginning of the devastating South Sudanese Civil War, which caused hundreds of thousands of deaths and displaced millions. The violence quickly spread to other parts of the country, with retaliatory killings occurring along ethnic lines in places like Bor and Bentiu. 

International Response and Accountability 
The events were well-documented by the United Nations, African Union, and Human Rights Watch. UN officials warned that targeted ethnic killings could be precursors to, or were already, widespread crimes and even genocide. 
However, to date, there has been no accountability for the atrocities committed. An internationally supported peace agreement included calls for a hybrid court to prosecute those responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but the government has stalled its establishment.

The situation is further complicated by the role of the presidency, which is perceived to be taking sides and fueling the conflict. The Nuer community feels that they are being deceived and manipulated into giving up their land, and this has sparked outrage and resistance.

In the face of these challenges, the Nuer community remains determined to protect their land, culture, and heritage. Panyagay is a symbol of their identity and resilience, and they will not let it be taken away. My #GetYourBellyOut story: Tashira
Hi, my name is Tashira, I’m from Puerto Rico, and I've had Ulcerative Colitis since I was 12 years old.

I struggled to live with it over the years, until my first surgery, which was in January 2017, where I had my colon removed, but they left my rectum in place.

It was in July of 2018, when I had my second surgery; however, this time it was an emergency!

My small intestine had burst inside of me, causing me to have sepsis. I had a bowel obstruction, and part of it was necrotic. They removed 1 and a half litres of pus from my stomach and hips, and abscesses from the top and bottom of my liver.

The surgeon had said to my family that he wasn’t sure if I was going to make it, but that he was going to do everything that he could.

So he cut my stomach open, and as a result of everything I was facing, I had an ileostomy made. It was the best thing that could have happened to me!

One of the downfalls after my super surgery was the loss of my hair; it was brutal. When I brushed it, tons of hair came out, and I had my entire hand full of it.

The fatigue is something real too, but there's no more rushing to the bathroom, no more pain and most of all, my daughter didn’t lose her mother.

God, the surgeon and the ileostomy saved my life. I’m very proud of it, so much so that I call it Lily. It has been one hell of a ride, but I love it.

My ileostomy saved my life, it brought me back my health and my energy. Everything turned out great.

Luminous Face Mist dari brand Gmecca adalah produk perawatan wajah multifungsi yang dirancang untuk memberikan hidrasi instan dan efek wajah tampak bercahaya (glowing).
​Berikut adalah beberapa manfaat utama dari penggunaan produk ini:

​1. Menghidrasi Kulit Secara Instan
​Produk ini bekerja sebagai penyegar yang langsung memberikan kelembapan pada kulit yang terasa kering atau kaku, terutama jika Anda sering berada di ruangan ber-AC atau terpapar sinar matahari.

​2. Memberikan Efek Luminous Glow
​Sesuai namanya, face mist ini diformulasikan untuk memberikan hasil akhir yang dewy dan sehat. Wajah akan terlihat lebih segar dan bercahaya seketika setelah disemprotkan.

​3. Membantu Makeup Tahan Lama & Natural
​Sebagai Primer: Digunakan sebelum makeup untuk menciptakan kanvas kulit yang lembap sehingga alas bedak lebih menempel.
​Sebagai Setting Spray: Digunakan setelah makeup untuk menghilangkan kesan "dempul" (cakey) dari bedak dan memberikan tampilan yang lebih menyatu dengan kulit.

​4. Menenangkan Kulit yang Iritasi
​Kandungan umum dalam produk luminous mist biasanya meliputi bahan penenang (seperti Aloe Vera atau Rose Water) yang membantu meredakan kemerahan atau sensasi terbakar akibat polusi dan cuaca panas.

​5. Perlindungan Antioksidan
​Banyak varian produk ini juga dilengkapi dengan vitamin atau ekstrak tumbuhan yang berfungsi melindungi kulit dari radikal bebas dan polusi lingkungan yang mempercepat penuaan dini.

​Tips Penggunaan:
​Jarak Semprot: Semprotkan dengan jarak sekitar 15–20 cm dari wajah dengan gerakan memutar.

​Kapan Saja: Bisa digunakan di pagi hari sebagai bagian dari skincare, atau kapan pun di tengah hari saat wajah terasa kusam.
​Kombinasi: Untuk hasil maksimal, gunakan sebelum mengaplikasikan serum agar penyerapan bahan aktif serum menjadi lebih optimal.

It is incredibly draining to manage the invisible side of this illness, the parts people don't see, like the crushing fatigue and the mental weight of just trying to survive the day.

The Reality of End-Stage Gastroparesis
I’m sharing this because I’ve realized many people don’t quite understand just how serious and life-altering end-stage Gastroparesis truly is. It isn't just about “not being able to eat” it’s so much more than that, it’s a constant daily battle for survival.

One of the most dangerous parts of this condition is the formation of bezoars (masses of undigested food trapped in the stomach). These are incredibly painful, deadly, and a constant reminder that my body isn't functioning the way it should.

But I will say this, the physical danger is only one layer. I want to be honest about the toll this takes on my mental and emotional health. Imagine waking up every day and immediately being hit with:
 
* Constant Nausea & Vomiting: It’s an exhausting cycle that never lets up.
 * Weakness & Tiredness: My body is running on empty because it can't process fuel.
 * Dizziness: Simple tasks like standing up or walking across a room become a challenge.

When you don’t have the energy for basic everyday tasks, it starts to wear on your mind, heart, & soul. It’s incredibly isolating to want to participate in life but be held back by a body that feels like it’s failing you. The mental weight of the “brain fog” and the emotional exhaustion of being in survival mode 24/7 is a heavy burden to carry.

I’m reiterating this so people have a better understanding of what I and others like myself face on a daily basis. It’s not just a physical diagnosis; it’s a fight for my quality of life every single minute.
 
My Invisible Struggle: People often see me when I up, out & about, but they don't see the hours spent lying down due to agonizing pain, nausea, weakness, dizziness, crying, frustration, or being curled up in a ball trying to make it from one minute to the next. I say this because there are parts of me no one sees, the parts of me I hide from the rest of the world, that are a part of my everyday life. I say this not to gain sympathy or for anyone to feel sorry for me. I say this because everyday so many people suffer from invisible illnesses the rest of the world doesn’t see. Out in public they look “fine” “presentable,” or “have it all together,” but in all reality, there are so many hidden layers under their struggle. 

Please remember that a smile doesn't always mean a lack of pain, and “fine” is often just the mask we wear to get through the day. Let’s be a little kinder to one another. We’re all fighting battles that don't make the evening news.

The Nuer of 21st century have shamed and tarnished the Nuer historical image and character whether in South Sudan or in Ethiopia

By Lul Gatkuoth Gatluak

Date:  Wednesday December 17, 2025

Commander Edward Lino Wuor Abyei.
Liberation Veteran • Military Commander • Security Strategist • Political Leader & Abyei National Advocate

Full Name: Edward Lino Wuor Abyei
Date of Birth: February 7, 1946.
Place of Birth: Abyei Area (Abieng), Sudan (disputed region)
Date of Death: April 15, 2020
Place of Death: Bangalore (Bengaluru), India 
Nationality: South Sudanese
Political Affiliation: Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM); later, Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in‑Opposition (SPLM‑IO) 
Professions: Military Commander, Security Strategist, Political Leader, Author, Historian

Early Life and Education

Edward Lino was born in the Abyei region in early 1946 into the Ngok Dinka community, a group central to the political and cultural history of Sudan and South Sudan. His father, Lino Wor Abyei, provided the early grounding for his commitment to his people’s heritage and rights. Edward Lino pursued higher education and initially studied law at the University of Khartoum, where he became actively involved in student politics. His early political activities, informed by progressive and nationalist ideas, led to persecution by the Sudanese authorities, shaping his later commitment to liberation and justice. 

Military and Liberation Struggle

Edward Lino entered the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement/Army (SPLM/SPLA) at the outbreak of the second Sudanese civil war in 1983, joining the ranks of those who sought to end oppression and secure dignity for Sudan’s marginalized peoples.

Command Roles and Frontline Leadership

Throughout the liberation struggle, Lino served in several key military positions:

Commander of SPLM forces in strategic regions, including Kapotea (1989) and Western Equatoria (1990–91) 

Commander of the Tonj‑Wau‑Raga axis (1995–97) 

Director General for External Security for the SPLM/SPLA (late 1990s) 

As Director of External Security, he was responsible for international operative coordination, diplomatic engagement, and strategic intelligence that supported SPLM’s political and military goals across Africa, the Middle East, Europe, and the United States. 

Edward Lino’s impact at the frontlines extended beyond pure military capacity. He was known among comrades as a morale booster and political educator, often articulating the political objectives of the struggle directly to soldiers under siege. Testimonies from frontline fighters credit him with strengthening resolve during some of the harshest campaigns of the liberation era. 

Political Leadership and Abyei Advocacy

Administrator and SPLM Leader in Abyei

Edward Lino played a central role in shaping the political landscape of the Abyei region, a contested border area rich in natural resources and a focal point of Sudan–South Sudan relations. In 2008, the Government of Southern Sudan appointed him as Chairman of SPLM in Abyei and Administrator of the region, entrusting him with implementing peace agreements, overseeing transitional governance, and coordinating humanitarian and development efforts. 

Abyei Joint Oversight Committee (AJOC)

After the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA), he was appointed South Sudanese Co‑Chair of the Abyei Joint Oversight Committee (AJOC), a key body responsible for managing the disputed territory and implementing protocols related to its administration. His leadership in AJOC underscored his strategic role in Abyei’s political future, actively representing the interests of Ngok Dinka communities. 

Political Positions on Abyei

Edward Lino publicly rejected proposals that threatened Abyei’s identity, including suggestions to divide the area or institute an ‘integrated administration’ under Sudanese dominance. He instead emphasized peaceful coexistence and unity grounded in respect for the will of Abyei’s people. 

Intellectual Contributions and Thought Leadership

Beyond military and political leadership, Edward Lino was a writer and historian who documented liberation history and leadership philosophy. His notable work, Dr John Garang de Mabior Atem: A Man to Know, provides unique firsthand perspectives on one of the leading architects of South Sudan’s struggle for liberation. His writings articulate the intellectual foundations of the movement and preserve key narratives for future generations. 

Later Years and Political Alignment

After South Sudan’s independence in 2011, Edward Lino continued to advocate for Abyei and national reconciliation. He eventually aligned with the SPLM‑IO, led by Dr. Riek Machar, following the eruption of internal conflict in South Sudan in 2013. His alignment reflected ongoing concerns over governance and the direction of the young nation, highlighting his lifelong commitment to the original ideals of liberation. 

Death and State Recognition

Edward Lino passed away in Bangalore, India, on April 15, 2020, after a prolonged battle with illness, including complications following medical procedures. He was 74 years old. 

His body was repatriated to South Sudan, where officials, including a delegation dispatched by SPLM‑IO leadership, accompanied it to Abyei for final rites and community homage, reflecting his standing as a national figure and historic veteran. 

Legacy and Historical Significance

Military and Strategic Legacy

Edward Lino’s contributions to the liberation of South Sudan and the broader struggle against oppression are acknowledged as foundational. His leadership in frontline operations, intelligence strategy, and political mobilization helped sustain the SPLM/SPLA through decades of conflict. He is remembered by many as an icon of bravery, selfless service, and revolutionary commitment. 

Political and Governance Legacy

As a political leader in Abyei, he championed autonomy, justice, and the rights of marginalized communities. His tenure as administrator and AJOC co‑chair placed him at the center of one of the most enduring post‑CPA political challenges, shaping Abyei’s governance trajectory and elevating its profile in regional diplomacy. 

Intellectual and Cultural Legacy

Through his writing, speeches, and public commentary, Edward Lino preserved the memory of the liberation struggle with depth and nuance. He provided future scholars and citizens with interpretations that bridge the military, political, and cultural dimensions of South Sudan’s history.

Commander Edward Lino Wuor Abyei stands as a towering figure in South Sudanese history: a soldier who bore arms for his country’s freedom, a strategist who shaped security and diplomacy, a political leader who fought for his homeland’s contested future, and a historian who gave language to its struggles.

He is remembered as:

> A liberator committed to justice, an administrator dedicated to his people, and a visionary whose voice enriched the historical record of a nation born of sacrifice.

Nuer expansion: territorial and political control

Murle raids: cattle and child abduction

Anuak resistance: land defense and survival

Collapsing these into a single “resource conflict” narrative is analytically flawed and ethically irresponsible (see Tasgara, 2021).

Peace built on distorted history is fragile. Real peace in Gambella requires:

Honest acknowledgment of indigenous land rights

Accountability for cross-border militias

Equal protection under Ethiopian law

Scholarship that reflects reality, not convenience

Until then, blaming Anuak communities for a conflict rooted in dispossession and militarization is not journalism, not scholarship, and not justice.

By doing that, they will regain their traditional practices and break the cycle of political manipulation that had ruined their forefathers; dignified reputation.

Respectively,

Lul Gatkuoth Gatluak

William Deng Nhial (1929–1968)

Founding Architect of Southern Sudanese Political Consciousness

Kolongdit Media Historical Archive | Official House Style Publication

Historical Profile

William Deng Nhial is universally recognized as one of the earliest and most principled architects of Southern Sudanese political consciousness. His life represents the transition of Southern Sudanese resistance from fragmented grievances to organized political nationalism. As a statesman, ideologue, and martyr, Deng occupies a foundational position in the historical evolution of South Sudan’s struggle for justice, equality, and self-determination.

Kolongdit Media preserves this biography as an authoritative historical record, written in accordance with its house standards: factual accuracy, institutional tone, national relevance, and respect for historical sacrifice.

Early Life and Socio‑Political Background

William Deng Nhial was born in 1929 in Tonj, within the former Bahr el Ghazal Province of Anglo‑Egyptian Sudan. He was a member of the Dinka community, whose people endured structural marginalization under colonial administration and later under post‑independence governments in Khartoum.

His formative years coincided with the final phase of colonial rule and the emergence of African nationalism across the continent. These forces shaped his political awareness and commitment to collective African dignity and self‑rule.

Education, Administration, and Political Maturation

Deng received formal education that enabled him to serve within the Sudanese administrative system. As a government administrator, he acquired direct exposure to the systemic exclusion of Southern Sudanese from meaningful participation in governance, development planning, and national identity formation.

Rather than internalizing the status quo, Deng transformed administrative insight into political resistance. His early career marked the transition from civil service to organized nationalist activism.

Political Thought and Ideological Orientation

William Deng Nhial was a committed African nationalist and Pan‑Africanist. He opposed the central state’s policies of Arabization, cultural erasure, and political domination. His vision advocated a pluralistic Sudan grounded in equality, dignity, and shared citizenship.

Core pillars of his political philosophy included:

Democratic participation and constitutional governance

Social justice and regional equity

Cultural and religious pluralism

Recognition of Southern Sudan’s right to self‑determination

Deng also pursued strategic alliances with marginalized African communities in northern Sudan, including the Nuba, Fur, Beja, and Nubian peoples, understanding Sudan’s crisis as national rather than regional.

Leadership of the Sudan African National Union (SANU)

In 1962, William Deng Nhial assumed leadership of the Sudan African National Union (SANU), emerging as its unchallenged political head. Under his stewardship, SANU became the principal political platform articulating Southern Sudanese demands within national and international forums.

SANU’s core objectives under Deng included:

Federal governance or regional autonomy

Political representation for Southern Sudanese

Legal and constitutional equality

He remained SANU’s leader until his assassination in 1968, providing ideological clarity during a period of intense repression and fragmentation.

Relationship with the Anyanya Liberation Struggle

William Deng was among the early political figures associated with the Anyanya Movement, the first organized armed resistance in Southern Sudan. While acknowledging the necessity of armed struggle under repression, Deng maintained that political engagement and negotiation were essential to achieving sustainable peace.

His position placed him uniquely between political diplomacy and armed resistance, earning him respect across divergent liberation circles.

Parliamentary Victory and National Significance

In the 1968 Sudanese parliamentary elections, William Deng Nhial won his constituency by an overwhelming margin. His election marked a historic moment: the elevation of a Southern nationalist voice through democratic means into the national legislature.

This victory signaled both popular legitimacy and the possibility of peaceful political transformation within Sudan.

Assassination and Historical Turning Point

In May 1968, while traveling from Rumbek to Tonj through Cueibet County, William Deng Nhial was ambushed and killed by elements of the Sudanese Armed Forces. Despite official denials, no independent investigation was conducted, and accountability was never pursued.

The assassination eliminated the most credible bridge between political dialogue and armed resistance, marking a decisive rupture in North–South relations. The location of his death later became known as William Bridge, symbolizing both loss and betrayal.

National Impact and Historical Consequences

The death of William Deng Nhial:

Destroyed fragile prospects for negotiated settlement

Accelerated militarization of the Southern struggle

Removed a unifying political figure capable of national coalition‑building

Many scholars regard his assassination as one of the pivotal events that prolonged Sudan’s civil conflict.

Legacy and Enduring Influence

William Deng Nhial is memorialized as:

A founding father of Southern Sudanese nationalism

A martyr of political principle

A moral reference point in South Sudan’s political history

His ideas influenced later liberation movements, including the SPLM, and contributed indirectly to milestones such as the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (2005) and the independence of South Sudan (2011).

Family and Continuity of Public Service

William Deng’s legacy continued through his son, Nhial Deng Nhial, who served the Republic of South Sudan in senior national roles, including Minister of Defense, Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Minister of Presidential Affairs.

This continuity underscores the enduring relevance of William Deng’s political ideals in state formation and governance.

Archival Conclusion

William Deng Nhial’s life and sacrifice remain inseparable from the historical identity of South Sudan. His commitment to justice through political means, even under existential threat, established a standard of leadership grounded in principle rather than expediency.

Early Life and Socio‑Political Background

William Deng Nhial was born in 1929 in Tonj, within the former Bahr el Ghazal Province of Anglo‑Egyptian Sudan. He was a member of the Dinka community, whose people endured structural marginalization under colonial administration and later under post‑independence governments in Khartoum.

His formative years coincided with the final phase of colonial rule and the emergence of African nationalism across the continent. These forces shaped his political awareness and commitment to collective African dignity and self‑rule.

Education, Administration, and Political Maturation

Deng received formal education that enabled him to serve within the Sudanese administrative system. As a government administrator, he acquired direct exposure to the systemic exclusion of Southern Sudanese from meaningful participation in governance, development planning, and national identity formation.

Rather than internalizing the status quo, Deng transformed administrative insight into political resistance. His early career marked the transition from civil service to organized nationalist activism.

Political Thought and Ideological Orientation

William Deng Nhial was a committed African nationalist and Pan‑Africanist. He opposed the central state’s policies of Arabization, cultural erasure, and political domination. His vision advocated a pluralistic Sudan grounded in equality, dignity, and shared citizenship.

Core pillars of his political philosophy included:

Democratic participation and constitutional governance

Social justice and regional equity

Cultural and religious pluralism

Recognition of Southern Sudan’s right to self‑determination

Deng also pursued strategic alliances with marginalized African communities in northern Sudan, including the Nuba, Fur, Beja, and Nubian peoples, understanding Sudan’s crisis as national rather than regional.

Leadership of the Sudan African National Union (SANU)

In 1962, William Deng Nhial assumed leadership of the Sudan African National Union (SANU), emerging as its unchallenged political head. Under his stewardship, SANU became the principal political platform articulating Southern Sudanese demands within national and international forums.

SANU’s core objectives under Deng included:

Federal governance or regional autonomy

Political representation for Southern Sudanese

Legal and constitutional equality

He remained SANU’s leader until his assassination in 1968, providing ideological clarity during a period of intense repression and fragmentation.

Relationship with the Anyanya Liberation Struggle

William Deng was among the early political figures associated with the Anyanya Movement, the first organized armed resistance in Southern Sudan. While acknowledging the necessity of armed struggle under repression, Deng maintained that political engagement and negotiation were essential to achieving sustainable peace.

His position placed him uniquely between political diplomacy and armed resistance, earning him respect across divergent liberation circles.

Parliamentary Victory and National Significance

In the 1968 Sudanese parliamentary elections, William Deng Nhial won his constituency by an overwhelming margin. His election marked a historic moment: the elevation of a Southern nationalist voice through democratic means into the national legislature.

This victory signaled both popular legitimacy and the possibility of peaceful political transformation within Sudan.

Assassination and Historical Turning Point

In May 1968, while traveling from Rumbek to Tonj through Cueibet County, William Deng Nhial was ambushed and killed by elements of the Sudanese Armed Forces. Despite official denials, no independent investigation was conducted, and accountability was never pursued.

The assassination eliminated the most credible bridge between political dialogue and armed resistance, marking a decisive rupture in North–South relations. The location of his death later became known as William Bridge, symbolizing both loss and betrayal.

National Impact and Historical Consequences

The death of William Deng Nhial:

Destroyed fragile prospects for negotiated settlement

Accelerated militarization of the Southern struggle

Removed a unifying political figure capable of national coalition‑building

Many scholars regard his assassination as one of the pivotal events that prolonged Sudan’s civil conflict.

Legacy and Enduring Influence

William Deng Nhial is memorialized as:

A founding father of Southern Sudanese nationalism

A martyr of political principle

A moral reference point in South Sudan’s political history

His ideas influenced later liberation movements, including the SPLM, and contributed indirectly to milestones such as the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (2005) and the independence of South Sudan (2011).

Family and Continuity of Public Service

William Deng’s legacy continued through his son, Nhial Deng Nhial, who served the Republic of South Sudan in senior national roles, including Minister of Defense, Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Minister of Presidential Affairs.

This continuity underscores the enduring relevance of William Deng’s political ideals in state formation and governance.

Archival Conclusion

William Deng Nhial’s life and sacrifice remain inseparable from the historical identity of South Sudan. His commitment to justice through political means, even under existential threat, established a standard of leadership grounded in principle rather than expediency.

The Governor underscored the urgent need for food assistance and other basic services to alleviate the humanitarian challenges faced by the returnees.

Governor Bol Wek reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to peace, stability, and the welfare of the people of Warrap State, calling on all stakeholders to play their part in fostering harmony and supporting vulnerable communities during the festive season and beyond.

The Dinka Resistance Against Anglo-Egyptian Domination and Rebellion of 1919–1920: Chiefs Kon Anok Nyingeer and Biar Abit Ayual’s Defiance of Colonial Rule

When the Aliab people rose in rebellion against the Anglo-Egyptian colonial administration on 8 November 1919 and again on 6 May 1920, they demonstrated extraordinary courage. Armed only with spears, they resisted the well-equipped British forces with remarkable determination.

During the uprising, Governor Chauncey Hugh Stigand, one of the most senior colonial officials in the southern provinces of Sudan, was killed by Aliab fighters. At the center of this resistance stood Paramount Chief Kon Anok Nyingeer, a man remembered for his valor, wisdom, and defiance in the face of empire.

The Attack on Mingkaman Police Post

Under Chief Kon Anok’s command, nearly 3,000 Aliab-Dinka men attacked the colonial police post at Mingkaman (Guolyar). They overpowered the police, killed several officers, and briefly captured the post. Word of this assault reached the provincial headquarters in Mongalla, leading to Kon Anok’s arrest and transfer there for interrogation.

The Interrogation of Chief Kon Anok

Unable to speak or write English, Chief Kon Anok requested a translator. A man with limited English proficiency was appointed to interpret.

Colonialist: “Interpreter, ask this man why he planned a bomb and killed the Governor.”

Kon Anok: “Wën wänmaath, lëkë mony kawaja kän, lëkë yεn an yin ë bëlit.”

(English: “My nephew, tell this white man that he is foolish.”)

The translator, fearing for his life, softened the message. Sensing this hesitation, Kon Anok reprimanded him:

Kon Anok: “Wën wänmaath, akënë luεl tëwën cha luεl, aŋuɔt ëcha tiŋ mony kawaja nyin ŋuɔt kë lëkë mony kawaja an yin ee bëlit sakit.”

(English: “My nephew, you did not tell him what I said. I can see it from the white man’s face. Tell him that he is indeed a foolish man.”)

The translator finally relayed the words exactly as spoken:

Translator: “Sir, this old man says that you are foolish.”

Outraged, the officer shouted,

Colonialist: “This old man calls me foolish? Guards, lock him up immediately!” The colonial officer immediately arrested Chief Kon Anok and imprisoned him.

The Awulian and Dachuek Resistance

While Kon Anok was in custody, the Awulian youth, led by Chief Biar Abit Ayual (Bany e Wut) and Biar Diing Ayual (Bany e Bith), ambushed a British convoy installing telegraph lines, a project the people of Jonglei (from Duk to Kolnyang) vehemently opposed.

That same night, most communities between Duk and Pakeer withdrew to the swamps (“Toc”) without informing the Awulian or Dachuek sections. When Chief Lual Ajueeny, leader of the Dachuek, learned of the withdrawal, he sent an urgent message to Pawuoi:

“Remain steadfast. Do not abandon Biar Diing and Biar Abit in the battle.”

Biar Diing responded firmly:

“We shall not retreat. Even if others flee, we will confront the enemy here at Pawuoi.”

The Battle of Pawuoi

At dawn, during the cold season of 1919, the Awulian warriors attacked from Lual Ajokbil to Padeloi, soon joined by the Dachuek (Mayom de Lual). The battle was fierce and costly; brave legendary men such as Duot de Mayen and Khamich de Bul were killed.

As the tide turned, Biar Diing invoked spiritual power from his sacred shrine, Luaŋ Yaath, calling forth a swarm of bees that attacked only the colonial soldiers. Panic spread through the British ranks; many soldiers were captured or killed. The Awulian and Dachuek warriors defeated the British Army. 

The Capture and Defiance of Chief Biar Abit

Chief Biar Abit Ayual was later captured and taken to Mongalla for interrogation. Before he was sentenced and confined behind bars, he made a striking request:

Biar Abit: “Mony Kawaja, na koor ba niin ëtënë, kε ɣεn Biar ɣεn cε niin ɣɔɔt, ɣεn ë niin ë ɣookiic, piaatë dhiën ëtëne ku ba tɔch ë ɣookiic.”

(English: “White man, if you want me to stay here, remember that I do not sleep in your houses. I rest only among my cattle.”)

Amused, the colonial officers surrounded his cell with herds of cattle. That night, Biar Abit and Kon Anok slept peacefully among the cattle.

Biar Abit: “ɣayoooow!! ëtenë yεn ka bë ya cool Pawuoi!”

(English: “Ah, yes! This place shall be called Pawuoi!”)

From that night onward, the area became known as Pawuoi Wut, located today in Mongalla.

Brotherhood in Captivity

While imprisoned together, Chief Kon Anok Nyingeer and Chief Biar Abit Ayual forged a deep bond of friendship. Upon their release, each honored the other by naming his son after his comrade, Biar Kon Anok and Kon Biar, ensuring that their unity lived on through generations.

Legacy and End of Dinka Colonial Oppression

In 1920, Chief Kon Anok Nyingeer was poisoned and killed, marking the end of a defining chapter in the Aliab resistance against British rule. 

Chief Biar Abit Ayual, the first Paramount Chief of today's Twi East County, was later released from prison and returned to his ranch at Pawuoi, where he died peacefully in 1930, surrounded by his family and the Awulian Community he dearly loved. 

The courage of Kon Anok Nyingeer and Biar Abit Ayual is not only a chapter in Sudan's history. It is a reminder that freedom is never granted; it is earned by those willing to stand for the truth and fight for their dignity and respect.

The wise chiefs faced the mighty empires of imperialism with nothing but faith, courage, and dignity, thereby protecting their homeland and their people. Their defiance stands as one of the earliest and most courageous acts of resistance against colonial oppression and a testament to the enduring spirit of freedom among the Dinka people.in what is today South Sudan.

The jewelled stink bug

Scutelleridae are true bugs (commonly known as jewel stink bugs, as they can produce an offensive odour when disturbed) with about 450 species worldwide. They feed by piercing and sucking plant juices, and are distinguished by an enlarged scutellum that forms a shield covering the abdomen and wings, often making them look beetle-like. They can have beautifully brilliant colours, but in some species the metallic colours come from microscopic structures in the cuticle that reflect light, rather than from pigment alone.
