Reconciliation and forgiveness are essential pillars for sustainable peace and social cohesion in the Upper Nile State Region. After years of conflict marked by communal violence, displacement, and deep social divisions, the people of Upper Nile face the critical task of healing wounds, rebuilding trust, and restoring relationships among communities.
The region is home to diverse communities with shared histories, cultures, and livelihoods. However, prolonged conflict has weakened traditional bonds, eroded mutual trust, and fueled cycles of revenge. In this context, reconciliation goes beyond political agreements; it requires honest dialogue, acknowledgment of harm, and collective commitment to peaceful coexistence.

Forgiveness plays a central role in the reconciliation process. It allows individuals and communities to release resentment and anger that perpetuate violence. While forgiveness does not mean forgetting past injustices or ignoring accountability, it opens space for healing and renewal. Community elders, faith leaders, women, and youth have been instrumental in promoting forgiveness through traditional justice mechanisms, peace dialogues, and inter-communal mediation.

Traditional practices in Upper Nile—such as community gatherings, truth-telling forums, and compensation rituals—remain powerful tools for restoring harmony. When combined with modern peacebuilding approaches, these mechanisms help address grievances, promote accountability, and rebuild social trust. Inclusive participation is critical, ensuring that women, youth, returnees, and displaced persons are actively involved in reconciliation efforts.
Reconciliation and forgiveness also contribute to long-term development. Peaceful communities are better positioned to restore livelihoods, access education and health services, and engage in governance. Without reconciliation, cycles of violence risk re-emerging, undermining stability and progress in the region.

In conclusion, reconciliation and forgiveness are not one-time events but continuous processes that require patience, leadership, and collective responsibility. For Upper Nile State to move forward, all stakeholders—communities, traditional leaders, government institutions, civil society, and partners—must work together to nurture healing, unity, and lasting peace. Only through genuine reconciliation can the region secure a peaceful and prosperous future for its people.

This is followed by the Anyuak (Anywaa), who make up about 20–25%. Those referred to as settlers—Oromo, Amhara, Tigrayans, Kafa, and others—constitute about 30–40%. In addition, around 0.3 million refugees displaced by the civil war in South Sudan (fighting between the Dinka and the Nuer) have fled to Gambella, and almost over 90% of them are from the Nuer ethnic group.
This demographic reality has major political implications in the region. However, it is not the only factor behind the insecurity there. Political power in the region is currently in the hands of what are considered the indigenous people, namely the Anyuak. The regional president, Ms. Alamitou, is Anyuak. Moreover, the government structure from top to bottom is dominated by the Anyuak group, which the Nuer perceive as political marginalization. The Nuer, being the larger population group, believe they should govern the region.
The Anyuak, on the other hand, in order to preserve their political power and keep the region exclusively under their control, do not want the Nuer population to be officially recognized or to increase. Based on this, they fear that the large number of Nuer refugees arriving from South Sudan and settling in refugee camps in Gambella would increase the Nuer population in the region, alter the demographic balance, and eventually dominate them. As a result, hostility toward refugees intensified, and on November 23, 2025, they broke into the refugee camp in Itang Woreda and inflicted severe harm on women, children, the elderly, and youths without distinction. The Anyuak do not want to see refugees coming from South Sudan because they believe they are only Nuer or Dinka. They fear that they may unite and dominate

In general, this is the underlying basis of the region’s politics and the ongoing conflict there.

The Second Scramble for Africa: Manufactured Conflict and the Plunder of a Continent – Sheikh Zakzaky

This is an excerpt from the concluding part of a speech delivered by Sheikh Ibraheem Zakzaky (H) to a massive gathering of thousands of participants at the Yaumush Shuhada commemoration, held on Saturday, 25th Rajab 1435 AH (24 May 2014), at the Polo Field near Husainiyyah Bakiyyatullah in Zaria, Nigeria.

As of today, 28 December 2025, the speech was delivered 11 years, 7 months, and 4 days ago.

The excerpt was written by the Media Forum of the Islamic movement. In the speech, the Sheikh explained the hidden schemes behind the attacks being carried out in the villages of Zamfara, Birnin Gwari, and other areas, as well as the renewed invasion plan of Africa.

The Invasion of Africa

Today, we are confronting a serious reality in this country. For a long time, I have been warning that something was approaching. I have emphasised this repeatedly in various sermons. Indeed, something is coming—and that is a renewed invasion of Africa. Long ago, through their research, they concluded that the century we were about to enter—even before the year 2000, as far back as the 1900s—would be known as “the African Century.” Their reasoning was that Africa holds nearly two-thirds of the world’s total wealth. Consequently, they planned to seize control of Africa once again through a second and more sophisticated form of domination.

What was once called the “Scramble for Africa” is now referred to as the “Second Scramble.” It represents a new kind of conquest. During the first scramble for Africa, European powers such as Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, and Belgium occupied territories across the continent. Each power claimed different regions until they eventually convened in Berlin, where a conference was held to divide Africa among themselves. Territories were allocated, borders were drawn, and each power was told, “This is yours.”

They now claim this process will be repeated. However, this time, the United States openly declared that it would employ terrorism as a tool to regain control of Africa. This explains what we are witnessing today. They executed this strategy in Libya. When they observed the Arab uprisings and the political awakening in Egypt, they became alarmed and decided to intervene. They moved into Libya, destroyed the country, and killed Gaddafi. Today, Libya is engulfed in violence—killings, tribal and ethnic conflicts, clashes among militias, and racial tensions—while foreign powers continue to exploit its resources. 

It has long been known that Libya and Nigeria possess what is referred to as “sweet crude oil.” Libya is now entirely under their control, and Nigeria, too, is effectively in their grasp. They simply install puppets—every day selecting individuals and declaring one the president, another the vice president, another a governor, and yet another a minister. Titles are distributed, while the nation’s wealth is systematically plundered.
 
The Method of Occupying Nations

They then introduced yet another strategy—the occupation of countries. Using this approach, they planned and invaded Mali. Even recently, the news has reported clashes in places like Kidal and Gao involving armed groups. Suddenly, gunmen appear in neighbourhoods, firing indiscriminately, and no one knows who is being targeted. The narrative presented is that “Islamic militants” have emerged and fighting has broken out.

In reality, gold was discovered in Mali, gold whose precise location had long been unknown. It had always been known that Mali possessed gold. After all, there was Mansa Musa, the famous ruler who travelled for Hajj and entered world history. It is said that he journeyed with thousands of camels carrying gold and thousands of slaves, each holding a staff of gold.

When he reached Egypt, the amount of gold he brought reportedly caused the price of gold to collapse—a decline from which it took years to recover. In Makkah, he constructed buildings, some of which were only recently demolished by the Saudi authorities during expansions around the Holy Mosque. Until just a few years ago, the buildings of Mansa Musa remained remarkable landmarks.
Yet the exact location of this gold remained unknown. Its existence was acknowledged, but where exactly was it? Where did Mansa Musa mine it? No one knew. One location would be suggested, people would go there and find nothing. Another would be mentioned, and again, nothing would be found. But now the gold has been discovered—and that is why they carefully planned the invasion of Mali.

They claimed that “Islamic extremists” had entered from Algeria. Not a single Malian was among them. They alleged that these fighters had captured more than half of Mali and had even established a so-called state named “Azawad.” Then France swiftly intervened, claiming to drive them out. France moved in ahead of the United States, even though the United States had originally planned the intervention. They declared that the militants had been defeated.

After that, France turned its attention to Central Africa, where diamonds are found. The true objective was diamond extraction, but it was disguised as a conflict involving mysterious groups whose identities were unclear. They claimed that a group called Seleka entered the Central African Republic, killing Christians and burning churches, supposedly in the name of Islam. Yet these individuals were not citizens of the Central African Republic. After carrying out the violence, they left the country. Once they departed, Christian militias known as Anti-Balaka were formed, and they began killing Muslims residing in the country, claiming it was retaliation.

But if those Seleka fighters came from elsewhere, killed people, and then left, were they truly citizens of the country? They were outsiders who entered and exited. And yet the local Muslims paid the price. The same pattern occurred in Mali with the military coup. A man named Sanogo was declared leader, claiming he had overthrown President Amadou Toumani Touré because he failed to defeat the northern rebels. Then it was later said that those same northern rebels had taken over most of the country under Sanogo’s watch.

Similarly, in the Central African Republic, it was claimed that a Muslim carried out a military coup, supposedly named Michel Djotodia. Have you ever heard of a Muslim named “Michel”? They said he was Muslim, yet his name was Michel Djotodia. They claimed a Muslim had seized power in a country where the majority are Christians.

But is it forbidden for a Muslim to be president in a Christian-majority country? If so, how did Christians become leaders in Nigeria, where Muslims are the majority? This was the excuse used to justify entering the Central African Republic and massacring Muslims—especially Fulani herders who had committed no crime and knew nothing of the conflict. The real objective was diamonds.
In South Sudan, when they realised they could not use the excuse of “Islamic extremism,” they engineered ethnic conflict between the Dinka and the Nuer. The aim was to block China’s access to oil. Since South Sudan had strong ties with China, they needed to sever that relationship.

As for Nigeria, they introduced something called Boko Haram. Long ago, some Westerners, particularly Americans, openly stated that Boko Haram was not an organic movement, but rather a creation engineered by the United States.

The Abduction of Schoolgirls: The Jonathan Government Is Responsible

Now they claim that Boko Haram abducted some schoolgirls from a school. But the girls themselves, and their parents, know exactly who took them. They know clearly that it was the Jonathan government. People say there are protests, and I ask: What exactly are they protesting? They even wear red clothing. Where did this idea of wearing red come from? They chant, “Bring back our girls.” But who is supposed to bring them back, Jonathan or Shekau? If it is Jonathan who is expected to return your daughters, then protest against him and demand that he produce them from wherever he has kept them, because he knows the military barracks where they were taken. But if it is Shekau, do you even know where Shekau is? When has he ever listened to you? He, too, is being held in a military barracks. Everything involved belongs to them.

There Is No Such Thing as Boko Haram

There is no such thing as Boko Haram. It is a complete fabrication, a deliberate falsehood. We will not accept this foolish deception. If you want to come and take oil, take gold, take wealth, then come openly and trade with us. Even if it is an unfair trade, let it still be a trade. We give you chickens, you give us eggs. We give you camels, you give us goats. We would rather accept that. 

But do not insult us or mock our religion. Do not tell us that we are suffering from “Islamic extremists” and that you have come to save us, when we know very well that you have come to exploit us.
 
The Real “Boko Haram” Is America

The so-called Boko Haram that has truly entered here is America. Wherever they go, there are killings, bombings, and destruction. This is exactly what they did in Afghanistan—and what they are still doing there. It is the same thing they did in Iraq.  In Afghanistan, they established dozens of air bases and began extracting resources, all under the pretext of war. They claimed they were searching for Bin Laden, even though no one knew where Bin Laden was. Later, they said they killed him somewhere that was not even Afghanistan. So what are they still doing in Afghanistan? They remain there to this day.

In Iraq, they invaded, claiming there were weapons of mass destruction. They destroyed the country, repeatedly insisting that the WMDs would be found. They searched everywhere, even after capturing Saddam Hussein, shining a torch into his mouth as if the weapons were hidden there. When they found nothing, they changed the narrative and said they had come to bring democracy. Today, they admit there were no WMDs, yet they have not left Iraq. They remain there, looting resources, while bombings and killings continue, carried out by them.

Now that they have entered here, what we are experiencing is exactly what they planned for us. What we once heard was happening in other countries has suddenly appeared in our own land. We are certain that there is no group of Islamic zealots called Boko Haram. We are completely certain that it does not exist. Where is it? In which town? On which street? In which neighbourhood?

Yet bombs continue to explode. They are the ones planting these bombs, digging shallow pits, burying explosives, detonating them remotely, or driving vehicles packed with bombs and blowing them up. That is their method. Sometimes armed men simply appear and open fire. And why? Because they have come to extract wealth.
In Zamfara lies gold. They aim to clear the people from the areas where the gold is found, leaving no one behind, so they can build airstrips and military bases and extract the gold freely. Between Zaria and Birnin Gwari lie gold and precious stones. They want to remove the population, establish airfields, and haul everything away.

From Sokoto to Borno lie uranium, gold, and platinum. That is what they have come for. So come to us openly and engage in trade. Even if it means you give us chickens and we give you camels, let it be fair, but leave us unharmed and do not interfere with our religion. Instead, you choose to deceive people, treating them like fools. Where, then, is your intelligence? When did America even exist? When did the Europeans exist before us? What real wisdom do they possess? Bring out European history and read it aloud—drunkenness, madness, and witchcraft. At what point did they suddenly become so wise that they now claim the right to deceive us? This is nothing but shameless arrogance.

Come and trade with us. We know you have weapons. We know you are capable of killing. But leave our religion out of this.
This is precisely why they came, and now calamity is spreading rapidly among us. You know what happened in Gwoza. They even advanced toward the town of Gwoza, but then said they would not enter because they feared the Shi‘a.

They had captured a brother, beheaded him, and completely severed his head. Yet they then heard words being spoken—the declaration of faith. They looked and saw that the head was reciting, “La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur Rasulullah,” while the body lay apart. At that point, they said they feared the town because of the Shi‘a. This is exactly the reality we are facing. And I know they have said it for a long time: the only thing they truly fear is this movement. They know it is the only force capable of stopping them.

A Call to Those Involved

We also address those individuals who have been summoned and elevated. We have heard that you were told you lost an election, yet you were still granted office. We have also heard it said that you are unqualified—that you are foolish, ignorant, weak-minded, or incompetent, and yet you were chosen. Very well, we have heard all of this.

But will you now accept money and positions in exchange for the killing of your own people? Do you have no conscience? Is it enough that you were given a title and wealth, such that your people must be slaughtered? Enough of silence. The community has endured more than enough. Do not imagine that they will spare you. Once they are finished using you, once you are drained of all value, they will kill you as well. That is their method. Saddam, whom they killed, was their own creation. Gaddafi, whom they killed, was their own creation. They built them up, then turned on them and destroyed them. And you, once they are done with you, they will cut you off as well. It will be over.

What Has Emerged in This Country Truly Concerns Us All

I know that today, on the occasion of the Day of the Martyrs, we have much to say, because what has emerged in this country truly concerns every one of us. Confronting this reality, using every lawful means available to us, is a duty owed to Islam. And whoever among us is killed in this struggle is a martyr. I am not telling you that because they carry guns, we should also carry guns. But we do have our own forms of weapons, and we will take them up, God willing.

O Allah, we ask You to allow us to witness the next Day of the Martyrs in good health and ample provision. O Exalted Lord, protect us with Your protection, support us with Your support, and grant us firmness over our enemies.

May Allah’s blessings be upon Muhammad and his pure and noble family. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah.

When the government publicly announced that the suspended First Vice President, Riek Machar, would be formally charged over allegations linked to the Nasir incident following his house arrest, public attention quickly turned to one key question: who would stand in his defense?

That question was answered during the opening court session in September 2025, when Dr. Geri Raimondo stepped into the spotlight as part of Riek’s defense team. Making his first submission before the court, Dr. Raimondo immediately distinguished himself with a confident and methodical legal argument.

From that moment on, he became a household name. With consistency and precision, he challenged the government’s case, urging the court to dismiss the charges on the grounds that they lacked legal standing. His arguments were firmly anchored in the constitution, which he repeatedly cited to defend not only his client, but the rule of law itself.

Dr. Geri Raimondo’s work is important to recognize because it represents a rare and courageous commitment to constitutionalism in a highly charged political environment. At a time when legal processes are often questioned, his performance reaffirmed the role of the judiciary, the supremacy of the constitution, and the right of every citizen to a fair trial—regardless of political status.

By standing firmly on legal principles and professional integrity, Dr. Raimondo has set an example for South Sudan’s legal fraternity and inspired public confidence in the justice system. His contribution in 2025 goes beyond one case; it speaks to the broader struggle for accountability, due process, and respect for the rule of law in South Sudan.

𝟑. 𝐃𝐫. 𝐈𝐬𝐚𝐚𝐜 𝐀𝐲𝐢𝐢 - 𝐄𝐝𝐮𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐮𝐫 (𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐲𝐢𝐢 𝐔𝐧𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲)

“If you are planning for a year, sow rice; if you are planning for a decade, plant trees; if you are planning for a lifetime, educate people.” This Chinese proverb captures the vision behind Isaac Ayii’s lifelong commitment to education and nation-building.

Long before it attained university status this year, Ayii’s dream took shape as the Juba Institute of Health Sciences. Founded to address the critical shortage of professional health training institutions in South Sudan, the institute set out to build local capacity in a country where skilled health workers are in short supply.

Through determination and persistence, the institute trained hundreds of health professionals, offering certificate, diploma, and degree programs that contributed directly to strengthening the health sector.

With the Ministry of Higher Education now issuing a certificate elevating the institution to full university status, Ayii University enters a new chapter. The transition opens the door to expanded degree programs and broader academic offerings at a time when higher education institutions in South Sudan remain few.

Isaac’s vision reflects a belief that sustainable national progress begins with investing in people—and that education remains one of the most enduring legacies one can build.

𝟒. 𝐍𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐀𝐫𝐞𝐦 𝐑𝐢𝐚𝐤 - 𝐄𝐝𝐮𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐮𝐫 (𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐃𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐖𝐢𝐬𝐝𝐨𝐦 𝐀𝐜𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐆𝐢𝐫𝐥𝐬 𝐒𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐥) 

Noble Arem Riak is a seasoned banker who previously served as a branch manager at KCB before making a bold shift into the education sector.

In a past interview, Noble recounted how his time in banking exposed him to a recurring concern among many parents. He often watched families struggle to secure scarce foreign currency so they could support children studying in Uganda or other countries. When he asked why they did not enroll their children in schools at home, the answer was almost always the same: there were not enough quality schools in the country.

That realization became a turning point. Determined to help address the gap in access to quality education, Noble left his banking career and founded Darling Wisdom Academy. Today, the school ranks among the leading private institutions in the country, offering both primary and secondary education across two campuses in Juba.

Building on that vision, he later established Amonto Girls School in Shirkat, a girls-only boarding secondary school dedicated to expanding educational opportunities for young women.

𝟓. 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐚 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐚 𝐆𝐚𝐤𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐠 - 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫

Maria Teresa Gakdeng rose to the occasion in unforgettable fashion as South Sudan’s Bright Starlets pulled off a historic breakthrough at the 2025 Women’s AfroBasket, stunning Egypt 75–65 to secure a dream debut victory and book a place in the Last Eight.

After enduring a winless group phase, the Starlets showed remarkable resilience and belief, with Gakdeng at the heart of their revival. The 22-year-old Hungary-based center dominated both ends of the floor, leading the debutants to their first-ever win at the tournament—and their first victory over Egypt—while inspiring one of the biggest upsets of the competition.

In just her first appearance for the Bright Starlets, Gakdeng not only powered South Sudan into the quarterfinals at the first attempt, but also broke a decade-long AfroBasket record, underlining the scale of her impact and the historic nature of the moment. Her performance symbolized the hunger, talent, and growing confidence of a young South Sudanese side determined to announce itself on the continental stage.

This landmark victory is more than a single win; it is a statement of progress for women’s basketball in South Sudan. We recognise and celebrate the players, coaches, and all those whose contributions continue to drive the nation’s excellence in basketball, opening new chapters and inspiring the next generation of athletes.

𝟔. 𝐉𝐨𝐡𝐧 𝐖𝐨𝐣𝐚 - 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥, 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐮𝐝𝐚𝐧 𝐂𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐥 𝐀𝐯𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 

John Woja was recently relieved of his role as Director General of the South Sudan Civil Aviation Authority, but his impact during a short tenure remains clear.

Before his appointment, Juba International Airport—the country’s only international gateway—had become a public embarrassment. Under John’s leadership, working closely with a new team that included Juba International Airport General Manager Kat Monyjok, a clear development plan was introduced and tangible changes followed. The airport underwent a visible facelift, restoring a sense of order, pride, and direction.

Although John did not stay long enough to complete all the projects he initiated, the progress made in that brief period set him apart. His work earned him a place on this year’s list.

At Civil Aviation headquarters, his tenure also marked a break from years of stagnation. While the airport generates millions of dollars every month, previous administrations failed to translate that revenue into development. Instead, resources were mismanaged and lost. John’s team began pushing for accountability and reinvestment.

Notably, his leadership also advanced efforts to reclaim control of South Sudan’s airspace from Sudan, a process that had reached an advanced stage under his watch.

𝟕. 𝐒𝐞𝐛𝐢𝐭 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐦 - 𝐉𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭

Sebit William is a veteran broadcast journalist and the long-serving host of the breakfast show on UNMISS-owned Radio Miraya. For years, his programme—focused on current affairs and news—has been a trusted source of information for millions of South Sudanese, especially in a country where most radio stations reach only limited areas.

Radio Miraya’s nationwide signal has made Sebit’s work accessible across the country, and through it, he has played a key role in keeping citizens informed on issues that matter most. Even during difficult moments, including periods when the government temporarily banned Radio Miraya over unclear accusations, Sebit remained committed to his professional duty.

We recognise and celebrate Sebit William’s enduring contribution to public information and responsible journalism in South Sudan.

𝟖. 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐥𝐨 - 𝐉𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭 

Mathiang Cirilo is a veteran journalist with a distinguished career spanning regional and international media. He has worked with globally respected news organizations, including Al Jazeera Arabic and Deutsche Welle (DW), where he built a reputation for professionalism, depth, and fearless journalism.

In 2012, Mathiang played a key role in establishing Al Masier, South Sudan’s first Arabic-language daily newspaper. Two years later, in 2014, he went on to found Al Mugif, further strengthening Arabic media in the country and expanding access to news and political discourse for a wider audience.

Known for his bold and uncompromising approach, Mathiang has never shied away from asking difficult questions. Whether engaging political leaders or senior public officials, he consistently presses for clarity and accountability. His television program, The Mathiang Cirilo Show, has earned a reputation for its hard-hitting interviews, with many describing it as South Sudan’s version of HardTalk due to the rigorous manner in which he challenges those in power on national issues.

Today, Hot in Juba recognizes Mathiang Cirilo for his outstanding contribution to journalism, his commitment to truth, and his unwavering dedication to holding leaders accountable in the public interest.

𝟗. 𝐏𝐚𝐮𝐥 𝐁𝐚𝐲𝐨𝐜𝐡 𝐆𝐚𝐭𝐥𝐮𝐚𝐤 - 𝐇𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐧/𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐭 

Paul Bayoch Gatluak is a humanitarian and activist based in Akobo town, Jonglei State, whose work goes beyond the delivery of aid to telling the human story of his community.

Through his humanitarian activities, Paul has become widely recognized not only for supporting vulnerable families but also for documenting the everyday lives of people in Akobo. His work highlights moments that are often overlooked—children at play, women at work, elders sharing stories, and communities coming together despite difficult circumstances. These images and videos offer a rare and honest window into life in one of South Sudan’s most remote areas.

What sets Paul apart is how seamlessly he combines service with storytelling. As he distributes assistance, supports local initiatives, or responds to emergencies, he captures the environment and the people around him with authenticity and respect. His content does not focus on despair alone; instead, it emphasizes resilience, dignity, and the quiet strength of ordinary citizens navigating economic hardship and the impact of conflict.

By showcasing the beauty of Akobo—its landscapes, culture, and people—Paul challenges common narratives that portray rural South Sudan only through the lens of crisis. His work reminds audiences that even in the face of adversity, communities continue to live, hope, and support one another.

Through his humanitarian efforts and visual documentation, Paul Bayoch Gatluak has become both a servant of his people and a voice for them, ensuring that the stories of Akobo’s citizens are seen, heard, and valued beyond their borders.

𝟭𝟬. 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝘂𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗷𝗲𝗻𝗴 - 𝗘𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁/𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 

As climate change continues to disrupt livelihoods across South Sudan, one young man is taking action at the grassroots level to protect the environment.

Through his self-funded nonprofit organization, Save the Nile, Makur Majeng is championing a cleaner and greener future. Alongside a team of volunteers, he leads regular clean-up drives, collecting trash and plastic waste—much of it washed into the Nile from Juba during the rainy season—and ensuring it is properly disposed of.

Makur is a Computer Science student at the University of Juba and also serves as a contributing editor at Hot in Juba, using both action and advocacy to push for environmental responsibility.

In recognition of his efforts, he was recently honored with a Climate Champion Award by the South Sudan Human Rights Defenders Network, which annually recognizes individuals working to advance human rights and social causes in the country.

Hot in Juba celebrates Makur’s commitment to environmental protection and his role in helping make South Sudan—and the world—a better place for all.

The Second Scramble for Africa: Manufactured Conflict and the Plunder of a Continent – Sheikh Zakzaky

This is an excerpt from the concluding part of a speech delivered by Sheikh Ibraheem Zakzaky (H) to a massive gathering of thousands of participants at the Yaumush Shuhada commemoration, held on Saturday, 25th Rajab 1435 AH (24 May 2014), at the Polo Field near Husainiyyah Bakiyyatullah in Zaria, Nigeria.

As of today, 28 December 2025, the speech was delivered 11 years, 7 months, and 4 days ago.

The excerpt was written by the Media Forum of the Islamic movement. In the speech, the Sheikh explained the hidden schemes behind the attacks being carried out in the villages of Zamfara, Birnin Gwari, and other areas, as well as the renewed invasion plan of Africa.

The Invasion of Africa

Today, we are confronting a serious reality in this country. For a long time, I have been warning that something was approaching. I have emphasised this repeatedly in various sermons. Indeed, something is coming—and that is a renewed invasion of Africa. Long ago, through their research, they concluded that the century we were about to enter—even before the year 2000, as far back as the 1900s—would be known as “the African Century.” Their reasoning was that Africa holds nearly two-thirds of the world’s total wealth. Consequently, they planned to seize control of Africa once again through a second and more sophisticated form of domination.

What was once called the “Scramble for Africa” is now referred to as the “Second Scramble.” It represents a new kind of conquest. During the first scramble for Africa, European powers such as Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, and Belgium occupied territories across the continent. Each power claimed different regions until they eventually convened in Berlin, where a conference was held to divide Africa among themselves. Territories were allocated, borders were drawn, and each power was told, “This is yours.”

They now claim this process will be repeated. However, this time, the United States openly declared that it would employ terrorism as a tool to regain control of Africa. This explains what we are witnessing today. They executed this strategy in Libya. When they observed the Arab uprisings and the political awakening in Egypt, they became alarmed and decided to intervene. They moved into Libya, destroyed the country, and killed Gaddafi. Today, Libya is engulfed in violence—killings, tribal and ethnic conflicts, clashes among militias, and racial tensions—while foreign powers continue to exploit its resources. 

It has long been known that Libya and Nigeria possess what is referred to as “sweet crude oil.” Libya is now entirely under their control, and Nigeria, too, is effectively in their grasp. They simply install puppets—every day selecting individuals and declaring one the president, another the vice president, another a governor, and yet another a minister. Titles are distributed, while the nation’s wealth is systematically plundered.
 
The Method of Occupying Nations

They then introduced yet another strategy—the occupation of countries. Using this approach, they planned and invaded Mali. Even recently, the news has reported clashes in places like Kidal and Gao involving armed groups. Suddenly, gunmen appear in neighbourhoods, firing indiscriminately, and no one knows who is being targeted. The narrative presented is that “Islamic militants” have emerged and fighting has broken out.

In reality, gold was discovered in Mali, gold whose precise location had long been unknown. It had always been known that Mali possessed gold. After all, there was Mansa Musa, the famous ruler who travelled for Hajj and entered world history. It is said that he journeyed with thousands of camels carrying gold and thousands of slaves, each holding a staff of gold.

When he reached Egypt, the amount of gold he brought reportedly caused the price of gold to collapse—a decline from which it took years to recover. In Makkah, he constructed buildings, some of which were only recently demolished by the Saudi authorities during expansions around the Holy Mosque. Until just a few years ago, the buildings of Mansa Musa remained remarkable landmarks.
Yet the exact location of this gold remained unknown. Its existence was acknowledged, but where exactly was it? Where did Mansa Musa mine it? No one knew. One location would be suggested, people would go there and find nothing. Another would be mentioned, and again, nothing would be found. But now the gold has been discovered—and that is why they carefully planned the invasion of Mali.

They claimed that “Islamic extremists” had entered from Algeria. Not a single Malian was among them. They alleged that these fighters had captured more than half of Mali and had even established a so-called state named “Azawad.” Then France swiftly intervened, claiming to drive them out. France moved in ahead of the United States, even though the United States had originally planned the intervention. They declared that the militants had been defeated.

After that, France turned its attention to Central Africa, where diamonds are found. The true objective was diamond extraction, but it was disguised as a conflict involving mysterious groups whose identities were unclear. They claimed that a group called Seleka entered the Central African Republic, killing Christians and burning churches, supposedly in the name of Islam. Yet these individuals were not citizens of the Central African Republic. After carrying out the violence, they left the country. Once they departed, Christian militias known as Anti-Balaka were formed, and they began killing Muslims residing in the country, claiming it was retaliation.

But if those Seleka fighters came from elsewhere, killed people, and then left, were they truly citizens of the country? They were outsiders who entered and exited. And yet the local Muslims paid the price. The same pattern occurred in Mali with the military coup. A man named Sanogo was declared leader, claiming he had overthrown President Amadou Toumani Touré because he failed to defeat the northern rebels. Then it was later said that those same northern rebels had taken over most of the country under Sanogo’s watch.

Similarly, in the Central African Republic, it was claimed that a Muslim carried out a military coup, supposedly named Michel Djotodia. Have you ever heard of a Muslim named “Michel”? They said he was Muslim, yet his name was Michel Djotodia. They claimed a Muslim had seized power in a country where the majority are Christians.

But is it forbidden for a Muslim to be president in a Christian-majority country? If so, how did Christians become leaders in Nigeria, where Muslims are the majority? This was the excuse used to justify entering the Central African Republic and massacring Muslims—especially Fulani herders who had committed no crime and knew nothing of the conflict. The real objective was diamonds.
In South Sudan, when they realised they could not use the excuse of “Islamic extremism,” they engineered ethnic conflict between the Dinka and the Nuer. The aim was to block China’s access to oil. Since South Sudan had strong ties with China, they needed to sever that relationship.

As for Nigeria, they introduced something called Boko Haram. Long ago, some Westerners, particularly Americans, openly stated that Boko Haram was not an organic movement, but rather a creation engineered by the United States.

The Abduction of Schoolgirls: The Jonathan Government Is Responsible

Now they claim that Boko Haram abducted some schoolgirls from a school. But the girls themselves, and their parents, know exactly who took them. They know clearly that it was the Jonathan government. People say there are protests, and I ask: What exactly are they protesting? They even wear red clothing. Where did this idea of wearing red come from? They chant, “Bring back our girls.” But who is supposed to bring them back, Jonathan or Shekau? If it is Jonathan who is expected to return your daughters, then protest against him and demand that he produce them from wherever he has kept them, because he knows the military barracks where they were taken. But if it is Shekau, do you even know where Shekau is? When has he ever listened to you? He, too, is being held in a military barracks. Everything involved belongs to them.

There Is No Such Thing as Boko Haram

There is no such thing as Boko Haram. It is a complete fabrication, a deliberate falsehood. We will not accept this foolish deception. If you want to come and take oil, take gold, take wealth, then come openly and trade with us. Even if it is an unfair trade, let it still be a trade. We give you chickens, you give us eggs. We give you camels, you give us goats. We would rather accept that. 

But do not insult us or mock our religion. Do not tell us that we are suffering from “Islamic extremists” and that you have come to save us, when we know very well that you have come to exploit us.
 
The Real “Boko Haram” Is America

The so-called Boko Haram that has truly entered here is America. Wherever they go, there are killings, bombings, and destruction. This is exactly what they did in Afghanistan—and what they are still doing there. It is the same thing they did in Iraq.  In Afghanistan, they established dozens of air bases and began extracting resources, all under the pretext of war. They claimed they were searching for Bin Laden, even though no one knew where Bin Laden was. Later, they said they killed him somewhere that was not even Afghanistan. So what are they still doing in Afghanistan? They remain there to this day.

In Iraq, they invaded, claiming there were weapons of mass destruction. They destroyed the country, repeatedly insisting that the WMDs would be found. They searched everywhere, even after capturing Saddam Hussein, shining a torch into his mouth as if the weapons were hidden there. When they found nothing, they changed the narrative and said they had come to bring democracy. Today, they admit there were no WMDs, yet they have not left Iraq. They remain there, looting resources, while bombings and killings continue, carried out by them.

Now that they have entered here, what we are experiencing is exactly what they planned for us. What we once heard was happening in other countries has suddenly appeared in our own land. We are certain that there is no group of Islamic zealots called Boko Haram. We are completely certain that it does not exist. Where is it? In which town? On which street? In which neighbourhood?

Yet bombs continue to explode. They are the ones planting these bombs, digging shallow pits, burying explosives, detonating them remotely, or driving vehicles packed with bombs and blowing them up. That is their method. Sometimes armed men simply appear and open fire. And why? Because they have come to extract wealth.
In Zamfara lies gold. They aim to clear the people from the areas where the gold is found, leaving no one behind, so they can build airstrips and military bases and extract the gold freely. Between Zaria and Birnin Gwari lie gold and precious stones. They want to remove the population, establish airfields, and haul everything away.

From Sokoto to Borno lie uranium, gold, and platinum. That is what they have come for. So come to us openly and engage in trade. Even if it means you give us chickens and we give you camels, let it be fair, but leave us unharmed and do not interfere with our religion. Instead, you choose to deceive people, treating them like fools. Where, then, is your intelligence? When did America even exist? When did the Europeans exist before us? What real wisdom do they possess? Bring out European history and read it aloud—drunkenness, madness, and witchcraft. At what point did they suddenly become so wise that they now claim the right to deceive us? This is nothing but shameless arrogance.

Come and trade with us. We know you have weapons. We know you are capable of killing. But leave our religion out of this.
This is precisely why they came, and now calamity is spreading rapidly among us. You know what happened in Gwoza. They even advanced toward the town of Gwoza, but then said they would not enter because they feared the Shi‘a.

They had captured a brother, beheaded him, and completely severed his head. Yet they then heard words being spoken—the declaration of faith. They looked and saw that the head was reciting, “La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur Rasulullah,” while the body lay apart. At that point, they said they feared the town because of the Shi‘a. This is exactly the reality we are facing. And I know they have said it for a long time: the only thing they truly fear is this movement. They know it is the only force capable of stopping them.

A Call to Those Involved

We also address those individuals who have been summoned and elevated. We have heard that you were told you lost an election, yet you were still granted office. We have also heard it said that you are unqualified—that you are foolish, ignorant, weak-minded, or incompetent, and yet you were chosen. Very well, we have heard all of this.

But will you now accept money and positions in exchange for the killing of your own people? Do you have no conscience? Is it enough that you were given a title and wealth, such that your people must be slaughtered? Enough of silence. The community has endured more than enough. Do not imagine that they will spare you. Once they are finished using you, once you are drained of all value, they will kill you as well. That is their method. Saddam, whom they killed, was their own creation. Gaddafi, whom they killed, was their own creation. They built them up, then turned on them and destroyed them. And you, once they are done with you, they will cut you off as well. It will be over.

What Has Emerged in This Country Truly Concerns Us All

I know that today, on the occasion of the Day of the Martyrs, we have much to say, because what has emerged in this country truly concerns every one of us. Confronting this reality, using every lawful means available to us, is a duty owed to Islam. And whoever among us is killed in this struggle is a martyr. I am not telling you that because they carry guns, we should also carry guns. But we do have our own forms of weapons, and we will take them up, God willing.

O Allah, we ask You to allow us to witness the next Day of the Martyrs in good health and ample provision. O Exalted Lord, protect us with Your protection, support us with Your support, and grant us firmness over our enemies.

May Allah’s blessings be upon Muhammad and his pure and noble family. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah.

GET TO KNOW THE PROBLEM BETWEEN MURLE AND DINKA BOR 

By HONORABLE MAKER LUAL 

HISTORICAL: Several Abortive Reconciliation Peace Conferences between the Greater Bor Dinka and the Murle Communities
Several Abortive Reconciliation Peace Conferences between the Greater Bor Dinka and the Murle Communities. When will this policy of ambiguity end?
By Hon. Maker Lual Kuol, Bor, Jonglei State
For nearly two centuries, Murle have continued to raid Bor; killing people, abducting children and robbing livestock to the extent that this inhuman and atrocious activity has become a lost a daily practice. It is not Bor alone that suffers from these raids but over other 12 communities such as Anyuak, Jie, Kachipo, Nuers, Toposa, Buoya, Pari, Lopit, Mundari, Bari, Lokoyo, Lotuka that surround the Murle suffer the same atrocities though at a lower magnitude.
Bor in this situation has the longest border extension with the Murle; approximately 250 kilometers from Bor South County border with Terekaka State to Duk North County Border with Fangak State. One fact known to all is that there are no contact areas where the two communities annually meet for water and pastures as these scarce resources are always the cause of disputes and conflicts between pastoralists.
The worst in this situation is that most Murle leaders and elites cover up the mistakes and crimes of their communities. Instead they consider the acts of the members of their communities as heroism and bravery of their people and the communities raided or affected are considered to be cowards. Unfortunately, those usual denials did not last in the face of the raids on Ethiopia in March 2016 when Ethiopia thrust armed to teeth forces into the South Sudanese borders.
And to evade the consequences, all the Murle leaders, hysterically in confusion, beginning from the governor of Boma State to the lowest in social hierarchy hurried up in recovering over one hundred abducted children in a very short period of time. Even for the first time, members of Murle who are always known for covering up of the devilish crimes of their people, started to point fingers at each other.
While the latest peace conference was on session in Pibor between the 1st and 4th December 2016, the Murle were actively busy in Greater Bor Area killing people, abducting children and robbing livestock. For instance, on 3rd Dec. 2016, two women were killed and a child abducted in Bor North County and on 5th Dec. 2016, the Murle greeted and welcomed back the returning delegation from the peace conference by killing two women (sisters) and abducting one child in Twic North County. Those activities were a clear defiance to the peace conference that was on process in Pibor.
Since independence of Sudan from the Condominium Rule in 1956 till independence of South Sudan from Sudan in 2011, 12 (Twelve)) major and minor peace conferences were held between the Murle and the Bor Dinka and after any of these peace conferences, the Murle commit more horrific crimes on the people of Bor. Below are the many conferences held between the two communities for over 50 years since 1962.
1. Bor Conference in 1962
----------------------------------
The first peace conference between Murleand Bor Dinka was held 52 years ago in 1962 in Bor. The conference was co-chaired by Abas Babikr, the commissioner of Bor District and al- Bashir al- Wagie, the commissioner of Pibor District. Also, some chiefs from the two communities headed by Paramount Chiefs of Bor District, Ajang Duot and Ajakoor of the Murle attended. As the conference was held in the open under trees, members of the public including us, as students at Bor Intermediate by the time used to hang around as spectators.
Among those colleagues, I could recall in witnessing the conference as spectators from Murle community, were late Rio Ajakoor (son of Murle Paramount Chief Ajakoor), Martin Lotigo and others. Unfortunately, the resolutions reached were not implemented and the Murle instead continued with their usual evil practices.
By that time, Murle had not acquired firearms. Only spears were the common weapons.
2. Pibor Conference in 1975
-----------------------------------
In 1975, another peace conference that involved most communities of Upper Nile was convened in Pibor. Senior authorities and officials from the Regional Government in Juba and Upper Nile Province led by Abel Alier, the vice president of the republic and president of the High Executive Council attended the conference. Other dignitaries included Enoch Mading de Garang, minister of culture and information and Peter Gatkuoth, commissioner of Upper Nile Province.
Among chief present were paramount Chief David Mabior Ngueny for Bor District, Ajakoor Korok for Pibor, Makuei Bil Kuei, Chief Andrea Farajala of Juba B court and many other chiefs from other communities of Upper Nile. Police inspectors of all the nine districts of Upper Nile attended the conference. At the conclusion of the conference, resolutions were drastic to the extent that some chiefs were dismissed for laxity in administering their communities.
The conference dispersed with high hopes of peace and tranquility but the Murle considered the affair to be a government affair and not theirs and as such continued to intensify their criminal activities against Bor Dinka in particular and the neighboring communities in general.
3. Gadiang Conference in 1981
----------------------------------------
The conference was attended by all communities of Jonglei Province that got sliced out from Upper Nile in 1976 when more provinces were created in Southern Sudan. Abel Alier, the vice president and president of the High Executive Council attended the conference among other dignitaries including Johnson Malual Leek, the Jonglei Commissioner by the time.
Paramount chiefs from the various communities such as David Mabior Ngueny of Bor District, Gatwich Dual, the current SPLM –IO Chief of General Staff representing Lou Nuer and the Murle Paramount Chief were also in attendance.
The glittering resolutions reached could not last as the Murle immediately resumed their culture of raids into Bor and other neighbors.
In 1983, especially after the rebellion of Battalion 105 in Bor, the Murles, during successive raids on Amoumeth, Anyidi, Machar Dehr, Alian and Paliau cattle camps where over 250 people were in a period of less than a year.
4. Liliir Conference in 2001
---------------------------------
While the peace negotiations between the SPLM and the Salvation Government were on at Machakos in Kenya, Sudan Council of Churches in coordination with South Sudan Law Society convened a peace conference at Liliir village north of Bor Town. The conference drew many from the communities of Jonglei State. Among the dignitaries who attended the conference were Cdr. John Koang Nyuon, the then governor of Upper Nile and His deputy Cdr. Peter Wal Athieu.
Some commissioners, including Nicodemos Arou Man, the hosting commissioner also attended. Dr. Harun from the Sudan Council of Churches and Justice Dengtiel Ayuen Kur acted as the facilitators of the conference. Even from Khartoum, elders such as late Isaiah Kulang Mabor and late Johnson Malual Leek among others attended the gathering.
But when the conference concluded its meetings, the Murle flexed their muscles for further deadly attacks on their usual vulnerable Bor People.
5. Boma Conference on 10th March 2004
--------------------------------------------------- 
A mini Peace Conference attended by both communities of Murle and Bor was convened in Boma. Unfortunately, Murle did not tune to the coexistence spirit.
6. Anyidi Conference on 20th March 2004
----------------------------------------------------
In 2004 when some Murle cattle camps migrated to Bor in search of water and pastures, the hosting communities dispersed them along the area in order to avoid congestion on water points. That opportunity was exploited by Philip Thon Nok, the peace project officer by the time in coordination with Bor South County Authorities to convene a mini peace conference between the Bor Dinka and the visiting Murle Community in the area led by chief Gulic.
Among the dignitaries who attended the conference included Cdr. Peter Wal Athieu, Cdr. Machar Akeu, Maker Chol Adol, Cdr. Kazakia Ruei Puot, the then Bor South County Commissioner and Panchol Jongkuc Kur, the SSRA Secretary.
That conference also ended with usual claims of opening a new page but the always defiant Murle continued their activities.
7. Bor Town Conference (November 2005)
-------------------------------------------------------
With the implementation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA), a peace conference was convened in Bor Town between the two communities of Murle and Bor. That conference was attended by Philip Thon Leek and Ismail Konyi, former Governors of Jonglei State, Jude Jonglei, speaker of Jonglei State and Isaiah Chol Aruei, Abraham Jok Ariing and Mayen Ngor, commissioners of Twic East, Bor and Duk Counties respectively. Members of Jonglei Assembly from both Communities attended the conference. That conference met the same fate of the previous ones and the Murle resumed their activities against the people of Bor.
8. Gumuruk Conference in 2006
------------------------------------------
The conference brought along all the six communities of Jonglei State and importantly, the conference was attended by the top leadership of the Government of Southern Sudan (GOSS) headed by Dr. Riek Machar, the former vice president of the Government of the Southern Sudan, Daniel Awet Akot, former minister of Interior, Clement Wani Konga, former Governor of Central Equatoria, Philip Thon Leek, former Governor of Jonglei State, commissioners of various counties of Jonglei State, king of Anyuak beside paramount chiefs and chiefs of various present communities.
Of course, with that high-level attendance by the government authorities, people thought that was the end of conflicts between the Murle and the neighboring communities, but instead the Murle continued to violate the agreement.
9. The Jonglei Reconciliation and Peace Conference (2011)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Government despite the continuous violations of agreements by Murles, Gen. Salva Kiir Mayardit, the President of the Republic of South Sudan thought of involving the church and as such decreed the formation of a peace and reconciliation committee under the chairmanship of His Grace Daniel Deng Bul, the Archbishop of the Episcopal Church of Sudan and South Sudan. And not to leave any stone unturned, committees were formed to visit all counties of Jonglei State in order to dig out the root causes of the conflicts.
When the committees compiled their reports, a general conference was convened in Bor where notes were compared and resolutions drowned. In order to assure commitment of all communities to the resolutions, the resolutions were signed by four paramount chiefs representing the Greater Counties of former Jonglei State; among them Ngatho, the paramount chief of Pibor.
The signing ceremony was witnessed by President Salva Kiir, Michael Makuei Lueth, the national minister of information, Gen. Kuol Manyang Juuk, former Governor of Jonglei State, His Grace Daniel Deng Bul, Archbishop of the Episcopal Church, myself as Bor County Commissioner by the time and many other dignitaries from the national and state governments.
The Murle did not care whether the president attended or not and as usual violated the agreement reached and vigorously continued to step up their raids into Bor and the neighboring communities.
10. Gumuruk Conference 19th August 2016
In trying to bring about peace between the Murle and Bor Dinka, both Baba Medan and Philip Aguer Panyang, the governors of Boma and Jonglei States thought of trying once more what the President, vice presidents, governors and church failed to achieve during 52 years period and as such convened a one day conference at Gumuruk in Boma State. Unfortunately, the conference did not bear fruits.
11. Bor Conference 20th 9 2016
-----------------------------------------
In reciprocating to the Gumuruk mini conference, another similar white washing conference was hurriedly convened at South Sudan Hotel in Bor amidst the roaring rotaries of UNMISS Choppers at Bor Airport. The result of the conference was launching more raids into Bor!
12. Pibor Conference 1st -4th Dec. 2016
---------------------------------------------------
Between 1st and 4th, the two states convened a peace conference in Pibor between the two communities of Murle and Bor Dinka attended by dignitaries from the two states of Jonglei and Boma led by the two governors Philip Aguer and Baba Medan. While the conferees were at the pomp of congratulating themselves on the great achievement for the lasting peace, the Murle were inflicting atrocities on the people of Bor.
On the 3rd December while the two parties were on the negotiating table, the Murle killed two women in Bor North County and abducted one child. On the 5th December 2016 when the conferees were returning to their places, the Murle attacked a village in Twic North County and killed two women who happened to be sisters, and walked away with one child.
It is reported that, while the two communities were negotiating, the Lou Nuer sent in an urgent message to the Boma State Government to immediately recover four Lou Nuer children the Murle abducted some few days earlier to the conference. The Lou Nuer gave an ultimatum of two days otherwise they would be forced to invade the area.
The Boma Government hysterically in no time recovered the four children among them a three-month-old baby! The Lou Nuer copied the example of the Ethiopian Government when she thrust thousands of her troops into the South Sudanese border. The usual techniques of denial by Mrule’s leaders could not work in front of the mighty Lou Nuer and the Ethiopian Government!!!
All the conferences held with the Murle are liken to a story of an Imam (A Muslim Cleric) who was advising a hyena against eating people’s sheep and goats as the consequences were going to be bad at the resurrection time. And while listening keenly to the Imam, a herd of sheep appeared in front of them. On seeing the sheep, the hyena appealed to the Imam to shorten his advice as he was going to miss the herd!!
Twelve Peace Conferences held in a span of 52 years of which some of them were attended by top leaders of South Sudan including President Salva Kiir, Vice President Abel Alier and Vice President Riek Machar but the Murle continued defiant!!!
The millions of Dollars or pounds spent on these twelve peace conferences between the Murles, Dinka, Nuers and others, had it been utilized on roads, water reservoirs, health facilities, schools and construction of security posts between the communities, at least the situation would have changed to some extent. It is not too late to catch up.
The unfortunate part is that Murle Community has no central authority. It is led by the generation group whose objective is to precede the previous generations in criminality. The best leader for them is the one who encourages malpractices ranging from robbery, child abduction to killing.
The International Community which is playing the role of sponsoring and supporting peace dialogue initiatives in South Sudan has no interest other than to continue accessing employment and training of their inexperience people such that when they return to their homes of origin, they would claim to be experts and to confer upon themselves the specialization in South Sudanese affairs.
From the above narrative, it is obvious that all the peace conferences failed miserably. No South Sudanese national in his full senses would applaud and support the death of his or her compatriots South Sudanese. Why not reverting to other options if the peace dialogues had reached a dead lock? It is time for the government to intervene in order to bring about a lasting peace among the communities of South Sudan.
If the IGAD, AU, TROIKA and UN could impose a solution on the opposition and the government on a conflict that lasted for two years only why not imposing a solution in order to resolve a conflict that lasted for nearly two centuries? The government should intervene in order to stop the bloodletting in the former Greater Jonglei State. But while the government is considering any other possible option, may I be allowed as a disturbed citizen to put forward the below suggestions:
(a) Short term solutions
Establishment of border security points.
Security roads to be constructed along the borders separating the neighboring communities that are consistently on conflicts. Security posts to be situated at every 10 kilometers’ interval. At Ajakgeer 53 kilometers east of Bor Town, UNDP constructed an observatory police post and wild life conservation office. Similar facilities were supposed to be concurrently constructed at Mach-Abol in Boma State.
2. Availing of Water for livestock and human.
As water is a crucial element for the pastoralist communities during the dry season, it is necessary that water reservoirs are constructed at strategic points for the drinking of both the livestock and the wild life. Also boreholes are to be drilled near the reservoirs for the provision of clean drinking water to the population.
3. A monitoring team where all the affected communities are to be represented. The team to be stationed in Pibor to monitor the criminal activities of the different communities.
(b) Long term Solution
There is a large semi empty area surrounded by the communities of the different states. That area is estimated at about five million hectares of arable land. That area could be converted into large agricultural schemes where by communities surrounding it can benefit from it. During the British Colonial period, a research conducted on sugar cane production in Mangala proved that sugar content in sugar cane planted was 14%.
That research made the area to be potential for the growth of sugar cane that could supply a sugar factory that can meet the country requirement from processed sugar. Unfortunately, our former colonialist, the Arab North constructed sugar factories at Geneid, Khashum al- Girba, Asalaya, West Sennar and Kenana. During Numiery industrial revolution, one sugar factory was constructed at Melut, but never started operations or production till present moment.
Initiatives for peaceful dialogues are commendable but if no progress seen in the horizon, other options are to be resorted to.

Monthly MPB Tips

January is a good time to be scouting your property and marking any of your green-attack trees – ones that contain live stages of the beetle.  
• This time of year MPB are still in their larval stage.  Larva are about the size of a piece of rice (about 1/4 “ long).  They are legless grubs with a dark head.  
• Other insects may be found under the bark too so looking at the shape of the galleries will help.  MPB galleries are vertical and packed with frass and sawdust with lateral larval galleries.
• Once you identify your infected trees, you will need to decide which method of control you will be using.  Control information can be found on the JCISM MPB website. www.jeffco.us/2738/Mountain-Pine-Beetle

Remember – Moving “green” logs that are infested will spread the beetle to new areas – Please don’t move fresh logs or firewood that have bark attached. Trees that faded last summer no longer contain MPB and are not a risk of spreading it.

Berikut adalah faktor-faktor kunci yang mempengaruhi kepuasan mereka:

Customer Maxim adalah pemburu nilai terbaik. Kepuasan mereka tercapai ketika mereka merasa mendapatkan layanan yang "layak" untuk harga yang "murah".
- Pemicu Puas: Diantar selamat dari A ke B dengan tarif hemat, tanpa ada drama tambahan dari driver (seperti mengeluh soal tarif atau jarak jemput). Bagi mereka, ini adalah transaksi yang sukses.

2. PREDIKTABILITAS DAN KONTROL (Waktu dan Rute)
Sifat mereka yang "buru-buru tapi irit" membuat mereka sangat menghargai kepastian.
- Pemicu Puas: Driver yang datang sesuai estimasi waktu, mengonfirmasi titik jemput dengan jelas, dan mengikuti rute tercepat (sesuai maps) tanpa banyak manuver yang membingungkan. Mereka puas jika mereka bisa mengontrol waktu kedatangan mereka.

3. JARAK PROFESIONAL YANG NYAMAN (The "Silent Service" Preference)
Mengingat banyaknya tipe "Silent Rider", interaksi sosial seringkali bukan prioritas utama mereka.

4. STANDAR DASAR FISIK (Kebersihan dan Keamanan)
Meskipun membayar murah, mereka tetap manusia yang punya standar dasar kenyamanan.
- Pemicu Puas: Kendaraan yang tidak bau (bau rokok/apek adalah musuh utama), driver berpakaian rapi (standar), dan cara menyetir yang tidak ugal-ugalan.

Auricularia Americana 
*Also known as 'Judas Ear', 'Jelly Ear' or 'Black Fungus'. 

Known for it's rubbery ear like shape, and chewy texture in dishes like soup. They are gelatinous and brown but as they dry out they become hard, and crisp (like apple chips) and turn a dark brown black color. When fresh they have a fleshy feel, When dried the back appears velvety.

Prized for its unique crunchy, jelly-like texture and ability to absorb flavors, makes it a popular addition to soups, stir-fries, and even salads. Can be used fresh or dried (rehydrated in water or milk). Dried mushrooms can last years; rehydrate before use and add to dishes to absorb flavors. 

❌ Do NOT eat raw! Woods Ear requires cooking to remove mild toxins and potential contaminants like bacteria or bugs. While considered an excellent edible with a unique crunchy texture when cooked, raw consumption can cause stomach upset and it's always best prepared in soups, salads, or stir-fries after proper cleaning and cooking. 

Woods Ear has also been used in traditional medicine and studied for potential properties like anticoagulant, anti-inflammatory, and  cholesterol-lowering effects.

 ⚠️Caution!  Avoid if taking blood-thinning medication due to its anticoagulant properties. Avoid if preparing for surgery soon. 

Key differentiator: Grows on conifers, unlike Auricularia angiospermarum which grows on hardwoods. Also, Spore print is  White.

Considered beginner-friendly as it has no toxic look-alikes, with the similar-looking amber jellyroll also being edible. 

• Contains compounds that act as natural anticoagulants 
(blood thinners)

• Helps lower total and "bad" (LDL) cholesterol levels, and may improve blood circulation.

• Rich in polyphenols and other antioxidants, Auricularia species help fight oxidative stress and may reduce inflammation, which are factors in numerous chronic diseases.

• Beta-glucans and other polysaccharides in the woods ear mushroom are believed to have immunomodulatory effects- which can help regulate and enhance the immune system.

• As a rich source of fiber and prebiotics, it helps promote healthy digestion, supports a balanced gut microbiome, and can aid in maintaining bowel regularity.

• Compounds that may inhibit an enzyme linked to degenerative brain diseases like Alzheimer's have been identified in lab studies, suggesting a potential role in supporting cognitive health. 

• Research indicates that polysaccharide-rich extracts can accelerate wound closure by promoting skin cell proliferation and enhancing collagen synthesis.

Ariath Makuei Bol Yel
Prophet and Spiritual Leader of the Dinka Malual
(c. 1896 – 1947)

KOLONGDIT MEDIA HISTORICAL ARCHIVE HOUSE
Preserving National Memory & Indigenous Knowledge

ARCHIVE IDENTIFICATION

Archive Title: Ariath Makuei Bol — Prophet and Spiritual Leader of the Dinka Malual
Alternative Names: Ariath Makuei; Ariathdit; Ariath Makueidit
Archive Code: KMHAH–ARIATH–001
Category: Spiritual Leadership | Indigenous Resistance | Oral History
Region: Northern Bahr el Ghazal (Aweil), South Sudan

I. INTRODUCTION

Ariath Makuei Bol;  also known as Ariath Makuei, Ariathdit, or Ariath Makueidit,  was one of the most influential indigenous spiritual leaders in the history of the Dinka Malual people of South Sudan. Born around 1896 and passing away in 1947, Ariath emerged as a prophet (Beny Bith), rainmaker, and moral authority whose influence extended beyond religion into culture and politics.

He is remembered as a man deeply rooted in Dinka traditions and cosmology, teaching belief in one supreme God, Nhialic Tok, long before the arrival and spread of Christianity and Islam in the Bahr el Ghazal region. His life, teachings, and spiritual authority left a lasting imprint on Dinka identity and later South Sudanese liberation consciousness.

II. ORIGINS AND EARLY LIFE

Ariath Makuei Bol was born around 1896 in Chimel Kuac, Bahr el Ghazal, in what is today Northern Bahr el Ghazal State, South Sudan. He belonged to the Dinka Malual community, a pastoral Nilotic society deeply rooted in spiritual cosmology, cattle culture, and communal governance.

He was born into a large family consisting of eleven siblings, a factor that placed him within extensive kinship networks across Malual land. These family connections later enhanced his influence and legitimacy as a mediator, spiritual guide, and leader.

From an early age, Ariath demonstrated exceptional spiritual awareness. Oral accounts consistently describe him as a man chosen through divine calling rather than inheritance or force, aligning with traditional Dinka beliefs that spiritual authority is granted by Nhialic, the supreme creator.

III. SPIRITUAL CALLING AND PROPHETIC ROLE

Ariath Makuei Bol is widely recognized as a prophet (Beny Bith) within Dinka spiritual tradition. His spiritual transformation is said to have begun after his initiation into adulthood. Following this rite, his demeanor changed profoundly,  he became quiet, deeply contemplative, and withdrawn, spending long periods in spiritual isolation.

For several years, Ariath lived away from public life, dedicating himself to meditation, communion with the divine, and reflection. In 1917, he re-emerged publicly, already recognized by elders and communities as a man chosen by Nhialic Tok, the one supreme creator God in Dinka belief.

His teachings emphasized:

The oneness and supremacy of Nhialic Tok

Moral discipline and communal harmony

Respect for ancestral traditions and sacred land

Peace, reconciliation, and unity among the Dinka

Unlike later organized religions, Ariath’s message was transmitted orally through proclamations, rituals, and symbolic acts, embedding his teachings deeply within cultural memory.

IV. LEADERSHIP AND COMMUNITY INFLUENCE

Ariath Makuei’s authority extended beyond spirituality into social leadership. He became a central figure in dispute resolution, cultural preservation, and communal mobilization. His influence was recognized across wide areas of Aweil and neighboring territories.

Marriage alliances and kinship ties strengthened his standing, consistent with the customs of the time, and enabled him to act as a unifying figure capable of bridging clan divisions.

Many oral historians describe Ariath as one of the earliest figures to envision unity beyond narrow clan identity, a concept that later evolved into broader Dinka and South Sudanese national consciousness.

V. SPIRITUAL AUTHORITY AND POLITICAL INSPIRATION

Although Ariath Makuei Bol was not a politician in the modern sense, his spiritual authority carried significant political weight. During the period of Anglo–Egyptian colonial expansion into Bahr el Ghazal, his influence represented indigenous sovereignty and resistance.

Colonial authorities perceived prophets and rainmakers as threats because they commanded loyalty beyond colonial structures. Ariath’s rejection of foreign domination was grounded in spiritual legitimacy rather than armed rebellion, yet it inspired later generations to view him as a symbol of self-determination.

His enduring political relevance is evident decades after his death. In 1991, during the South Sudanese liberation struggle, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement/Army (SPLM/A) named one of its battalions “Ariath Makuei”, recognizing him as a foundational figure of resistance, identity, and unity.

VI. FINAL YEARS AND DEATH

Ariath Makuei Bol passed away in 1947 in the Aweil region. His death marked the physical end of his mission but not the conclusion of his influence. He left behind no written texts, yet his teachings survived through oral transmission, ritual memory, and cultural reverence.

VII. LEGACY AND CONTINUING INFLUENCE

Ariath Makuei Bol’s legacy remains deeply embedded in the spiritual, cultural, and political consciousness of the Dinka Malual and wider South Sudanese society.

Spiritual Legacy

He is revered as a rainmaker, a role of immense importance in pastoral and agricultural Dinka life. Rainmaking symbolizes divine favor, survival, and harmony between humanity and nature. His reputation as a rain-associated spiritual authority endures in oral tradition.

Cultural and Religious Identity

Ariath’s teaching of belief in one God (Nhialic Tok) positioned him as a precursor to later monotheistic interpretations within South Sudan while remaining firmly grounded in indigenous belief systems

Contemporary Continuity

His spiritual lineage is believed to continue today. In recent years, Mayen Akech Koot has emerged in the Aweil region as a spiritual leader widely regarded by elders and followers as a successor within the Ariath Makuei tradition, reviving rituals of rainmaking, peace, and communal reconciliation.

Ariath Makuei Bol thus stands not only as a historical figure but as a living spiritual reference point whose influence continues to shape identity, belief, and leadership.

VIII. HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE

Ariath Makuei Bol represents the intersection of African traditional religion, communal leadership, and anti‑colonial consciousness. His story underscores the role of spirituality as a form of governance and resistance long before the emergence of modern political movements.

IX. ARCHIVAL STATUS

I got married at a very young age.
At that time, life looked promising. I was beautiful, young, and hardworking. I was a nurse in one of the federal hospitals in the country, and people respected me. From the outside, my life looked perfect. But behind closed doors, my marriage was slowly destroying me.
My only problem was infertility.
My husband and I tried everything. We went to different hospitals. We saw doctors. We tried herbal treatments. We prayed. We waited. Nothing worked. As the years passed without a child, his love turned into anger.
He started threatening me with divorce.
Every small misunderstanding became a big fight. He would beat me, drag me out of the house, and bundle me with my clothes back to my village like unwanted luggage. Each time, my family would call him, beg him, kneel emotionally, and plead with him to take me back. And he would—only to repeat the same cruelty again.
One incident broke me forever.
I didn’t even know I was pregnant. After one of his beatings, he sent me back to my village again. The stress, the pain, the shame—I lost the pregnancy. I had a miscarriage without ever knowing I was carrying life inside me. That loss stayed with me. It was silent, deep, and unbearable.
From that day, something in me died.
The humiliation never stopped. Then one evening, I saw a text message on his phone. It was clear he was seeing another woman. When I confronted him, he beat me again and shouted that once he returned from work the next day, he would send me back to my people for good.
That night, I made a decision.
I called a truck. I called some boys. While he slept peacefully, I packed everything he owned—his clothes, shoes, furniture, electronics—everything. Before morning came, I left the house empty. I switched off my phone and traveled very far away, to a place where nobody could find me.
I disappeared.
Years later, I heard the news of his death.
Since then, my life has not known peace.
I see him in my dreams. He accuses me of killing him. He looks at me with anger and blame. I wake up shaking, sweating, crying. I did not poison him. I did not harm him. I did nothing to cause his death. Yet his spirit haunts me.
I can’t sleep well. I can’t rest. My mind is always troubled. Sometimes I feel like I’m losing my sanity.
I escaped his hands while he was alive, but now, even in death, he won’t let me go.
And I don’t know how to be free.

I write this message to remind you about the future of South Sudan, which is in your hands. This country can be united if you put aside your emotions and look at the future of South Sudan objectively. Remember that tomorrow is there and it is always a day to reflect deeply.

Do not allow those from Gogrial in Warrap State to exploit your emotions as members of the Dinka tribe and push you into decisions that can destroy your own future. I know what is going as some individuals watch out just to compile a case against Nuer so that you put aside you decision to support the unity of South Sudan and make sure Nuer are defeated.

Meanwhile, you will be left to face the consequences. Yes, the SSPDF are being paid today, some are being promoted in the army, and the SPLM-IG leadership may meet you easily but know that they are doing this only because they need something from you.

If you do not want to fight, then do not support those who would remain in power only to destroy you later. 

 In Summary, think of tomorrow, think of the future of South Sudan, and think of the freedom that was achieved through sacrifice. Tribal divisions can kill you, but the country in unity can build you.
