My name is Leah, and when I was eight years old, my entire understanding of family shattered in the middle of a crowded airport terminal.

Back then, my world revolved completely around my mother, Annette. After my parents divorced when I was five, she became my anchor, my safe place, the person I trusted without question. My father, Gordon, vanished from my life almost overnight. Or at least, that’s how it was explained to me. Mom told me he chose his business empire over us, that he didn’t want the responsibility of being a father anymore. I believed her, because at that age, you believe the story that hurts the least when it comes from the person you love most.

When my mother remarried a man named Calvin, everything changed in ways I didn’t yet have the words to describe. Calvin came with two children of his own—Kylie, who was ten, and Noah, who was nine. They were loud, confident, demanding, and immediately treated like royalty. I was quiet, observant, careful not to take up too much space. From the moment we became a “family,” it was clear there were different rules for me.

Calvin never pretended otherwise. He doted on his biological children openly, praising their smallest achievements while barely acknowledging my existence. If Kylie spoke, everyone listened. If Noah complained, something was immediately done. If I needed something, I was told to wait, to stop being dramatic, to figure it out myself. My mother watched all of this happen and did nothing. Worse, she adapted to it, reshaping herself to fit Calvin’s expectations, even when it meant slowly erasing me.

Kylie mastered subtle cruelty. She smiled sweetly in front of adults, then whispered insults when no one was looking. She borrowed my things without asking and returned them broken. Noah was less strategic but just as hurtful, knocking things over, ripping pages out of my notebooks, laughing when I cried. If I protested, Calvin accused me of exaggerating. If I cried, my mother sighed like I was an inconvenience she hadn’t planned for.

The signs were everywhere, even then. Family movie nights where there “wasn’t enough room” for me on the couch. Birthday parties where Kylie and Noah got themed decorations, gifts piled high, while mine passed with a single cake bought at the last minute. Vacation photos where I was placed at the edge, half out of frame, or missing entirely. I didn’t understand what exclusion was, but I felt it in my bones.

Everything came to a breaking point during spring break of my second-grade year.

Calvin announced we were going to Hawaii for two full weeks. I remember the way my chest filled with excitement so intense it made it hard to breathe. I had never been on a real vacation before. I imagined beaches, warm sand, maybe my mom holding my hand again like she used to before Calvin entered our lives. I told myself this trip would be different. This would be the moment we finally felt like a real family.

The night before we left, I barely slept. I packed my small purple backpack again and again, making sure my favorite stuffed animal was safe inside, along with a few books and the swimsuit my mom had bought me weeks earlier. She’d smiled when she handed it to me, and I’d clung to that smile like proof that she still cared.

The drive to the airport felt strange. Calvin was quiet, his jaw tight. Kylie and Noah kept exchanging glances and whispering to each other, breaking into laughter when I looked their way. Something in my stomach twisted, but I ignored it. I was eight. I wanted to believe.

At the airport, everything seemed normal at first. We checked in, handed over our bags, and walked toward the gate. I held my boarding pass like it was something precious, reading the destination over and over. Honolulu. It felt magical just seeing the word.

Then Calvin said he needed to use the restroom and took Kylie and Noah with him. My mom told me she was going to grab coffee and that I should wait by the gate. She said it casually, like it was nothing, like she’d be back in a minute.

I waited.

Minutes passed. Then more. Families lined up to board. Children clung to their parents, laughing, bouncing with excitement. I checked the large clock on the wall again and again. Our boarding time was approaching. My stomach began to hurt.

Finally, I pulled out the phone my mom had given me for emergencies and called her.

When she answered, there was loud music in the background, mixed with laughter. It didn’t sound like an airport café.

“Mom?” I said, my voice small. “Where are you? Our plane is about to leave.”

There was a pause. A long one. Then her voice came through, colder than I had ever heard it.

“Leah, listen carefully. You’re not coming with us.”

I didn’t understand the words at first. “What do you mean? I have my ticket. I’m at the gate.”

“You’re staying there,” she said flatly. “Calvin thinks it’s better if it’s just our new family on this trip.”

My chest tightened. “But… how do I get home?”

Her tone sharpened. “You can figure it out. I’m not ruining my perfect family vacation for your worthless drama.”

I started crying, panic crashing over me in waves. “Mom, I’m eight. I don’t know what to do.”

Calvin’s voice cut in, harsh and dismissive. “Some brats just need to learn real independence the hard way.”

In the background, I heard laughter. Kylie’s voice carried clearly, delighted. “Finally. A vacation without the unwanted baggage.”

My mother came back on the line, irritation thick in her voice. “Stop being so pathetic, Leah. You’re smart. Figure it out.”

The call ended.

I stood there in the middle of Denver International Airport, clutching my backpack and phone, my entire body shaking. Around me, life went on. Planes boarded. Announcements echoed overhead. People hurried past without noticing the little girl who had just been abandoned.

Airport security found me about twenty minutes later, curled up near the gate, sobbing so hard I could barely breathe. From the moment Adeline laid eyes on the woman beside her brother, everything clicked into place.

She'd heard bits and pieces before-Alberto had once dated someone seriously.

No one knew exactly why they broke up, but judging by the look in their eyes now, former girlfriend might no longer be the right label.

Adeline was genuinely happy for them. After all, what sister wouldn't be glad to see her brother reunited with someone he clearly loved?

"Adeline, Harrison," Alberto called out, practically glowing. "Let me introduce you-this is Connie. My girlfriend."

There was no hesitation in his voice. He said it with certainty, and pride.

Connie smiled and greeted them warmly, her gaze resting on Adeline with admiration. "I always imagined the daughter of the Mendoza family would be beautiful, but you... You're something else entirely. I've seen beauty, but you? You're in a league of your own."

The compliment was so earnest that Adeline couldn't help but feel a little embarrassed.

Alberto, however, immediately put on a mock-stern face. "What? Are you saying my sister is the most beautiful woman you've ever seen? What about me?"

Connie shot him a playful glance and quipped,"Please. Compu. ed to your sister, you ve got a long way to go."

Despite the teasing, Alberto looked at Connie with such soft affection that Adeline instinctively recognized the expression.

It was a look she was more than familiar with - because that was exactly how Harrison looked at her.

Soon after, Isaac and Gracie came downstairs.

They paused the moment they spotted Connie.

Their eyes met briefly, silently exchanging the same question, "Is that who we think it is?"

But after living half a lifetime, they'd learned to keep their expressions in check.

Connie greeted them politely, and they responded with warmth, just as they would have years ago.

That evening, Connie stayed for dinner at the Mendoza family.

Afterward, she and Adeline took a quiet walk in the garden, chatting side by side.

It was during this stroll that Adeline finally heard the full story of how she and Alberto had broken up.

As it turned out  there had been no dramatic
betrayal. No earth-shattering secret. Just...
distance.

Alberto had been overwhelmed with work for a while. They hadn't seen each other in weeks.

Connie had felt neglected-but she understood the pressure Alberto was under as the Mendoza heir, so she said nothing.

Then, one night, while Alberto was away on a business trip, a friend of Connie's happened to be in the same city. That friend spotted Alberto at a restaurant, sitting beside another woman who was pouring him a drink a little too intimately.

She snapped a photo and sent it to Connie.

Connie had been with Alberto for ten years. 

She knew his character. She didn't really believe he a cheat. But still-seeing that image had lit a fire in her chest.
She had been so patient, giving him space, never demanding more than he could give... only to see him, in another city, with some woman leaning in like that.

She lost it.

And that, Adeline thought, was how it started—a spark that caught on old insecurities.

Alberto, exhausted from work, didn't know why Connie was suddenly cold and angry. 

He tried to soothe her, but when she wouldn't say what was wrong, he snapped too.

One fight turned into a blowout. Words were exchanged. And then came the fatal one-breakup.

They hadn't meant it. Not really. After ten years together, how could it be that easy to walk away?

But just a few days later, Connie heard a rumor.

Alberto was getting engaged.

She tried calling him. He didn't pick up.

She asked aroud.

Every answer was the same: he was engaged, and the woman came from a powerful family. It was all so detailed. So convincing.

Connie was devastated. "Have I really meant so little?" she thought.

She cried for days. When Alberto finally called, she was still so hurt, she refused to answer.

Instead, she sent him a flurry of angry texts, then blocked him.

Just like that, ten years unraveled.

Adeline couldn't help but wince. "Seriously? Ten years together and they still didn't know how to talk to each other?"

All of this... could've been avoided with one honest conversation.

She thought of her and Harrison. They'd had their fair share of miscommunication
too.

She smiled bitterly.

"Anyway," Connie said, rubbing the back of her neck sheepishlv "we talked it all out this afternoon. Tur out, that woman at the dinner was just someone the business partner brought along. She poured him one drink, and Alberto immediately had her sent away. Unfortunately, that's the exact moment my friend walked in..."

She gave a helpless shrug. "And the whole engagement thing? Total nonsense. Neither of us knows where that rumor even came from. The day I called him, he really was just tied up with something urgent."

If she'd just waited, asked, and trusted him.

And as for the whole "I'm getting married" thing? Connie sighed. "That night, I went to a bar to drink away my misery. Someone said something about Alberto getting engaged, and I-I just snapped. I said I'd get married too. It was a joke.

But apparently, one of Alberto's friends was there, overheard it... and the rumor started." At the Livingston banquet, when Alberto confronted her, she'd doubled down. Just to save face.

But today, they had finally laid it all bare because neither of them had ever really moved on.

If they had, there would've been no reason to make up.

Connie took Adeline's hand, her tone gentle and sincere. "Adeline, I can see how much you and your boyfriend love each other. But trust me, even the best relationships can fall apart without proper communication. Take it from me and your brother-don't make the same mistake. If something's bothering you, talk to him. Don't let it fester."

Adeline nodded. "I know."

She had learned that the hard way already.
And now, Alberto and Connie's story had only driven the lesson home further.

"But there's still one thing that bothers me," Adeline said thoughtfully. "Where did that engagement rumor even come from?"

Connie gave a wry smile. "Neither of us knows. I even called the people who told me about it originally. They all said the same thing-that they'd heard it from someone else. No one knows who started it."

Adeline frowned slightly. "You two should probably look into it. I have a bad feeling.
Something tells me it wasn't just idle gossip.
Maybe someone out there wanted to tear you apart. I hope I'm wrong... but better to be sure."

Connie's smile slowly faded as her expression turned serious.

But it hadn't just been a month of relaxation-they carved out time each day to handle work remotely, keeping tabs on company matters online.

Though it wasn't quite as convenient as being at the office daily, the Thomson Group was already a well-oiled machine. A brief absence wouldn't cause any real disruption.

Spring had warmed the city by then.

During that time, Sam had taken Joyce to see the aurora borealis.

Naturally, Callan had followed them there.

But with security guards watching his every move, Callan never had the chance to get close.

He could only trail them from afar like an unwanted shadow.

But neither Sam nor Joyce cared.

If anything, it only made their trip more relaxing, they could simply pretend he didn't
 exist. The only one suffering from this awkward cat-and-mouse game was Callan himself.

They remained still, but Jamarion couldn't.

Worried that Callan might snap and do something reckless, he eventually sent people to drag him back.

Not long after, Adeline and Harrison returned to Orianto.

As soon as eir plane landed, Myra was already waiting at the airport.

It had been over two months since they last saw each other.

And though Adeline couldn't quite pinpoint what had changed, she could feel it-Myra's entire presence seemed subtly different.

She was more at ease and happier. Her smile alone said she'd been doing well.

To welcome them back, Myra took them out for dinner.

During the meal, she casually brought up Edward.

"He came to see me," she said in a tone so light it was almost indifferent.

Harrison's brow immediately furrowed. "What did he want?"

Myra said, "He asked if I could convince Lorenzo to let his current wife into the Thomson family."

The way she said it-calm, detached -made it clear she was truly over him. It sounded like she was talking abou a stranger's life, not her own.

Harrison, on the other hand, didn't take it nearly as well. His face darkened.

Edward still had the nerve to come crawling back and ask Myra for favors?
Adeline noticed Harrison's reaction and gently ran her fingers over the back of his hand, silently reminding him to stay calm.

"I turned him down, of course," Myra said with a soft smile. "Told him his affairs have nothing to do with me anymore, and that he should stop bothering me."

To his credit, Edward hadn't pushed the matter.

Maybe even he realized how ridiculous it was to make such a request.

After being firmly rejected, he left quietly.

After dinner, Myra handed Adeline a small box.

Surprised, Adeline looked up. "Myra, this is...”

"My mother left it to me," Myra said as she opened the box.

Inside,  there was an exquisite emerald bracelet. The stone glee with a gentle warmth, its quality unmistakably top-tier.

"Now it's yours," Myra said with a warm smile.

Adeline was stunned. This wasn't just a gift-it was a deeply personal heirloom. She could feel her heart pounding. "Myra, I... This was your mother's..."

"I hope you'll accept it," Myra said sincerely. 

"I won't claim I can treat you like my own daughter just yet... but I can promise to try-to do my best to be a good mother to you."

With words like that, Adeline could no longer refuse.

She was touched, truly.

If nothing else, it showed that Myra had opened her heart to her.

"Thank you," Adeline said, her voice soft.

Myra's smile deepened. She personally fastened the bracelet around Adeline's wrist.

On the way home, Adeline couldn't stop glancing at the bracelet.

"You really like it, huh?" Harrison asked, smiling.

"I do," she said honestly. "It's beautiful... and it means a lot."

"I'm glad," he replied. "One day, you can pass it down to our daughter."

"Mm..." Adeline hummed instinctively-then her eyes widened as she processed what he'd just said.

She shot him a glare. "Who said anything about having a daughter with you?"

"No daughter?" Harrison frowned. "So you want a son instead? Wow. Gender bias? That's disappointing."

"You—!" Adeline couldn't help but laugh.

She didn't mean that.

If she ever had a child, she'd love nothing more than to have a soft, sweet little girl calling her Mommy.

But clearly, Harrison was playing dumb on purpose.

Still, she'd on y said it to be playful.

In truth, there was no one else she could imagine building a future with but him.

And Harrison? He was already picturing their daughter in vivid detail.

"She'd definitely look more like you," he mused dreamily. "Maybe like a miniature version of you."

Adeline, unintentionally drawn into the fantasy, smiled. "What if she looks more like you?"

"That works too," Harrison said. "Our genes are excellent either way."

Adeline laughed. "You're so full of yourself."

"I'm just being honest."

"How did I not realize you were this narcissistic before?"

"Oh, there's plenty about me you ve yet to discover."

The way he said it was casual... but Adeline caught the underlying tone and felt her cheeks heat up.

To cover it, she gave his thigh a sharp pinch.

Their car pulled into the Shurford Residence.

When they arrived downstairs, Adeline got out-only to spot another car nearby. 

Standing by it was Rowen, who waved at her with a bright smile.

"Rowen?" Adeline called. "What are you doing here?"

"I brought Mr. Thomson's luggage," Rowen said cheerfully.

Adeline blinked and thought, "Luggage?
Harrison's luggage? Why was Harrison's luggage being brought here?"

She turned to shoot him a look-calm but deadly.

Harrison was in without even telling her.

Harrison pretended not to notice her expression.

Instead, he said to Rowen, "Bring it all upstairs."

"Got it." Rowen quickly began directing several movers.

Adeline gave Harrison a swift kick. "Who said you could move in?"

"I did," Harrison replied with zero shame. 

"I'm your boyfriend."

"You..." Adeline was momentarily speechless at his audacity.

Wait a second. She'd just remembered something important.

This apartment... belonged to Harrison.

Technically, she didn't even have the authority to tell him not to move in.

She sighed and thought, "Forget it. Let him do what he wants."

Besides, a part of her-though she'd never admit it aloud-was a little excited at the thought of living together.

With the help of the elevator, it didn't take long for the movers to carry everything upstairs.

Once Rowen gave the all-clear, he led the team out, leaving the two of them alone again.

Without hesitation, Harrison walked into her room and started filling her closet with his clothes.

Toiletries and personal items were neatly arranged in the bathroom.

An incomplete comprehensive attempt to list all spiritual practices of the World:

DECOLONIZED FRAMEWORK
(Excluding colonizer / missionary frameworks)

This framework is used in Indigenous studies, decolonial anthropology, and critical religious studies. It does not rank traditions, does not universalize belief, and does not assume “religion” is the correct category for all spiritual systems.

Core Principles:
 • Land-based before belief-based
 • Relational before doctrinal
 • Ancestral continuity over conversion
 • Plural truths, not universal truth claims
 • No “founder = legitimacy” assumption

⸻

I. ʻĀINA / LAND-BASED & ANCESTRAL COSMOLOGIES
Spiritual systems inseparable from place, genealogy, and ecology. These are complete knowledge systems, not “primitive religions.”

Examples:
 • Kānaka Maoli: ʻIke kūpuna, akua–ʻāina–aliʻi relational system
 • Māori: Whakapapa-based cosmology
 • Aboriginal Australians: Dreaming / Songlines
 • Native American Nations: Lakota, Diné, Hopi, Haudenosaunee, etc.
 • Sámi: Noaidi traditions
 • Ainu: Kamuy system
 • Andean peoples: Pachamama cosmology
 • African nations: Yoruba, Akan, Dinka, Igbo, etc.
 • Pacific Islanders: Moana-based ancestral systems
 • Amazonian peoples: Animist-relational cosmologies

Key feature:
Land is alive. Humans are not above it.

⸻

II. ANCESTRAL-STATE & CIVILIZATIONAL COSMOLOGIES
Pre-colonial systems later rebranded as “religions.”

Examples:
 • Kemet (Egypt): Maʻat-based cosmology
 • Sumer / Akkad: Mesopotamian cosmology
 • Indus Valley: Proto-Dharmic systems
 • Shang / Zhou China: Tian–ancestral order
 • Greco-Roman world: Polis-based cosmologies
 • Maya / Aztec: Cyclical cosmic systems

Key feature:
Spiritual order equals cosmic and social order.

⸻

III. DHARMIC / CYCLE-BASED PATH SYSTEMS
Paths of practice rather than belief systems.

Examples:
 • Hindu traditions: Dharma, karma, moksha
 • Buddhism: Liberation from suffering
 • Jainism: Non-harm and liberation
 • Sikhism: Devotion and justice

Key feature:
Reality is cyclical; no single creator authority.

⸻

IV. RELATIONAL ETHICAL PHILOSOPHIES
Often mislabeled as “religions.”

Examples:
 • Confucian traditions: Social harmony
 • Tao / Dao traditions: Natural balance
 • Stoicism (ancient): Virtue and reason

Key feature:
Focus on how to live well, not who to worship.

⸻

V. MONOTHEISTIC IMPERIAL THEOLOGIES
Text-centered systems that expanded alongside empires.

Examples:
 • Judaism: Tribal-law covenant
 • Christianity: Roman imperial adoption
 • Islam: Caliphate-linked expansion

Key features:
 • Exclusive truth claims
 • Conversion imperative
 • Scripture prioritized over land
 • Portable across empires

This names historical structure, not the worth of practitioners.

⸻

VI. DIASPORA & RESISTANCE SPIRITUALITIES
Formed under enslavement, occupation, or forced exile.

Examples:
 • Vodou: Enslaved African survival system
 • Santería (Lukumi): Colonial Cuba
 • Candomblé: Brazil
 • Rastafari: Anti-colonial Black theology
 • Palo: Survival cosmology

Key feature:
Spiritual survival against domination.

⸻

VII. REVIVAL, RECLAMATION & CONTINUITY MOVEMENTS
Not “neo-pagan” — reclamation, not invention.

Examples:
 • Kemetic revival: Cultural restoration
 • Norse Heathenry: Reclaimed ancestry
 • Hawaiian ʻŌiwi resurgence: Continuity, not revival
 • Andean resurgence: Land and identity reclamation

Key feature:
Memory reclaimed, not created.

⸻

VIII. MODERN SYNTHETIC & POST-INDUSTRIAL SYSTEMS
Formed in modern and post-industrial contexts.

Examples:
 • Baháʼí: Universalist synthesis
 • Scientology: Technology-spiritual hybrid
 • New Thought: Mind-centered metaphysics
 • Secular Humanism: Ethics without metaphysics

⸻

WHAT THIS FRAMEWORK CORRECTS:
 • Removes “world religion” hierarchy
 • Centers Indigenous sovereignty
 • Separates belief, practice, and power
 • Rejects missionary and imperial language
 • Treats land, ancestry, and place as primary

⸻

ONE-LINE TRUTH:
“Religion” is a Western category imposed on many systems that never defined themselves that way.

Violence in South Sudan does not recognize tribal boundaries; it affects all communities. a) In 2020 Surge in civilian harm across hotspots:

Nationwide spread of lethal incidents as the ACLED-based annual synthesis shows multiple provinces experiencing fatal events, reflecting subnational conflicts and cattle-raiding cycles escalating through the year.

b) 2021Violence remains widespread, though some metrics decrease: 

UNMISS annual brief notes a reduction in total victims compared to 2020, but persistent subnational communal violence continues to drive killings and injuries, particularly in Jonglei, Warrap, and Lakes. UN investigators warn of country-scale engulfment: UN News reports investigators describing extreme violence, with clashes involving thousands of fighters across three-quarters of the country—underscoring the scale of gun involvement and communal mobilization. ACLED summary confirms continued fatal incidents: Province-level mapping shows ongoing conflicts with recurrent lethal events across multiple regions.

c) 2022 Deadly Q4 spike: 

UNMISS reported 450 civilians killed between October and December alone, alongside injuries, abductions, and CRSV, marking a sharp quarter-on-quarter rise and reflecting both party-based fighting and community militia attacks. Annual victim count rises despite fewer incidents: UNMISS press release records at least 3,469 civilian victims throughout 2022; while incidents attributed to parties to the conflict decreased, the number of victims increased significantly, indicating greater lethality per event. Illustrative major events: Notable mass-casualty clashes include January killings in Jonglei and April attacks in Abyei area, demonstrating intercommunal and cross-border militia dynamics tied to land and cattle disputes.

d) 2023 High lethality concentrated in Warrap: 

UNMISS documented 885 incidents affecting 3,340 civilians, including 1,524 killed; Warrap accounted for 45% of killed and injured, highlighting intense communal gun violence and revenge cycles in that state. ACLED annual mapping shows persistent fatal events: Countrywide distribution of killings continues, with provincial clusters aligning to cattle-raiding corridors and contested territories.

e) 2024 UNMISS reported that more incidents and civilian harm than prior year: 

The UN News reports 1,019 violent incidents affecting 3,657 civilians in 2024, including 1,561 killed and 1,299 injured, which was an increase in civilians harmed by parties to the conflict and armed groups, with subnational violence driving most casualties. Civil society gun-violence census: OCND’s Truth Lab finds 755 gun-violence deaths nationwide in 2024 (657 civilians, 81 soldiers, 17 foreign nationals), largely from cattle raiding, inter/intra-communal conflicts, ambushes, and criminal attacks—offering a gun-specific lens that complements UNMISS’s broader civilian-harm metrics.

f) 2025 (to mid-year) Exceptional lethality in H1:

The refusal of President Kiir to build a professional security sector capable of protecting civilians has been the major cause. This is because it allows the communal violence to flourish as a tool of control. The current ongoing conflict is due to the refusal of President to implement the security sector reforms in accordance with the Revitalized Agreement.

President Kiir governs not as a national leader but as a tribal elder, mixing tribal, military, and political tactics. His reliance on tribal loyalty isolates communities that refuse to cooperate, leaving them targeted and marginalized. This decentralized dictatorship perpetuates fear, division and instability with destructive impact.

The Dinka should not pay attention to tribal language used by some Nuer who are fighting for their own survival against the system of President Kiir that contains the elements of tribal rule.

Nuer communities who view the government as “Dinka-led” are victims of Kiir’s tribalized rule. They are not enemies of the Dinka people. Listening to divisive rhetoric only strengthens Kiir’s destructive governance. True change requires rejecting tribal mobilization and embracing leadership that prioritizes national unity and civilian protection.

6) Conclusion

The only option is to remove President Kiir in order to save both the country and the people of South Sudan and in particular Dinka Communities. The Dinka people need to ignore other voices but concentrate on how to liberate themselves from President Kiir by cooperating with other communities who are victims of President Kiir’s rule.  Supporting SPLM-IG under President Kiir is not saving the Dinka people but it is saving the continuation of communal violence. corruption and exploitation, salary arrears and economic failure, regional and international humiliation and loss of sovereignty. Two women leaned into a front-facing phone camera at Homeland Inn along Thika Road.

The afternoon light was kind.

It looked like sisterhood.

Love.

At the centre of this slow-burning tragedy stood Joseph Kori Karue, a man whose rise was spoken of in business circles as proof that the Kenyan hustle still worked.

His life did not begin in comfort.

It began in a single room in Kayole, where he lived with Grace, his first wife, his partner in hunger and faith.

They owned little beyond each other.

In 2007, they buried their first child.

The grief was quiet and heavy, the kind that either breaks a home or binds it tighter.

For them, it bound.

A KSh 53 million tender from the Rural Electrification Authority to supply power poles.

She suspected.

Grace pleaded.

A customary marriage followed in 2012.

Peace did not.

Game drives where children pointed at lions.

Water parks at Village Market.

Go-kart tracks and laughter.

Malaysia.

Nairobi never apologises.

A glance became conversation.

Conversation became exchanged numbers.

It was powered by interest.

She observed everything.

The cars.

The trips.

Not some of it.

All of it.

Mary and Judy sat together at Homeland Inn.

Two men joined them later, witnesses would say.

Laughter.

Photos.

Normalcy.

Accusations.

Betrayal.

A struggle.

Usman Khawaja and the Quiet Question of Power, Respect, and Race in Australian Cricket

Usman Khawaja has served Australian cricket for nearly 15 years; as an opener, a top-order batsman, and one of the most technically sound players of his generation. Yet, as his career approaches its twilight, the manner in which he has been treated raises uncomfortable questions about respect, authority, and systemic bias within Cricket Australia (CA).

Khawaja is an established opener. That is his role, his craft, and his contribution to the team over more than a decade. Asking a senior, retiring player; who has carried the batting order countless times- to bat down the lower middle order is not a tactical adjustment; it is a symbolic demotion. On what may well be his last day in Test cricket, basic respect demanded he be allowed to open, where he belongs.

Any cricket enthusiast watching that innings could see it clearly:
his body language was saying something was wrong. This was not a player being eased out gracefully; it was a player being pushed aside.

RACISM IN AUSTRALIA IS NOT ALWAYS LOUD - IT IS SYSTEMIC

As stated in an earlier article on Usman Khawaja, racism in Australia is rarely overt. It is not shouted. It is systemic, subtle, and deeply embedded in power structures; especially those that cannot be challenged without consequences.

Khawaja himself has openly stated that he feels he is treated as non-white within the Australian dressing room culture. When a player of his stature makes such a claim, it should trigger reflection- not defensiveness.

This is where authority becomes the problem.

 Cricket Australia and the Culture of Control

The word authority immediately reminds many Australians of 2018, when Cameron Bancroft was caught ball-tampering, with Steve Smith and David Warner implicated. During subsequent interviews, it became clear that pressure existed from above i.e. pressure to win at any cost. Someone within the system, within Cricket Australia’s authority structure, created an environment where unethical decisions felt justified.

That scandal was not an accident. It was a symptom.

Cricket Australia operates not merely as an administrator, but as an authoritative system; one where decisions flow top-down, dissent is discouraged, and narratives are tightly controlled. In such a system, players who do not “fit” the traditional mould - or who speak openly - are quietly marginalised and Usman Khwaja is one just instance.

This is not leadership, this is authoritarianism.

Australian Cricket Belongs to the People.

Australians are deeply passionate about cricket. We pride ourselves on fair play, equality, and giving respect where it is earned. When decisions appear political rather than cricketing, when senior players are sidelined without transparent justification, and when voices like Khawaja’s are dismissed, the game itself suffers.

This is not about one innings position, It is about dignity. The fans are watching, And so is history.

Support for Salva Kiir among the Dinka—South Sudan's largest ethnic group—is not monolithic, but it is deeply entrenched. It is driven by a combination of historical legitimacy, ethnic insecurity, and a vast system of political and economic patronage.
​Here is a breakdown of why the Dinka community largely supports Salva Kiir:
​1. Ethnic Solidarity and "Existential" Security
​The most powerful driver of support is the fear of ethnic rivalry, specifically with the Nuer (the second-largest ethnic group), led historically by Riek Machar.
​The "Us vs. Them" Narrative: The civil war (which began in 2013) was quickly framed as an ethnic conflict. Many Dinka view Kiir not just as a president, but as a protector against perceived existential threats from Nuer militias or other groups.  
​The "One of Our Own" Factor: In a country where political identity is almost entirely synonymous with ethnic identity, Kiir represents Dinka dominance. Losing him is often equated with the Dinka losing their grip on the state and its resources.
​2. Historical Legitimacy (The SPLM Legacy)
​Salva Kiir commands respect as a "liberator."
​Founding Father: Kiir is one of the founding members of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM). After the death of John Garang (the father of the nation) in 2005, Kiir became the natural successor.  
​Continuity: For many Dinka, supporting Kiir is a way of honoring the legacy of the independence struggle. He is seen as the custodian of the freedom they fought for against the north (Sudan).
​3. The "Jieng Council of Elders" (Institutional Influence)
​Kiir’s support is structurally maintained by the Jieng Council of Elders (JCE).
​This is a powerful, self-appointed group of influential Dinka politicians and traditional leaders. They surround the President and shape government policy to favor Dinka interests ("Jieng" is the native term for Dinka).

Crabby Shrimp-Stuffed Garlic Bread Bombs 

Your next quick party hit is right here—perfect crowd-pleaser!

Ingredients :

1 French baguette, cut into thick slices

1 lb shrimp, peeled, deveined, and cooked

1/2 cup lump crab meat (optional but highly recommended!)

2 tbsp olive oil

3 tbsp unsalted butter, melted

4 cloves garlic, minced

1 1/2 cups shredded mozzarella cheese

1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese

2 tbsp chopped parsley

Salt and pepper, to taste

Pinch of red pepper flakes (optional, for kick)

🍽️ How to Make It :

1️⃣ Prep the Bread Base:

Slice your baguette into thick rounds—perfect for loading! Lightly toast each piece in a hot skillet with a drizzle of olive oil for that crispy golden crunch.

2️⃣ Sauté the Garlic Shrimp:

In a skillet, combine melted butter and garlic. Add the shrimp, a pinch of salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Cook until shrimp are tender and juicy, a real easy weeknight win.

3️⃣ Mix the Cheesy Seafood Blend:

In a bowl, combine the cooked shrimp, crab meat, mozzarella, Parmesan, and parsley. This cheesy seafood bomb mix is what makes these bites totally next-level delicious.

4️⃣ Stuff & Stack It Up:

Pile the seafood-cheese mixture generously on each toast slice. The cheesy garlic shrimp magic starts now—this is your ultimate appetizer moment!

5️⃣ Bake Until Melty Perfection:

Place loaded bread slices on a baking sheet and broil for 3–5 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and slightly golden. Finish with a sprinkle of parsley for that gourmet appetizer vibe.

Calories: ~330 per serving | Protein: ~22g per serving

Who was Ngundeng Bong?

Ngundeng belonged to the Nuer people. His father (Bong Chan) was from the Bul-Nuer, while his mother (Nyayiel Malual) came from the Lou-Nuer. 

According to Nuer oral tradition, his birth was considered miraculous (his mother was believed to be barren for a long time), and because of the unusual circumstances, he was named “Ngundeng” meaning “God-given” or “Gift of Deng.” 

From around the 1850s–1860s, he began to prophesy and act as a spiritual leader. Many among the Nuer came to believe he was possessed by the divinity of Deng (the sky-god of Nuer religion), and that he served as Deng’s earthly representative. 

-His Role and Prophecies

Ngundeng built a spiritual and political centre at a place called Wec Deng in present-day Jonglei State. There he gathered followers, gave prophecies through songs and trance-induced pronouncements, and ruled (in spiritual / moral terms) over many Nuer. 

He preached against internal Nuer feuds, cattle-raids, and inter-communal violence; he emphasized peace among Nilotic peoples and co-existence. 

His prophecies reportedly included predictions about major upheavals: division of Sudan, civil war, and future suffering for his people — warnings and promises delivered decades before modern conflicts. . 
-The Monument: Ngundeng Pyramid & What It
 Symbolized

Under Ngundeng’s guidance, between the 1870s and early 1880s, his followers built a large cone-shaped earth mound/shrine at Wec Deng. This mound — called the “Ngundeng Pyramid” — was about 300 feet in circumference and 50–60 feet high. 
It was surrounded by elephant tusks and served as a sacred and political centre. 

The pyramid was a symbol of spiritual authority, Nuer unity, and resistance against outside domination (colonial intrusion).

ايرادات فيلم Dhurandhar اجمالى 831.40 كرور روبية وما زال العدد في ازدياد من فيلم ضخم إلى فيلم يحطم الأرقام القياسية، يتجاوز فيلم Dhurandhar فيلمي Pushpa 2 - The Rule  و Jawan ليصبح الفيلم الأعلى إيرادًا في تاريخ السينما الهندية

أعاد فيلم Dhurandhar كتابة قواعد شباك التذاكر الهندي رسميًا. فمع إيرادات مذهلة بلغت 831.40 كرور روبية، تصدّر الفيلم قائمة الأفلام الأعلى إيرادًا على الإطلاق، مُطيحًا ببعضٍ من أضخم أفلام العصر الحديث، ومُرسّخًا مكانته في تاريخ السينما.
بذلك، تفوّق فيلم Dhurandhar على فيلم Pushpa 2 - The Rule  الذي بلغت إيراداته 830.10 كرور روبية، مما جعل المنافسة على الصدارة من أشدّ المنافسات وأكثرها شراسة في الآونة الأخيرة. ويؤكد هذا الفارق الضئيل على مدى استثنائية نجاح Dhurandhar في دور العرض، والذي استمر بفضل التوصيات الشفهية الرائعة والإقبال الجماهيري الكبير حتى بعد الأسابيع الأولى من عرضه.

ويبدو إنجاز الفيلم Dhurandhar أكثر عظمةً عند مقارنته بالأفلام الضخمة التي تفوّق عليها. ففيلم Jawan  لشاروخان، الذي أعاد تعريف مفهوم الجاذبية الجماهيرية والحماس الجماهيري، يحقق حاليًا إيرادات بلغت 643.87 كرور روبية، بينما يليه فيلم Stree 2 بإيرادات بلغت 627.02 كرور روبية، مما يثبت أن الأفلام الترفيهية ذات المحتوى الهادف قادرة على منافسة الأفلام الضخمة بقوة. كما حقق فيلم Chhaava  نجاحًا تاريخيًا، متجاوزًا إيرادات بلغت 830.10 كرور روبية. بلغت إيرادات فيلم Dhurandhar اجمالى 600.10 كرور روبية، مما يؤكد مجددًا كيف كان عام 2025 عامًا ذا زخم غير مسبوق في شباك التذاكر.

وتليها في القائمة أفلامٌ كانت تُعتبر في السابق بعيدة المنال. فقد حصد فيلم Animal اجمالى 556.36 كرور روبية، بينما اختتم فيلم Pathaan عرضه التاريخي بإيرادات بلغت 543.05 كرور روبية، وقد لعب كلا الفيلمين دورًا محوريًا في إعادة تشكيل المشهد السينمائي بعد الجائحة. أما فيلم Gadar 2 من بطولة سوني ديول، والذي استمد قوته من الحنين إلى الماضي وجاذبيته الجماهيرية، فقد جمع 525.45 كرور روبية، مما يعزز جاذبية سلاسل الأفلام العريقة.

وما يجعل إنجاز Dhurandhar أكثر تميزًا هو أنه تجاوز ظواهر عالمية بارزة مثل فيلم Baahubali 2 - The Conclusion الذي حقق 510.99 كرور روبية، وفيلم KGF - Chapter 2 الذي كان قد رفع سقف التوقعات سابقًا بإيرادات بلغت 434.70 كرور روبية. لطالما اعتُبرت هذه الأفلام معايير للنجاح على مستوى الهند، مما يجعل صعود دوراندهار إلى القمة أكثر أهمية.

Good riddance Usman Khawaja — what a disgrace. 

Shooting a parting shot as you retire from the sport and country that gave you everything. 

Invoking “racial stereotypes” as a grievance while being one of the most privileged people to ever wear an Australian jersey is completely detached from reality.

 If You Don’t Love Australia, Don’t Wear the Jersey

This might shock the commentariat, but wearing the Australian jersey is not a personal branding exercise.

It’s a privilege.

When you play for Australia, you are not representing a religion, a cause, or a grievance. 

You are representing a nation built on shared civic values that gave you opportunity, safety, wealth, and global recognition.

Australia didn’t owe you a career.
Australia didn’t owe you fame.
Australia didn’t owe you the baggy green.

It gave it anyway.

That comes with expectations.

No one is asking you to abandon your faith. 

Australians of every religion live freely here. That freedom is the point. 

But when you step onto the field for the national team, you step into something bigger than yourself.

Unity matters.
Respect matters.
Standing with the country that lifted you matters.

Here’s the question no one in the media dares ask.

When will a white Christian boy play international cricket for Pakistan?

When will Pakistan celebrate “diversity” by elevating someone who openly challenges its dominant religious norms?

When will a player criticise Pakistan’s treatment of minorities and still be protected, praised, and platformed?

Everyone knows the answer.

They wouldn’t.
They couldn’t.
They’d be finished.

Australia, by contrast, bends over backwards to accommodate difference. That generosity is a strength. 

But it becomes weakness when it’s exploited.

National teams are not protest platforms.
They are symbols of unity.

If representing Australia feels like a burden.
If standing with Australians feels optional.
If our national symbols are treated as inconveniences.

Then step aside.

Let someone else wear the jersey.

Because millions of Australians who grew up bowling bowls at tge wheelie bins for stumps would give anything for the chance you were handed.

And they wouldn’t treat it with contempt.

My Parents Called Me The 'Spare Twin, They Said, "Your Sister Is The One." Years Later, She Begged For My Inheritance, And I Had Proof To Destroy Her.
The day my own mother whispered, “We kept the better child,” something inside me went silent… and never came back.

I was born in America, a twin—but not an equal one. Chloe was the “angel.” Blonde hair, green eyes, dimples… the kind of kid strangers complimented like she was a miracle. Me? I was the extra. The spare twin. The one told to stand in the back of family photos so the lighting wouldn’t “ruin the picture.” The one who got socks while she got iPads. The one who carried bags, washed dishes, took the blame—then got sent away at 14 like unwanted luggage.

And they didn’t even pretend it was temporary.
My mom’s last words weren’t “we’ll miss you.” They were: “Don’t cause them as much trouble as you caused us.”

Uncle James and Aunt Laura saved me. They gave me a room, food, and something I’d never had—a place where I wasn’t competing for permission to exist. I grew up. I healed. I learned one brutal truth: if someone treats you like disposable, they’ll only come back when they need you.

Years later, Chloe calls out of nowhere—sweet voice, fake concern… then the punchline: “You should split your inheritance. We’re twins.”
And that’s when I realized… she didn’t just want money.

She wanted to erase what they did to me and rewrite the story like I owed her.
But I had receipts. Proof. Screenshots. Spreadsheets. Even the things they thought they’d buried forever.

And when Chloe tried to shame me publicly for refusing… I didn’t defend myself.
I didn’t argue.
I simply uploaded the truth where they couldn’t delete it.

The family chat went quiet. Then it exploded.
Because once the mask slips, it never goes back on the same way again.

But the most satisfying part? That came later… in a place she never expected to see me… when I saw her wearing something blue, holding a mop, and trying not to be recognized.

What did I post that made Chloe’s GoFundMe vanish overnight?
What did my parents do when the whole family finally saw the “spare twin” truth?
And why did Chloe’s last message prove she still hadn’t learned a single thing…?

At my sister Emily’s wedding, I sat alone at the far-right table, the one closest to the exit. It wasn’t by accident. It never was. I had learned long ago where I belonged in my family’s hierarchy.

The venue was a renovated barn in upstate New York, all white roses and fairy lights. Emily looked radiant in her lace gown, laughing easily, soaking up the attention she believed she deserved. I adjusted my simple navy dress and glanced at my son, Noah, who was quietly coloring beside me, unaware of how little he was wanted in this room.

When the speeches began, I felt a familiar tightening in my chest.

Emily took the microphone, smiling sweetly. “I just want to thank everyone for coming,” she said. Then her eyes flicked toward me. “Especially my big sister, Rachel.”

Some guests turned to look at me. I forced a polite smile.

“You know,” Emily continued, laughing, “Rachel’s been such an inspiration. She showed me exactly what not to do with my life.” The room chuckled. “She’s a single mom, unwanted by anyone. Laughter erupted.

My hands trembled. I looked down at Noah. He looked up at me, confused.

Then my mother, Linda, leaned into her microphone from her seat. “Oh please,” she laughed loudly. “She’s a used product, but still functional! And she even comes with a defective son! Ha!”

A chair scraped loudly across the floor.

Defending the Dignity of Madiing Aweil: A Community of Sacrifice, Leadership, and National Service

      By: Garang Nyang Mel Anguei
If the suffering of Madiing Aweil during the liberation period represents the sacrifice for our country's liberty and freedom, despite being labeled a "cheap community," then the person using such derogatory language towards this community must be held accountable by God until the end of his life, for no individual is greater than the community.

Madiing Aweil has leaders who have brought transformation and development in various roles, yet we are still labeled as a "cheap community" by an unknown individual. We should not be subjected to abuse, as we have the following leaders who contribute tirelessly to the development of South Sudan:

1. Gen. Paul Malong Awan, former Chief of Staff, is a respected general and veteran leader whose contributions continue to benefit the people of South Sudan. He played a vital role in supporting leadership and its people in 2013 and 2016 by recruiting the Mathiang Anyor army. As Chief of Staff in 2014, he established the Bilpham military headquarters and the Giade military fence. He also built several military colleges and opened military training facilities, further improving military administration by providing essential support to soldiers.

2. Dr. Benjamin Bol Mel, former Vice President, is a rising politician and young entrepreneur dedicated to serving his community through infrastructure development. He oversaw the completion of the Bor road and renovations of roads in Bhar El-Ghazal and internal roads in Juba. He is recognized for providing important services to the country and is proud to come from Aweil.

3. Dr. Dhieu Mathok Diing Wol, former Minister of Investment, is a respected politician who significantly improved access to electricity in Juba and contributed valuable research to the country.

4. Honourable Ateny Wek Ateny, Minister of Information, Communication, Technology, and Postal Services, is a popular leader and motivator. He inspired young people across the country, reduced the cost of digital services, and promoted digital literacy, making a great impact on those affected by economic challenges.

5. Mr. Luol Aldo Ajou, president of the South Sudan Basketball Federation, is the first South Sudanese athlete to raise the nation’s profile on the world stage, using his resources for the benefit of South Sudan.

6. Dr. Albino Bol Dhieu, former Minister of Youth and Sports, made significant contributions to sports, enhancing youth development across the country, completing the Juba National Stadium, and providing financial support for the national team, the Bright Stars.

7. General Satino Deng Wol, a respected veteran leader, served loyally in the South Sudan People's Defense Forces and was crucial in protecting leadership and its people during critical times in 2013 and 2016.

8. General Deng Wal Achien, the Executive Director in the Office of the President, managed the presidential office with integrity, effectively addressing previous issues.

9. Ayii Duang Ayii is a pioneering businessman who built hotels and hospitals across South Sudan, providing accommodation and care for thousands of government officials over the years.

10. Honourable Garang Majak Bol, former Undersecretary in the Ministry of Finance and Planning, played a key role in building the ministry's main structure and transforming the economy in several ways.

Do we truly deserve such negative remarks when our leaders have significantly contributed to the development of our country? We fought for our nation, and our leaders fought for our freedom, often sacrificing their lives, only to be labeled as a "cheap community." May God address this injustice.

Good riddance Usman Khawaja — what a disgrace. 

Shooting a parting shot as you retire from the sport and country that gave you everything. 

Invoking “racial stereotypes” as a grievance while being one of the most privileged people to ever wear an Australian jersey is completely detached from reality.

 If You Don’t Love Australia, Don’t Wear the Jersey

This might shock the commentariat, but wearing the Australian jersey is not a personal branding exercise.

It’s a privilege.

When you play for Australia, you are not representing a religion, a cause, or a grievance. 

You are representing a nation built on shared civic values that gave you opportunity, safety, wealth, and global recognition.

Australia didn’t owe you a career.
Australia didn’t owe you fame.
Australia didn’t owe you the baggy green.

It gave it anyway.

That comes with expectations.

No one is asking you to abandon your faith. 

Australians of every religion live freely here. That freedom is the point. 

But when you step onto the field for the national team, you step into something bigger than yourself.

Unity matters.
Respect matters.
Standing with the country that lifted you matters.

Here’s the question no one in the media dares ask.

When will a white Christian boy play international cricket for Pakistan?

When will Pakistan celebrate “diversity” by elevating someone who openly challenges its dominant religious norms?

When will a player criticise Pakistan’s treatment of minorities and still be protected, praised, and platformed?

Everyone knows the answer.

They wouldn’t.
They couldn’t.
They’d be finished.

Australia, by contrast, bends over backwards to accommodate difference. That generosity is a strength. 

But it becomes weakness when it’s exploited.

National teams are not protest platforms.
They are symbols of unity.

If representing Australia feels like a burden.
If standing with Australians feels optional.
If our national symbols are treated as inconveniences.

Then step aside.

Let someone else wear the jersey.

Because millions of Australians who grew up bowling bowls at tge wheelie bins for stumps would give anything for the chance you were handed.

And they wouldn’t treat it with contempt.

The Ilemi Triangle: Historical Origins, Colonial Boundaries, and the Legacy of Anuak King Ilemi Akwon.

Abstract

The Ilemi Triangle is a roughly triangular tract of land bounded by modern South Sudan, Kenya, and Ethiopia, whose ownership remains disputed due to a legacy of colonial boundary ambiguities. Named after the Anuak chief Ilemi Akwon, the territory illustrates the interaction of indigenous authority with imperial mapping, pastoral use, and post-colonial state claims. This paper reconstructs the history of the Ilemi Triangle from late 19th-century local dynamics through colonial demarcations to modern contestations, emphasizing Ilemi Akwon’s role and the region’s changing geopolitical status.

1. Introduction

The Ilemi Triangle occupies approximately 8,000–14,000 square kilometers of semi-arid rangeland in East Africa. It lies northwest of Lake Turkana, with its tri-junction created by colonial-era borders between Sudan (now South Sudan), Kenya, and Ethiopia. While largely uninhabited by large sedentary populations, it serves as vital seasonal grazing land for pastoralist groups and remains a point of long-standing boundary dispute shaped by colonial surveys and international treaties. 

2. Ethnic and Local Context before Colonial Intervention

Before European incursions, the broader region functioned as a fluid pastoralist frontier with no fixed state borders, used seasonally by groups such as the Toposa (Jiye), Dassanech, Nyangatom, Turkana, and Anuak. Pastoral mobility, cattle raids, and informal arrangements governed access to scarce water and grazing. This ecological and social fluidity meant that early European powers encountered complex patterns of land use that did not align with fixed boundary concepts. 

3. The Anuak and Chief Ilemi Akwon: Local Authority in the Borderlands

3.1. The Anuak People

The Anuak (Anyuak, Anywaa) are a Nilotic ethnic group whose traditional homeland spans the floodplains of the Akobo, Baro, and Pibor rivers on what is now the Ethiopia–South Sudan border region. They were organized in chiefdoms and clan networks, with little centralized authority but recognized local leaders. 

3.2. Ilemi Akwon: Biography and Local Significance

The name “Ilemi” commemorates a prominent Anuak chief, Ilemi Akwon (also recorded as Ulimi Akwon, Ilembi, Ilimi, Chamchar), whose village lay on the Sudanese bank of the Akobo River near its junction with the Ajibur. His authority stemmed from ancestral lineage and regional influence among pastoralist and riverine communities. His mother was a Murle woman from the Boma Plateau, illustrating inter-ethnic kinship ties in frontier contexts; his father was of the Anuak royal house. 

In 1934, Ilemi joined Murle kin in a raid against the Kichepo, a group displaced to the Boma Plateau during drought. Despite warnings from colonial officials not to intercede, Ilemi was killed in January 1936 by the Kichepo while visiting his maternal relatives. Later that year, Anuak and Murle forces avenged his death. These events highlight the local military and social significance of Ilemi himself. 

3.3. Naming of the Territory

Colonial administrators, operating with limited geographic knowledge and a practice of naming regions after prominent local figures or places, began referring to the pastoral zone around Ilemi Akwon’s village as the Ilemi Triangle. This naming preserved his legacy even as imperial mapping delineated the contested area. 

4. Colonial Boundary Making (1900–1950s)

4.1. Early Imperial Treaties and Surveys

The Maud Line — surveyed in 1902–1903 by British Royal Engineer Philip Maud — became a key reference for borders between Sudan and British East Africa and was later incorporated into treaties such as the 1907 Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement. This placed the Ilemi region within Sudanese territorial claims, though with vague delineation on the Kenya–Sudan connection. 

Subsequent agreements, such as the 1914 Uganda-Sudan Boundary Commission, extended Sudanese access to Lake Turkana, revealing early diplomatic complexity and layered claims. 

4.2. Red, Blue, and Patrol Lines

From the 1920s to 1950s, colonial authorities drew administrative “lines” — including the Red Line (1931) and Blue Line (1944) — to manage pastoral movements, largely reflecting grazing boundaries rather than formal state borders. In 1950, the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan established its own patrol line further northwest, though treaties clarified that it did not alter sovereignty. 

4.3. Kenyan Administration

By the 1930s, Sudan often ceded administrative control in practice to British Kenya to protect Turkana pastoralists against raids and conduct governance. Kenya maintained posts and security presence into the post-World War II era. 

5. Post-Colonial Landscape and Modern Contestations

5.1. Independence and Diverging Claims

After Sudan’s independence (1956), Sudan’s capacity to administer the region weakened due to internal conflict. Meanwhile, Kenya continued its de facto administration. When South Sudan gained independence in 2011, it inherited Sudan’s claim to the triangle. 

5.2. Kenya’s Cartographic Shift

In 1967 and 1986, Kenya began publishing official maps asserting the Ilemi Triangle as part of Kenyan territory, replacing earlier provisional markers with continuous boundary lines, reflecting a shift toward claiming sovereignty. 

5.3. Ethiopia’s Position

Ethiopia has historically not pressed formal claims to Ilemi, and bilateral treaties with Kenya reinforced mutual boundaries that place the triangle outside Ethiopian territory. 

6. The Triangle in International Law and Local Use

The unresolved colonial demarcations — multiple interpretative boundary lines and contested treaties — have left the Ilemi Triangle’s legal status ambiguous. Scholarly analyses note this colonial legacy as central to the persistent dispute between Kenya and South Sudan, and the de facto administration by Kenya since pre-independence times. 

Despite these geopolitical wrangles, the triangle remains vital pastoral land, seasonally shared by Turkana, Toposa, Nyangatom, and Dassanech pastoralists, whose movements have long pre-dated colonial boundaries. 

7. Conclusion

The Ilemi Triangle exemplifies how colonial boundary practices layered European geopolitical aims atop indigenous social landscapes, producing enduring disputes. Its name memorializes Beaufort-aged authority — the Anuak chief Ilemi Akwon — whose influence at the local frontier became entwined with imperial cartography. Though sparsely inhabited, the territory remains contested, shaped by historic treaties, administrative pragmatism, and persistent claims from both Kenya and South Sudan. Contemporary negotiations continue to grapple with colonial legacies in determining sovereignty, jurisdiction, and rights over this frontier zone.

THEY MADE ME SIT ON THE FLOOR LIKE A DOG! Then the Chairman WALKED IN and bowed to ME.

The linoleum was freezing against my tailbone. Every time someone walked past, their shoes clicked inches from my head. "Get comfortable, mutt," Janet had sneered, adjusting her power suit. "Maybe you'll learn something by osmosis."

I wanted to disappear. I'd arrived early, prepped the conference room, even brewed a fresh pot of the good stuff – Kona blend, Janet's favorite. But none of it mattered. I was still the temp, the outsider, the one they could kick around without consequence. All because of the company merger. After the acquisition, the old guard at Sterling Dynamics made it clear they saw us from the smaller firm as nothing more than unwanted baggage.

I tried to focus on the presentation deck flickering on the screen, but Janet's words kept echoing in my head. Mutt. Osmosis. Like I wasn't even worth a real chair. Like my ideas, my experience, meant nothing. It wasn't just the humiliation, but the sheer, calculated cruelty of it all. I glanced around the room. Everyone avoided my gaze, pretending not to notice the woman sitting on the floor. Cowards.

My phone vibrated in my pocket. I ignored it. Probably another email from my landlord, reminding me rent was due. Or a message from Mom, asking if I'd heard back about any full-time positions. The irony wasn't lost on me: here I was, helping run a crucial strategy meeting for a multi-million dollar company, while simultaneously teetering on the edge of homelessness. I clenched my fists, digging my nails into my palms. I wouldn't cry. I wouldn't give them the satisfaction.

The door swung open, and a hush fell over the room. "Good morning, everyone," a voice boomed. It was Mr. Thompson, the CEO. Janet practically vibrated with excitement. This was her moment, her chance to shine in front of the boss. I sank lower, trying to become invisible. But then, something completely unexpected happened.

Mr. Thompson stopped just inside the doorway, his eyes scanning the room. He paused when he saw me, a flicker of… something… crossing his face. Disgust? Pity? I couldn't tell. And then, he did something that made my jaw drop. He bowed. A deep, respectful bow, right in my direction. The room erupted in a cacophony of whispers. Janet's face turned a shade of purple I didn't think was humanly possible. "Ms. Ramirez," Mr. Thompson said, his voice cutting through the noise like a laser. "Please, forgive our… oversight. There seems to be a distinct lack of hospitality in this room."

He gestured to one of the senior executives, a portly man named Mr. Peterson, who immediately jumped to his feet. "Peterson, give Ms. Ramirez your chair." Peterson sputtered, his face turning redder than Janet's. But he didn't argue. He scrambled to find another seat, while I hesitantly stood up, brushing off the wrinkles from my skirt. All eyes were on me. I could feel the heat of their stares, the mixture of confusion, resentment, and… fear? It was intoxicating.

"Thank you, Mr. Thompson," I said, trying to keep my voice steady. "But please, call me Sofia."

He smiled, a genuine, warm smile that reached his eyes. "Of course, Sofia. Now, shall we begin?"

As I settled into Mr. Peterson's ridiculously oversized chair, I couldn't help but feel a surge of vindication. But it was a hollow victory. I knew this was just the beginning. The old guard at Sterling Dynamics wouldn't let this go easily. They'd see me as a threat, an upstart who dared to challenge their authority. And they'd be right. Because after today, things were going to change.

I took a deep breath and opened my laptop. Time to show them what this 'mutt' was really made of. The presentation began, but inside, my mind was already racing. I had to figure out why Mr. Thompson had defended me so publicly. Was it genuine respect? Or was there something else at play? A power struggle, perhaps? Whatever the reason, I knew I had to be careful. Because in the corporate jungle, even a single act of kindness could be a trap.

The meeting droned on, filled with jargon and PowerPoint slides. But I couldn't shake the feeling that I was being watched. Every time I looked up, I caught Janet staring at me, her eyes filled with a cold, calculating rage. It was unnerving, to say the least. I’d known that corporate life could be a battlefield, but until today, I’d never felt the crosshairs aimed directly at me. I found myself reflecting on my career choices and recent life events, but always the central feeling was confusion. Who was I to be treated like this by someone I worked with? 

The hours crawled by. I presented my portion of the strategy deck, outlining a bold new plan for expanding into emerging markets. My voice was clear and confident, but inside, I was a mess of nerves. When I finished, Mr. Thompson was the first to applaud. Janet remained silent, her arms crossed tightly over her chest. The tension in the room was so thick you could cut it with a knife.

Finally, the meeting adjourned. As people filed out, Mr. Thompson approached me. "Sofia, could I have a word?" he asked, his voice low.

I nodded, my heart pounding in my chest. We walked to his office, a sprawling corner suite with panoramic views of the city. He closed the door behind us and turned to face me.

"I wanted to apologize again for what happened in there," he said, gesturing back towards the conference room. "It was unacceptable."

"Thank you, Mr. Thompson," I said. "I appreciate that."

"Please, call me Richard," he insisted. "And I want you to know that I value your contributions to this company. Your insights are invaluable."

I raised an eyebrow, skeptical. "Is that why I was sitting on the floor?"

He winced. "No, of course not. That was… a misunderstanding. A terrible lapse in judgment on Janet's part."

"A misunderstanding?" I repeated, my voice rising. "It felt like a deliberate act of humiliation."

He sighed. "I know. And I assure you, it won't happen again. I'll deal with Janet personally."

I looked him in the eye, trying to gauge his sincerity. Was he being genuine? Or was he just trying to smooth things over? I couldn't tell. But I knew one thing: I wasn't going to let this go. I deserved respect, just like everyone else. And I was going to fight for it, no matter what it took.

"Richard," I said, using his first name for the first time. "I appreciate your apology. But I need more than words. I need to see real change. I need to know that Sterling Dynamics is a place where everyone is treated with dignity and respect."

He nodded, his expression serious. "I understand. And I promise you, you will see change. I'm committed to creating a culture of inclusivity and respect here. And I need your help to do it."

I stared at him, surprised. "My help?"

"Yes," he said. "I want you to be my advisor on this issue. I want you to help me identify the problems and develop solutions. Will you do it?"

I hesitated for a moment. This was a huge opportunity. A chance to make a real difference. But it was also a huge risk. If I took on this role, I'd be making enemies. Powerful enemies. But I couldn't back down now. Not after everything that had happened. Not after the humiliation, the disrespect, the feeling of being less than human.

"Yes, Richard," I said, my voice firm. "I'll do it."

He smiled, relief washing over his face. "Thank you, Sofia. I knew I could count on you."

As I left his office, I felt a surge of determination. I was no longer just a temp, an outsider. I was an advisor, a change agent. And I was ready to fight for what was right, even if it meant taking on the entire corporate machine. As I stepped out of the glass doors, I noticed Janet at her desk, glaring in my direction. I straightened my back, held my head high, and walked past her without a word. The battle had just begun.

The rest of the day passed in a blur. I was bombarded with emails and phone calls, all related to my new role as Richard's advisor. It was overwhelming, but exhilarating. I felt like I was finally making a difference, finally using my skills and experience to create positive change. But beneath the surface, I was still wary. I knew that Janet and her allies wouldn't give up easily. They would fight back, using every dirty trick in the book. And I had to be prepared.

As I packed up my things to leave for the day, I received a text message from an unknown number. It read: "Watch your back, Sofia. You're playing with fire." I deleted the message and turned off my phone. It was time to go home, to rest, to prepare for the battles ahead. Because in the corporate jungle, survival of the fittest was the only rule that mattered. When I pulled up to my apartment complex, I noticed a black car parked across the street, its headlights off. I couldn't see who was inside, but I had a feeling I knew. I parked my car, grabbed my purse, and walked quickly towards my building, glancing over my shoulder every few steps. I unlocked the front door and slipped inside, breathing a sigh of relief. But I knew I wasn't safe yet. The corporate jungle had followed me home. And I had a feeling it was about to get a whole lot more dangerous. I turned on all the lights, double-locked the door, and peeked through the blinds. The black car was still there, its headlights still off. Waiting. Watching. I shivered, despite the warmth of the apartment. This wasn't just about a job anymore. It was about power, control, and survival. And I was caught in the middle.

As I settled in for the night, I tried to distract myself with a book, but my mind kept racing back to the events of the day. The humiliation, the apology, the new role, the threatening text message, the black car. It was all too much to process. I tossed and turned in bed, unable to sleep. Finally, I gave up and got out of bed. I poured myself a glass of water and walked over to the window. The black car was still there. Watching. Waiting. I closed the blinds and turned off the lights. I crawled back into bed, pulling the covers over my head. But I couldn't escape the feeling that I was being watched. That I was in danger. That my life was about to change forever.

I need to decide who I can trust and who are the enemies.

“Let’s see how they survive without us,” the children joked—never realizing the old man carried a fortune no one knew about.

I never imagined a quiet Tuesday could fracture my sense of humanity.

The day had been ordinary. I finished my last appointment early and left the clinic while the sun pressed down mercilessly, turning the road into a shimmering ribbon of heat. The air felt heavy, like it was holding its breath.

I was driving the old highway that connects the city to the surrounding towns when something caught my eye near an overpass.

Two figures.

They sat beneath a rusted streetlight that offered no shade at all. An elderly couple. Their belongings—tattered bags, a single battered suitcase—were scattered at their feet like the remains of a life hastily abandoned.

I slowed instinctively.

You don’t usually see elderly people sitting on the roadside in that kind of heat. Not unless something has gone terribly wrong.

I pulled over and stepped out, gravel crunching under my shoes.

Up close, the truth was written all over them.

The woman’s face was streaked with dried tears, her eyes red and swollen. The man stared at the asphalt, his shoulders slumped, his straw hat casting a shadow over a face carved by exhaustion and quiet despair.

“Good morning,” I said gently. “Are you alright? Can I help you with anything?”

The woman looked up slowly, as if lifting her head took every ounce of strength she had left. Shame and heartbreak flickered across her expression.

After a long pause, her voice broke.

“Our children brought us here,” she whispered. “They said they needed to stop for a moment… told us to wait. That they’d be right back.”

She swallowed hard.

“That was over two hours ago.”

Something inside my chest gave way.

The man finally spoke, his voice rough, hollow.

“Please don’t worry about us, miss,” he said quietly. “They’ll come back… or they won’t. We’ve been a burden for a long time now.”

The words cut deeper than any scream.

I stood there, frozen, staring at two people who had once been someone’s entire world—now left on the side of the road like unwanted luggage.

And as the wind swept dust across the pavement, one thought kept echoing in my mind:

How could anyone do this… without knowing who they were leaving behind?

​Pelarian Sang Raja dan Panglima🥷🤴
​Di Pulau Jawa, sebuah kerajaan besar sedang bergolak. Perebutan kekuasaan yang berdarah membuat sang Raja Muda Aryasatya Digdaya berada dalam posisi terjepit. Ia enggan menumpahkan darah saudaranya sendiri, namun ia juga tidak setuju dengan tirani yang dijalankan oleh Maha Raja (ayahandanya) dan para tetua kerajaan yang haus perang.

​Di samping sang Raja Muda Aryasatya Digdaya, berdirilah Panglima Mahawira Swarnabhumi, seorang ksatria perkasa asal Sumatera yang bertahun-tahun lamanya merantau ke Jawa hingga menjadi orang kepercayaan tertinggi kerajaan.
​Melihat kekacauan yang tak terbendung, Panglima Mahawira Swarnabhumi berbisik kepada sang Raja Aryasatya Digdaya:
​"Gusti, jika kita tetap di sini, pedang kita hanya akan memutus tali persaudaraan. Ikutlah hamba ke tanah seberang, ke desa tempat hamba dilahirkan. Di sana, kita bisa membangun kedamaian tanpa harus membunuh darah daging sendiri."
​Maka, di bawah rembulan yang redup, sebuah kapal besar berlayar meninggalkan pelabuhan Jawa secara diam-diam.

​Kemurkaan dan Sumpah Maha Raja👹🎤📜
​Kepergian sang Raja Muda Aryasatya Digdaya dan Panglima Mahawira Swarnabhumi  dianggap sebagai pengkhianatan terbesar. Maha Raja dan para Tetua Kerajaan murka karena mereka kehilangan panglima terkuat dan pewaris takhta di saat ancaman pemberontakan lain sedang memuncak.
​Di atas singgasana emasnya, Maha Raja menghunus keris pusaka dan menghentakkannya ke bumi. 

Ia mengucap sumpah kutukan yang menggetarkan langit:
​"Barangsiapa raja yang melarikan diri dan pengikutnya, diharamkan bagi mereka menginjakkan kaki kembali di Tanah Jawa. Jika ia atau keturunannya melanggar, maka seluruh makhluk di Pulau Jawa—baik yang terlihat maupun yang gaib—diperintahkan untuk menyesatkan mereka.
