​The Legend of Vyanasaka: "The Javanese Oath and the Three Seals of Sumatra"
​Long ago, when the oceans were still the primary path for rulers, there stood a serene village on the coast of Sumatra known as Muara Langit. This village became the silent witness to the return of a local son who brought with him the destiny of a king: Aryasatya Digdaya.

​The Flight of the King and the Commander 🥷🤴
​On the island of Java, a great kingdom was in turmoil. A bloody struggle for power had left the young King, Aryasatya Digdaya, in a cornered position. He was unwilling to shed the blood of his own kin, yet he could not abide by the tyranny of the Great King (his father) and the war-hungry elders of the court.
​Standing beside King Aryasatya Digdaya was Commander Mahiwa, a mighty warrior originally from Sumatra. He had spent many years traveling through Java until he became the kingdom’s most trusted confidant.

​Seeing the unstoppable chaos, Commander Mahawira Swarnabhumi whispered to King Aryasatya:
​"My Lord, if we remain here, our swords will only sever the ties of brotherhood. Follow me to the lands across the sea, to the village where I was born. There, we can build peace without having to kill our own flesh and blood."

​Here is the translation for Part II of the legend, capturing the intensity of the King's wrath and the mystical atmosphere of Sumatra.
​The Wrath and the Sovereign's Oath 👹🎤📜
​The departure of young King Aryasatya Digdaya and Commander Mahawira Swarnabhumi was condemned as the ultimate betrayal. The Great King and the Court Elders were consumed by rage; they had lost their strongest commander and the rightful heir to the throne at the very moment a rebellion was reaching its peak.
​Upon his golden throne, the Great King unsheathed a sacred keris and struck it against the earth. He uttered a cursed oath that shook the very heavens:
​"Whosoever be the fleeing King and his followers, they are forbidden from ever setting foot on Javanese soil again. Should he or his descendants break this decree, then every creature on the Island of Java—both the seen and the unseen—is commanded to lead them astray. They shall be blinded of direction, stripped of memory, and trapped in an eternal mist until they can never find their way home again!"
​Thunder rolled across the sky as lightning struck the keris; the Sovereign’s oath had been bound to the earth.
​As their ship drifted away from the Javanese coastline, Commander Mahawira Swarnabhumi spoke to King Aryasatya: "My Lord, let the Great King's oath remain behind with the dust of that land. In Swarnabhumi, I shall guard your blood from the curse that pursues us." Yet, in the distance, the elders continued to scream toward the ocean, calling out Aryasatya’s name so that the nature of Java would never again recognize his footsteps.
​Life in the Village of Muara Langit 🛖
​After days of slicing through the ocean waves, the great ship finally moored on the coast of Sumatra. King Aryasatya and his small entourage followed the steady footsteps of Commander Mahawira through the dense jungle toward Muara Langit Village.
​However, right before the giant wooden gates that marked the village entrance, the air grew deathly silent. The wind ceased to rustle. From behind the dark thickets emerged a pack of weretigers (siluman harimau) with glowing red eyes and fangs dripping with the saliva of hunger. They growled, surrounding the exhausted King and his followers.
​The Presence of the Weretiger Queen 🐅
​As the largest beast prepared to pounce on Mahawira, a shadow darted as fast as lightning. A hunched old woman with disheveled white hair appeared out of nowhere. She was barefoot, her skin wrinkled yet as tough as tree bark, wearing clothes woven from coarse palm fiber. In her hand, she clutched a long, ancient wooden staff.
​Thwack! Thwack! Thwack!
​With movements impossible for a human of her age, the old woman struck the heads of the tigers one by one. Miraculously, the ferocious beasts froze instantly, stiff and motionless as stone.
​The Decree of the Forest Queen 🐅👸
​The hunched woman stood tall before Commander Mahawira, her back to the royal party. Her voice was raspy yet thunderous, echoing through every corner of the jungle:
​"Listen, O dwellers of the wild! Not a single spirit in this forest shall harm Commander Mahawira Swarnabhumi, King Aryasatya Digdaya, their followers, or any of their descendants!"
​She turned slightly, her sharp eyes piercing the frozen spirits.
​"Remember your history! Long ago, it was Mahawira’s ancestors who risked their lives to save your kind from the slaughter of the power-hungry Black Shamans. Without them, the spirit race would have been extinct, sacrificed as offerings."
​She struck her staff against the ground. She was indeed the Queen of the Forest Spirits. She gave a stern warning: anyone who dared touch the Commander’s lineage or his guests would face a terrifying punishment.
​At her command, the magic locking the tigers was released. Without a second's delay, the beasts scrambled into the darkness, trembling in fear.

​A New Beginning 🎉🎊
​The old woman turned to Mahawira and Aryasatya with an unreadable gaze before vanishing into the mist as quickly as she had arrived. But before she fully disappeared, she left a legacy—a talismanic promise for their descendants for thousands of years.

​The Will of the Weretiger Queen 👸👑
​The Queen raised her staff and spoke with a voice vibrating with authority:
​"O Mahawira, if one day you or your kin are lost in the deep wild, or if you are cornered by danger and need aid, do this one thing: Light a fire until the smoke rises high into the heavens, and call out loudly: 'Grandmother, Hunched Grandmother! I am Mahawira, I need your help!'"

​She smiled thinly, revealing a face full of mystery.
​"In that instant, I and the entire army of forest spirits will emerge from the darkness to aid you. This forest is your home, and I am your guardian."
​With those words, she was swallowed by the fog, leaving only the scent of damp earth and aged wood.
​The gates of Muara Langit opened. Mahawira was greeted with tears of joy by the villagers, and the King’s party was welcomed by the village elder, Datu Dharmasraya—a wise leader respected across the reaches of Sumatra.

​The young King shed his robes of grandeur and chose a humble life. They settled there, blending with the locals, teaching advanced farming and defense strategies. Muara Langit flourished into a prosperous realm—the King was an exile, yet he now possessed the most powerful protector in Sumatra.

​The Union of Two Bloodlines 🤴👸
​Datu Dharmasraya had a youngest daughter, the sister of Commander Mahawira. Her beauty was the talk of the land, and her temperament was as soft as silk yet as firm as a coral reef. Her name was Dinda Citrakirana Swarnamala.
​King Aryasatya found peace in her presence. With the blessing of Datu Dharmasraya and the spirits of the land, the two were wed. This marriage was more than a union of two people; it was the merging of Javanese royal blood with the mystical power and local wisdom of Sumatra.

​Notes: Myth and Reality in the Future 📋👣
​Thousands of years have passed. Kingdoms may have fallen, but the Queen’s promise lives on in Muara Langit. To this day, if a villager goes missing while gathering wood or wanders too deep into the fierce Sumatran wilderness, the people do not panic. They seek out the village elder—a direct descendant of Mahawira.

​The descendant stands at the edge of the forest, lights a small fire, and calls out:
"Grandmother, Hunched Grandmother! I am a descendant of Mahawira, I need your help!"
​A miracle always follows. A thick mist guides the lost soul back. Many who were lost tell of a mysterious barefoot woman who took their hand, leading them through thorny thickets without a single scratch until they reached the forest's edge.

​However, beneath this protection, the shadow of the Javanese Sovereign's Oath still haunts them. The Forest Queen can guard them in Sumatra, but her power ends where the ocean begins. If they dare cross back to the "Cursed Land," the old curse waits.

لیکچر: قوم پرستی (Nationalism) — شناخت اور وفاداری کا جذبہ

1. تعریف (Definition)
• 
بنیادی تصور: قوم پرستی ایک ایسا نظریہ ہے جو اس بات پر زور دیتا ہے کہ ایک جیسے کلچر، تاریخ، زبان یا جغرافیے سے تعلق رکھنے والے لوگوں کا گروہ ایک "قوم" ہے اور اس قوم کو اپنی آزاد ریاست بنانے اور اسے چلانے کا مکمل حق حاصل ہے۔
• وفاداری: اس نظام میں انسان کی اولین وفاداری کسی بادشاہ یا قبیلے کے بجائے اپنی "قوم" اور "وطن" سے ہوتی ہے۔

2. وجہ تسمیہ (Etymology)
• 
لفظی معنی: لفظ "نشنلزم" انگریزی لفظ 'Nation' سے نکلا ہے، جو لاطینی لفظ 'Natio' سے ماخوذ ہے، جس کا مطلب ہے "پیدائش" یا "نسل"۔
• مفہوم: شروع میں اس سے مراد ایک ہی نسل کے لوگ تھے، لیکن وقت کے ساتھ اس کا مطلب ایک ایسی کمیونٹی بن گیا جو ایک سیاسی اکائی (ریاست) کے طور پر متحد ہو۔

3. تاریخ (History)

• نشو و نما: قوم پرستی کا جدید تصور 18ویں صدی کے آخر میں فرانسیسی انقلاب (1789) کے دوران ابھرا، جب لوگوں نے بادشاہ کے بجائے "فرانسیسی قوم" کے نام پر متحد ہونا شروع کیا۔
• 19ویں صدی: یہ وہ دور تھا جب یورپ میں جرمنی اور اٹلی جیسے ممالک قوم پرستی کی بنیاد پر متحد ہوئے، جبکہ سلطنتِ عثمانیہ جیسی بڑی ریاستیں قوم پرستی کی وجہ سے تقسیم ہوئیں۔
• تحریکِ آزادی: برصغیر پاک و ہند سمیت دنیا بھر میں نوآبادیاتی نظام (Colonialism) کے خلاف چلنے والی تحریکیں (جیسے تحریکِ پاکستان) قوم پرستی ہی کی مرہونِ منت تھیں۔

4. کور پوائنٹس (Core Principles)

قوم پرستی کے بنیادی ستون یہ ہیں:
• 
خود ارادیت (Self-Determination): ہر قوم کو حق ہے کہ وہ اپنی حکومت خود چنے اور کسی بیرونی طاقت کی غلام نہ رہے۔
• مشترکہ شناخت: زبان، مذہب، تاریخ یا ثقافت وہ دھاگے ہیں جو لوگوں کو ایک قوم کی شکل میں پروتے ہیں۔
• قومی اتحاد: قوم کے مفاد کو ذاتی یا گروہی مفاد پر ترجیح دینا۔
• قومی علامات: جھنڈا، قومی ترانہ اور قومی ہیروز کا احترام کرنا جو اتحاد کی علامت ہوتے ہیں۔

5. روزمرہ زندگی سے مثال (Real-life Example)
• 
مثال: کرکٹ یا فٹ بال کا میچ یاد کریں۔ جب پاکستان اور کسی دوسرے ملک کا میچ ہوتا ہے، تو ہم سب اپنے تمام ذاتی، لسانی اور سیاسی فرق بھول کر صرف "پاکستان" کی جیت کی دعا کرتے ہیں۔
• نشنلسٹ پہلو: سبز ہلالی پرچم دیکھ کر جو فخر محسوس ہوتا ہے اور قومی ترانے پر جو جذبہ پیدا ہوتا ہے، وہی قوم پرستی کی سادہ ترین مثال ہے جو ہمیں ایک لڑی میں پرو دیتی ہے۔

6. کریٹیکل پرسپکٹیو (Critical Perspective/Criticism)

• انتہا پسندی (Jingoism): جب قوم پرستی "میرے ملک سے محبت" کے بجائے "دوسرے ملکوں سے نفرت" میں بدل جائے، تو یہ جنگوں کا باعث بنتی ہے (جیسے پہلی اور دوسری عالمی جنگ)۔
• اقلیتوں کا مسئلہ: بعض اوقات اکثریت کی قوم پرستی کے چکر میں ملک کے اندر موجود چھوٹی زبانیں یا مذاہب بولنے والے لوگ خود کو غیر محفوظ محسوس کرنے لگتے ہیں۔
• تنگ نظری: "میرا ملک صحیح ہو یا غلط، میں اسے سپورٹ کروں گا" والا رویہ اخلاقی طور پر غلط فیصلے کروا سکتا ہے۔

RELEASING SUPPRESSED EMOTIONS. 

So, at the beginning of this New Year, let's talk about releasing suppressed emotions in particular. It's time to address the emotions that we always hide, to deal with at a later time. An airline employee shared one of the most infuriating and irresponsible passenger incidents they ever witnessed when a grandfather attempted to check in an 11-year-old boy as an unaccompanied minor but refused to follow proper airline procedures requiring family members to stay until the child boards.

The airline staff didn't know this unconscionable abandonment had occurred until the confused and worried child returned to the check-in desk an hour later asking if his aunt had checked in with them to pick him up as his grandfather promised. 

After discovering the grandfather had literally stranded his own grandson alone in a busy airport terminal, one of the ground staff members stayed with the boy and kept him company until his aunt finally arrived to collect him from the coffee shop. 

The employee stated "I will never not be furious at that man for embarrassing a child then stranding him" in an airport environment where anything could have happened to an unattended 11-year-old left alone for over an hour. The traumatized kid is probably close to 30 years old now, and the employee wonders if he still even speaks to his grandfather after being abandoned like unwanted luggage at an airport.

I faked bankruptcy to see my wife’s true colors, but on Christmas Eve, she dragged my daughters into a blizzard. “You’re just baggage now!” she screamed, leaving them to freeze in pajamas. I watched from the shadows, recording every second. She drove off laughing, but she didn’t know the "poverty" was a lie and the police were waiting...
The snow falls heavy over the South Bronx tonight, draping a mournful shroud over the city. Each flake drifts through the December darkness like a tiny, frozen witness to a crime in progress.
The temperature is 28 degrees. Cold enough to hurt. Cold enough to kill.
I sit motionless in the shadows of an armored black SUV, gripping the steering wheel until my knuckles turn bone-white with pain. My heart feels like someone has poured molten lead into my chest. Beside me, Tom—a veteran ex-FBI agent—has his telephoto lens trained through the gloom, locked onto the abandoned bus station 100 yards away.
"Is she... is she actually doing it?" I whisper, my voice thick and broken.
"She’s stopping," Tom says, his tone grim, cold as tempered steel. "Keep your head down, Chris. We need ironclad proof. If you move now, she walks away a free woman. You lose the girls forever. Stay. STILL."
I grind my teeth, watching through the monitor. My wife, Isabella—the woman I once thought was the missing piece of my soul—steps out of our black Escalade. She looks like a million dollars in her cashmere coat and designer boots, a gleaming contradiction amidst the filth of the slums.
But her soul? Her soul is a rotting void.
The back door opens. My heart stops dead. She grabs Rose by her arm—the same arm I saw bruises on last week—and yanks her violently out into the dirty slush. Rose is seven years old. She’s wearing matching Christmas pajamas covered in reindeer. No coat. Just thin cotton pajamas and slippers.
Then comes Lily. She stumbles out, her glasses fogging up instantly in the biting wind. She’s clutching Mr. Buttons, the teddy bear I bought them the day the adoption was finalized.
"SLEEP HERE!" Isabella screams. Her voice cuts sharply through the microphone hidden deep in the bear’s ear. "Sleep right here at this pathetic bus stop!"
"Mommy, please!" Lily’s high-pitched wail shatters me like glass. "It’s cold! We’ll be good! We promise!"
"Don't call me that," Isabella sneers, her beautiful face twisted into a mask of pure loathing. The façade she’s worn for a year has finally shattered. "I never wanted you. You were just the ticket to your father’s billions. But now? Now he’s bankrupt. He’s a loser. He’s a criminal. And I’m not spending another second as a babysitter for two foster brats nobody wanted."
She hurls their backpacks into the black mud.
"Your father can't afford you anymore," she says, her voice dropping to a low, cruel hiss like venom. "You're baggage. Unwanted trash. Stay here and maybe someone will pick you up before you freeze. Not my problem."
She turns her back, coldly getting into the car. She doesn't look back once. The Escalade revs its engine and speeds away, tires kicking gray slush onto my daughters' pajamas.
I don't wait for Tom to say the word. I explode out of the SUV like a wounded beast.
My lungs feel like they might burst. My feet pound through the snow. I see them—two tiny figures huddled together under the flickering yellow light of a dying streetlamp. They are shaking so hard they can barely stand.
"DADDY!"
The scream comes from both of them at once. It’s a sound of pure, raw terror transforming into impossible hope.
I hit the pavement on my knees, sliding through the ice, scooping them both into my arms, pulling them deep inside my heavy wool coat. I hold them so tight I can feel their tiny hearts racing against my chest like trapped birds.
"I've got you," I sob into Lily’s hair. "I’m here. I’m here. I never left you. I would never leave you."
"She said you didn't want us," Rose whispers, her face buried in my neck, soaked with tears. "She said we were trash."
I pull back, cupping her freezing face in my warm hands. I look her straight in the eye.
"THAT WAS THE LAST LIE SHE WILL EVER TELL YOU," I say, my voice vibrating with a rage so cold it rivals the storm. "You are my daughters. You are my world. And that woman? She’s never coming back."
Behind us, Robert, my driver and bodyguard, is already on the phone with the NYPD. "Target vehicle heading toward George Washington Bridge. Intercept now."
I look down at Mr. Buttons, lying forgotten and soggy in the snow. I pick up the bear and tuck it under my arm.
Isabella thinks she’s escaping with the $50,000 she stole from our "household" safe. She thinks she’s flying to the Caymans to start over while I rot in a federal cell for a bankruptcy that doesn't exist.
She has no idea that every venomous word, every shove, every cruel look, was recorded in crystal-clear 4K.
She thinks she won. But she just signed her own confession.
And this? This is only the beginning of her nightmare...

Citizenship 2.0 

When I said that citizenship should be grounded in lived reality, many people rushed to dispute the idea. But the problem with much of the thinking around this debate is that we often reduce citizenship to a single archetype, what I’ll call, for the sake of this discussion, the “NGO-jobs, fake citizen” narrative. This usually points to highly visible cases: a Ugandan or Kenyan in a well-paying job, or someone occupying elite professional spaces. That scenario exists, yes, but it is only a very small and unrepresentative slice of a much broader national reality. 

Our country is shaped by many other lived experiences that rarely make it into these debates.

Two years ago, I was in Yirol and had lunch at a friend’s family home. Like many small towns across South Sudan, Yirol is home to people from nearby and distant villages who have settled there over time. It is also home to many foreigners who run shops and small trading businesses. As I listened to children playing outside, I was struck by something unexpected: some Ethiopian looking kids were speaking fluent Atuot. When I asked about it, I was told they were the children of an Ethiopian trader, the kids were born and raised there. Ironically, Atuot is their first language; they speak Arabic and some Amharic with their parents, and often even translate for them.
This is not an isolated case. Similar stories exist across the country. In Yirol alone, you will find Darfuris who married local women and raised families there. Walk across Bahr el Ghazal and you will meet many foreigners who have integrated so deeply that local families have adopted them and given them indigenous names.

Go to Terekeka and you will find local restaurants run by Mundukuru families. The mistake people often make is assuming these Mundukuru “arrived yesterday” or don’t understand local languages. In reality, many have been there for generations, to the point that they have virtually lost contact with their places of origin. You will find similar histories in  among communities often loosely referred to as “Zaireans” or Congolese, people who have been part of this land since long before the modern state existed.

Traditional South Sudanese cultures have historically been generous and pragmatic in matters of belonging. Many communities had clear but flexible ways of granting what was once understood as custodianship of the land. Similar traditions exist among the Naath, where a foreigner could, and often still can be fully assimilated into the community.

The real problem with today’s debate is that many people insist on narrowing it to a “work permit” or “NGO citizenship” argument. That is not the only discussion being had here. This is a much wider, deeper, and more consequential conversation about belonging, identity, and lived reality.

Try standing in Yirol and telling the Atuot-speaking Habasha child that they are not a citizen. It will be the Atuot people themselves who push back, not out of law or ideology, but because their daily lived experience tells them otherwise. 

Once again, I am a social critic who is trying to widen your thinking to accommodate more experiences for the sake of public discourse.

My own mother abandoned me at an airport when I was just eight years old, leaving me with nothing but a backpack, all so she could enjoy a luxury vacation with her new husband and his children. That sentence still feels unreal to write, even now, because no child ever imagines their mother as someone capable of walking away like that. At eight, your world is small. It revolves around safety, routine, and the belief that the adults who love you will always come back for you. I didn’t know it then, but that day would tear that belief apart so completely that nothing would ever feel the same again.

My name is Leah, and when I was eight, my entire universe was my mom, Annette. My parents had divorced when I was five, and from that moment on, it was just the two of us. At least, that’s how it felt to me. My father, Gordon, vanished from my daily life after the divorce. My mom told me he cared more about his business than he ever did about us, that he chose money over being a father. She said it so often and with such certainty that I never questioned it. Children believe what they’re told, especially when it comes from the person they trust most.

When my mom remarried, everything shifted. Her new husband, Calvin, entered our lives with a confidence that filled every room. He had two kids of his own—Kylie, who was ten, and Noah, who was nine—and from the start, it was clear that this new family had already been formed long before I arrived. I was the extra piece, the one that didn’t quite fit. Calvin didn’t hide his favoritism. Kylie and Noah were loud, demanding, and sure of themselves, and he rewarded them for it. I learned quickly that staying quiet was safer.

The changes came in small, almost invisible ways at first. Movie nights where there was “no space” for me on the couch. Family photos where I was asked to stand off to the side. Birthday parties where Kylie and Noah received elaborate celebrations while mine felt rushed, almost like an obligation. I didn’t have the words for what was happening, but I felt it. A coldness growing where warmth used to be. My mom noticed it too, I think—but she never stopped it. She always chose the path that kept Calvin happy.

By the time spring break of second grade rolled around, I was desperate for things to feel normal again. Calvin announced we were taking a two-week vacation to Hawaii, and the idea felt magical. I had never been on a real vacation before. I imagined sandy beaches, warm water, and maybe—just maybe—feeling like part of the family. I clung to that hope with everything I had.

The morning of the trip, I woke up before my alarm. My heart raced as I carefully packed my small purple backpack, folding my swimsuit just right, tucking my favorite stuffed animal inside, making sure I didn’t forget the book I was halfway through. I wanted everything to be perfect. I wanted no reason for anyone to be annoyed with me. In the car ride to the airport, Calvin barely spoke. Kylie and Noah exchanged glances and whispered to each other, then laughed. I told myself I was imagining it.

At the airport, the energy buzzed with excitement. Families rushed past us dragging suitcases, kids bouncing with anticipation, parents juggling coffee cups and boarding passes. I clutched my ticket tightly, staring at the word “Honolulu” printed across it like it might disappear if I looked away. This was real. I was really going.

Then, without warning, everything unraveled.

Calvin said he needed to use the restroom and took Kylie and Noah with him. My mom told me she was going to grab coffee and instructed me to wait by the gate. I sat down obediently, swinging my legs, watching people line up to board flights. Minutes passed. Then more. The gate agent announced pre-boarding. I checked the clock again and again, my stomach tightening each time.

Finally, I called my mom.

When she answered, I could hear laughter and music in the background. It didn’t sound like an airport anymore. “Mom?” I asked, my voice shaking. “Where are you? The plane is boarding.”

There was a pause. Then her voice came back cold, unfamiliar. “Leah, listen carefully. You’re not coming with us.”

I didn’t understand the words. I remember staring at the floor, convinced I had misheard. “What do you mean? I have my ticket. I’m at the gate.”

“I mean you’re staying there,” she said flatly. “Calvin thinks it’s better if it’s just our family on this trip.”

My chest hurt. “But… I don’t know how to get home.”

Her response crushed something inside me that never fully healed. “You can figure it out. I’m not ruining my perfect family trip for your worthless drama.”

Then Calvin’s voice cut in, sharp and dismissive. “Some brats need to learn real independence the hard way.”

In the background, I heard laughter. Kylie’s voice rang out clearly, cruel and amused. “Finally, a real vacation without the unwanted baggage.”

My mom came back on the line one last time. “Stop being so pathetic and needy. Find your own way home.”

The call ended.

I stood there frozen, phone in my hand, backpack digging into my shoulders, surrounded by strangers rushing to places they belonged. The noise of the airport faded into a dull roar as the reality settled in. My own mother had left me. Not by accident. Not because of an emergency. She chose to walk away.

I don’t remember how long I stood there before airport security noticed me. I was crying so hard I could barely breathe. They led me to a small office filled with bright posters meant to comfort children, but nothing felt comforting. A woman sat with me, speaking softly, asking questions. They tried calling my mom again. Straight to voicemail.

“Is there anyone else we can call?” she asked gently.

I hesitated. My mom had spent years telling me my father didn’t care. But his phone number lived somewhere deep in my memory, carefully guarded. I whispered it like a secret.

When he answered, his voice was calm and professional. “Gordon Calvinson speaking.”

“Daddy?” I said, barely louder than a breath.

The silence that followed felt endless.

“Leah?” His voice cracked. “Where are you?”

“I’m at the airport,” I sobbed. “Mom left me. I’m scared.”

Everything changed after that. His tone sharpened, urgent. He asked questions quickly. Then he told me to stay exactly where I was and handed instructions to the adults with me. When the woman ended the call, she looked at me differently.

“Your father is coming,” she said slowly. “He’ll be here in three hours.”

I didn’t know what that meant yet. I only knew that for the first time that day, I wasn’t completely alone.

Qu'est-ce que le Shirk ?

En Islam, le shirk est considéré comme le plus grand péché. Mais, qu’est-ce que le shirk ? De manière générale, le polythéisme consiste en l’association de quiconque à Allah (Exalté soit-Il) dans Sa Seigneurie, Son adoration et Ses Noms et Attributs.

Malheureusement, cet « associationnisme » ou « idolâtrie » existe depuis longtemps. Par ailleurs, tous les prophètes ont combattu ce danger extrême. Voyons donc, de plus près, quelle est cette action qui est le seul péché impardonnable auprès d’Allah, s’il n’est pas suivi d’un repentir sincère sur Terre ?

ÉTYMOLOGIE DU SHIRK
Le « Shirk » ou « Chirk » est un mot d’origine arabe qui s’écrit « شِرْك ». Dans la terminologie juridique islamique, ce terme désigne le fait d’associer à Allah (Exalté soit-Il). Il est, ainsi, l’opposé du « Tawhid », qui est le fait d’unifier Allah (Soubhanahou wa Ta3ala). Ou encore, c’est le contraire de la « Hanifiyyah », c’est-à-dire la religion du prophète Ibrahim (Paix d’Allah sur lui) « le Hanif ». Ces 2 termes consistent à unifier Allah et se désavouer du shirk ainsi que ses adeptes.

En effet, dans la religion musulmane, Allah (Gloire et Pureté à Lui) est le « Dieu » Unique et la Seule Divinité digne d’être adorée. Ainsi, l’association à Allah d’autres « dieux », « puissances » ou « divinités » (qui sont, en réalité, faux) s’appelle « Shirk ». Et celui qui commet cet acte abominable est appelé « Moushrik » (مُشْرِك ou مُشْرِكون au pluriel) ou « associateur ».

Qu’Est-ce Que le Shirk ?
Comme indiqué ci-dessus, en principe, le shirk est le fait d’associer à Allah (Le Très Haut) dans les trois points suivants :

Sa Seigneurie ;
Son Adoration ;
Et Ses Noms et Attributs.
C’est aussi le plus grand des péchés aux yeux d’Allah (Exalté soit-Il). Car, Allah (Gloire et Pureté à Lui) déteste le fait que l’on associe à Lui qui que ce soit, ou que l’on Le mette à égalité avec quelqu’un d’autre. Pire encore, Allah (3azza wa Jalla) n’accepte pas que l’on essaie de mettre une personne ou une législation au-dessus de Lui ou de Sa Législation (Charia).

Qu’Est-ce Que le Tawhid ?
En réalité, il faut comprendre ce qu’est le « Tawhid » pour mieux savoir : Qu’est-ce que le shirk ? Effectivement, le Tawhid (ou l’Unification) d’Allah (Soubhanahou wa Ta3ala) dans Sa Seigneurie, Son Adoration et Ses Noms et Attributs est le Droit d’Allah.

Dans un hadith rapporté par Boukhari et Mouslim, le prophète Mohammed (Paix et Salut d’Allah sur lui) nous enseigne cela : « Ô Mou’adh, sais-tu quel est le droit d’Allah sur Ses serviteurs et quel est le droit de Ses serviteurs par rapport à Lui ?
Je répondais : “Allah et Son Messager en sont plus savants.”
Il dit : “Le droit d’Allah sur Ses serviteurs est qu’ils L’adorent sans rien Lui associer. Et le droit des serviteurs par rapport à Allah est qu’Il ne châtie pas celui qui ne Lui aura rien associé”. »

Et au contraire, le Shirk est une injustice (« Dhoulm » en phonétique et « ظُلْم » en arabe) dans la mesure où il tente de donner à autrui le droit d’Allah, ou une partie de ce droit. C’est pour cela que Louqman « le sage » dit à son fils pour le conseiller, comme cela est mentionné dans le Coran (traduction approximative des sens) : « Et lorsque Luqmān dit à son fils tout en l’exhortant : « Ô mon fils, ne donne pas d’associé à Allah, car l’association à [Allah] est vraiment une injustice énorme ». » [Sourate 31, verset 13].

LES DIFFÉRENTS TYPES DE SHIRK
Le shirk ou le polythéisme s’avère être le contraire du monothéisme. Nous allons maintenant voir : Qu’est-ce que le shirk d’un point de vue de ses types ? En fait, celui-ci se divise en deux formes :

Le Shirk Akbar « شِرْكٌ أَكْبَر » ou le polythéisme majeur ;
Le Shirk Asghar « شِرْكٌ أَصْغَر » ou le polythéisme mineur.
Shirk Akbar ou le Polythéisme Majeur

Le shirk akbar se compose de 3 catégories :

Le shirk dans « Tawhid Ar-Rouboubiyyah » (l’Unicité de la Seigneurie). Il s’agit du polythéisme dans l’Unicité d’Allah dans Ses Actes, Sa Création, Son Royaume, etc.
Le shirk dans « Tawhid Al Oulouhiyyah » (l’Unicité de l’Adoration). C’est-à-dire le polythéisme dans l’Unicité d’Allah dans l’Adoration.
Le shirk dans « Tawhid Al Asma` wa As-Siffat » (l’Unicité des Noms et Attributs). À savoir : le polythéisme dans l’Unicité des Noms et Attributs d’Allah (Gloire et Pureté à Lui).
Le shirk akbar est le plus grave des péchés, car il fait sortir de l’Islam la personne qui le commet.

LE SHIRK ASGHAR OU LE POLYTHÉISME MINEUR
Le shirk asghar est l’ensemble des interdits de la Charia qui porte ce jugement dans les textes religieux, mais qui n’a pas atteint le niveau du shirk akbar. Ce péché est appelé « shirk », mais n’est pas considéré comme le polythéisme majeur qui rend son auteur « mécréant » ou « apostat ».

Ceci dit, cette forme d’association, qui est une « mécréance mineure », est très dangereuse dans la mesure où elle conduit au polythéisme majeur. Les exemples du polythéisme mineur sont nombreux, notamment :

Le fait de jurer par autre qu’Allah (Exalté soit-Il) ;
Certaines œuvres pieuses (mineures) faites par ostentation ;
La préciosité vis-à-vis des gens.
LA GRAVITÉ DE CET ACTE SELON LE NOBLE CORAN
Qu’est-ce que le shirk en matière de dangerosité ? Dans le Coran, l’association est considéré comme la plus grande transgression. Voici quelques versets coraniques qui montrent cela :

Le verset 13 dans la sourate 31 (traduction approximative des sens) : « car l’association à [Allah] est vraiment une injustice énorme. » ;
Dans la sourate 4 au verset 48 (traduction approximative des sens) : « Certes Allah ne pardonne pas qu’on Lui donne quelqu’associé. À part cela, Il pardonne à qui Il veut. »
LE DANGER DU SHIRK DANS LA SOUNNAH
Même dans la Sounnah, il se place au rang des plus grands péchés. À une occasion, le prophète Mohammed (Paix et Salut sur Lui) a expliqué que le polythéisme est le plus grand péché, lorsqu’il dit : « Les grands péchés sont : le shirk (associer à Allah), l’ingratitude envers les parents… ».

Le hadith complet se trouve dans les recueils « Sahih Al Boukhari » et « Sahih Mouslim ». Bien entendu, il y a plein d’autres hadiths qui vont dans ce sens.

Do you have a Vinted pile?!

On last night's Can You Make £10K in 10 Days, Scarlett Moffat met a reseller who made £85k in a year from selling items she's picked up at car boot sales or lost luggage sales! 

Scarlett then tried her hand at selling items on online marketplaces. After some initial excitement, she noted that it took more time than she expected, it could feel a bit overwhelming, and it had the potential to become more like a full-time job than a side hustle. 

The subject of selling unwanted items online frequently comes up during decluttering sessions. Clients are usually keen to recoup some money from their unwanted items, and will identify potential pieces to sell. But it's often the case that the Vinted pile is left untouched, or sales don't go as well as expected, resulting in disappointment. 

If you're looking to make some cash from your clutter, it is always worth doing a quick check of previously listed items to see the potential resale value (and get a feel for how many didn't sell), prioritising high-value items first and foremost, and having an alternative exit plan in the near future for items that don't shift.

Bear in mind, car boot sales can be a one-stop shop for selling multiple mixed items in one go. Potential buyers can see and feel the items, negotiations can be done face-to-face, and you don't have to worry about photographs, descriptions, packing or posting.

The range of other options is endless, but includes trading in or selling tech (at electrical retailers or via tech exchange shops), bundling books to send to We Buy Books, or contacting local auction houses and specialist shops that specialise in reselling second-hand items. 

What's been your favourite method of turning your clutter into cash? Please share in the comments!

🔷️ In shirk vervallen door misleiding en onwetendheid || Sh. al-Rādjiĥī

Vragensteller: Wat is het oordeel over iemand die anderen dan Allāh aanroept, terwijl hij tussen de moslims leeft en de Qur'ān hem heeft bereikt? Is deze persoon een moslim die met shirk (afgoderij) is besmet, of is hij een mushrik (afgodenaanbidder)?

Sh  'Abd al-'Azīz al-Rādjiĥī:

Deze persoon is een mushrik, want hij is niet verontschuldigd als hij tussen de moslims leeft. 

Vanwege de uitspraak van Allāh: "En aan mij is deze Qur'ān geopenbaard om jullie ermee te waarschuwen, en degenen die het bereikt." 

Dus wie de Qur'ān heeft bereikt, voor hem is het bewijs geleverd. 

Allāh de Verhevene zegt: "En Wij straffen nooit totdat Wij een boodschapper sturen." 

Dus wie de Qur'an heeft bereikt en de boodschap heeft ontvangen, en shirk (afgoderij) verricht terwijl hij tussen de moslims leeft, is een mushrik.

Sommige geleerden zeggen echter dat als het voor  de persoon verborgen is van wat hij aan shirk begaat, door toedoen van de predikers die uitnodigen naar dwaling en het plegen van shirk  en door toedoen van de vele misleiders om hem heen, en de zaak is voor hem onduidelijk, dan wordt zijn situatie overgelaten aan Allāh de Verhevene. In dat geval wordt hij beoordeeld zoals de Ahl al Fatrah (degenen die leefden in al djaahiliyyah vòòrdat de Boodschapper kwam).

MAAR als hij sterft (in die toestand) dan wordt hij  gewoon behandeld als een mushrik: hij wordt niet gewassen, er wordt geen gebed voor hem verricht en hij wordt niet begraven met de moslims in de begraafplaatsen.

Dus het fundamentele uitgangspunt is dat hij niet verontschuldigd is (laa yu`dhar). Maar (zoals eerder aangegeven) als iemand van de mensen in een situatie verkeert waarin het voor hem verborgen is gebleven door de predikers van shirk en dwaling, en hij weet het niet, dan wordt er gezegd: dat hij verontschuldigd is in die (specifieke) situatie en zijn toestand (qua eind oordeel in het Hiernamaals) wordt overgelaten aan Allāh de Verhevene. 

Maar in elk geval is het voor hem verplicht om de waarheid te zoeken en te achterhalen, en zich daarvoor in te spannen, net zoals hij zich inspant voor zijn levensonderhoud en navraag doet naar het verdienen van inkomsten. Dus het is verplicht voor hem dat hij vraagt over zijn godsdienst en over de zaken die voor hem onduidelijk zijn. Het feit dat hij de waarheid niet heeft gehoord, niet heeft aanvaard of doof is geweest voor het horen van de waarheid, is geen excuus voor hem; dat is de Asl (het fundamentele uitgangspunt).

✒️ Abu Hudayfa Musa ibn Yusuf

 of tribalism has become the altar upon which national progress is
 sacrificed.

 co-opt and manipulate, while suppressing dissent and legitimizing
 authoritarianism.
Theology teaches us that idolatry is 
the worship of false gods, and in South Sudan, the idolization of tribalism
 has become a perverse form
 of worship.
It is a rejection of the transcendent, a denial of the nation's higher purpose,
and a betrayal of the people's 
trust.
To break free from this cycle, South Sudan must undergo a profound conversion, one that rejects the false gods of tribalism and embraces a politics of inclusion and justice.

Dear Mr. Bichiia Maisango,

I have no problem with your advocacy or your calls for Hausa consciousness. However, I am concerned about the way many of you in this movement conduct yourselves. What you are doing increasingly appears to be less about Hausa consciousness and more about promoting hatred against the entire Fulani ethnic group.

Your approach reminds me of some atheists who, instead of making their beliefs attractive by explaining why godlessness is better, focus mainly on attacking, insulting, and blackmailing other religions. This often suggests that without attacking others, they have little to offer. In the same way, your advocacy seems largely focused on attacking the Fulani people. You rarely acknowledge anything positive about them and rarely miss an opportunity to criticize or incite hostility against them.

The language you use when speaking about the Fulani is often filled with anger and rage, and I wonder what has made you so intolerant. It appears you have gone to an extreme, and it is troubling to see someone who once advocated religious tolerance now leaning toward tribal extremism and jingoism. Does this mean that intolerance is only wrong when it concerns religion?

What you are doing does not uplift the Hausa people; rather, it demeans them. Hausa will continue to grow and thrive with or without tribal warriors. Hausa is not just a Nigerian language. It is one of the largest trans-Saharan languages, spoken proudly by millions. It reached this level not through hostility, but through tolerance and accommodation of others, even when others mocked or undermined the Hausa people.

Although most northern tribes accept Hausa as a lingua franca, fears of domination still linger in their minds, which is why they sometimes attribute various vices to the Hausa. The Hausa people largely ignore this, and that is part of what makes them unique.

I believe it is time for you and your colleagues to reflect and retrace your steps before drifting further into extremism.

My parents, Julian and Beatrice Thorne, didn’t even pretend it was temporary.

Elena was a forensic accountant, and Silas was a retired architect. They didn't see a "spare." They saw a girl with a mathematical mind and a heart that had been starved. They Hugged Each Other — While I Walked Away Alone

The day my own mother leaned close and whispered, “We chose the better child,” something inside me went silent. And it never woke up again.

I was born in Seattle — a twin, but never an equal. My sister, Celeste, was the “perfect one.” Soft golden hair, bright blue eyes, and a smile that made strangers stop and tell my parents how lucky they were.

I was the other one.

My name was Iris.

I was the background twin. The extra. The child pushed to the edge of photos so I wouldn’t “distract” from Celeste’s beauty. While she received the newest phones and designer clothes, I got hand-me-downs and silence. I carried her bags. I cleaned her messes. I apologized for her tantrums.

Until the day I was sent away at fourteen — like unwanted luggage.

My parents, Nathan and Lorraine Whitmore, didn’t even pretend it was temporary.

“Don’t embarrass your uncle the way you embarrassed us,” my mother said, sipping her coffee without looking at me.

Those were her last words to me for ten years.

A PLACE TO BREATHE

My mother’s brother, Uncle Raymond, and his wife, Marisol, saved me.

They lived on a quiet ranch in Wyoming, far from the mirrors and whispers of the Whitmore estate. They gave me a room, warm meals, and something I had never known: a place where I didn’t have to compete just to exist.

Marisol was a forensic analyst. Raymond was a retired engineer.

They didn’t see a “spare.”
They saw a girl who needed to heal.

They taught me that worth isn’t measured by beauty — but by truth, discipline, and integrity.

I grew stronger.
I studied.
I became a senior financial auditor at a global firm.

And I learned one painful truth:
People who treat you as disposable only return when you become valuable.

THE $100 MILLION SILENCE

Two years ago, Raymond and Marisol died in a car accident.

They left me everything.

The ranch.
Their investments.
A private trust they had built in my name since I was fourteen.

Total value: $100 million.

I didn’t tell my parents.
I didn’t tell Celeste.
I mourned quietly — the way I had learned to survive.

Then, six months ago, Celeste called.

Her voice was sweet. Fake.

“Iris, sweetheart! We miss you so much. Mom and Dad are heartbroken we lost touch. We heard about the inheritance… and honestly, we think it should be shared. We’re twins, after all. What’s yours is ours, right?”

I laughed for the first time in years.

“I don’t have a family, Celeste. I have a balance sheet. And your name isn’t on it.”

She didn’t accept no.

She went online.

She posted a tearful video that went viral, calling me a “cold, greedy sister” who was hoarding money while our “sick parents” struggled to survive.

She even launched a GoFundMe — painting me as the villain of the Whitmore legacy.

The old family group chat exploded.

Relatives I barely remembered called me heartless.

I didn’t argue.
I didn’t explain.
I didn’t send legal threats.

I opened the digital archive Marisol helped me build.

It wasn’t just money.
It was proof.

Videos of birthdays where I was pushed out of the frame.
Texts where my mother called me a “mistake.”
Receipts showing the money I had sent for my father’s surgery had actually paid for Celeste’s luxury vacation in Spain.

I uploaded everything.

I named the folder:
“The Whitmore Audit.”

And I tagged every journalist who had shared her video.

The silence was instant.

The GoFundMe vanished within hours.
Support turned to disgust.
My mother called, crying about “misunderstandings.”

Her number is still blocked.

"The Flight Attendant Held Her Nose And Pointed To The Cargo Hold, Telling The Passengers I Smelled Like ""Rotting Garbage."" They Didn't Know The ""Garbage"" In My Pocket Was The Only Thing Stopping A Global Meltdown. Ten Minutes Later, The Pilot Started Screaming. He Wasn't Screaming Because Of The Turbulence—He Was Screaming Because A Massive AC-130 Ghostrider Had Just Decloaked Off The Left Wing, And The Radio Command Was Simple: ""Put The General Back In Seat 1A, Or Learn To Fly Without Wings.""

CHAPTER 1: THE UNWANTED PASSENGER

The rain at O'Hare International Airport was coming down in sheets, looking like grey static against the terminal windows. I stood at the gate for Flight 294 to D.C., clutching a leather satchel that had seen better decades. I caught my reflection in the glass. I looked like a nightmare. My trench coat was stained with mud and what looked like motor oil, my beard was matted, and there was a distinct, sharp odor clinging to me—a mix of ozone, burnt cordite, and sulfur. To the average civilian, I smelled like death. To anyone who’s been downrange, I smelled like a job well done.

I wasn’t homeless, and I certainly wasn’t a drifter. I was Neo. Call sign ""Ghost."" And the contents of that battered satchel were classified way above Top Secret. It was the ""Football""—not the whole thing, but the authentication drives required to reset the nuclear launch protocols after a localized breach in Seattle three hours ago. I had to get this to the Pentagon. Physically. No digital transmission. The airspace was supposed to be clear, my ticket was First Class, purchased by a frantic Department of Defense algorithm, and I was exhausted.

""Boarding Group 1,"" the gate agent announced, her voice tinny over the speaker.

I stepped forward. I could feel the eyes of the other passengers boring into my back. A guy in a tailored suit, probably a lobbyist, actually audibly gagged as I shuffled past him. I ignored it. I just needed to sit down, keep the satchel against my chest, and close my eyes for ninety minutes.

I walked down the jet bridge, the smell of jet fuel mixing with the sulfur on my coat. I stepped onto the plane and turned left toward First Class. Seat 1A. The best seat in the house.

""Excuse me, sir?""

The voice was sharp, like breaking glass. I stopped and looked up. The lead flight attendant—let's call her Brenda—was standing there, her arm blocked across the aisle like a barrier. Her nametag glinted under the harsh cabin lights. She looked me up and down, her nose wrinkling in exaggerated disgust.

""Can I help you?"" I rasped. My throat was raw from the smoke inhalation back in Seattle.

""You are not sitting here,"" Brenda said, her voice loud enough that the boarding passengers behind me stopped to watch the show. ""First Class is for paying customers. The shelter is downtown.""

I sighed, reaching into my pocket with a slow, deliberate movement so I didn't spook anyone. I pulled out the crumpled boarding pass. ""Seat 1A. I paid full fare. Actually, the government paid full fare. Now, if you’ll excuse me.""

I tried to step around her, but she didn't budge. She put a hand on my chest. A fatal mistake in my line of work, but I restrained the reflex to snap her wrist.

""I don't care what that paper says,"" she hissed. ""You smell like a sewer. We have elite members on this flight. I will not have you stinking up the cabin and ruining their experience. You are a health hazard.""

""Ma'am,"" I said, my voice dropping to a low growl. ""I suggest you let me sit down. This bag needs to remain with me at all times, and I need to be in D.C. by 2100 hours. It’s a matter of national security.""

Someone in the line laughed. ""National security? Buddy, the only security risk here is the biohazard coming off your coat!""

The lobbyist from the gate chimed in. ""Get him off the plane! I paid three grand for my seat; I'm not sitting next to a hobo!""

Brenda smirked, emboldened by the crowd. ""You hear that? You’re disrupting the flight. Now, I can have the Air Marshals drag you off, or we can make... an arrangement.""

I looked at my watch. We were already behind schedule. If I got dragged off, there would be paperwork, delays, and a potential security leak. I couldn't risk the delay.

""What arrangement?"" I asked, my grip tightening on the satchel.

""The cargo hold has a jumpseat for the loadmaster. It’s accessible through the rear galley hatch. It’s unpressurized comfort, freezing cold, and loud. Perfect for trash,"" she smiled sweetly, a smile that didn't reach her cold, dead eyes. ""You sit there, or you don't fly.""

I looked at the passengers. They were sneering, filming with their phones, eager to see the 'bum' get thrown out. They had no idea that if I didn't make this flight, the safety umbrella protecting their suburban lives would collapse by midnight.

""Fine,"" I said. ""Show me the hole.""

CHAPTER 2: THE VIPER IN THE SKY

They marched me through the plane like a prisoner. The walk of shame. I passed through First Class, through Economy Plus, all the way to the back of the bus. People covered their noses. Mothers pulled their children closer. I kept my head down, not out of shame, but to memorize faces. You never know who’s a threat.

Brenda opened a narrow access panel in the rear floor near the galley. A steep ladder led down into a small, cramped transition space next to the baggage containers. It wasn't the main cargo hold, but a maintenance jumpseat used for checking hydraulics in flight. It was dark, it smelled of grease, and the temperature was already dropping.

""Enjoy the flight, Sir,"" she mocked, slamming the hatch shut above me. I heard the lock engage.

I was alone in the dark.

I sat on the cold metal crate, clutching the satchel. The vibration of the engines firing up rattled my teeth. As we taxied, I pulled a small, ruggedized tactical tablet from my coat. I authenticated my biometrics.

STATUS: ASSET COMPROMISED. LOCATION: CARGO.

I didn't send a text. I initiated ""Protocol Black."" It’s a distress signal reserved for when a carrier of the Codes is under duress or removed from a secure environment. By forcing me into the cargo hold, Brenda had technically ""kidnapped"" the nuclear launch authority. The Pentagon's automated defense network doesn't understand ""rude flight attendants."" It only understands ""Asset Removed from Command Position.""

The plane lurched into the sky. It was freezing down here. My breath plumed in the red emergency light. I watched the tablet. The signal was out.

Ten minutes into the flight, the turbulence hit. But it wasn't wind. It was the specific, rhythmic thrumming of high-grade military countermeasures.

Above me, in the cockpit, the world was ending.

Captain Miller was sipping his coffee when his altimeter spun crazy circles. The GPS navigation screen flickered and went dead. The radio, usually filled with the chatter of Air Traffic Control, blasted a screeching static that made him tear his headset off.

""What the hell is going on?"" Miller shouted to his co-pilot. ""Are we in a storm?""

""No storm on the radar, Cap! But look at the TCAS! It's lighting up like a Christmas tree!""

The Traffic Collision Avoidance System was screaming that something was close. Extremely close.

""I have visual!"" the co-pilot screamed, pointing out the left window.

Captain Miller looked. His coffee cup slipped from his hand and shattered on the floor.

Flying parallel to their Boeing 737, less than fifty yards off the wingtip, was a monster. It was painted matte black, absorbing the moonlight. The massive propellers were churning the air into a frenzy. It was an AC-130J Ghostrider gunship.

And it wasn't just flying along. Its 105mm Howitzer cannon was traversed, locked, and pointed directly at the cockpit window.

Miller froze. He was staring down the barrel of a gun that could turn his plane into confetti in a fraction of a second.

Suddenly, the static on the radio cut out, replaced by a voice so clear and cold it sounded like it was coming from inside his own head.

""Commercial Flight 294. This is U.S. Special Operations Command Air Defense. You are in violation of Federal Protocol 7-Alpha.""

Miller grabbed the mic, his hands shaking. ""This is Flight 294! We are a civilian aircraft! What is the meaning of this? You’re going to cause a collision!""

The voice on the radio didn't change pitch. ""You have incorrectly stowed sensitive military cargo. You have a VIP in your cargo hold. The man you treated like garbage is the only reason we haven't vaporized your engines yet.""

Miller felt the blood drain from his face. ""The... the homeless guy?""

""That 'homeless guy' is General Neo. And you have exactly three minutes to restore him to his assigned seat in First Class and offer him your personal apologies. If you do not, we will assume this aircraft has been hijacked by hostiles and we will neutralize the threat. Do you copy?""

Miller looked out the window. The Gunship dipped its wing slightly, revealing the 30mm chain gun spinning up.

""Brenda!"" Miller screamed into the cabin intercom. ""Get to the back! NOW!""

“Nobody Wants You!” My Foster Mother Screamed, Throwing My Life Into The Mud. I Stood There Waiting To Freeze, Until 200 Engines Shook The Earth.

Chapter 1

They say the sound of a heart breaking is silent. That’s a lie.

My heart breaking sounded exactly like a black plastic garbage bag hitting a wet pavement.

“Get out!” Brenda screamed, her voice cracking the suburban silence. “I am done! I am done with the silence, the staring, and the… the weirdness! You’re a curse, Toby. Just like the agency said.”

I stood on the lawn of 412 Maple Drive, the rain soaking through my thin gray hoodie in seconds. It was a cold rain, the kind that settles in your marrow and refuses to leave.

“Brenda, please,” I whispered, though I knew it was useless. “I have nowhere to go. It’s forty degrees out here.”

“Not my problem!” she shrieked, clutching the lapels of her pink bathrobe. She kicked a pair of my jeans off the porch. They landed in a puddle of muddy water. “I called your caseworker. She can come pick up the trash. But you are not stepping foot in my house again. You scare the cat. You scare my kids. You’re broken!”

Broken.

I’d heard that word in seven different homes over the last ten years. Too quiet. Too angry. Too much baggage.

I was sixteen years old, and my entire worldly possession fit into the Hefty bag I was clutching like a lifeline. A sketchbook, a toothbrush, two t-shirts, and a photo of a mother I couldn't remember.

I looked around the neighborhood. I saw the curtains twitching next door. Mr. Henderson was watching. Mrs. Gable across the street was watching. They saw a skinny kid getting thrown out in a storm, and they did what people always do: they closed their blinds and turned up the TV.

I was invisible. I was a statistic. I was a check that bounced.

I bent down to pick up my wet jeans, my hands shaking so hard I could barely grip the denim.

Just walk, I told myself. Just start walking until you hit the highway. Maybe a truck will hit you. Maybe the cold will take you.

That’s when I felt it.

It wasn't a sound at first. It was a vibration.

The water in the puddle by my feet started to ripple. Then, the glass in the front window of Brenda’s house rattled.

Brenda stopped screaming. She looked around, confused. “What is that?”

Then came the noise.

It started as a low growl, like a beast waking up underground, and then it exploded into a roar that drowned out the thunder.

Lights. Blinding, white LED beams cutting through the rain.

One motorcycle turned the corner. Then two. Then ten. Then fifty.

They didn't stop coming.

It was a river of chrome and black iron. Harleys, Indians, custom choppers. They filled the street, hopping the curbs, parking on the manicured lawns of the neighbors. The air filled with the smell of gasoline and exhaust, choking out the smell of rain and despair.

There must have been two hundred of them.

Brenda backed up against her front door, her face draining of color. “Who… who are these people? Did you call them? Did you bring a gang here, you little freak?”

I couldn't speak. I was paralyzed. I had never seen a motorcycle club in real life. They looked like monsters. Men with beards down to their chests, arms covered in tattoos, wearing leather vests with patches I couldn't read.

The engines cut off.

The silence that followed was heavier than the noise.

Two hundred men stepped off their bikes. They didn't say a word. They just stood there, a wall of leather and violence, staring at the house.

Then, the crowd parted.

A man walked through the center. He was a giant. He had to be six-foot-five, with shoulders like a linebacker and a gray beard that was braided at the end. He wore a cut that said PRESIDENT on the chest. He wasn't wearing a helmet. His face was a map of scars, weathered by wind and fights.

He walked past the bikes. He walked onto the grass. He walked straight toward me.

I flinched. I closed my eyes, waiting for the hit. That’s what men did. They hit.

But the hit never came.

I opened my eyes. The giant was standing two feet away from me. He wasn't looking at me with anger. He was looking at me like… like he was searching for something.

He looked at my blue eyes. He looked at the jagged scar on my chin.

Then, he looked at Brenda.

His expression changed. It went from searching to homicidal.

“You the one who put him out here?” the man asked. His voice sounded like gravel grinding together.

Brenda stammered, trying to find her authority. “This… this is private property! I’m calling the police! This boy is a ward of the state, and you have no business—”

“I asked you a question,” the man roared, and the sound was terrifying. “Did you put this boy out in the rain like garbage?”

“He is garbage!” Brenda yelled back, her fear making her stupid. “He’s unwanted!”

The giant turned back to me. He saw the trash bag in my hand. He saw the shivering.

He slowly unbuttoned his leather vest. He took it off. It was heavy, warm, and smelled like tobacco and freedom.

He draped it over my shoulders. It swallowed me whole.

Then he knelt down. One knee in the mud. He grabbed my shoulders with hands the size of shovels.

“Toby,” he said.

My breath hitched. “How do you know my name?”

The man’s eyes, terrifying to everyone else, filled with water.

“I know your name,” he whispered, “because I’m the one who gave it to you.”

He stood up, turning to face his army of bikers. He raised a fist in the air.

“BOYS!” he shouted. “WE FOUND HIM! WE FOUND THE PUP!”

A cheer went up that shook the shingles off the roof. Horns honked. Engines revved.

The giant looked back at Brenda, who was now trembling against her doorframe.

“You said nobody wants him?” The giant stepped onto the porch, towering over her. “Lady, you just made a mistake that’s gonna haunt you for the rest of your miserable life. Nobody throws a Reaper’s son in the mud.”

He turned back to me and extended a hand.

“Let’s go, Toby. Your room is ready. And it ain’t in a place like this.”

“I know your name,” he whispered, “because I’m the one who gave it to you.”

A cheer went up that shook the shingles off the roof. Horns honked. Engines revved.

The giant looked back at Brenda, who was now trembling against her doorframe.

“You said nobody wants him?” The giant stepped onto the porch, towering over her. “Lady, you just made a mistake that’s gonna haunt you for the rest of your miserable life. Nobody throws a Reaper’s son in the mud.”

He turned back to me and extended a hand.

“Let’s go, Toby. Your room is ready. And it ain’t in a place like this.”

Mr. Amunga,Amunga Akhanyalabandu
Your remarks regarding the leadership of Lugulu Girls High School are deeply troubling, unbecoming of an educator, and a profound embarrassment to the teaching fraternity you claim to represent. One is left wondering whether, during your teacher training, you were prepared to educate and nurture all Kenyan children or only those who share your ethnicity.

Education, by its very nature, is national, merit-based, and unifying. Schools;especially national schools exist to rise above parochial identities and tribal sentiments. To reduce leadership in such institutions to ethnic entitlement is not only intellectually bankrupt but also dangerous to the social fabric of this country.

This kind of thinking is precisely what continues to cripple our nation: the belief that public institutions must be captured, owned, or led by specific communities. Your rhetoric mirrors the very tribal jingoism we have repeatedly condemned in our political class. What, then, makes your position morally superior to the tribal generals you seem to criticize when you advance the same divisive ideology?

You have often spoken with pride about your children attending prestigious schools across the country. Are they taught exclusively by members of your community because they are Luhyas? Do you demand the removal of principals and teachers in those schools if they do not share your ethnicity? If not, why should Lugulu Girls be subjected to a standard you yourself do not uphold?

Leadership in education must be founded on competence, integrity, performance, and commitment to learners not on surname, tribe, or place of origin. To publicly call for the removal of a principal purely on ethnic grounds, while issuing veiled threats of “taking matters into our own hands,” is reckless, inflammatory, and unbecoming of a professional educator.

Lugulu Girls High School does not belong to any single community; it belongs to Kenya. Its success has been built by educators from diverse backgrounds who have served with distinction. To weaponize ethnicity in the name of “pride” is to betray the very values education is meant to instill tolerance, unity, and critical thinking.

History has taught us, painfully, where such thinking leads. As educators and opinion leaders, we should be the first to dismantle tribal barriers, not entrench them. Kenya will not be saved by ethnic entitlement, but by merit, fairness, and national consciousness.

You owe the profession, the learners, and the nation a deep moment of reflection.

Asif vinculó su argumento a las órdenes de arresto emitidas por la Corte Penal Internacional (CPI) contra Netanyahu por presuntos crímenes de guerra, y comparó su propuesta con la reciente captura del presidente venezolano por parte de Estados Unidos.

My Mom Chose a Luxury Trip with Her New Family Over Me
-She Said, 'You Can Take Care of Yourself, Then Walked Away Forever
When I was eight, I stood in the middle of a crowded airport clutching a small pink backpack-the last piece of home I had left-as my mother walked away. Her heels clicked against the floor, each step echoing like a countdown to the end of my childhood.
She turned once, her sunglasses slipping just enough for me to see the irritation in her eyes. "You can take care of yourself," she said, her tone cold and dismissive, as if I were an unwanted package she couldn't wait to drop off.
Her new husband smirked. "Some spoiled kids need to learn independence the hard way."
His children-two polished, picture-perfect twins-laughed.
"Finally, a real vacation without the extra baggage!"
Their laughter followed them as they disappeared toward the gate. My throat burned, but I refused to cry. Not for them. Not for her. All I whispered was, "This isn't over."
For an hour, I waited -convinced she'd come back. That she'd realize she'd made a mistake. But the announcement board kept flashing Flight to Paris boarding now, and the hope inside me slowly cracked.
I sat on a bench, hugging my backpack like it could protect me from the truth. Inside was a photo of me and my mom from before her remarriage-back when she braided my hair and called me her little girl. I stared at it until the colors bled together.
Then a security guard approached, kneeling to meet my eyes. "Sweetheart," he asked softly, "where are your parents?"

SPANGLED NATION SPEWING

From Vancouver’s waterfront 
to Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge,
border cities must bear our boisterous, 
swaggering neighbour’s weight—
as they snarl and skid into us
through gritted fences.

There have been glimmerings 
into the mood of the nation—
as when a hoodie becomes a hood,
a mask, camouflage, 
a phone, a concealed weapon,
youth perceived as threats,
and hence, targets.

Along with all the other targets,
targeted for daring to deviate 
from ‘the norm,’ 
the almighty, righteous, 
white man’s ordained normal.

As when the spangled nation
salivates or spews, 
with nothing in between—
might abused, might enough 

to drag us along 
via rousing dogmata, 
endless expansionism
and drone-striking jingoism,

as the coastline burns,
gray whale blubber boils,
pretzel-stuffed crows stagger
and eagles, lungs tarred, plummet.

Dazzled into deference too long,
our messages mauled mid-delivery,
we no longer hold our tongues.
 
We unmask, unsheathe, 
sever your bomb-lit screeds, 
hack out truth 
from the wreckage.

Definition. Jingoism.n.

Jingoism is extreme, aggressive nationalism, characterized by fervent patriotism, a belief in national superiority, and a strong advocacy for aggressive foreign policies, often involving threats or force, rather than peaceful diplomacy, to promote perceived national interests, stemming from a popular English song in the 1870s. It's an excessive form of patriotism that glorifies the military and sees other nations as inferior, differing from healthy patriotism by its confrontational and bellicose nature.

I found this book while I was in the middle of a massive "planning" phase of my life. I had spreadsheets for my goals, five-year plans for my career, and a constant, low-grade anxiety that if I didn't white-knuckle every decision, my life would fall apart. I saw The Surrender Experiment on a shelf and, honestly, the title annoyed me. "Surrender" sounded like giving up. It sounded passive. But I was so tired of fighting the current that I bought it, mostly out of a desperate curiosity to see if someone could actually live a life without "trying" so hard.

I expected a series of vague, mystical anecdotes about a guy who sat in a forest and had things magically fall into his lap. I thought Michael Singer was going to tell me to stop working, stop planning, and just "trust the universe" in a way that would probably result in me being evicted. I expected a book that was disconnected from the reality of business, money, and "real world" stakes.

I was floored by how practical—and how wildly successful—this "experiment" actually was. This isn't just a book about meditation; it’s the story of how a man decided to stop letting his personal likes and dislikes run his life and instead said "yes" to whatever the flow of life brought him.

Watching him go from a lone hippie in the woods to the CEO of a billion-dollar public company, simply by not resisting, was a total brain-shift for me. It wasn't about being passive; it was about being incredibly active in service of what was happening right in front of him. I found myself looking at my own life and realizing how much energy I spend fighting things that are already happening. Reading it felt like a permission slip to let go of the steering wheel for a second and see where the road actually wants to go.

10 Lessons and Insights

1. The Voice in Your Head is a Preference Machine: Most of our internal dialogue is just us complaining about things we don't like or obsessing over things we do. Surrender is about ignoring that chatter and looking at the facts instead.

2. Life Knows Better Than You Do: The forces that create galaxies and manage the weather are also managing your life. Singer suggests that the "flow of life" has a much better perspective on what you need than your limited ego does.

3. Saying "Yes" to the Unpleasant: The experiment started when he decided to do things he didn't want to do, simply because life asked him to. These "unwanted" tasks often led to his greatest breakthroughs.

4. Non-Resistance is a Superpower: When you stop fighting reality, you have 100% of your energy available to actually deal with reality. Resistance is just a leak in your gas tank.

5. Your "Personal Self" is a Prison: We build a cage out of our "likes" and "dislikes." We only feel okay if the world matches our specific preferences. Surrender breaks the bars of that cage.

6. The "Invisible Hand" of Opportunity: Singer shows that when you stop trying to force your own agenda, opportunities appear that you couldn't have possibly planned or imagined.

7. Do the Task, Not the Ego: Whatever job was in front of him—building a house or writing code—he did it with total focus, as if it were a gift from the universe. Quality comes from presence, not from personal ambition.

8. Internal Peace is the Only Metric: The goal of the experiment wasn't wealth or success; it was to see if he could stay peaceful regardless of what was happening. The success was just a side effect of that peace.

9. Letting Go of the "Inner Judge": We spend so much time judging whether an event is "good" or "bad." Surrender teaches you to view events as "what is happening," which removes the emotional baggage.

10. The Experiment Never Ends: Surrender isn't a one-time decision; it’s a moment-by-moment practice. Every time you feel that internal "clinch" of resistance, it’s a signal to let go and dive back into the flow.

The First Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly, Ambrose Lomin, has strongly condemned armed rebellions that target innocent civilians and questioned the credibility of opposition groups that claim to pursue political power while subjecting their own communities to violence and suffering.

“If I am from Juba, I should not go to Juba land and kill my people. If I am Nuer, I should not go to Nuer land and kill Nuer civilians. If I were Dinka, I would not go to Dinka land and kill my own people. The government is here in Juba,” Lomin said on Monday during the reception ceremony for the newly appointed Minister of Mining, Lasuba Ludoru Wongo.

He added that such violence undermines the legitimacy of rebellion and justifies interim leaders remaining in the capital rather than returning to communities affected by conflict.

Meanwhile, the Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, Onyoti Adigo, criticized divisions within the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement–in Opposition (SPLM-IO), highlighting the fragmentation into multiple factions with differing views on peace.

He pointed to Machar’s faction, a faction led by a self-styled interim chairperson, Stephen Par Kuol, and a faction he accused of mobilizing for renewed conflict, hinting at Oyet Nathaniel Pierino, the former First Deputy Speaker of the Transitional National Legislative Assembly.

“There is another group headed by a former deputy speaker who has declared war against the people of South Sudan. This is unacceptable; such actions undermine the peace agreement and contradict the position of SPLM-IO leader Dr. Riek Machar, who does not support a return to armed conflict.

“Even Dr. Riek Machar is not for war. How can someone declare war on behalf of a chairman who does not support war?”

He accused the faction of collaborating with non-signatories to the peace agreement, describing these actions as contrary to national interests.

“Nobody will stand with those who are enemies of peace. We are for peace,” he said, while commending other opposition groups that have rejected violence and noting their contribution to national stability.

 Kiristaanummaan baay’inaan Ameerikaa, Awurooppaa fi Afrikaa Sahaaraa gadii keessatti babal’ateera.  Addunyaa irratti amantii guddaa yoo ta'u, addunyaa guutuutti hordoftoota biliyoonaan lakkaa'aman qaba.

 Kiristaanummaan Yesus akka Ilma Waaqayyoo fi Fayyisaa dhala namaatti amanuu cimsee kan ibsu yoo ta’u, amantiiwwan ijoo jaalala, dhiifama, fayyinaa fi abdii jireenya bara baraa dabalatee.

 Waaqeffannaan kiristaanaa akkaataa adda addaatiin kadhannaa, dubbisa macaafa qulqulluu, icciitii akka cuuphaa fi irbaata, fi waldaa hawaasa amantii keessatti of keessatti qabata.

➨Walumaa galattii:-

Kiristaanummaan amantii waaqa tokkicha addunyaa irratti isa guddaa yoo ta’u, jireenya, barsiisa, du’aa fi du’aa ka’uu Iyyesuus Kiristoos kan hordoftoonni Ilma Waaqayyoo fi Masiihii abdachiifame ta’uu isaa amanan irratti kan xiyyeeffate dha.  Hordoftoonni, Kiristaana jedhamuun kan beekaman, aarsaan Yesus cubbuu namaaf araara, hariiroo dhala namaa Waaqayyoo wajjin qabu isa cabe deebisee fi fayyinaa fi jireenya bara baraa karaa amantii isaatti dhiyeessuun, macaafa qulqulluu, Macaafa Qulqulluu (Kakuu Moofaa fi Kakuu Haaraa)tiin qajeelfamuun ni amanu.  Dameewwan gurguddoon Roomaa Kaatolikii, Ortodoksii Bahaa fi Pirootestaantii kan dabalatu yoo ta’u, sochiiwwan adda addaa kan akka Peentaaqosteezimii fi Wangeelaas ni jiru.

➨ Amantii_fi_Hojiiwwan_Ijoo:
 ➨ Waaqayyo:-  Waaqa tokko, akka Abbaa, Ilma (Yesuus Kiristoos), fi Hafuura Qulqulluu ta’ee kan jiru.

 ➨ Macaafa Qulqulluu:- Sagalee Waaqayyoo hafuura Qulqulluutiin barreeffame, amantii fi jireenyaaf qajeelfama isa dhumaa ta’ee kan tajaajilu, Kakuu Moofaa fi Kakuu Haaraa kan of keessaa qabudha.

 ➨ Barsiisota Ijoo:- Waaqayyoon jaalladhu, ollaa kee jaalladhu, namoota biroof dhiifama godhi, dhiifama Waaqayyoo barbaadi, warra rakkatan tajaajili. 

 Gama Ijoo:-
 ➨ Ka’umsa:- Dh.K.D jaarraa 1ffaa keessa Yihudoota irraa kan jalqabe Yihudaa keessattidha.
➨ Hawaasa:- Waldaa, hawaasa fi amantootaa irratti kan xiyyeeffate yoo ta’u, jaalala, gara laafina fi haqa hawaasummaa cimsee kan ibsu ture.
