ETT SKAKANDE VITTNESMÅL FRÅN EN DRABBAD FAMILJ
Från DN 13 januari om Christian Sonesson (M), KO i Staffanstorp, som 2022 ville prioritera ukrainska flyktingar framför människor från Mellanöstern:

"Snart fyra år har gått sedan han blåste till strid – mot kvotflyktingmottagande, bosättningslagen och Migrationsverket. Efter att han fått veta att en kvotflyktingfamilj med fyra syriska flyktingar hade anvisats till Staffanstorp – föreslog han att kommunen skulle sätta stopp.

– Vi kommer inte möta dem på flygplatsen, sa Sonesson om kvotflyktingfamiljen till DN i maj 2022.

Nu möter han dem i stället i en rättssal i Lunds tingsrätt. Sonesson och ytterligare fem kommunpolitiker står åtalade för grovt tjänstefel – efter att ha beslutat om ett totalstopp för mottagande av kvotflyktingar i kommunen."

Hela åtalet och rättegången är som en enda stor fars, som inte blir bättre när den syriska familjen avger sitt skakande vittnesmål: 

"I rättssalen beskriver mamman i familjen, Yasmine Al-Fadel, hur ledsen hon blev när hon förstod att familjen inte var välkommen.

– Det var en chock för oss, säger Yasmine Al-Fadel. Jag kände mig bruten. I Ukraina hade krig utbrutit, men även hos oss, säger hon."

Naturligtvis blev den hårt prövade Yasmine bruten. Här hade hon i hela sitt liv suttit i Syrien och drömt om ett liv i lilla skånska Staffanstorp och så hamnade familjen i Vellinge istället. Vilket nerköp, vilken besvikelse, vilket svek!  

Familjen Al-Hariri/Al-Fadel hade dock inte valt Sverige, till Fredrik Reinfeldts stora förtret, utan Sverige hade genom UNHCR handplockat dem som kvotflyktingar just hit. Och den fullständiga och slutliga katastrofen för den hårt krigsdrabbade familjen blev ett faktum. 

Inte nog med att de förflyttades till det genomrasistiska Sverige, de tvingades dessutom bo i Vellinge, en av Sveriges mest vackra, välmående, lugna och trygga kommuner. Inte undra på att mamma Yasmine blev helt knäckt. 

Av alla märkligheter och vansinnigheter jag genom åren upplevt som konsult inom socialtjänsten var mitt uppdrag i en mindre kommun 2018 det allra mest bisarra. Jag och en anställd kollega tog emot kvotflyktingar, och detaljer om hur det gick till återkommer jag till i en kommande krönika i Bulletin. 

Fakta: Det svenska kvotflyktingmottagandet år 2020 var högst i Europa sett till faktiskt antal. Sverige stod för 39 procent av alla överföringar. Sett till landets storlek var Sverige då världens största mottagare av kvotflyktingar. I faktiska tal var det enbart USA, Kanada och Tyskland som tog emot fler. Numera tar vi emot 900 kvotflyktingar per år. 

Min erfarenhet av hur otroligt besvikna, missnöjda och fly förbannade alla dessa kvotflyktingar alltid blir när de anländer till den svenska kommun som tar emot dem föreslår jag att vi helt slopar denna grymma verksamhet. 

Innan vi helt förstör livet för ännu fler hårt drabbade flyktingfamiljer från Mellanöstern! 😎

Data terhimpun, peristiwa tragis itu terjadi sekitar pukul 11.15 WIB ketika korban sedang membereskan tempat tidur. Korban diketahui bernama Erat (58 tahun), warga Kampung Sukabakti RT 026 RW 010 , Desa Gunung Karamat, Kecamatan Cisolok.

Diketahui Lokasi kejadian merupakan rumah anak korban, yakni di Kampung Gunungsari.

Camat Cisolok, Okih Pazri Assidiq, saat di komfrimasi membenarkan kejadian tersebut. Menurutnya saat kejadian, korban tengah membereskan tempat tidur seorang diri di dalam kamar.

"Menurut keterangan saksi, sat itu Korban sedang membereskan Tempat Tidur sendirian di kamarnya. Kemudian korban Terperosok kedalam Septitank dengan kedalaman kurang lebih 6 Meter yang posisinya berada disamping tempat tidurnya," terang Okih, Selasa (13/01). 

Lebih lanjut Camat Cisolok mengatakan, peristiwa tersebut pertama kali diketahui  oleh Anak Perempuanya.

"Anak perempuan nya yang mengetahui peristiwa itu kemudian meminta tolong kepada tetangga sekitar TKP. kemudian Tetangga Korban melaporkan kejadian tersebut kepada Kepala Dusun dan diteruskan Kepada Kasi Trantib Kecamatan Cisolok untuk segera melakukan penyelamatan," 

Upaya evakuasi pun segera dilakukan oleh aparat bersama warga sekitar, namun, nyawa korban tidak dapat diselamatkan.

"Pada saat korban di evakuasi dari dalam Septik tank Korban sudah dalam Keadaan Meninggal Dunia," sambung Okih. 

Selanjutnya korban sementara di semayamkan dirumah duka di Kampung Gunungsari Desa Cicadas Kecamatan Cisolok untuk selanjutnya dibawa Ke Kampung halamanya di Kampumg Sukabakti Desa Gunung Karamat Kecamatan Cisolok untuk dikebumikan.

ຝົນກົດແມ່ນ ຝົນ, ຫິມະ, ໝອກ ຫຼື ຝຸ່ນ ທີ່ມີກົດ(ອາຊິດ)ອັນຕະລາຍປະປົນຢູ່ ມັນເກີດຂຶ້ນເມື່ອອາກາດປົນເປື້ອນມົນລະພິດປະສົມກັບນໍ້າ ແລະ ອົກຊີແຊນໃນຊັ້ນບັນຍາກາດ.

Acid rain is rain, snow, fog, or dry dust that contains harmful acids. It happens when dirty air mixes with water and oxygen in the atmosphere
Normal rain: pH ≈ 5.6
Acid rain: pH ≈ 4.2–4.4 (much more acidic)
 
The main cause of acid rain is human activity, especially:
Burning coal, oil, and gas Power plants, factories, and vehicles
These activities release:
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂)
Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)
These gases mix with water and oxygen and later fall back to the ground as acid rain.
 
Acid rain harms nature in many ways. It makes lakes and rivers too acidic, which can kill fish and other water animals. It also damages forests by removing important nutrients from the soil and weakening trees. Over time, this can cause many plants and animals to disappear. For people, breathing polluted air or acid fog can cause eye irritation, breathing problems, and asthma.
 
To stop acid rain, we need to reduce air pollution. This means using less fossil fuel, switching to clean energy like solar and wind power, and controlling pollution from factories and power plants.

O Tribunal de Justiça do Rio de Janeiro decidiu manter Jairo Souza Santos Junior, conhecido como Dr. Jairinho, no Tribunal do Júri que irá julgar a morte do menino Henry Borel, de apenas 4 anos. O julgamento está marcado para o dia 23 de março.

A decisão foi proferida pelo desembargador Joaquim Domingos de Almeida Neto, da 7ª Câmara Criminal, que rejeitou o pedido de liminar apresentado pela defesa do ex-vereador. Os advogados tentavam suspender o julgamento sob a alegação de supostas irregularidades processuais e aguardavam análise de recursos em instâncias superiores.

Para o magistrado, a defesa não conseguiu demonstrar qualquer risco concreto de prejuízo irreparável caso o julgamento prossiga. No entendimento do tribunal, não ficou comprovado que a continuidade do processo violaria direitos fundamentais do réu ou tornaria eventual decisão futura ineficaz.

O desembargador ressaltou que a concessão de liminar em habeas corpus exige prova clara da plausibilidade jurídica do pedido e da urgência extrema, requisitos que, segundo ele, não foram atendidos no caso.

Com isso, o processo segue seu curso normal e Dr. Jairinho permanece como réu no julgamento popular, que deverá decidir sua responsabilidade pela morte da criança.

O crime que chocou o Brasil

Henry Borel morreu em março de 2021 após dar entrada em um hospital na Barra da Tijuca, no Rio de Janeiro, apresentando múltiplas lesões pelo corpo. À época, a mãe, Monique Medeiros, e o padrasto alegaram que a criança havia sofrido um acidente doméstico.

As investigações, porém, desmontaram essa versão. Laudos e depoimentos apontaram que Henry foi vítima de agressões repetidas e tortura. Dr. Jairinho é acusado de ter cometido o crime, enquanto Monique responde por omissão.

A brutalidade do caso gerou comoção nacional e levou à criação da Lei Henry Borel, que endureceu as punições para crimes de violência contra crianças e adolescentes, classificando o homicídio de menores de 14 anos como crime hediondo. #JustiçaPorHenry #TribunalDoJúri #CrimeHediondo #LeiHenryBorel #ViolênciaInfantil #ImpunidadeNão #BrasilIndignado #DireitosDasCrianças #CasoHenryBorel

The Greater Giyani Municipality has responded to complaints about the lack of drainage in the town's CBD, saying that businessmen who built shops without proper planning are to blame. These individuals have allegedly blocked the drainage system, causing water to accumulate in the area.

This beat-up car was blocking the last available pull-through spot, buried under fresh snow. I wiped the frost from the window, ready to shout at whoever was inside to move.

I didn't scream. I froze.

The windows were iced over from the inside. Through the haze, I saw a woman in the driver’s seat, slumped over the wheel, wearing a bright blue warehouse vest. In the back, under a pile of laundry, was a mound of blankets that rose and fell with the rhythm of breathing.

They were freezing to death.

I tapped the glass. The woman, Elena, jerked awake with a look of pure terror. Her fingers were too stiff with cold to even work the door lock.

"Easy, ma'am," I yelled, holding up my hands. "I'm a driver. You’re just... you’re in a truck spot."

She cracked the window, and the air that escaped was colder than the night itself. "I'm sorry," she chattered. "The engine... it overheats if we idle, but the battery dies if we stop." She turned the key. The engine let out a sickening, metal-on-metal groan. Then, silence.

From the back, a small voice whispered, "Mom? Is it time for school?"

"No, Leo, go back to sleep," she replied, her voice breaking.

Leo was maybe eight years old, pale and shivering. Next to him was a medical cooler. "He's diabetic," Elena said. "The heater died hours ago. I’m trying to keep his insulin from freezing, but I can’t keep him warm at the same time."

She had a job. She had a car. But she was one bad winter night away from a total catastrophe. My instinct was to dial 911, but I hesitated. I’ve been on the road since the nineties; I know how that goes. The system often punishes poverty. If I called, they might take the car—and the boy.

"Please," she begged, seeing my phone. "I have a shift at 6 AM. If I miss it, I lose the job. Just give us a jump."

A jump wouldn't fix a seized alternator.

The Network Activates
"I'm not calling the cops," I said. "Turn off your lights."

I walked back to my rig and picked up the CB mic. "Breaker one-nine. This is Big Mack at Mile Marker 402. I’ve got a human situation. Not a police one."

Static cleared. "Go ahead, Mack. This is Iron Man, five minutes out."

"I’ve got a car here. Mom and a sick kid. No heat. Kid needs meds kept stable. I need a mechanic, a temperature-controlled pack, and I need a wall."

"A wall?"

"Wind is forty knots from the north. I need a windbreak."

Ten minutes later, the ground vibrated. Elena watched in shock as three massive rigs rolled in. They didn't honk. They moved with surgical precision. Iron Man pulled his rig parallel on her left. Another driver, 'Diesel,' pulled up on her right. I backed my trailer across the front. We boxed her in, creating a steel fortress that killed the wind instantly.

Diesel jumped out with a heavy toolbox. He didn't ask questions; he popped her hood. "Belt's shredded, alternator's seized," he grunted. "You got sixty bucks?"

She looked at the ground. "I have fifteen."

"Keep it," Diesel said. He pulled a spare belt and a refurbished alternator from his own truck’s stash. "I can make this fit. Give me twenty minutes."

Iron Man, hauling refrigerated produce, brought over a thermal bag. "Put the meds in here," he said gently. "It’ll stay at exactly thirty-six degrees."

I opened my cab door. "Elena," I said. "Take Leo. My bunk heater is at seventy. Get two hours of real sleep. We’ll fix the car."

She hesitated, looking at three rough-looking men in the snow. Then she looked at her son's blue lips. "Why?" she asked.

"Because we're heading the same way," I told her. "Forward."

The Payload Delivered
They slept in my cab while I sat in her car, drinking coffee, watching Diesel work in sub-zero temperatures. We didn't talk about politics or the economy. We just passed wrenches and held flashlights.

By 5:30 AM, the sedan was purring and the heat was blasting. I woke Elena. After a few hours of warmth and a breakfast sandwich Iron Man had bought, she looked human again. When she tried to give me her fifteen dollars, I pushed it back.

Diesel handed her a scrap of paper. "My number," he said. "And Iron Man's, and Mack's. If you break down on this interstate, you don't call a tow truck. You call us. We’ll find someone."

She drove off as the sun cracked the horizon—a small silver car disappearing into the American morning. She made her shift.

"You good, Mack?" Iron Man asked over the radio.

"Yeah," I replied, putting my rig in gear. "Payload delivered."

The Lesson: The Real Safety Net
Here is the truth: The real safety net isn't a government program or a policy written in a distant building. The safety net is us. It’s the person who stops when they don’t have to. It’s the driver who shares a spare part in a blizzard. It’s the understanding that we are all just one bad break away from the cold.

America is a vast, lonely highway. But if you listen to the static, you’ll realize you aren't alone. Look for the helpers—or better yet, be one. The most valuable cargo you will ever carry is a little bit of kindness.

هذه سيرة عَلمٍ من أعلام هذه الأمَّة ، وبطل مِن أبطالها ، صحابيٍ جليل مِن أصحاب النبي ﷺ ، هذا الصحابي كان من السابقين إلى الإسلام ممن شهد بدراً و أُحد ،

Satuan Reserse Kriminal (Satreskrim) Polres Kediri Kota berhasil mengungkap kasus pencurian sepeda motor (curanmor) yang beraksi di sejumlah tempat kejadian perkara (TKP). Dalam pengungkapan tersebut, polisi mengamankan pasangan suami istri siri sebagai tersangka.

Kedua tersangka masing-masing berinisial WN (29), warga Kecamatan Prambon, Kabupaten Nganjuk, dan istrinya SN (33), warga Kabupaten Sidoarjo.

Kasat Reskrim Polres Kediri Kota, AKP Cipto Dwi Leksana, menyampaikan pengungkapan kasus tersebut saat konferensi pers di Mapolres Kediri Kota, Rabu (14/1/2026).

“Kami berhasil mengamankan barang bukti berupa empat unit sepeda motor hasil curian dan satu unit sepeda motor yang digunakan sebagai sarana pelaku dalam melakukan aksi curanmor,” ungkap AKP Cipto.

AKP Cipto menjelaskan, kasus curanmor ini terungkap berawal dari laporan seorang korban warga Desa/Kecamatan Tarokan, Kabupaten Kediri. Saat itu, korban memarkir sepeda motornya di pinggir sawah ketika pergi memupuk tanaman jagung.

“Setelah selesai beraktivitas di sawah, korban mendapati sepeda motor Honda Supra X 125 miliknya sudah tidak ada di tempat,” jelasnya.

Menindaklanjuti laporan tersebut, Unit Resmob Satreskrim Polres Kediri Kota bersama Unit Reskrim Polsek Tarokan langsung melakukan olah TKP dan penyisiran lokasi yang terpantau kamera CCTV. Dari hasil analisis rekaman tersebut, petugas berhasil mengantongi petunjuk arah pergerakan pelaku.

“Petugas mendapati pelaku berhenti di sebuah ruko. Setelah dilakukan pengecekan, ruko tersebut diketahui milik tersangka. Saat dilakukan penangkapan, ditemukan sepeda motor Yamaha Mio dan Honda Supra X 125,” terang AKP Cipto.

Sevty Utami Nandha (40), residivis kasus obat terlarang asal Bandung, kembali ditangkap polisi di Bali setelah diduga mengedarkan obat terlarang kepada wisatawan. Sevty sebelumnya divonis 16 tahun penjara pada 2010 dan bebas pada 2019 setelah mendapat remisi.

Kasatnarkoba Polresta Denpasar Kompol M. Akbar Ekaputra menyebut Sevty pindah ke Bali karena aktivitasnya di Jakarta sudah terpantau aparat. Di Bali, ia diduga memanfaatkan ramainya turis untuk kembali menjalankan peredaran obat terlarang.

Sevty ditangkap bersama rekannya, Grace Natalia (53), usai polisi menindaklanjuti laporan warga terkait aktivitas mencurigakan di sebuah rumah kos di Jalan Pura Demak, Denpasar. Dari penggeledahan, polisi menyita sejumlah barang bukti berupa sabu, ekstasi, dan ganja.

Polisi menduga jaringan Sevty di Bali berbeda dengan jaringan yang pernah ia miliki di Jakarta. Penyelidikan masih dilakukan untuk menelusuri pemasok barang terlarang tersebut.

Keduanya dijerat pasal dalam UU Narkotika dan KUHP baru, dengan ancaman hukuman maksimal 12 tahun penjara.

She saved thousands of lives with a cookie.
In 1942, Japanese soldiers patrolled the streets of Manila, and thousands of Allied prisoners were starving to death in internment camps.
Maria Orosa—a 49-year-old food scientist—was supposed to evacuate. Her family begged her to flee to safety in Batangas. Friends pleaded with her to leave before it was too late.
She refused.
"I'm a soldier," she said. "I stay at my post."
And her post? A chemistry laboratory that had become the most important battlefield in the Philippines.
Because Maria Orosa had discovered something extraordinary: she could keep people alive with science.

This was 1942. The year Casablanca premiered in theaters. The year the Manhattan Project began. And in the Philippines, the year Japanese occupation brought systematic starvation to imprisoned Americans and Filipinos.
The Santo Tomás Internment Camp held over 4,000 civilians—teachers, businessmen, missionaries, families. They were given rice water and scraps. Children's ribs showed through their skin. Adults weighed less than 100 pounds. People were dying of malnutrition, beriberi, and starvation.
The Japanese guards watched. And waited for them to die.
But Maria Orosa had other plans.

She had spent two decades preparing for this moment, though she didn't know it.
Born in 1893 in Taal, Batangas, Maria was brilliant. She earned degrees in pharmaceutical chemistry and food chemistry from the University of Washington—during a time when Filipino women weren't supposed to pursue science, when women of any nationality rarely earned advanced degrees.
She returned to the Philippines in 1922 with a mission: make her country self-sufficient through food innovation.
While other scientists worked in ivory towers, Maria worked in villages. She taught rural women how to preserve food, raise poultry, plan nutritious meals. She created the palayok oven—a clay cooking device for families without electricity. By 1924, her "4H Clubs" had over 22,000 members.
But her most famous invention seemed almost silly at first.
Tomato ketchup was popular in the Philippines—an American import that Filipinos loved. But it was expensive. And tomatoes didn't grow well in tropical climates.
So in the 1930s, Maria looked at the abundance around her and thought: Why tomatoes when we have bananas everywhere?
She created a ketchup from mashed bananas, vinegar, spices, and a dash of red food coloring. Sweet. Tangy. Brilliantly red.
Banana ketchup became a national obsession. Today, it's in every Filipino kitchen, manufactured by major corporations, beloved across generations.
Maria Orosa had given the Philippines a taste of independence—one condiment at a time.
But then the war came. And Maria's gifts became weapons.

When Japan invaded in 1941, Maria didn't flee. She joined Marking's Guerrillas—a resistance movement fighting the occupation—and was given the rank of captain.
But Captain Orosa didn't carry a rifle.
She carried a chemistry degree and 700 recipes in her head.
Working in her laboratory with 400 students, Maria invented two products that would save thousands of lives:
Soyalac – a powdered soybean drink so nutrient-dense it was called "magic food." One serving contained complete nutrition. It could keep a starving person alive.
Darak – rice bran cookies packed with vitamin B-1. As guerrilla leader Valeria Panlilio wrote: "One teaspoon a day could keep a starving man's digestive system functioning. A palmful could keep him on his feet. Two palmfuls? He could fight."
Maria had turned local, abundant resources—soybeans and rice bran that others discarded—into concentrated life itself.
But creating the food wasn't enough. She had to get it into the camps.

The plan was audacious.
Maria hired local carpenters who could move freely through the city. They hollowed out bamboo sticks and filled them with Soyalac and Darak powder. Then they walked into Santo Tomás and other prison camps, pretending to deliver construction materials.
The guards never suspected.
Bamboo by bamboo, Maria Orosa smuggled nutrition to dying prisoners. American soldiers. Filipino civilians. Children who had forgotten what it felt like to have energy.
They called it "magic food" because it seemed like magic—people who could barely stand were suddenly able to walk. To think. To hope.
One American POW later wrote: "We didn't know her name. We didn't know where the food came from. We just knew that someone, somewhere, was fighting to keep us alive."
That someone was a 50-year-old chemist risking her life every single day.
If the Japanese had discovered what she was doing, they would have executed her immediately. But Maria kept working. Kept cooking. Kept smuggling.
Because science wasn't just her profession. It was her resistance.

By early 1945, American forces were fighting to retake Manila.
The Battle of Manila became one of the most devastating urban battles of World War II. The city was being destroyed. Buildings crumbled. Artillery shells fell constantly.
Maria's family begged her—one last time—to evacuate.
She refused.
"I'm a soldier," she repeated. "I stay at my post."
On February 13, 1945, Maria was working in her laboratory when the shelling intensified. Her colleagues urged her toward the bomb shelter.
On the way, shrapnel tore through her body.
A colleague found a pushcart—the only transportation available during the bombardment—and rushed her to Remedios Hospital in Malate.
The hospital was overwhelmed. Volunteers were treating hundreds of wounded. Maria was brought inside, bleeding, fighting to survive.
And then another shell hit the hospital.
Over 400 people died instantly—doctors, nurses, patients, civilians seeking refuge.
Maria Orosa was among them.
She was 51 years old. She had invented over 700 recipes. She had fed a nation. She had saved thousands from starvation.
And she died at her post, just as she said she would.

For decades, her story was nearly forgotten.
Corporations commercialized her inventions without crediting her. Banana ketchup became ubiquitous, but few knew who created it. Streets bore her name, but people didn't know why.
It wasn't until recently that historians, chefs, and activists began resurrecting her legacy.
Google honored her with a Doodle in 2019. The National Historical Institute placed a marker at the Bureau of Plant Industry. Her remains, lost for decades, were finally given a proper burial in 2025 at San Agustin Church.
And slowly, the world is remembering what Maria Orosa proved:
That science can be an act of love. That feeding people is revolutionary. That a woman in a laboratory can save more lives than an army with guns.

Here's what they don't tell you about heroes:
They don't always carry weapons. They don't always fight on battlefields.
Sometimes they carry test tubes and mixing bowls. Sometimes they fight with chemistry and ingenuity and quiet, relentless determination.
Sometimes they invent a condiment that makes people smile—and then weaponize that same creativity to keep prisoners of war alive.
Sometimes they refuse to evacuate because they understand something essential: that their work matters more than their safety.
Maria Orosa could have fled. Could have survived the war. Could have lived a long, celebrated life.
But she chose to stay. Because thousands of people were starving, and she knew how to feed them.
She invented banana ketchup to make her country smile.
She invented Soyalac and Darak to keep her country alive.
And when they told her to run, she stayed at her post—because that's what soldiers do.
The next time you see banana ketchup in a Filipino kitchen, remember:
It's not just a condiment.
It's a reminder that one woman's genius, courage, and refusal to abandon her people changed history—one recipe, one bamboo stick, one life at a time.
She was a scientist. A patriot. A captain.
And she saved thousands with nothing but chemistry, creativity, and unshakable courage.

At just four years old, he saw his world fall apart. Until then, his days followed gentle routines: his mother’s voice coming from the kitchen, his father lifting him high as if he could reach the clouds, and the strong sense of safety that only a child knows.

Then the war shattered everything. 

Then the soldiers came.

Joseph Schlipstein was his name. He was taken with his parents, held close to his father, not understanding what was happening. 

The trains were crowded with people and fear, the air thick with silent screams. When the doors opened, he saw the sign:

 "Jedem das Seine"—"To each his own." This was Buchenwald. This was hell.

In a place where children were not meant to survive, Joseph did not belong. He was too small to work, seen as too weak to live.

His father knew the only way to protect him was to hide him. Every day, with great courage, he placed Joseph in a suitcase. He opened it just to let him breathe, give him water, and offer comforting words. When she could, his mother left him a piece of bread. While sirens, shouts, and footsteps echoed outside, Joseph learned to stay silent in his small hiding place.

But one day, the suitcase was found.

The soldiers opened the suitcase and found Joseph shaking, his eyes wide with fear. They beat his father, but not him. For reasons no one understood, they let him live. They called him "the little one of the camp." He was given scraps of food and cloth. He became a strange symbol—a living child in a place ruled by death.

Joseph did not know why he was still alive. He remembered the cold, the smoke from the chimneys, and the men who left and never came back. He remembered his father's face, full of love and fear, saying goodbye.

When the camp was freed in 1945, Joseph had just turned five. He was thin and weak, but he was alive.

Three years later, an American journalist took his photo and it was seen around the world. He still wore his striped uniform and sat on a chair much too big for him, looking as if he had seen everything. He was only seven, but his eyes looked old.

His story became a symbol of hope. The boy in the suitcase had survived against all odds, but not by himself. He lived because of an act of love that broke through hatred.

As years passed, Joseph shared his story with anyone who wanted to hear it. He spoke quietly and calmly, knowing that words cannot change the past, but they can help stop it from happening again. He said he did not remember every face, but he remembered every hand: his father's, who protected him, and the soldiers', who, for reasons he never understood, let him live.

Joseph kept that suitcase for the rest of his life. It was not a symbol of fear, but a reminder of a love so strong it overcame death.

Today, whenever we remember Joseph Schlipstein, the child who survived the war, we are reminded of one important truth: even in the darkest times, life finds a way to shine.

In the face of systemic evil, individual mercy is a revolutionary act. Joseph survived because of a father’s devotion and a soldier’s inexplicable choice to look away. 

This reminds us that in every moment, we hold the power to choose compassion over cruelty, and those choices can echo through generations. 

No cage is small enough to crush the human spirit.

For more than a hundred years Yellowstone’s bison moved in broken groups cut off by fences roads and human control. Yellowstone’s bison herds are merging and moving as one again following paths their ancestors walked generations ago.

This matters more than it sounds. Bison migration helps grasslands stay healthy spreads seeds naturally and supports countless other species. Their hooves aerate soil. Their grazing patterns prevent overgrowth. Even birds and insects depend on their movement. What shocked researchers most is that no one taught them these routes. The bison simply knew. Somewhere deep in instinct and memory the map survived.

Stories of Service and Sacrifice

Christian Nix was born on August 2, 1836, in Ederbach, Baden, Germany. He immigrated to the United States age 14 with his parents. Nix became a naturalized U.S. citizen on November 3, 1857, in Milwaukee County, Wisconsin.

On June 4, 1861, Nix married Maria Kasper, who had been born in Crenznach, Prussia, on March 13, 1840. Shortly after the war began, Nix enlisted in Company F of the 6th Wisconsin Infantry on June 6, 1861. He rose to the rank of third sergeant while serving in the area that became West Virginia. After approximately one year of service, mustered out of the 6th Wisconsin to sign on as a second lieutenant in the 24th Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, Company D.

Nix and the 24th Wisconsin found themselves caught up in the collapse of the Union right wing during the opening hours of the Battle of Stones River. On December 31, 1862, Nix was shot during the fighting and taken to a hospital at the Gresham house that was soon overrun. He died from his wounds on January 5 or 6, 1863.

On January 14, 1863, Company D's Captain Alvah Philbrook wrote a letter to Maria stating:

“You have lost your best friend on Earth and we deeply feel with you in this sad bereavement for we too have lost an esteemed friend and a true soldier.”

Lt. Christian Nix is buried in plot N-5390 of Stones River National Cemetery where his story continues to represent the sacrifice of immigrant soldiers who fought and died their adopted country. You can see a copy of Capt. Philbrook's letter along with Lt. Nix's sword and officer's sash displayed in our museum.

You can read more about Christian Nix and other stories spanning more than 160 years of service to our nation and its ideals at go.nps.gov/sacrifice.
Stories of Service and Sacrifice is an initiative remembering at least 250 individuals buried at Stones River National Cemetery and their contributions to our nation’s 250-year story.

On the week I won 47 million, I asked my family for five thousand and watched them turn my panic into entertainment. My mom texted, “Cassie, stop calling people. You’re making us look bad,” like my rent was a PR problem. My stepdad’s voice went flat: “You’re not my daughter.” My sister offered “maybe three hundred,” and my brother vanished until he needed “two grand” for a “sure thing.” Meanwhile the winning ticket sat in my kitchen, hidden behind a tiny US flag magnet on the fridge, holding a handwritten list of ten names I planned to call. I wasn’t trying to be cruel. I just wanted to know who would show up before money made strangers out of everyone.

Before that ticket, I was invisible in every room. I balanced spreadsheets at a small Portland office while my boss recycled my ideas with his name attached, and a coworker slipped out early, leaving me to clean up. At home, my family treated me the same way: reliable, quiet, always available. Jason’s “emergencies,” Lisa’s “shortfalls,” Dad’s lectures, Mom’s warmth — it all landed on me like unpaid labor.

Every Friday I stopped at Gus’s market for one ticket. On my birthday I bought an extra, ate Thai takeout, and checked the numbers with zero hope. When they matched, my hands shook and the remote slipped from my grip. Sinatra crackled, iced tea sweated onto the table, and I stared until it felt real. By morning, I was in a lawyer’s office asking if my name could stay out of it.

Three weeks later, I staged a crisis. I said my company was shutting down and I needed five thousand. Mom sighed about a lake house deposit. Warren hung up. Dad lectured me about “six months of expenses.” Lisa’s concern faded. Paul barely looked up. Jason finally called — cheerful — and pitched me an “investment.”

Then the gossip hit. Quotes about “handouts,” whispers at work, a smirk from Derek, and a warning from Arnold about “instability.” That night, Aunt Martha met me at a diner with an envelope — three thousand dollars, nearly everything she had.

I invited her over, told her the truth, and she only said, “You don’t owe them access to you.”
So I scheduled a Sunday announcement, looked at the US flag magnet on my fridge, took one breath, and said, “The truth is—”👇🫢

She weighed just 68 pounds, her hair turned white from starvation, her will almost gone. Then an American soldier opened a door, and everything shifted.
May 7, 1945. Volary, Czechoslovakia.
Gerda Weissmann could no longer walk. After more than six years of persecution, ghettos, forced labor camps, and a death march stretching over 300 miles, her body finally failed her. Snow still covered the ground. Her shoes had disintegrated long before, so she wrapped her feet in scraps of cloth. Every step felt like blades slicing into frozen flesh.
She was only 20 years old, yet she looked far older. Hunger had drained the color from her skin and bleached her dark hair completely white. She weighed less than many children. Her body was barely holding on.
What truly crushed her, though, was not only the cold or the hunger. It was the loss of everyone she loved.
Her parents were gone. Her brother was gone. Friends from her hometown and the girls she had worked beside in labor camps were gone as well. One after another, they vanished, shot, gassed, beaten, or left to die in the snow. Gerda survived when almost no one else did, and she no longer knew whether survival was a blessing or a burden.
The death march had begun in January 1945, as Nazi guards evacuated camps ahead of the advancing Soviet army. Starving women were forced to march through winter with no destination except collapse. Anyone who fell behind was shot. Bodies were left in ditches as warnings.
Gerda watched women who had endured years in camps fall and die just weeks before liberation. By May, only about 120 women remained from a group that had once numbered in the hundreds. For months they had marched through snow, hunger, and terror.
Then they heard engines.
American vehicles.
The SS guards fled without a word, leaving the women behind. Liberation had arrived, but Gerda felt nothing. Hope had drained out of her long before. She stood near the entrance of an empty bicycle factory, barely conscious and barely upright.
A jeep stopped nearby. American soldiers stepped out.
One of them walked toward the building. His name was Lieutenant Kurt Klein. He was 25 years old. He wore an American uniform and spoke fluent German. He was Jewish, born in Germany, and had escaped to the United States in 1937. His parents had not escaped. They were murdered at Auschwitz.
Kurt had already helped liberate camps. He had seen starvation, death, and despair. He thought nothing could surprise him anymore.
Then he saw Gerda.
A young woman with white hair, hollow eyes, and rags wrapped around her feet. She swayed as she stood, struggling to remain upright. In that instant, something inside him shifted.
Kurt walked to the door of the factory.
And he opened it for her.
He did not shout. He did not issue commands. He did not rush her or grab her. He simply held the door open and motioned for her to go first.
For six years, Gerda had been forced through doors into trains, camps, barracks, and toward death. For six years, no one had treated her as a human being.
She later said, “He was the first person in six years who opened a door for me.”
That single gesture restored something the Nazis had tried to erase: her dignity.
Kurt spoke gently. He asked if she was Jewish. He asked if there was anything he could do for her. No one had asked her such questions in years.
Gerda was taken to a hospital, where doctors doubted she would survive. Her organs were failing. Her body was dangerously weak. Recovery seemed unlikely.
Kurt kept returning.
He brought food. He talked with her. He listened. He treated her not as a case or a number, but as a person. He shared his own losses, including the parents he would never see again.
They shared grief and understanding. Slowly, Gerda began to heal.
As her strength returned, something else grew.
They fell in love.
It was not a fairy tale that erased the past, but a bond formed by two people who had seen the worst and still believed in something better.
Kurt asked her to marry him.
In June 1946, just over a year after liberation, they were married in Paris. Gerda wore a wedding dress. She was no longer a prisoner or a number. She was choosing her future.
They moved to the United States, settled in Buffalo, New York, and built a family. Together, they made a promise to speak for those who could not.
Gerda wrote her memoir, All But My Life. She and Kurt spent decades educating students, soldiers, and leaders about the Holocaust. They spoke with honesty, not hatred.
Their marriage lasted 57 years. Kurt died in 2002. Gerda held his hand, just as he had once held a door open for her. She was remembered not only as a survivor, but as a witness. She transformed unspeakable loss into testimony, and testimony into purpose.
One open door became the beginning of a life filled with love, learning, and remembrance.
Survival is only the first step. Living is the greater victory. Gerda’s story shows that even when the spirit is nearly destroyed, the human heart can still mend.
We cannot choose what happens to us, but we can choose to turn our scars into testimony, and testimony into light.
Those who survive carry the responsibility to speak for those who cannot.
Remembrance is not only about facing the darkness of the past. It is about carrying truth forward, so the white hair of hunger is never seen again.
Our stories are our legacy. Our empathy is our strength.

"Today I had my first kiss. It wasn’t planned. It was also with a complete stranger.
I’ve always had my first kiss envisioned from the moment I learned what real love was. I imagined the sparks we would feel as we share that passionate moment. I imagined what my wolf would feel like when she recognizes him as our mate.
Going to a large college, I thought I would at least find one person that would make me want to give him everything my heart had to offer.
But I never felt what my mother felt for my father.
I’ve had a boyfriend for a couple of months, but it still never felt right. I keep thinking that when I turn 18 and get my wolf, maybe she would recognize him as our mate. Maybe he’s the one I’m supposed to be with for the rest of my life, even if I don’t see it yet.
But the moon goddess thought otherwise.
As I walked through the halls of my school, Higala Shifter Academy, I paused when a familiar sense washed over me. My boyfriend, Scott, was nearby, and he wasn’t alone. The halls were growing quiet as students went to class. It was only the sounds my heartbeat left as I made my way around the corner, only pausing when I heard a familiar giggle of a she-wolf, Sarah, and the husky growls of Scott.
“You are so naughty, Scott,” Sarah chuckled.
“Only for you, babe,” he replied, muffled as her lips closed around his.
At that moment, I felt sick to my stomach.
My next class, ceramics, was with Scott. I didn’t even want to take that class, but he thought it would be fun to take a class together. I was an art student, so I agreed.
As I stepped away, I paused as I saw a tall and broad gentleman across the hall, staring in my direction. Our eyes met only briefly and I had to admit that he was strikingly handsome.
“Oh, Scott. Stop it. You know we can’t be seen together. What if your girlfriend finds us?”
“She’s in class. She’s never late. You don’t need to worry.”
My heart was heavy in my chest, but also a wave of fury and resentment crossed me.
A crease formed between the gentlemen’s brows. I realized tears had escaped my eyes. They weren’t so much as tears of heartbreak, more like tears of disappointment. I wiped my face with the back of my hand and was about to walk past him.
I didn’t want anyone to see me like this.
Just as Scott came around the corner, I felt him freezing as he saw me. Sarah stood beside him, and I heard her gasp. I met her beautiful blue eyes.
“Lila?” Scott breathed, staring at me in shock “What are you—”
Before he could get the entire question out, I turned to the gentleman beside me, placing my hands on his shoulders and pulling him toward me. He went easily, though his eyes showed nothing but confusion. I closed my eyes tightly so I wouldn’t have to see his expression any longer.
Then, our lips touched.
His lips were soft, and they tasted so sweet, almost like marshmallows. However, his lips remained unmoving. His hands rested lazily by his sides, though mine moved comfortably around his neck.
My heart was beating rapidly in my chest. I had no idea what I was doing. I’m not sure why I did it; maybe to hurt Scott. Maybe because I was sick of holding out for something that might never be good enough in comparison to the role models I grew up with.
Either way, I seized the moment.
Though, I had no idea who this man was.
I pulled away from him, breathlessly gazing up at his grey eyes. They were growing darker as he stared into me. I wasn’t sure what lingered in his gaze, but he didn’t pull away from me. My hands continued to rest behind his neck, and I realized I was pressing my body into him.
My face grew warm as I stepped away, touching my fingers to my lips.
That was my first-ever kiss.
What. Did. I. Do?
“I need to get to class,” he said, his tone was low and almost husky. That was the first thing he’s ever said to me.
I was too stunned at my own actions to even ask him what his name was. But I nodded, brushing my dark hair out of my face with my fingers.
Scott and Sarah had already gone to class. I turned away from him, without saying anything and went in the direction of the main office. All I could think about at that moment was getting out of my next class.
I couldn’t face Scott again after that.
Even as I walked away, I could feel the gentlemen’s eyes on the back of my head, watching me.
…
“Unfortunately, there’s only one class available. All other seats are filled,” the receptionist, at the main office, said, glancing at her computer.
“And what class would that be?” I asked, trying to keep the tears from resurfacing in my eyes.
“Shifting and Combat,” she answered, staring up at me. “Would that be all right?”
Shifting? I had yet to obtain my wolf; so, that class might be difficult. However, I was skilled in combat.
“Anything but ceramics,” I said to her in return.
She frowned for a moment.
“Is everything all right, Lila? You aren’t being bullied in that class, are you?” She asked. “I can give your father—”
“No!” I said quickly; the last thing I wanted was for my father to find anything out about what had happened. He was the head of the Alpha Committee and worked closely with Scott’s dad, another Alpha. “It’s nothing like that,” I assured her.
She looked unconvinced, but she nodded just the same as she looked back at her computer, typing away. She soon printed out a new schedule, handing it to me.
“You are now in Shifting and Combat 101 with Professor Enzo. It’s in the school arena. You can head there right now.”
The arena was on the opposite end of the school; I’ve only been there a few times to practice my combatting.
But how was I going to get through a semester of shifting classes when I couldn’t even shift?
My 18(th) birthday was only a few days away; I was supposed to be heading home for the weekend to celebrate with my family. I thought I would have obtained my wolf by now, but I was mistaken.
I was the youngest wolf to get accepted into the Higala Shifting Academy; one of the largest schools for werewolf and bear shifters. I was also the only one who didn’t have a wolf yet. But that didn’t mean I was incapable.
Like my mother, I am a Volana wolf. Volanas are more powerful than regular wolves. The moon goddess had gifted us with many different abilities. Although, I haven’t received these abilities just yet.
However, I’ve studied and practiced my entire life, with some of the greatest gamma warriors and my father, on how to fight and defend myself.
I reached the arena and stood outside the doors; I could already hear the growling of wolves as they practiced their combat with one another.
Stepping inside, my eyes scanned the area briefly. Not one wolf was paying me any attention, they were fixated on each other. They were large and ferocious looking; it reminded me of the gamma training I used to watch growing up.
Stepping further into the arena, I allowed the door to shut firmly behind me. The biggest wolf stood on the far side of the arena, overlooking the combat unfolding before him.
That had to have been the professor.
He was a beautiful dark wolf that almost looked blue from the crystal lighting that danced off his thick fur. His dark eyes scanned the arena briefly before they landed on mine.
He looked oddly familiar; it wasn’t until he shifted back into his human form that I realized who he was.
It was him…
The man I kissed only moments ago in the hallway.
The man I had given my first kiss to, was my professor.

Little Girl Paid a Mafia Boss $5 to Help Her Mom — What She Said Made Him Freeze

The mafia boss was stepping out of his car when something small tapped his hand. Not a gun. Not a knife. A crumpled five-dollar bill, soft with age and folded too many times to count. He looked down.

A little girl stood in front of him.

Her hair was messy, pulled back with a cracked plastic clip. Her shoes were worn thin at the toes. Both hands were shaking as she held the bill up like it was everything she owned.

“Please,” she said quietly. “This is all I have.”

The U.S. flag magnet on the black Cadillac’s rear bumper caught the streetlight as Vincent Torino’s men moved instantly—too close, too fast. Hands drifted toward jackets. Eyes scanned for threats.

Vincent raised one hand. They froze.

Nobody paid Vincent Torino five dollars. People paid him in fear, in envelopes thick with cash, in silence. He crouched down until he was eye level with her.

“What do you want, kid?”

She swallowed, forcing the words out. “I want you to help me. Because the police won’t.”

That made him pause.

She leaned closer, voice trembling. “They said if I told anyone, my mom wouldn’t come home.”

That was when he noticed the bruised knuckles. The torn sleeve. The way her eyes kept flicking toward the dark end of the block like she expected someone to appear.

Vincent took the five dollars—not because he needed it, but because whatever she was about to ask was worth far more than money.

This was the moment that would come back later. The one he didn’t walk away from.

Friends, in today’s Gospel (Mark 1:29–39), Jesus heals many of the townspeople of Capernaum. His healing of physical ailments points to his spiritual healing—to his being the doctor of the soul.

The Gospels are filled with accounts of Jesus’s healing encounters with those whose spiritual energies are unable to flow. Much of Jesus’s ministry consisted in teaching people how to see (the kingdom of God), how to hear (the voice of the Spirit), how to walk (overcoming the paralysis of the heart), and how to be free of themselves so as to discover God.

Jesus was referred to in the early Church as the Savior (“Salvator” in Latin). The term speaks of the one who brings healing—indeed, our word “salve” is closely related to “salvus,” meaning health. When the soul is healthy, it is in a living relationship with God. When the soul is sick, the entire person becomes ill, because all flows from and depends upon the dynamic encounter with the source of being and life who is God.

We heal the soul by bringing to bear the Salvator, the healer, the one who in his person reconciled us with God and opened the soul to the divine power.

After speaking to a dear old friend and what she went through with her Nicu babies, we headed out to the hospital yesterday early afternoon on a mission. After expressing our concerns to the doctor she agreed that I knew my baby better than anyone else and agreed to pull the NG tube. Also, the ridiculous amount of 54ml of his formula every 3 hours is a bit excessive and a goal that’s just not going to be reachable for a baby of his size. So they set a minimum of 45ml every 3 hours and he’s able to have more if he wants more. Friday or sooner they will wean the oxygen (he doesn’t need it) and hopefully we get him home over the weekend or early next week. Needless to say I’m done playing the sit and wait game when my baby is ready. He doesn’t have any issues with me feeding him. The issue was the nurses have way too many babies under their care and they are only one person. So an NG tube is so much quicker and easier than to sit for 30 mins each baby to feed them. Well, that’s their problem not Westins. He deserves a fighting chance to have his 30 mins to finish his bottle. The ONLY reason he even needs 30 mins is because they have him on such high protein and added protein and it makes him extremely gassy. He struggles to burp. I’ve over heard nurses complaining about how the doctors try to grow these babies so quickly and how bad it hurts their tummy’s. There are babies that cry constantly unless being held due to upset belly’s. It’s not rocket science. I also feel they try to slow walk these babies for the insurance money as I can’t even begin to imagine what the bill is for Westin. I’ve come into the nicu to a dry bottle right after feeding time with a snotty nurse who claimed Westin ate 12 ml only just so she could justify not even trying to bottle feed him. Don’t get me wrong guys, I’m so appreciative for the doctors and nurses who’ve all cared for all babies in the nicu and I can’t ever repay them for the gratitude I have but at some point these hospitals have got to think outside of the protocol. These are humans. Not science projects. Needless to say I’m glad my tubes are tied and my uterus will be removed as soon as I’m off blood thinners and I won’t ever need to experience this part of life ever again. I love my little dude but my heart can’t handle the distance. I can’t be patient anymore. Not when I’m not seeing an issue with my baby. He’s going to thrive better with his family at home.

He was too drunk to drive. I agreed to give him a ride home. He was a friend of a friend who lived across the river. He rode in the backseat of my car, and I worried the whole time he would be sick. I got to his apartment complex, and he stumbled out of my 1973 Cutlass Supreme. I gave my backseat a quick check to make sure it was vomit-free. The guy had written something on the car window with his finger.  
It said, "Guns and Roses."
He had written it backward so that it was correct on the outside. I had no idea what the significance of those three words was. It was completely random. It was so odd I couldn't help but remember. About six months later, I would find out what those words represented along with the rest of the world.  
I taught guitar lessons at McGuire Music in Lafayette, Indiana. Axl Rose and Izzy Stradlin had grown up in the area and headed west to follow their dream. I was seven years younger and not in their musical circle. What I did see was the wave of kids who were inspired to buy guitars and take music lessons because of the popularity of Guns N' Roses. Heavy Metal wasn't my cup of tea, but I could see what music was turning kids on. Bon Jovi, Motley Crue, and Metallica all had a hand in selling guitars and amplifiers. As a music teacher, I felt obligated to keep up with what was popular. So I learned how to play most every song on Master of Puppets, …And Justice For All, Appetite for Destruction, Dr. Feelgood, and OU812. I still wanted to play rockabilly and swing for fun, but learning those songs paid my rent.  
One night, Izzy Stradlin bought some things at the guitar store. He browsed a bit and left with a conga drum and a pre-amp. Slash gets all of the attention as the lead guitarist, but I feel that Izzy was the real soul of that band. I like his song "Dust and Bones" on Use Your Illusion.
Another kid was knocking around Lafayette. His name was Shannon Hoon. He played in a band called Styff Kytten. I was in a band called The Other Side, and we shared a couple of bills with them. He was a really nice guy. Well, he got called out to Los Angeles and got hooked up with the GnR guys, and you probably know the rest of his story.
Seeing how many kids were turned on by Guns N' Roses was inspiring. They made it seem like anything was possible. You COULD escape from a small Indiana town and make something of yourself.  
From three random words on a car window to The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Who would have believed that?

1. May hawak silang warrant of arrest issued by a competent court.
2. Na-announce nila ang kanilang authority at purpose.
3. Ang refusal ng occupant ang nagbigay ng legal ground for forced entry.

Kung wala ang mga ito, ang pagpasok ay magiging unlawful. Article III, Section 2, 1987 Constitution: “The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures of whatever nature and for any purpose shall be inviolable…”

Entry into a dwelling generally requires consent of the occupant or a valid judicial process (search warrant or arrest warrant).

Rule 113, Sec. 11, Rules of Court: “The officer may break into any building or enclosure to effect an arrest if he is refused admittance thereto after he has announced his authority and purpose.” This means:

Police must first announce their authority and purpose (i.e., that they have a warrant of arrest).

If the occupant refuses to open the door, they are legally allowed to break in or use reasonable means (like climbing over a fence) to execute the arrest.

Doctrine of “knock and announce”: Officers must give notice before forced entry.

Excessive force or entry without proper announcement may render the arrest irregular and expose officers to liability.

People v. Doria (G.R. No. 125299, Jan. 22, 1999) emphasized strict compliance with warrant requirements to protect constitutional rights.

Yes, police may force entry when serving a valid arrest warrant if refused entry, but only after proper announcement of authority and purpose. | #abogadangbayan

Polemik pertemuan Eggi Sudjana dengan Presiden Republik Indonesia ke-7 Joko Widodo kembali mencuat setelah Refly Harun mengungkap pesan WhatsApp (WA) dari Eggi dalam acara talkshow Rakyat Bersuara di Inews TV, Selasa (13/1/2026) malam.

Refly Harun menyebut Eggi menegaskan bahwa kunjungannya ke rumah Joko Widodo tidak dilandasi kepentingan pribadi, tekanan politik, maupun permintaan maaf, melainkan alasan ideologis dan religius. Eggi bahkan mengaitkan keputusannya dengan perenungan Al-Qur’an Surah Taha ayat 41–46.

“Demi Allah, Subhanallāh wa ta‘ala, saya BES (Bang Eggi Sudjana-Red) ke rumah Pak Joko Widodo atas imbauan banyak pihak dan segala kepentingan mereka. Itu semua saya tolak mulai dari 4 bulan lalu,” kata Refly Harun membacakan pesan Eggi.

Dalam pesan tersebut, Eggi menganalogikan pertemuannya dengan Jokowi seperti kisah Nabi Musa yang diperintahkan Allah untuk menemui Firaun dengan sikap lemah lembut.

“Kemudian saya membaca Al-Qur’an Surah Taha ayat 41 sampai ayat 46, intinya Allah perintah kepada Nabi Musa dan Nabi Harun untuk datangi Firaun… Tapi kalian berdua berkatalah kepada Firaun dengan lemah lembut,” ujar Refly Harun mengutip pesan WhatsApp Eggi.

Eggi menegaskan, “Itulah alasan ideologis saya mau berkunjung ke JKW. Bagi yang tidak percaya, no problem.”

Pernyataan tersebut menuai kritik dari Razman Arif Nasution yang juga hadir dalam acara tersebut. Razman menilai terdapat kontradiksi antara tujuan silaturahmi dengan analogi yang digunakan Eggi.

“Datang bersilaturahmi, tapi yang ditemui dianalogikan seperti Firaun dalam Surah Taha. Itu yang membuat saya bingung,” ujar Razman.

Razman juga mengingatkan Eggi agar tidak memperpanjang polemik yang berpotensi menimbulkan persoalan hukum baru, serta meminta seniornya lebih fokus pada kesehatan.
“Saya tidak rela abang harus masuk persidangan. Saya tahu hati abang tidak seperti itu,” katanya.

Di sisi lain, peluang penerapan restorative justice atau keadilan restoratif bagi Eggi Sudjana dan Damai Hari Lubis disebut terbuka. Hal itu disampaikan Sekretaris Jenderal Peradi Bersatu, Ade Darmawan, usai memenuhi panggilan penyidik Polda Metro Jaya, Senin (12/1/2026).

“Peradi Bersatu membuka peluang penerapan restorative justice terhadap Eggi Sudjana dan Damai Hari Lubis dalam perkara dugaan pencemaran nama baik,” kata Ade.

Namun, Ade menegaskan keputusan tersebut bergantung pada persetujuan pelapor utama, yakni Joko Widodo, serta perkembangan proses penyidikan.

Sementara itu, Direktur Reserse Kriminal Umum Polda Metro Jaya Kombes Iman Imanuddin menyatakan kepolisian membuka ruang keadilan restoratif jika kedua belah pihak sepakat.

“Untuk restorative justice, kami mengakomodir hal itu, dan kami pegang sebagai proses penegakan hukum,” katanya.

Mallards of the Blue Ridge Mountains

Most people think of mallards as park ducks, but in the Blue Ridge Mountains they’re something entirely different. Here, they ride fast, cold streams, slip between fog-covered banks, and glow with iridescent green and chestnut in the soft mountain light.

Did you know:
They’re the genetic blueprint for most domestic ducks.
Nearly all common farm ducks (Pekin, Rouen, etc.) descend from wild mallards.

Their famous green head is structural color, not pigment.
Microscopic feather structures reflect light to create that emerald sheen—change the angle and the color shifts.

Females choose mates by voice, not looks.
A louder, clearer quack often signals better health and stronger genetics.

They can sleep with one eye open.
Half their brain stays awake to watch for predators—true “unihemispheric sleep.”

Frustrating Fallow Deer Management in
Ireland 

(Below you find posted an older but still very worthwhile to read article published again thanks to the permission of the author Jim Daly.)

Frustrating Fallow Deer Management in
Ireland 

Deer stalkers in Ireland have often asked why Fallow Deer heads compare so unfavourably to the best
English Fallow. Certainly this is the case and by way of answer all I can do is give you an account of my
efforts and experience.
There is no doubt that Fallow Deer are the most difficult and gregarious of our Irish species to manage for trophy
heads. They are particularly faithful to certain areas of ground and left unchecked can achieve large densities in
relatively small areas. Fallow depend on grass as a food source much more than our other species and therefore are
more likely to come into conflict with farmers. Consequently they are very accessible as most of the fields they graze
are close to roads or tracks, unlike open moor land or mountainous regions. Their size and weight is considerably
less than Red Deer making them easier to extract from the field. Hunting fallow deer is generally less demanding
physically than hunting the other species.
2
Twenty four years ago a group of friends and I got together to formulate a deer management plan. Locally, there was
growing concern regarding the rapidly increasing deer herd. Farmers, Foresters and Motorists were complaining. At
that time we were the first deer hunting license holders in our extensive fallow deer area. We decided to reduce deer
numbers drastically to alleviate the problems and try and improve the quality of the animals by selective culling. We
knew enough to realise that antler quality acts as a barometer indicating the health and quality of the herd and antler
quality in our area was very poor. We rapidly reduced the overall numbers by culling does and every buck below our
local ‘pass standard’. Recognising that a pass standard for one area might be a fail standard in a good area, we set a
realistic benchmark and improved on this as time went on. We culled prickets that had short spikes and poor body
weight and bucks that did not show decent palmate by their third head. Bucks with split palmate, fishtail or keyhole
palmate were culled on sight. Many bucks had good palmate on one antler and fishtail or keyhole on the other. Deer
that were apart from the herd usually were sick or carrying an injury and these also were culled. We frequently
observed such deer lying down when all the others were feeding. They were also bullied by other deer. This is
nature’s way of keeping sick deer from spreading illness. Weak or late fawns were not spared either. As a rule we
always shot the fawn first. If the doe escaped she would live. If we shot the doe first and the fawn ran with the group,
it could slowly die especially if taken early in the season.
Many hunters ignore the fact that does provide 50% of the genetics. If we knew that a given doe was fathered by a
great buck then obviously we would spare her as breeding doe. Also the dominant does usually have the heaviest
fawns. It has been proven that the heaviest buck fawns become the Master Bucks later on. The point here is that
body weight and aggression win mating rights, not the biggest antler, although everything helps.
In only a few years we noticed a huge improvement. By our twelfth year there were over ten really good Master
Bucks around with some great prospects nipping at their heels. Some were as good as the best in Dublin’s Phoenix
Park.
As for our management group, we experienced a great sense of achievement and satisfaction at producing a well
managed, well balanced herd. This programme reduced traffic accidents and minimised damage to woodland and
3
farmland. Best of all we had exceptional trophies emerging.  The plan was for each hunter to harvest a trophy in turn
when it was time to do so. That way each member of the management group would be rewarded with a great trophy
without damaging the herd.
While we have met with great success it was to be followed by great disappointment and frustration. Unfortunately we
became the authors of our own demise. News of the big trophy bucks spread. Just as they started to dominated the
herds, hunters from outside the area decimated them in only three years over two seasons. These “hunters“, and I
use the term loosely, continued to bring friends to get their trophies too. If they encountered resistance they bad
mouthed us to landowners saying we wanted to keep all the hunting for ourselves. They even said we were making
money selling trophies. In truth they took all the trophies they could and made even the culling of does difficult with
the constant disturbance. In no time at all we were back where we started. We found many dead and injured deer,
almost all were large antlered bucks. The experience has taught me a lot. Some individuals are prepared and
determined to shoot trophies generated by other people’s good management. While every hunter deserves a good
representative trophy, many are not prepared to wait and put in the management effort.
It became blatantly apparent that the only way to counter this was for locals to control the sporting rights in a given
area. It is not enough to have permission from the odd farmer here and there. To accomplish this one needs to be
wealthy or part of a very organised group of hunters and landowners. Such a gathering of like minded local people
can form a club or syndicate and jointly buy or lease the sporting rights in the area they want to wish to manage.
There is no doubt it can be done. It is essential that local licensed hunters are accommodated, providing they agree
to and abide by the management plan.  The local Gun Clubs have by now largely rectified the situation in our area.
Too late I’m afraid, there are a lot more deer hunters these days and it is increasingly difficult to get consensus to
selectively manage deer.
The whole concept of managing deer for trophies raise a lot of questions, such as - Do you want to have the biggest
trophy to announce you are a great hunter? Or do you want the best trophies to show that the deer are managed to
4
the best possible standard? Maybe you want to sell trophies to pay for your hunting leases or just to make money. If it
is sustainable and the deer are managed correctly, does that matter? Very often it is not sustainable simply because
greed takes over and the goose that laid the golden egg is killed. There are other frictions too. Some people resent
not being able to access other hunter’s areas especially for big antlered deer. Poaching, lamping and other methods
are employed to get that ‘huge one’.
Regarding trophy measurement, (politics and personalities aside) I personally favour the CIC system of trophy
measurement simply because it encourages hunters to leave trophy animals until they have reached their best or
gone past their best. CIC does this by giving double points for weight of antler in Red and Fallow. Other big scores
come from the circumference of the beams. The antler weight and mass are only achieved by the attainment of good
age. Most antlers attain their adult width and height as fourth or fifth heads - the basic antler shape remaining the
same throughout the animals life. Reds may gain a few points or ends.  Fallow palmate size and antler mass will
increase. Accordingly the trophy or medal class will increase with age especially when  the stock comes from a well
managed herd. The heaviest heads for Fallow Bucks and Sika Stags occur from 8 to 11 years of age. Red Stags
between 10 and 13 years. Unfortunately Fallow Deer suffer greatly from liver fluke and accordingly lose condition just
at the age when the antler should be attaining its maximum mass and weight. In the area I hunt, infestation by liver
fluke usually dictates that most fallow buck heads start to degenerate by 7 or 8 years of age. Indeed, with all the
uncontrolled hunting they would be very wily and lucky to reach that age. Liver fluke proliferate on limestone ground
and not at all on acid ground.  Fallow, of course greatly prefer limestone grasslands, particularly if it is near mixed
woodland.
Inbreeding only becomes a problem in established herds when there are not enough bucks to generate competition.
The doe, like all female deer will drive away her buck calf by February/March. It is natures way of prevent inbreeding.
Where bachelor buck herd numbers are adequate, all will be well as normal genetic diversity is assured.. A
competitive testosterone driven arms race also increases antler quality.
5
Fallow bucks, like all our deer, form bachelor groups, often far from the nearest does. In fact they are the pioneers
when populating a new area. The does, in contrast generally stay in the area in which they were born. Hunting
pressure and in particular worrying by dogs moves them on, usually to ‘new’ areas pioneered by the bucks who in
turn move on again.
Their big weakness is of course, the rut. Often bucks that are not seen from year to year except during the rut,
become easy targets. Easy, because the rutting stands are  traditional. The best stands are in areas with high doe
populations and obviously these areas become ‘Master Buck’ magnets. Interestingly,  primary rutting stands are often
located over an energy source such as a strong magnetic field or over underground water springs. Bucks, during the
peak of the rut are very vocal with their constant groaning/belching call.  Rutting stands that are dominated by young
bucks are symptomatic of poorly managed areas. For this reason some countries have a closed season period during
the peak of the rut. Fallow bucks are the most determined and vicious fighters. I assume nature equipped them with
palmate antlers to help avoid serious injury. Such fights occur despite prolonged parallel walking and posturing when
evenly matched animals refuse to back down. It almost always occurs when two males from different bachelor groups
meet during the rut. The hierarchy within a bachelor group is well established prior to the rut. Like all male deer,
bucks within a group remain ‘friends’ most if not all their natural life.
Fallow bucks are the only palmate antlered small deer. As such they are unique. A buck with  little or no palmate, split
palmate, fish tail or keyhole palmate will pass this trait on to the next generation if he is the dominant buck.
Unfortunately, in Ireland such bucks are very often dominant because the strong antlered well-palamated bucks are
shot as trophies. This would not be a problem if they were left until late in their breeding life and given the chance to
pass on their superior genes. Fallow antlers when poor are very obviously poor and as such are ignored by trophy
hunters. Relatively speaking poor Sika and Red antlers are less obvious with their pointed configuration and can
make a reasonable trophy with age. Poor prospect fallow heads will always look poor.
6
Ireland has only three established species of deer, Red, Sika, Fallow and a fledgling population of recently introduced
Muntjac that may not survive. We have nothing like the populations of deer in England, Scotland and Europe. The
escalating unemployment situation here and venison prices paid by ever more ‘weigh and pay’ game dealers play a
major part in the reducing numbers. It has destroyed many efforts at selective deer management. In parts of Ireland
there has already been mention of ‘deer wars’. Deer numbers in accessible areas have been reduced  by as much as
60%. Small satellite groups have been wiped out.  Heavy densities are still a problem in areas of Wicklow and east
Galway but not for long.
My constant mantra to landowners is ---  Its easy to separate the hunters who want to manage deer from the trophy
hunters. You will see the trophy hunters out day in day out, often at night, during the rut but very rarely in January and
February when the doe cull needs to be completed. A lot of those same people shoot many trophies, constantly trying
to get a bigger buck. They send each other photos by phone and email.  ‘Look what I got, mine is bigger than yours !’
and so the short sighted greed continues.
On the flip side, many agree with the sentiments expressed by a friend. I have often heard him say to farmers and
foresters. “There will always be deer, we might as well leave the best healthy ones, but not too many”. Good advice
indeed if only all those concerned would listen.
Jim Daly

DRIVER ARRESTED AFTER PURSUIT, BARRICADING IN VEHICLE ON I-293

LONDONDERRY, N.H. – A Merrimack woman was arrested after barricading herself in a vehicle following a pursuit that started in Londonderry.
 
At 1:06 a.m. on Wednesday, Jan. 14, 2026, State Troopers responded to assist members of the Londonderry Police Department after they encountered a suspicious vehicle parked near Citizens Bank on Route 102 in Londonderry.
 
When Londonderry officers attempted to speak with the driver, she fled, and a pursuit ensued westbound on Route 102 toward Hudson. The driver then pulled into the Circle K gas station at the Londonderry town line. Members of the Londonderry and Hudson police departments attempted to stop the vehicle, a 2016 Volkswagen GTI, from leaving the gas station, but the driver drove down an embankment, hit a guardrail, and got onto Route 102 back in the direction of Londonderry.
 
The driver then entered Interstate 93 northbound from Exit 4, at which point State Troopers took over the pursuit and deployed tire deflation devices in an attempt to stop the vehicle. The driver continued northbound, taking the left ramp onto I-293. The driver then attempted to drive northbound in the southbound direction of I-293, but a Trooper used his cruiser to stop the vehicle. The driver then refused to get out of the vehicle.
 
The interstate was closed in the area for approximately two hours while Troopers and officers from the Londonderry Police Department attempted negotiations with the driver. Ultimately, a State Police K-9 and less-lethal munitions were deployed before the driver was taken into custody.
 
The driver was identified as Heather Lewis, 34, of Merrimack. She was transported to Elliot Hospital to be treated for minor injuries.
 
Lewis has been charged by both the State Police and the Londonderry Police Department for multiple counts of felony reckless conduct with a deadly weapon, disobeying an officer, resisting arrest or detention, criminal mischief, and operating after suspension. Lewis will be scheduled to be arraigned in Manchester District Court later this week.
 
No booking photo is available at this time.

MOVING BACKWARDS
I was in the passenger seat of my wife’s car the other day as we were backing out of our driveway. I happened to glance over at the dashboard as we were moving backwards and noticed that the digital speedometer registered “4 miles per hour.” I never noticed that before, but most newer cars with digital output actually record the tire rotation (whether the car is moving forward or backwards). Older models, with mechanical speedometers, didn’t register speed while the car was moving in reverse. They only took note of forward movement … both on the speedometer and the odometer. So, newer models of cars register backward movement the same as forward movement.

Isn’t that just like our society? We assume that if you’re moving at all, whether forward or backwards, that it counts as a positive action. The main thing is that you’re moving. But, I’m pretty sure that’s not the way God sees things. As a matter of fact, the book of Jeremiah often mentions God’s disdain for backsliding (“moving backwards spiritually” … read Jeremiah 2:19, 3:8, 14:7 and 15:6). Hosea also tells a similar story as he records these words of God: “My people are bent on backsliding from Me. Though they call to the Most High, None at all exalt Him” (Hosea 11:7). And, in Hebrews 10:38, God says, “If any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him.”

Jesus had some things to say about backward movement as well. One of his followers wanted to become a disciple, but wanted to go back to bid his family farewell before leaving with Him. Jesus told him, “No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). And, in one of the shortest verses in the Bible (Luke 17:32) Jesus said, “Remember Lot’s wife,” reminding us that those who want to move backwards to embrace the world they’re leaving behind will not fare well in the kingdom of God.

I don’t know about you, but I want to move forward. I don’t want any backward movement in my life. I don’t want to “go back” to simpler times or to “the good old days.” I want to move forward and upward to what God is calling me to.

Make this confession over your life today: 
“Lord, may my eyes be fixed on what is ahead of me and may I always be focused on moving forward. The past is behind me … both the good and the bad. I don’t want to go back and revisit it. I don’t want to go back to old ways that separated me from You. I hear Your call to move forward and upward, so I will move in Your direction. In Jesus’ Name!”

Philippians 3:14
I press toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

– Importante para sa heart health at muscles, lalo na kung active ka o mahilig sumayaw 💃🕺

– Tumutulong sa brain function at mood, malaking tulong sa mental health ng diabetes warriors 💙

Save this to know why Khichdi is the King of Indian Food! 👇

Why is an entire festival (Makar Sankranti) dedicated to this humble dish? It’s not just tradition; it’s Science.

1. The "Complete Protein" Hack: 🧬 Rice is low in Lysine. Dal is low in Methionine. But when you mix them? They create a Complete Amino Acid Profile equivalent to egg or meat protein! Our ancestors hacked nutrition without labs.

2. The "New Harvest" Logic: 🌾 Sankranti marks the arrival of the fresh crop (New Rice & Pulses). Freshly harvested grain has high water content and is harder to digest. Cooking it as a mushy "Khichdi" was the safest way to consume the new harvest without upsetting the stomach.

3. The "Gut Reset": 🩺 Winter digestion is naturally slow. After the heavy fried foods of the wedding season, Khichdi acts as a "System Reboot." It is alkaline, soothing, and easy on the gut.

Fun Fact: Legend says Khichdi was popularized by Baba Gorakhnath to feed hungry warriors quickly during war! ⚔️

🐾 My 18-year-old son was working at Tractor Supply one evening when a gentleman came in just before closing to buy food for his beloved Bernese Mountain Dog 🐕‍🦺. There was a long line at the register, and when the man tried to pay, his card was declined 😞. He tried again — still declined.
Seeing the disappointment and embarrassment on the man’s face, my son quietly took out his own debit card and paid for the entire order without saying a word 💳❤️. When the man thanked him, my son simply smiled and nodded — just happy to help someone in need 🌟.
A few days later, the same gentleman returned to the store, found my son, thanked him again, and paid him back. But my son didn’t keep the money — he donated it to the American Cancer Society in memory of his late great uncle 🎗️.
In today’s busy world, I take nothing for granted. My son’s compassion, kindness, and willingness to help others make me incredibly proud 🥹💙🐾.

🚨 #POLICIACA 🔥 || ​QUERÉTARO, QRO.– En un operativo conjunto de fuerzas federales y estatales, se logró la captura de seis presuntos delincuentes, entre ellos Ramón “N”, alias “Moncho”, identificado como líder operativo de la célula delictiva “Los Lavadora”. El grupo criminal es señalado como el principal generador de violencia y robo al transporte de carga en la región.

​La detención fue resultado de diversas órdenes de cateo cumplimentadas por elementos de la Defensa (SEDENA), Secretaría de Marina (SEMAR), la Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana (SSPC) y la Fiscalía General de la República (FGR), contando con el respaldo logístico del Gobierno del Estado de Querétaro.

​
​Según el informe oficial, el "Moncho" era el encargado de coordinar el robo a autotransporte mediante agresiones físicas y la privación de la libertad de los choferes, operando principalmente sobre la carretera México-Querétaro.

​Además del robo a transportistas, las investigaciones vinculan a esta célula con una amplia gama de delitos de alto impacto, que incluyen:
​Narcomenudeo y secuestro.
​Robo de hidrocarburos (huachicol).
​Robo a casa habitación y hom1c1dio.

​Aseguramiento de armamento y droga
​Durante las diligencias en los inmuebles intervenidos, las autoridades aseguraron un arma de fuego, cartuchos útiles, un tractocamión (tráiler) relacionado con actividades ilícitas y diversas dosis de estupefacientes.

​Los seis detenidos y los objetos asegurados fueron puestos a disposición de la autoridad ministerial correspondiente para determinar su situación jurídica. Con esta acción, las fuerzas federales buscan reducir la incidencia delictiva en una de las rutas comerciales más importantes del país.
