لقد كرَّم الدين الاسلامي الحنيف المسلمَ ميتاً ، كما كرَّمه حياً، فبعد موت المسلم أمر الاسلام بتغسيله ،وتطييبه ، وتكفينه، ثم الصلاة عليه ، ومواراته في القبر. ونهى الاسلام عن امتهان القبور، فحرَّم المشي فوقها ، أو القعود عليها، ودعا إلى زيارتها، والسلام على أهلها، والدعاء لهم .ففي صحيح مسلم : (عَنْ جَابِرٍ قَالَ نَهَى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ -صلى الله عليه وسلم- أَنْ يُجَصَّصَ الْقَبْرُ وَأَنْ يُقْعَدَ عَلَيْهِ وَأَنْ يُبْنَى عَلَيْهِ ).  كما حَرِص الدين الاسلامي على عقائد الناس وتوحيدهم، فسدَّ أبواب الفتنة ،ومنع ما يؤدي إلى الغلوِّ في القبور ، أو أصحاب القبور، فنهى عن الصلاة في المقابر، ونهى عن تشييد البناء والقباب فوق القبور، كما أمر بتسوية القبور المشرفة المرتفعة فوق الأرض ، كما هو واضح في الحديث الذي بين أيدينا اليوم ، والذي رواه مسلم في صحيحه (عَنْ أَبِى الْهَيَّاجِ الأَسَدِيِّ قَالَ ،قَالَ لِي عَلِىُّ بْنُ أَبِى طَالِبٍ :أَلاَّ أَبْعَثُكَ عَلَى مَا بَعَثَنِي عَلَيْهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ -صلى الله عليه وسلم-:(أَنْ لاَ تَدَعَ تِمْثَالاً إِلاَّ طَمَسْتَهُ وَلاَ قَبْرًا مُشْرِفًا إِلاَّ سَوَّيْتَهُ) ،قال النووي في شرح صحيح مسلم:(وَلاَ قَبْرًا مُشْرِفًا إِلاَّ سَوَّيْتَهُ  ): فيه أن من السنة ألا يرفع القبر على الأرض رفعا كثيرا، ولا يجوز البناء عليه ولا تجصيصه ، ولا كتابة آيات القرآن عليه ، ولا غير ذلك مما تعظم به القبور

 أيها المسلمون

والحكمة من قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم (وَلاَ قَبْرًا مُشْرِفًا إِلاَّ سَوَّيْتَهُ ) ،هو عدم الغلو في الصالحين ، فبناء القباب على قبورهم ، وكذا المساجد على قبورهم ، كان من أهم الأسباب التي ساعدت على انتشار دعاء غير الله عز وجل وكانت سببا في فساد عقائد الكثير من الناس فقد قال ابن جرير في تفسيره لقوله تعالى : (وَقَالُوا لَا تَذَرُنَّ آلِهَتَكُمْ وَلَا تَذَرُنَّ وَدًّا وَلَا سُوَاعًا وَلَا يَغُوثَ وَيَعُوقَ وَنَسْرًا) (23) نوح ،  قال : ( كانوا قوما صالحين بين آدم ونوح ،وكان لهم أتباع يقتدون بهم ، فلما ماتوا ، قال أصحابهم الذين كانوا يقتدون بهم : لو صورناهم كان أشوق لنا إلى العبادة إذا ذكرناهم ، فصوروهم ، فلما ماتوا وجاء آخرون دب إليهم إبليس فقال :إنما كانوا يعبدونهم وبهم يسقون المطر ، فعبدوهم. وعَنْ عَائِشَةَ أَنَّ أُمَّ حَبِيبَةَ وَأُمَّ سَلَمَةَ (رضي الله عنهما) : (ذَكَرَتَا كَنِيسَةً رَأَيْنَهَا بِالْحَبَشَةِ فِيهَا تَصَاوِيرُ، فَذَكَرَتَا لِلنَّبِيِّ (صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ) فَقَالَ: إِنَّ أُولَئِكَ إِذَا كَانَ فِيهِمْ الرَّجُلُ الصَّالِحُ فَمَاتَ بَنَوْا عَلَى قَبْرِهِ مَسْجِدًا وَصَوَّرُوا فِيهِ تِلْكَ الصُّوَرَ، فَأُولَئِكَ شِرَارُ الْخَلْقِ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ) متفق عليه. قال ابن رجب “هذا الحديث يدل على تحريم بناء المساجد على قبور الصالحين”. وعَن عَائِشَةَ وَعَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ عَبَّاسٍ (رَضيَ اللهُ عنهما) قَالَا: (لَمَّا نَزَلَ بِرَسُولِ اللَّهِ (صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ) طَفِقَ يَطْرَحُ خَمِيصَةً لَهُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ، فَإِذَا اغْتَمَّ بِهَا كَشَفَهَا عَنْ وَجْهِهِ، فَقَالَ وَهُوَ كَذَلِكَ: (لَعْنَةُ اللَّهِ عَلَى الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى اتَّخَذُوا قُبُورَ أَنْبِيَائِهِمْ مَسَاجِدَ، يُحَذِّرُ مَا صَنَعُوا) رواه البخاري.  وقال ابن كثير (رحمه الله) في “تفسيره”: أن أمير المؤمنين عمر بن الخطاب (رضي الله عنه) لما وجد قبر (دانيال) (أحد أنبياء بني إسرائيل بالعراق)، أمر أن يُخفى عن الناس، وأن تُدفن تلك الرقعة التي وجدوها عنده”؛ وذلك حفاظاً على عقائد الناس وتوحيدهم، حيث أن أهل فارس كانوا يغالون فيه، فأمر(رضي الله عنه) بإخفائه خشية الغلو فيه ، فيدعى ويعبد من دون الله ، فمن الأسباب التي أدت إلى انتشار الفتنة بأصحاب القبور هو الغلو في تعظيم المقبورين ، وقد جاءت النصوص الكثيرة في التحذير من هذا الداء العضال ،فعُبَّاد القبور اليوم، يلجؤون إلى الموتى وينادونهم من مكان بعيد: يا سيدي، أنا في جاهك، أنا في حسبك، ليس لي إلا الله وأنت، لا تردني خائبًا، رد غائبنا ، اشف مريضنا ، خذ بيدنا ، فرج همنا وفك كربنا ، ويسر أمرنا ، بل وإذا حضر أحدهم أمام القبر أو من داخل الضريح، سالت دموعه ، وخشعت جوارحه ، وهذا كله شرك ، لأن ذلك لا يكون إلا لله ، قال الله تعالى: ﴿ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ عِبَادٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ فَادْعُوهُمْ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ صَادِقِينَ ﴾ [الأعراف: 194]، وقال الله تعالى : ﴿ وَلَا تَدْعُ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَنْفَعُكَ وَلَا يَضُرُّكَ فَإِنْ فَعَلْتَ فَإِنَّكَ إِذًا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ ﴾ [يونس: 106]، فزيارة القبور شُرِعت للعبرة وللزهد في الدنيا – وتذكرة الآخرة، والإحسان إلى الأموات بالدعاء لهم والاستغفار، ولكن للأسف بدل الذين ظلموا قولاً غير الذي قيل لهم، فبدلاً من أن يدعوا لهم ، دعوهم من دون الله، حتى أقرُّوا بذلك عين إبليس اللعين، معرضين عن كتاب ربهم وسُنة نبيِّهم، وهدْي سلف الأمة الصالح، وهذا شأن مَن أضلَّه الله، فلا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله العلي العظيم

The last word

From the courtroom

Transcript of Felix Makhammadiev's speech at the Leninsky District Court of Saratov on September 19, 2019.

Transcript of the court session dated 09/19/2019

F. H. Makhammadiev: I also cannot help but begin my last word with words of gratitude. This is a very important moment to thank others. It's worth a lot. My dear family, Zhenya, mother, sisters, and nephews, my dear ones, you have passed this difficult part of the journey with dignity. Your devotion has warmed and warms my heart. You are the most precious material thing I have. I love you very much. I admire your strength. There is nothing better and more pleasant in the world than friendship. To exclude friendship from life is like depriving the world of sunlight. My dear friends, you are our sunshine. It's hard for me to imagine the sacrifices you're making to support the six of us and our families. I am very grateful to you.

Your Honor, you listened to us attentively, attached important documents to us, and met us halfway when we asked for breaks. Thank you for that. Anastasia Vladimirovna and Alexander Valentinovich are your loyal assistants. They have always treated us with respect, and for that I am very grateful to them. Thank you.

I also can't help but mention the bailiffs. Thank you for your hard work. Please tell the others who attended this meeting that your kindness and respect for us was sometimes a kind of painkiller. Thank you.

I also want to say a few words to Mr. Prosecutor. Alexander Nikolaevich, you have good natural features. For example, you can listen carefully. I also noticed that you know how not to take personally those of our counterarguments that were voiced today and in other hearings on the case. Thank you for your respect.

Your Honor, during my last statement, I would like to express my attitude towards the criminal case against me and my friends, based on the word of God, the Bible. My speech will take about 20 minutes. I really hope that the respected court will listen to me carefully. I will not talk about extremism, but everything I will say concerns this criminal case. "My mindset was on freedom," Colvin said in 2021 of her refusal to give up her seat. "So I was not going to move that day. I told them that history had me glued to the seat."

Polícia Federal cumpre mandado de busca e apreensão em Santa Maria.

A Polícia Federal deflagrou, na manhã desta quarta-feira (14), a segunda fase da operação Compliance Zero, que visa apurar a prática dos crimes de organização criminosa, gestão fraudulenta de instituição financeira, manipulação de mercado e lavagem de capitais. A nova fase da operação mira endereços ligados a Daniel Vorcaro, dono do Banco Master. 

Segundo a corporação, estão sendo cumpridos 42 mandados de busca e apreensão, expedidos pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), além de medidas de sequestro e bloqueio de bens e valores que superam R$ 5,7 bilhões. 

Os mandados estão sendo cumpridos em São Paulo, Bahia, Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul e Rio de Janeiro. No RS, conforme apurado pela reportagem da Rádio Imembui, um dos mandados de busca e apreensão está sendo cumprido nesse momento em Santa Maria. A PF não deu detalhes, apenas informou que está recolhendo computadores e outros materiais à pedido da corporação em Brasília, onde as investigações estão centralizadas.

Most of us know the story of Rosa Parks, the Black seamstress whose refusal to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus to a white person sparked the boycott and invigorated the civil rights movement as we know it. 

While that story is true, it is also woefully incomplete. Because before Ms. Parks there was fifteen year-old Claudette Colvin. 

Some excerpts from a profile in Mother Jones:

“On March 2, 1955, a full nine months before Rosa Parks took her famous stand, Colvin boarded a city bus with her friends, taking a seat behind the first five rows, which were reserved for whites. Although the practice was illegal, drivers would routinely clear whole rows to accommodate a white rider if the white section was full—even if it meant those Black riders would have to stand.

That’s what happened that day. When the driver shouted, “I need those seats!” Colvin’s friends dutifully moved to the back, but she stayed put. The driver chewed her out, to no avail. A couple of stops later, city police were there to meet the bus. 

Still Colvin refused to leave her seat. “It’s my constitutional right!” she shrieked again and again as the police dragged her from the bus.

Somehow one of the cops got scratched in [the] Colvin fracas, and the girl was charged with resisting arrest and assaulting a police officer in addition to breaking the city’s segregation law. On the ride to the station, Colvin told author Hoose, the police called her a “n___ bitch,” and took turns trying to guess her bra size. When she arrived, other officers called her “thing” and “wh*re.” After booking, she was thrown in the city’s adult jail.

**

On her day in court, Colvin was found guilty of all charges by a hostile judge. The verdict, as one movement leader recalled, “was a bombshell.” The people were ready for action. 

**

When Rosa Parks boarded the bus that fateful day and refused to relinquish her seat, it wasn’t that she was simply tired; she was sick and tired—and inspired in no small part by her rebellious protégé. She acted knowing full well what she was about to unleash.

**

Although few remember Colvin’s name, it was she who may have had the most clout in the final tally. 

**

Some time after Colvin’s defeat, and the birth of her baby, lawyer Fred Gray had taken the city to trial in federal court, this time in a lawsuit intended to quash segregation altogether in the city bus system. 

Among the plaintiffs—and she turned out to be the most powerful witness—was Claudette Colvin. In a 2-1 vote, the three-judge panel ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, spelling the beginning of the end of segregation in Montgomery.”

Ms. Colvin died yesterday, at the age of 86. Her story could not be more timely, her example more powerful, her inspiration more urgent. May her memory continue to spark outrage, courage, and change.

IAT APLICA MAIS DE 8 MIL MULTAS POR CRIMES AMBIENTAIS EM 2025

O Governo do Estado, por meio do Instituto Água e Terra (IAT), aplicou 8.184 multas por crimes ambientais no Paraná em 2025. O valor representa uma queda de 14,7% em relação às 9.602 multas aplicadas em 2024, reforçando a eficácia do trabalho desenvolvido pelo IAT no combate ao desmatamento criminoso no Estado. Os dados do Sistema de Informações Ambientais (SIA) do IAT revelam ainda que o valor total em autuações foi de R$ 231 milhões em 2025.

Segundo o gerente de Monitoramento e Fiscalização do IAT, Alvaro Cesar de Góes, os números refletem os esforços do Estado em combater o desmatamento ilegal e outros crimes ambientais. "Desde 2022, o IAT vem reduzindo de forma significativa a supressão de vegetação nativa no Estado. E com esse trabalho de monitoramento e fiscalização já realizado, e que atualmente ainda vem sendo executado pelo órgão ambiental, a tendência é de redução do número de autos de infração ambiental", diz. 

O valor recolhido pelo Estado com as infrações é repassado integralmente ao Fundo Estadual do Meio Ambiente. A reserva financeira tem como finalidade financiar planos, programas ou projetos que objetivem o controle, a preservação, a conservação e a recuperação do meio ambiente, conforme a Lei Estadual 12.945/2000.

Um dos casos, por exemplo, aconteceu em Cruz Machado. O IAT multou em R$ 25 mil a prefeitura pela utilização irregular de equipamentos do município para a prática de crimes ambientais em Área de Proteção Permanente (APP). Foram dois Autos de Infração Ambiental (AIA) emitidos pelo escritório regional do órgão em União da Vitória contra o município: danificar área de APP de 1.800 metros quadrados mediante movimentação do solo (R$ 5 mil) e depositar resíduos e rejeitos também em local de proteção (R$ 20 mil).

Por meio da vigilância, o Paraná conseguiu reduzir em 64,9% a supressão ilegal da Mata Atlântica entre 2023 e 2024. De acordo com levantamento da Plataforma MapBiomas, vinculada ao Observatório do Clima, a área desmatada caiu de 1.230 hectares em 2023 para 432 hectares em 2024. O estudo também aponta que 75% dos municípios paranaenses ampliaram suas áreas de mata nativa entre 2019 e 2023, enquanto 71% registraram desmatamento zero em 2024.

Dados do próprio IAT também apontam que o Paraná reduziu em 95,2% o desmatamento ilegal da Mata Atlântica entre 2021 e 2024, de 6.939 hectares para 329 hectares. No mesmo período, o número de Autos de Infração Ambiental (AIAs) ligados a crimes contra a flora aumentou em 65%, passando de 3.183 para 5.252.

My Family Made My 15-Year-Old Daughter Walk 3 Hours on a Broken Leg. They Called Her "Sensitive" and Left Her Alone. They Laughed. I Didn't Scream. I Got on a Plane, Got the X-Rays, and Got My Revenge.

They Called My 15-Year-Old Daughter a "Drama Queen" For Breaking Her Leg and Left Her Alone in a Hotel. They Forgot I Was a Criminal Investigator. I Didn't Yell. I Waited. Four Days Later, They Were Screaming in Panic.

It was a Tuesday, just another mind-numbing, paper-stack Tuesday. I sat at my desk, my eyes burning from staring at documents for too long, gnawing on a pen that had run out of ink. The air in my office was thick with the scent of stale coffee and filtered ventilation—the kind of smell that clings to your clothes and seeps into your bones, the smell of recycled air and quiet desperation.

Then I saw it. "Sophie" lighting up my phone on FaceTime.

I smiled instinctively. It was probably a vacation update. Maybe she’d show me a bracelet she'd bargained for, or some weird, colorful snack with a name I’d butcher trying to pronounce. The whole trip had been her idea—joining my parents, my brother Mark, and her cousins on a sightseeing break three states over.

It lined up perfectly with her spring break. I couldn’t go. Neither could my husband. Work, for both of us. And I don’t fly.

I mean, I really don’t fly. Haven’t in over ten years. It's not just a preference; it’s a full-on, crippling phobia. Sweaty hands, racing heart, the distinct, metallic taste of panic rising in my throat the second I’m near a boarding gate. Even the scent of jet fuel makes my throat feel like it’s closing.
So, we drive. We take trains. We stay grounded. That’s how I stay functional.

The point is, I wasn’t bracing for trauma. I was expecting a selfie from a street market. I answered the call, a smile already on my face.
The smile died instantly.
There was no noise. Just Sophie, my 15-year-old daughter, sitting rigid on the edge of a generic hotel bed.
"I'm tired," she said softly. Then, "Hey, Mom."
She paused, and her eyes, even through the pixelated screen, looked… hunted.
"Can I tell you something," she whispered, "but promise not to freak out?"
Spoiler: I absolutely freaked out.
Not on the outside. My voice didn't even raise a decibel. But inside, it was a full-blown, five-alarm internal meltdown. "What’s going on, honey?" I asked, my voice terrifyingly calm as I slowly got to my feet.
She turned the camera. Her leg was resting on a hotel pillow. It was swollen, red, and a deep, angry purple. The skin was stretched taut along her ankle and shin. It wasn't just bruised; it was ballooned. It looked wrong.
"I think I broke it," she said, her voice flat.
My mind blanked. "What do you mean, you think you broke it?"
"I fell yesterday," she replied. "On the stairs at that old palace place. Yesterday."
I sank slowly back into my chair, like gravity had suddenly doubled. "Yesterday? Who’s looked at it? Where is everyone?"
"Grandma, Grandpa, and Uncle Mark," she said. "They... they didn’t think it looked that bad. It wasn't really swollen at first. They figured it was just bruising."
I blinked, the information failing to compute. "So... they didn’t take you anywhere? To a doctor?"
She shook her head, her hair falling over her face. "No. We kept going. I just... walked through it."
I shut my eyes, a cold sickness rising in my stomach. "How long, Sophie? How long did you walk?"
"Three hours? Maybe more."
"Three... hours."
She nodded, finally looking at me. "They told me I was overreacting."
That line. That classic, familiar line. "They said I’d feel better once the tour was over," she added, her tone so casual it made me want to scream. "And now... now it hurts a lot more."
My voice was ice. "Where are they now, Sophie?"
She hesitated, and that's when I knew. "Out. They... they said I could stay at the hotel and rest."
I froze. "You’re by yourself?"
She nodded again, a small, jerky motion.
"In another state. Alone." I stared at the screen, at my child, who was clearly in agonizing pain and had been abandoned.
"Hey," I said, my voice sharp, professional. "Don't move. I’m coming to get you."
"What? Mom, you don't have to..."
"I do. But you'd have to fly."
"I'm aware."
She blinked. "You haven't flown since..."
"I know." I was already on my laptop, my fingers flying across the keys. "I'm already checking flights."
This time, she didn't argue. Her voice grew quiet. "Okay."
I hung up. I found one flight. One single, non-stop seat, leaving in 90 minutes. There was no time for fear. No time for logic. No time for anything but motion.
I booked it.
Then I called my parents. Voicemail. Tried again. Voicemail.
I called Mark. He answered, chipper. "Hey, Erica! How's it going?"
"You left Sophie alone in a hotel room with a possibly broken leg."
The chipper tone vanished. "Whoa, hold on. She said she was fine. She's 15, she can..."
"She can't walk, Mark. She told you it hurt yesterday, and you made her walk for three hours."
"We didn't make her. She’s always been a little sensitive, come on. It's probably just a sprain. The swelling didn't even start until last night."
"Sensitive," I repeated. The word felt like acid on my tongue. "You saw her leg and you left her alone because she 'couldn't move'?"
He sighed, a sound of pure, unadulterated annoyance. "You're blowing this out of proportion. Just like you always do."
There it was. Always. Me. Her. I hung up without another word. I didn't have time to shout.
I grabbed my bag, shut my laptop, and bolted. My boss looked up as I burst into his office, halfway out the door.
"Family emergency," I said. "I have to go."
"What kind of emergency?"
"The kind where I leave right now."
He frowned. "You were just assigned..."
"I know. I'm sorry." I didn't wait to hear the rest. I was already in the elevator, booking a cab. In the cab, I texted Sophie. I'm coming. Don't take anything. Stay in bed.
She replied with a single heart emoji. I stared at that tiny red heart the whole ride to the airport, a single point of focus in a sea of rising panic.
I ran. Through check-in, through security. Sweaty, disoriented, fighting the irrational, screaming itch in my brain to turn back, to get on solid ground. But I didn't. I ran like I was being chased.
Maybe I was. Chased by the ghost of every time I’d been told I was too sensitive, too much, too scared.

I made it to the gate with minutes to spare. No checked bags, no clean shirt, just me, my credit card, and a phobia I didn't have time to entertain.
I hate flying. I really, really hate it. But I hate what they did to her more.
So, I boarded the plane. I didn't shout. Not yet.
But four days later, they were the ones screaming.

Chapter 1: The Ghost in the Rain
The rain at Fort Bragg doesn’t just fall; it hammers you. It feels personal, like the sky is trying to drive you into the pavement. It was 0300 hours on a Tuesday, the kind of graveyard shift that makes you question every life choice that led you to a guard shack in North Carolina.

I was three coffees deep and feeling none of it. My partner, Corporal “Hitch” Hitchins, was slumped over the logbook, pretending to read while actually catching a nap with his eyes open—a skill specific to the infantry.

“Visibility is zero, Sarge,” Hitch mumbled, wiping condensation off the bulletproof glass. “If anyone tries to breach tonight, they’re either specialized or stupid.”

“Or lost,” I muttered, staring into the gray wash of the floodlights. The perimeter lights were just hazy halos in the downpour.

That’s when the sensor tripped.

Beep. Beep.

It wasn’t a vehicle. The weight triggers on the access road were set for heavy tonnage. This was the motion sensor on the pedestrian shoulder, about fifty yards out.

“Movement,” I said, voice dropping into that automatic, flat tone of alert. “Sector Four.”

Hitch snapped awake, hand going to his sidearm. I grabbed the spotlight controls and swung the beam toward the darkness.

At first, I saw nothing but rain slashing sideways. Then, a shape materialized from the fog. It was low to the ground, moving with a staggering, uneven rhythm.

“Is that a coyote?” Hitch squinted.

“Too big,” I said. My stomach tightened. “It’s... it’s a dog.”

But it wasn’t just a dog. As the figure drew closer, fighting every inch against the wind, I saw the distinctive silhouette. The high ears, the slope of the back. A German Shepherd. But he looked wrecked. He was limping badly on his rear right leg, his coat was a matted mess of mud and burrs, and his head hung low.

And he was dragging something.

Clamped in his jaws was the neck of a heavy burlap feed sack. It was soaking wet, dragging heavily on the asphalt. Scrape. Step. Scrape. Step. The sound was audible even over the storm.

“Sarge, look at his movement,” Hitch whispered, his hand hovering over the gate release. “That’s not a stray. He’s marching.”

He was right. The dog wasn’t skulking. He was on a mission. He reached the yellow line that marked the kill zone—the point where we are authorized to engage—and he stopped. He dropped the sack. He sat down, trembling violently from cold and exhaustion.

Then, he looked up at the guard shack. He didn't bark. He just stared.

I hit the PA system. “Step away!” I yelled, out of habit, before realizing how stupid I sounded.

The dog didn’t flinch. He lifted his right paw and held it in the air.

My blood ran cold. I knew that signal. It was the ‘Freeze/Alert’ command used by the EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) units. This dog was signaling a find.

I grabbed my poncho and my rifle. “Cover me. Keep the light on him.”

“Sarge, protocol says—”

“Screw protocol,” I snapped. “Look at his eyes.”

I stepped out into the deluge. The wind nearly knocked me over. I approached slowly, weapon low. The dog watched me come. His amber eyes were glassy, filled with a pain so deep it radiated off him like heat. As I got within ten feet, the smell hit me. Wet fur. Swamp mud. And the metallic, copper tang of fresh blood.

“Easy, boy,” I said, keeping my voice level.

The dog whined—a high, broken sound that tore through the noise of the rain. I squinted. There was a patch of white fur on his chest shaped like a lightning bolt.

I froze.

“Gunner?” I whispered.

The dog’s tail gave a single, weak thump against the wet tarmac.

It was impossible. Gunner was a legend. A Purple Heart recipient. He’d sniffed out three daisy-chained IEDs in the Arghandab Valley five years ago, saving an entire squad. He had been retired with honors and adopted by his handler, Master Sergeant Miller. They lived off-grid in the Blue Ridge Mountains, three hours away.

“Gunner, what are you doing here?” I dropped to my knees, ignoring the water soaking my fatigues.

He was in bad shape. His paws were raw, the pads shredded as if he’d run on sandpaper for miles. There was a gash over his eye.

He nudged the burlap sack toward me with his nose. Then he nudged it again, harder, and let out a sharp bark.

Open it.

My hands were shaking. Not from the cold, but from a sudden, crushing dread. I looked at the sack. It was tied with a piece of electrical cord. The bottom was stained dark.

“Hitch!” I yelled over my shoulder. “Call the Commander! Get the vet! Now!”

I turned back to the sack. “Okay, Gunner. Okay.”

I pulled my knife and cut the cord. The mouth of the sack fell open. I clicked on my tactical flashlight and shone it inside.

The world stopped. The rain stopped. The only thing that existed was the object inside that bag.

It was a leg.

A prosthetic leg. Matte black carbon fiber, battered and scratched. And stuck to the calf was a fading sticker: First to Fight.

I knew this leg. I had seen Miller pour beer into it at the VFW hall. I had seen him run on it during the Warrior Games. Miller couldn’t walk ten feet without it.

I reached in further. My fingers brushed against wet paper. I pulled it out. It was a torn piece of a map, soaked in blood. On the back, scrawled in charcoal or grease, were three words. The handwriting was jagged, frantic, written by a man who knew he was running out of time.

THEY ARE HERE.

I sat back on my heels, the rain mixing with the hot tears suddenly stinging my eyes. Gunner collapsed against my chest, his job finally done.

Miller was out there. He was crippled, he was bleeding, and he was being hunted. And his only hope had just walked twenty miles through a hurricane to let us know.

I looked at the camera in the guard shack.

“Open the gate,” I roared into the radio, my voice breaking. “Wake everyone up. We’re going to war.”

Some days I don’t talk about this out loud because it feels heavy, and unless you’re living it, it’s hard to fully understand.

Being a special needs parent isn’t just one hard thing. It’s layers of hard stacked on top of each other, woven into everyday life. It’s working full time and then coming home to years of potty training that don’t follow the timeline you thought they would. Timer. Potty. Timer. Potty. Accident. Accident. Accident. And somehow you still clap for the tiniest win because you know how much effort it took to get there.

It’s communication that looks nothing like what people expect. Trying sign language. Modeling words. Using AAC. Prompting. Prompt, prompt, prompt. Over and over again. It’s knowing that asking something as simple as “are you hungry?” might take five or ten minutes to work through together, not because he doesn’t want to answer, but because his brain processes the world differently.

It’s therapy schedules that run your calendar. Sleepless nights that blur into mornings. Dysregulation that shows up without warning. A constant undercurrent of worry that hums quietly in the background, even on good days.

And then, right when it feels like too much, something happens.

He looks at me with his eyes and gives me that cheesy grin. He grabs my face, and without words, I know he’s saying I love you. He sits at the piano, banging away, singing the ABCs with absolute joy and zero concern for how it sounds. He starts talking about the solar system with a level of detail that leaves me in awe, especially since I can’t even name all the planets in order most days.

That’s the part people don’t always see.

This journey is messy. It’s exhausting. It’s not linear. But it’s also breathtakingly beautiful in ways I never expected. The hard doesn’t cancel out the hope. Somehow they exist side by side.

And I’m holding onto the belief that someday it gets a little easier. Until then, I’ll keep choosing hope, noticing the magic in the middle, and loving this kid with everything I have. ❤️

Why It’s Not Good to Buy a Woman Through Payments of Bride Price – A Response to My Article Published on Nyamilepedia on August 27, 2020 Entitled “Why We Should Abolish Bride Price in South  Sudan".

When this article was published, I received several emails from readers appreciating my advocacy for respecting the rights and dignity of women, particularly regarding the abolition of bride price payments and other culturally demeaning practices. Among the emails that caught my attention was one from Tatiana Bol—a white woman married to a Nuer man in Australia—whose marriage suddenly came to an end due to multiple cultural differences, including her husband’s habit of contributing money to his relatives to “buy” wives.
I stopped communicating with Tatiana Bol in 2020 after my email inbox became full and I deleted some files to save space. Unfortunately, I also deleted her email and attachments. However, while going through my archive today, November 22, 2025, I came across printed copies of her response that I had shelved. After reading her four-page letter, I felt the need to make her voice and frustration heard.
Being a woman from a different background, she was in a better position to speak out—as she did—on issues that many Nuer women do not dare to discuss. She clearly still loves her dear husband and wishes him all the best. But the cultural odds within Nuer traditions were too much for her to bear. Here is the original excerpt of her email to me. I only wish her husband had changed his mind and listened to the advice of his devoted wife, who deeply cared for him – the guy definitely lost a caring wife – I wish he could reunite with her one day.

Dear Paul,
The opinion piece you wrote on the issue of bride price was excellent—a well-balanced article with all the points you wished to raise clearly supported by evidence and statistics.
I am a white (non-Anglo-Saxon) woman who, until recently, was married to a Nuer man. The South Sudanese practice of bride price was one of the main issues that contributed to disagreement in our marriage. I told him I could not respect a man who regularly participated in making monetary contributions within his Nuer community to help men raise enough money to “buy” a wife.
My ethnic background is Russian Cossack, and I explained to my husband how, in the past, Cossack clans also had a dowry system. However, this tradition—along with other practices such as putting an unfaithful husband alive into a sack and drowning him in the river—was abandoned as people became more Christian and educated.
I asked him to consider how life would be if cultures and traditions never moved on. For example, if the Chinese still practiced foot binding, women today would still have tiny, deformed feet. Or if white people had not abolished slavery, they might still consider it “normal” to travel to Africa to buy people and keep them in chains as slaves.
A point to consider: how interesting it is that South Sudanese cultural practices which negatively affect males—such as the ritual of the gaar or, in some tribes, knocking out several teeth when a boy becomes a man—have slowly disappeared and are now seen as too brutal and old-fashioned.
I have had South Sudanese friends for over 15 years (having been in a relationship with my ex-husband since 2006), and during that time I have spoken with numerous South Sudanese women. My being non-African has often meant they felt “safe” to confide in me about issues of concern:
1. Women said that because their husbands had paid a bride price for them, the husbands believed they could do whatever they liked with their wives.
2. Husbands forcing wives to have sex (i.e., marital rape).a
3. Husbands forcing them to have one child after another, leaving them unable to attend English classes or pursue any kind of study, as they were continually pregnant and caring for newborns.
4. Husbands taking the child benefit money provided by the government to mothers, resulting in children not receiving decent food or clothing.
5. Husbands believing it is “normal and okay” to beat their wives. Even though the women know this behavior is illegal in Australia and other Western countries, they shrug their shoulders and say, “What can we do? This is our culture.”
6. Husbands threatening to throw out their wives and children if the wife does not “obey.” For women with six or more children and little English, obedience becomes the only option, as welfare housing rarely accommodates large families, and without language or work skills, finding employment is nearly impossible.
I have also seen how some South Sudanese men in Australia maintain one legally recognized wife while having additional “wives” with whom they have children, then take money from those women as well. I witnessed a distressing incident in an English class: one South Sudanese woman told other students that her husband had paid a couple of cows and several chickens for her bride price. Another woman from a different tribe mocked her, boasting that her husband had paid $70,000 AUD for her. The first woman became sad and upset, and tension grew between them, even though they had previously gotten along well.
In my view, once you put a price on the life of a human being—some kind of monetary value—you dehumanize them. They become a commodity, an object to be bought and sold. How, then, does paying a bride price differ from human trafficking? While the terminology may be different, essentially, if a human being is bought in a monetary or in-kind transaction, is it not the same thing?
Unfortunately, I believe it will be extremely difficult to abolish the bride price practice among South Sudanese because of three major obstacles: poverty, greed, and pride/competition. The “revenge mentality” is also a huge obstacle. As long as families continue to live in poverty—especially under the dire circumstances in many regions of South Sudan—daughters will be “sold” to secure money for basic necessities. Greedy individuals with no conscience will continue to sell girls out of lust for wealth.
The obstacle of pride and competition is particularly strong among South Sudanese in the diaspora, even those who are university educated. They condone and continue the practice, saying, “This is our culture. This is what our families have always done, and we want to continue this tradition even if we’re not in South Sudan.” This competitive aspect creates rifts within communities and between tribes, with families boasting that their daughter received a higher bride price than another’s, or that their son was a better match because he could afford to pay more. Such attitudes have led to arguments within and between families.
I told my husband how lucky he was that he did not have to pay anything for me—he got me “for free,” along with a home he did not have to pay for. His failure to adequately provide financially for me and our marriage was a breaking point. Although he gave me a small portion of his salary, he was essentially living off me, despite earning twice what I received. He was always sending money to relatives and friends or making “contributions” within the Nuer community.

Dear Paul,
I agree with you that the family unit is the fundamental cornerstone of any society. Yet there is another Nuer practice which I believe contributes to destroying positive family dynamics, as it devalues and demeans women and prevents vital dinner-table discussions from taking place. This is the cultural practice of men eating before women and children, with women and children receiving only what is left after the men have finished.
This issue was a major contributor to the breakdown of my marriage. My husband accused me of not respecting his culture, while I repeatedly told him that I had not been raised to accept being treated like a dog fed scraps from its master’s table. I told him that if we attended South Sudanese social events where this behavior occurred, I would simply not eat. If he went ahead and ate with the men, I would lose all respect for him. On several occasions he compromised by bringing me a plate of food at the same time as he served himself, but I refused it, saying I could not eat while the women around me had none.
This caused great friction between us. He told me I embarrassed him and made him feel ashamed in front of his relatives and friends, as it showed them he could not “control” me. To them, I was a “disobedient” wife who did not “obey” her husband. When his female cousin visited our home and he made her a cup of tea instead of me, she was livid, considering it demeaning for a man to do “women’s work.” Yet five days a week I had dinner ready for him the moment he came home from work. A friend of his once tried to “put me in my place” in front of other South Sudanese men by clicking his fingers and whistling at me like a dog, ordering me to make him tea. Needless to say, I ignored him and walked away.
Satan’s strategy to destroy humanity is one of division and conquest, while God’s strategy is unity, forgiveness, love, and peace—to treat all as equal. God allows the sun to shine equally on all human beings: female, male, honest, dishonest. As it stands, Satan is succeeding in destroying South Sudan by ensuring divisions and friction remain inflamed—between tribes, clans, sub-clans, families, and even between men and women within the family. The more divisions, the greater the scope for conflict.
Paul, I pray that God grants you all you need to bring about positive change regarding South Sudanese cultural practices that bring so much heartache to women.
For the record, I married my husband because I respected his intelligence, humor, and potential—not for monetary gain. When he first arrived in Australia, he had no money and little formal education. Within four years, he had earned a diploma (plus two “Student of the Year” awards), secured a good job, and bought a car. Despite leaving me devastated and heartbroken by divorcing me, I continue to hold love in my heart for him. I know he is fundamentally a good and decent man. But as I often told him: “I am just one tiny white woman whose voice is trying to compete with the hundreds of voices of your relatives and tribe members shouting in your ear.” In the end, his need for approval from his relatives and tribe—to be seen as upholding Nuer traditions—was greater than any love he had for me.
May God be with you and keep you safe.
With warmest wishes, Tatiana Bol

About 63 returnees from Nyolo Boma in Magwi County Return From Refugee Camps in Uganda Back Home.

By Lamson David

Over 60 households from Nyolo Boma have returned from settlement camps in Uganda. 

The Boma chief of Nyolo Boma, Mr. Owan David, disclosed that 63 households have made the journey back due to the lack of social service centers and cut-off food rations, which made continued stay in the camps unsustainable.

Speaking to the Voice of Freedom, Mr. David said that life had become exceedingly difficult for the refugees in neighboring Uganda, prompting their return home to rebuild their hope.

He attributed the mass return to the ration cuts, limited access to social service centers due to financial difficulties, and the absence of land for cultivation.

The Boma chief noted that returnees who arrived in July had already managed to cultivate land, while those arriving now are occupied with cutting grasses to build houses for accommodation. 

He anticipates that a larger influx of people will arrive in Nyolo Boma in January 2026 and will require substantial support from the government and implementing partners.

Voice of Freedom quoted Mr. David as saying that he had sent several reports to the Magwi County Relief and Rehabilitation Commission requesting support, but no feedback had been given.
 
This lack of response has forced the returnees to rely heavily on their relatives for assistance.

Mr. David highlighted that some returnees have resorted to mining in an effort to secure financial support and stabilize their lives, while others are dependent on relatives who have cultivated crops for food.

In May this year, a family of seven was forced to walk on foot from Palabek Camp to Magwi due to inadequate food, limited access to clean water, and a general lack of social services within the settlement.

Haram Things in Islam: In Islam, haram means anything that Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) have clearly forbidden. These limits are not meant to restrict us, but to protect our heart, body, faith, and dignity. Every prohibition carries wisdom, nothing is forbidden without purpose.

1. Shirk (Associating partners with Allah)

Reference:
“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him…” — Surah An-Nisa 4:48

Shirk destroys the foundation of faith and is the greatest sin.

2. Alcohol & Intoxicants

Reference:
“Intoxicants and gambling… are filth from the work of Shaytan.” — Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:90

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Every intoxicant is haram.” — Muslim

3. Zina (Fornication & Adultery)

Reference:
“Do not approach zina…” — Surah Al-Isra 17:32

Islam blocks every doorway that leads to temptation and heartbreak.

4. Riba (Interest/Usury)

Reference:
“Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.” — Surah Al-Baqarah 2:275

Riba creates injustice, exploitation, and social imbalance.

5. Gambling

Reference:
“Intoxicants, gambling… are an abomination from Shaytan.” — Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:90

It destroys wealth, creates addiction, and feeds false hopes.

6. Eating Pork & Carrion (dead animals)

Reference:
“Forbidden to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine…” — Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:3

These foods harm both body and spiritual purity.

7. Stealing, Lying, Cheating & Fraud

Reference:
The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
“Whoever deceives us is not from us.” — Muslim

Islam promotes honesty in every action, contract and relationship.

8. Backbiting & Slander

Reference:
“Do not backbite one another…” — Surah Al-Hujurat 49:12

Allah compares it to eating the flesh of your dead brother — a powerful warning.

9. Oppression & Injustice

Reference:
“O My servants, I have forbidden oppression upon Myself and made it haram among you…” — Hadith Qudsi (Muslim)

Every form of abuse, harm, or injustice is strictly forbidden.

10. Cutting Family Ties

Reference:
The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
“The one who severs family ties will not enter Paradise.” — Bukhari & Muslim

Family bonds are sacred in Islam.

11. Magic, Sorcery & Fortune-Telling

Reference:
“…but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic.” — Surah Al-Baqarah 2:102
The Prophet (ﷺ) said fortune-tellers are not to be believed. — Muslim

These acts open the door to shirk and deception.

12. Extravagance, Arrogance & Showing Off

Reference:
“Indeed, Allah does not like the arrogant and prideful.” — Surah An-Nisa 4:36

Arrogance destroys the heart and distances one from Allah.

A Beautiful Reminder:

Allah does not forbid things to take joy away from us. He forbids what wounds the soul,
destroys the heart, breaks the family, or distances us from Him.

Every haram protects a blessing.
Every halal brings peace.
And every command is a doorway to Jannah.

After the death of the Arabian Prophet Muhammad  there were TWO ORIGINAL theological positions of "TASHBIH" (anthropomorphism) and "TANZIH" (Immaterial transcendence) competed stridently for orthodox status within early Islam until the 10th century. 

TANZIH emphasizes God's absolute Immaterial transcendence and incomparability, asserting "Nothing is like Him" (Quran 42:11), and seeking to purify God from human faults or limitations.

TASHBIH, in its extreme form (often associated with tajsīm or corporealism), describes God and divine attributes using human characteristics or physical analogies, sometimes interpreting Quranic descriptions of God's "hands," "face," or "throne" literally. 

The debate was a dominant feature of early and classical theological thought. The rationalist Muʿtazilite school strongly advocated for tanzih, while some traditionalist scholars, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and early Hanbalis, were accused of holding more anthropomorphic or corporeal views (though they themselves repudiated the label of tashbih). 

By the 10th century, the Ash'ari school of theology, founded by Al-Ashʿarī, emerged and sought a middle ground, accepting the reality of God's attributes as mentioned in scripture "without asking how" ( bi-lā kayf), thus avoiding outright tashbih while also rejecting the excessive allegorical interpretation (ta'wil) of the Mu'tazilites. The Ash'ari position eventually became a dominant strand of Sunni orthodoxy, and tanzih is now widely accepted in mainstream Islam.

Rethinking Satan, the Divine Council, and the Supernatural Worldview of Scripture

One of the most overlooked realities in modern Christianity is that the biblical authors did not view “Satan” as a single, identical figure throughout Scripture. When we flatten the text, we lose the richness of the worldview the Bible assumes. But when we read Scripture the way its original audience understood it, the picture becomes much clearer.

This is where Dr. David Bernard’s hermeneutic is crucial. He frequently emphasizes that we must read the Bible left to right — letting the Old Testament establish the categories that the New Testament later builds upon. Apostolics rely on this method to articulate Oneness Christology with precision, because it anchors our theology in the world of ancient Israel. That same method also compels us to understand spiritual beings, supernatural cosmology, and the satan figure through the lens of the Old Testament first.

In Job 1–2, the figure called ha-satan (“the adversary”) is not the fallen serpent of Genesis 3 or the dragon of Revelation 12. In Job, he appears as a legitimate member of the Divine Council functioning as a prosecutor — an office-holder, not a rebel. He has authorized access to Yahweh’s throne room and operates under divine command. Nothing in Job portrays him as the cosmic enemy of God.

But the serpent of Genesis 3 is an entirely different being. He is cursed, cast down, stripped of his former glory, and exiled from the divine presence. His rebellion is not tolerated among the sons of God. He operates outside Yahweh’s government, against it, in open defiance. This is the being Revelation 12 identifies as the ancient serpent, the devil, and Satan — the one Christ will ultimately destroy in the eschaton.

To collapse these two figures into one creates serious theological consequences. It implies that Yahweh allows a fallen, treasonous rebel to stand in His council chamber, participate in heavenly deliberations, and attack humanity with divine permission. But Scripture never presents Yahweh as negotiating with a cosmic rebel. His throne room is holy. His council is loyal. The original rebel does not operate within Yahweh’s administration.

This is why the Divine Council worldview matters. It preserves the integrity of God’s heavenly government, aligns with ancient Near Eastern and Second Temple Jewish context, and reflects the worldview Jesus and the apostles assumed. It also explains why Jewish interpreters — ancient and modern — consistently differentiate between the adversarial office-holder in Job and the cosmic rebel of later literature. The biblical authors did not treat them as the same figure.

Many Apostolic teachers apply the ancient worldview rigorously when defending the identity of God. Yet when the same worldview expands into supernatural cosmology, they often default to later evangelical interpretations. If we trust ancient Israel’s worldview for monotheism and Christology, we should trust it for everything the apostles inherited from them. The Divine Council does not undermine the oneness of God; it magnifies His supremacy.

Here are some key apologetic questions worth wrestling with:
 1. If the adversary in Job were the devil, why does the text depict him as a loyal council participant rather than as a fallen rebel?
 2. If the serpent in Genesis 3 was cursed and cast down, how could he still function freely in Yahweh’s throne room and participate in heavenly decisions?
 3. If we interpret Scripture left to right, why should Revelation 12 redefine the categories established in Job rather than the other way around?
 4. Why do ancient and modern Jewish interpreters strongly distinguish between the heavenly accuser and the cosmic rebel, while later Christian tradition merges them?
 5. If ancient Israel’s worldview is essential for understanding Oneness Christology, why ignore that same worldview when it comes to the Divine Council, spiritual beings, and supernatural cosmology?

Recovering the biblical worldview does not weaken our theology; it strengthens it. It allows us to read Scripture as the biblical authors intended — not through later traditions, but through the lens of the world in which the Bible was written.

If we want to think biblically, we must see the world the way the biblical authors saw it. This includes their understanding of God, His heavenly host, the adversary, the serpent, and the cosmic conflict that unfolds from Genesis to Revelation.

Tazkiyah — Part Two: The Next Level

In the beginning, tazkiyah is about cleaning.
Removing obvious stains: anger, arrogance, heedlessness, excess.

At the next level, tazkiyah becomes something else.

It becomes refinement.

Not dramatic change.
Not visible transformation.
But a quieter, more demanding work: purifying intention, perception, and attachment.

This is where many stop — because this stage cannot be performed or displayed.

---

From Behavior to Intention

At the first level, you correct what you do.
At the next level, you examine why you do it.

The same action can be:

worship

habit

ego

fear

image-management

Tazkiyah at this stage asks uncomfortable questions:

Would I still do this if no one saw it?

Do I want Allah’s pleasure — or approval?

Am I sincere, or merely disciplined?

This is harder than quitting sins.
Because ego can hide inside good deeds.

---

Letting Go of Control

Early tazkiyah teaches restraint.
Advanced tazkiyah teaches surrender.

Not passivity — but acceptance.

You begin to notice how much inner tension comes from:

needing outcomes

needing recognition

needing certainty

At this stage, purification means releasing the illusion of control.

You still act.
You still strive.
But you stop demanding that life obey you.

The heart becomes lighter — not because life is easier, but because grip loosens.

---

Purifying Perception

The next level of tazkiyah is not about changing the world.
It is about changing how you see it.

You begin to notice:

resentment is a form of attachment

constant judgment clouds clarity

anger often masks wounded pride

Tazkiyah here means learning to see clearly without reacting immediately.

This produces a rare quality in modern life: inner space.

---

Silence Becomes Work

At early stages, words and actions dominate.
At advanced stages, silence becomes a discipline.

Not silence of withdrawal —
silence of presence.

You speak less, but more precisely.
You react less, but more truthfully.
You explain less, but stand more firmly.

This silence is not emptiness.
It is containment.

---

Living Between Two Worlds

At this level, the believer becomes aware of something subtle:

Life is happening in two realms at once.

The visible world of work, family, and responsibility.
And the unseen world of intention, meaning, and accountability.

Tazkiyah trains you to live responsibly in both.

You don’t escape the material world.
You inhabit it without being consumed.

---

The Cost of the Next Level

This stage is not comfortable.

You may feel:

less reactive, but more alone

calmer, but less entertained

clearer, but less impressed

The ego resists this stage fiercely — because it loses its stage.

But what replaces it is better:

steadiness

sincerity

trust

inner dignity

---

In One Sentence

The next level of tazkiyah is when purification shifts from what you remove from your life — to what you release from your heart.

On a family trip to Miami, my parents left my seven-year-old daughter at a stranger’s door and drove off like she was nothing more than unwanted baggage. When I pulled her into my arms, she was shaking and sobbing: “Mom… they said it wouldn’t hurt… but it hurts a lot.” I didn’t shout. I took immediate action. And the next day, their lives started to fall apart…

My name is Laura Bennett, and until that afternoon in Miami, I believed I understood my parents, even if we had never been close. They were strict, image-obsessed people who believed discipline solved everything. What I did not believe—what I could never have imagined—was that they were capable of abandoning my child.

It happened on the fourth day of our family trip. I had stayed back at the hotel to finish a remote work call while my parents insisted on taking my seven-year-old daughter, Emily, out for ice cream. They said I was “too soft” and that Emily needed to learn independence. I remember hesitating, a tight feeling in my chest, but I let them go. I still replay that decision in my mind.

An hour passed. Then two. My phone rang, but it wasn’t my parents. It was a woman named Rachel Moore, her voice trembling as she explained that a little girl was standing barefoot on her doorstep, crying uncontrollably. Rachel lived three miles away. She had found Emily alone, clutching a pink backpack, repeating my phone number like a prayer.

I ran.

When I arrived, Emily was sitting on the steps, her knees scraped, her cheeks streaked with tears. The moment she saw me, she collapsed into my arms, shaking so hard I could feel it in my bones.

“Mom,” she whispered, her voice hoarse, “they said it wouldn’t hurt… but it hurts a lot.”

Those words shattered something inside me.

Rachel explained that my parents had parked, walked Emily to the door, rang the bell, and driven away before anyone answered. No explanation. No note. Nothing. Just a child left with strangers.

I didn’t scream. I didn’t cry. I thanked Rachel, carried my daughter back to the car, and buckled her in with hands that felt eerily calm.

That night, as Emily slept curled against me, I sat in the dark hotel room, staring at my phone. I didn’t confront my parents. Not yet. Because somewhere between rage and clarity, a decision had settled in my chest.

He handed down to Moses minute details concerning a special portable structure called the tabernacle, which the people had built and which would occupy a dominant position in the camp, whenever they were stationary, and in the ranks, when they marched toward their destiny. God said, “I want the people of Israel to build me a sacred residence where I can live among them. You must make this Tabernacle and its furnishings exactly according to the plans I will show you” (Exod. 25:8-9).
The details given to Moses about the architecture, materials, and furnishings seem at first glance to be both extravagant and unnecessary, in light of the fact that the escaping slaves were heading for the Promised Land. But as time would show, the details of the Tabernacle were specifically designed to model spiritual principles. The people could hardly fail to see and appreciate these principles as the tabernacle was built and as it stood prominently in their midst.
The tabernacle was divided into two sections that were separated by a thick curtain. The priests went in and out of the first section daily, but no priest was allowed to enter behind the curtain in the daily liturgy. Only the high priest could go behind the curtain, and that only on one day per year, the Day of Atonement, and then only under the strictest circumstances. The inescapable lesson for the Israelites was that the presence of God could not be entered glibly and casually. The sins of the people were offensive to a holy God, and as a result, man was separated from God and could only approach God as God himself ordained and allowed.
This dramatic ritual not only portrayed the holiness of God to the children of Israel, it prefigured the wonderful work of Christ on the cross. For when Jesus died and rose again, he entered into the unmediated presence of God as our High Priest. In so doing, he went behind the curtain into the holiest place and “secured our salvation for ever” (Heb. 9:12). Only Jesus could offer “himself to God as a perfect sacrifice for our sins” (9:14). Therefore, only Jesus could enter the presence of God and make it possible for forgiven men to do so, too. Jesus drew back the curtain and invited forgiven men to meet God. God is no longer hidden and remote. So now, men once estranged from God by sin can enjoy through Christ an intimacy with him that satisfies their deepest longings and meets their profoundest needs

#Kabbalistic Tree of Life (Etz #Chaim), a central symbol in #Kabbalah representing the structure of creation, the divine #emanations, and the human soul’s ascent toward the divine. This particular version appears to be influenced by #Hermetic #Qabalah (as developed in Western esoteric traditions like the Golden Dawn and earlier #Renaissance sources), with unique planetary attributions and psychological/soul correspondences.
Standard #Structure of the Tree of Life
The Tree consists of 10 Sephirot (spheres/emanations) connected by 22 paths (often linked to #Hebrew letters and #Tarot majors). It is divided into three pillars:
 • Left Pillar (#Severity): Restriction, judgment.
 • Middle Pillar (Mildness): Balance, harmony.
 • Right Pillar (Mercy): Expansion, force.
There is also an “11th” non-Sephirah called Daath (#Knowledge), shown here as a “Bridge” across the #Abyss (the gap between the upper divine triad and the lower worlds).🔺🔻
The #Sephirot from top to bottom are typically:
 1 Kether (Crown)
 2 Chokhmah (Wisdom)
 3 Binah (Understanding)
 4 Chesed (Mercy)
 5 Geburah (Severity)
 6 Tiphareth (Beauty)
 7 Netzach (Victory/Eternity)
 8 Hod (Glory/Splendor)
 9 Yesod (Foundation)
 10 Malkuth (Kingdom) — often implied at the bottom, though numbered 0 or 10 here as G’uph (body).
Key Features in This Diagram
 • #Numbering: The spheres are numbered from 9 (top, Yesod?) down to 0 (Malkuth), with Daath as a bridge. This is non-standard (usually Kether is 1 at the top, Malkuth 10 at the bottom) and may reflect a “descending” view of creation or a specific esoteric mapping.
 • Planetary Associations (listed with symbols):
 ◦ Luna (Moon) at the top (9?)
 ◦ Mercury (8)
 ◦ Venus (7)
 ◦ Sol (Sun) (6)
 ◦ Mars (5)
 ◦ Jupiter (4)
 ◦ Saturn (3)
 • This follows an older pre-modern attribution seen in some Renaissance and geo-centric models (e.g., Ptolemaic order from closest to farthest planets, with Malkuth as Earth). It differs from the common Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn system, where:
 ◦ 3 Binah = #Saturn
 ◦ 4 Chesed = Jupiter
 ◦ 5 Geburah = Mars
 ◦ 6 Tiphareth = Sun
 ◦ 7 Netzach = Venus
 ◦ 8 Hod = Mercury
 ◦ 9 Yesod = Moon
 • Psychological/Soul Correspondences (Hermetic view of the soul’s levels):
 ◦ Yesod: Nephesh — The animal/vital soul (instincts, emotions, basic life force; often tied to Malkuth in standard systems).
 ◦ Hod: Intellect — Rational mind, logic.
 ◦ Netzach: Emotion — Desires, feelings.
 ◦ Tiphareth: Imagination — Creative visualization, harmony of self.
 ◦ Geburah: Will — Discipline, power.
 ◦ Chesed: Memory — Expansion, benevolence.
 ◦ Binah: Neshamah — Higher intuition/soul.
 ◦ Chokhmah: Chiah — Creative life force.
 ◦ Kether: Yechidah — Divine spark/unity with God.
 • These align with esoteric teachings on the multi-layered soul (#Nephesh = lower/animal; Ruach = middle intellect/emotions; #Neshamah/Chiah/#Yechidah = higher divine aspects).
 • Descriptive Texts: The diagram includes poetic explanations, e.g.:
 ◦ “Nine is the father… forming and changing…” (top sphere).
 ◦ “Three holds the key of all #hidden magic…” (Saturn sphere).
 ◦ These evoke mystical qualities of each level.
Purpose and Meaning
The Tree maps:
 • #Macrocosm: How divine energy emanates from the infinite (Ein Sof) into creation.
 • #Microcosm: The human psyche and spiritual path (ascent via meditation, ritual, or pathworking).
 • #Daath as Bridge: Represents “knowledge” that crosses the Abyss — often a point of illusion or enlightenment.
This variant emphasizes astrological/planetary influences on the soul’s faculties and may come from older sources blending Kabbalah with astrology (e.g., pre-Golden Dawn Hermeticism). It’s a tool for meditation, magic, and self-understanding

The Varangian Guard (Greek: Τάγμα τῶν Βαράγγων, Tágma tōn Varángōn) was an elite unit of the Byzantine Army from the tenth to the fourteenth century. The members served as personal bodyguards to the Byzantine emperors. The Varangian Guard was known for being primarily composed of recruits from northern Europe, including mainly Norsemen from Scandinavia but also Anglo-Saxons from England.[1] The recruitment of distant foreigners from outside Byzantium to serve as the emperor's personal guard was pursued as a deliberate policy, as they lacked local political loyalties and could be counted upon to suppress revolts by disloyal Byzantine factions.[2]

"The best interests of the constitution" refers to actions, policies, and interpretations that align with the constitution's fundamental purposes, such as establishing a stable government, protecting citizens' rights and liberties, and maintaining the balance of power among government branches. This concept involves upholding the principles of fundamental justice, preventing the concentration of power to avoid tyranny, and ensuring that all laws conform to the constitution's supreme law status. 
Key Aspects of "Best Interests"
Establishing and Maintaining Government: A constitution's primary interest is to create and sustain a functional national government, including its legislative, executive, and judicial branches. 
Protecting Fundamental Rights: It involves safeguarding the inherent rights and liberties of individuals, such as life, liberty, and security of person. 
Preventing Tyranny: The "best interests" include ensuring that authority is distributed and balanced among different branches of government, preventing any single entity from becoming too powerful, as advocated by thinkers like Montesquieu. 
Upholding Supremacy of the Constitution: Acting in the constitution's best interests means recognizing its status as the supreme law, meaning any inconsistent law is invalid. 
Adhering to Principles of Justice: Interpretations and actions should be consistent with the fundamental principles of justice that underpin the legal and constitutional system. 
How It's Applied
Judicial Interpretation: Courts, particularly Supreme Courts, interpret the constitution's provisions to determine what actions or laws are consistent with its best interests, often referencing foundational texts and historical precedents. 
Legislative Action: Lawmakers must create legislation that respects the constitutional framework and fundamental rights. 
Public and Citizen Engagement: Citizens and public discourse play a role in advocating for and upholding policies that align with the constitution's enduring principles.

Subversion (from Latin subvertere 'overthrow') refers to a process by which the values and principles of a system in place are contradicted or reversed in an attempt to sabotage the established social order and its structures of power, authority, tradition, hierarchy, and social norms. Subversion can be described as an attack on the public morale and, "the will to resist intervention are the products of combined political and social or class loyalties which are usually attached to national symbols. Following penetration, and parallel with the forced disintegration of political and social institutions of the state, these tendencies may be detached and transferred to the political or ideological cause of the aggressor".[1]

Subversion is used as a tool to achieve political goals because it generally carries less risk, cost, and difficulty as opposed to open belligerency. Furthermore, it is a relatively cheap form of warfare that does not require large amounts of training.[2] A subversive is something or someone carrying the potential for some degree of subversion. In this context, a "subversive" is sometimes called a "traitor" with respect to (and usually by) the government in power. Subversion is also often a goal of comedians, artists and people in those careers.[3] In this case, being subversive can mean questioning, poking fun at, and undermining the established order in general.[4]

Terrorist groups generally do not employ subversion as a tool to achieve their goals. Subversion is a manpower-intensive strategy and many groups lack the manpower and political and social connections to carry out subversive activities.[5] However, actions taken by terrorists may have a subversive effect on society. Subversion can imply the use of insidious, dishonest, monetary, or violent methods to bring about such change. This is in contrast to protest, a coup d'état, or working through traditional means in a political system to bring about change. Furthermore, external subversion is where, "the aggressor state attempts to recruit and assist indigenous political and military actors to overthrow their government by coup d’état".[6] If subversion fails in its goal of bringing about a coup it is possible that the actors and actions of the subversive group could transition to insurrection, insurgency, and/or guerrilla warfare.[7]

COURT DOCUMENTS DETAIL THURSTON COUNTY ROAD RAGE HOMICIDE: A man is dead and another man is in jail on murder charges following a road rage incident in Lacey on Friday, Dec. 19. 

Tucker S. Shirk, 24, of Lacey, is accused of fatally shooting Eddie Y. Park, 48, also of Lacey, in the 2400 block of Marvin Road Northeast. 

Shirk is reportedly an active duty member of the military and had a concealed carry license at the time of the shooting. 

Shirk allegedly called 911 at approximately 8:51 p.m. to report that he was involved in an incident with another man whom he had shot with a firearm. 

According to documents filed in Thurston County Superior Court on Monday, Dec. 22, Shirk refused to perform CPR on the man who had been shot. 

That man was later identified as Park. 

Responding officers with the Lacey Police Department arrived at the scene at approximately 8:54 p.m. and began CPR on Park, who had been shot in the neck and was struggling to breathe.

One of the detectives reportedly “asked in a loud tone about where the shooter was located,” at which point Shirk, standing about 25 years away and “looking nervous,” identified himself as the shooter. 

He was detained in handcuffs while Lacey medics took over CPR. 

“The Lacey Fire Department continued with lifesaving measures, but Mr. Park was ultimately declared deceased,” the Thurston County Prosecutor’s Office stated in the affidavit of probable cause. 

When questioned by detectives, Shirk gave his recollection of the events leading up to the shooting. His narrative was repeated by the Thurston County Prosecutor's Office in the affidavit of probable cause. 

Shirk allegedly told detectives that he was returning to his Lacey home on Birdseye Avenue Northeast in Lacey after picking up dinner from a restaurant in the 1100 block of Marvin Road Northeast. 

He reported that he was driving northbound on Marvin Road Northeast near the bridge and exit lane to southbound Interstate 5 when a grey Tesla suddenly merged out of the exit lane, cutting Shirk off. 

Frustrated, Shirk reported that he started honking his horn and flipping off the other driver, who was later identified as Park. 

According to Shirk, Park slowed down to 20 mph in a 35 mph zone “on purpose,” then began switching between brake-checking him and “maliciously” driving slowly. 

Shirk then reportedly again honked and flipped Park off. 

As they continued, Park reportedly moved over into the far right lane, then into a turn lane toward the Lacey dump and dog park, before speeding up to pass him and flip him off. 

Park then reportedly maneuvered "aggressively" back behind Shirk’s vehicle, “staying very close to his number in an ‘aggressive’ manner,” according to Shirk. 

Shirk said he brake-checked Park twice as they both continued driving on Martin Road Northeast. 

The two continued past a roundabout near the 2300 block of Marvin Road Northeast before getting stuck side-by-side behind traffic before a crosswalk in the 2400 block of Marvin Road Northeast.  Shirk was reportedly in the left lane, while Park was in the right. 

Shirk reported that Park had his driver’s side window rolled down and had motioned for Shirk to roll his window down. 

Shirk reported that he rolled his passenger window down and yelled expletives at Park. 

Park then got out of his car “aggressively,” according to Shirk. 

Shirk allegedly said he “ immediately” drew his Shadow Systems MR920 from the front holster on his belt under his shirt, pointed it at Park out the open passenger window, and said “Get in your car. I will shoot you. Get in your car.” 

Shirk allegedly said he repeated the command four to five times. 

According to Shirk, Park said “shoot me, shoot me,” and reached into Shirk’s open window and began “pawing” at the gun. 

Shirk reported that Park’s hand didn’t touch the gun outside of a “graze” with his fingertips, according to court documents. 

Shirk reported that he pulled the gun back towards his body, and that Park began to step back from Shirk’s car. 

Shirk then allegedly fired a single shot.

He allegedly told a detective that “he was not aiming any particular place, as the distance between them left the male still very close to his vehicle.” 

When asked by a detective if he had thought to shoot Park while he was reaching for the gun, Shirk allegedly said “he had a brief thought to shoot the driver then, but even in that moment thought that he did not want to shoot the man.” 

Shirk allegedly said “his adrenaline was high, and he perceived ongoing hostility from the driver.” 

Park had no visible weapons on his person at the time, Shirk confirmed to a detective. 

Immediately after the shooting, Shirk said, he put his car in park, stepped out, and called 911. He reportedly unloaded the remaining 16 rounds from his firearm while on the phone with dispatchers. He then reportedly stepped 15 to 20 feet away from the vehicles to await police, saying he didn’t want to be holding the weapon when they arrived. 

When asked by dispatch if Park was breathing, Shirk said he approached Park, shook him, said “sir, sir,” and saw “what he observed to be agonal breathing,” according to court documents. 

At that point, Shirk said he noticed two children in Park’s car -– one in the front seat and one in the backseat.  

The children were reportedly still in the car when Lacey officers arrived. 

Several bystanders began to exit their own vehicles, but did not interact with Shirk. 

Shirk reportedly told detectives that this was his “first self-defense situation,” describing how he has had a concealed carry permit for two-to-three years and has never been in a situation where he “had to use it.” He reported that he had military and concealed carry experience, and had expressed instant “panic” after the shooting. 

A detective described Shirk’s demeanor during his interview as “calm,” noting how he described the incident as self-defense. 

His description of the road rage leading up to the shooting was reportedly consistent with witness statements from two other drivers, according to court documents. 

Shirk was booked into the Thurston County Jail on Saturday, Dec. 20, after being interviewed by detectives. 

A Thurston County Superior Court judge found probable cause Monday, Dec. 22, to charge Shirk with second-degree murder while armed with a firearm, second-degree assault while armed with a firearm, and first-degree manslaughter while armed with a firearm. 

The same judge also revoked bail for Shirk, meaning he will remain in custody until his case is resolved, or his conditions of release are changed. 

Arraignment was scheduled for Friday, Dec. 26.

Your Stomach Gets a New Lining Every Few Days!

Your stomach is a powerhouse of digestion, producing strong acids that help break down food into nutrients your body can absorb. But did you know that your stomach has a remarkable self-defense system? It replaces its lining every 3 to 4 days to protect itself from its own harsh digestive acids!

The Science Behind the Fact

Your stomach secretes hydrochloric acid—a substance so powerful that it can break down proteins and even dissolve metal under certain conditions. To prevent this acid from digesting the stomach itself, a thick layer of mucus and specialized epithelial cells form a protective lining.

These cells are constantly under attack from stomach acids and digestive enzymes, so the body rapidly replaces them every few days to maintain a fresh, healthy barrier. Without this natural renewal process, painful stomach ulcers could easily form.

Research and Medical Insights

Researchers studying stomach cell regeneration have found insights into gastrointestinal health and disorders like gastritis and peptic ulcers. Understanding how the stomach lining renews itself helps scientists develop treatments for conditions caused by bacteria like Helicobacter pylori—a common culprit behind ulcers.

Real-Life Applications
 • Medication Development: Drugs like proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) help reduce acid production in people with ulcers or acid reflux.
 • Cancer Research: Studying stomach cell renewal also aids in understanding how cancer cells grow and how to stop them.
 • Digestive Health: Understanding this renewal process emphasizes the importance of diets that support gut health, including foods rich in fiber and probiotics.

Why It Matters

Your stomach’s ability to renew itself is a perfect example of how your body’s natural systems are designed for resilience. Maintaining a healthy stomach lining is essential for proper digestion and overall health—so taking care of your gut through a balanced diet, hydration, and regular checkups can help keep this incredible process running smoothly.

What does “gullible women” mean in 2 Timothy 3:6?

Answer

In 2 Timothy 3:6, Paul explains how false teachers “creep into households and make captives of gullible women loaded down with sins, led away by various lusts” (NKJV). The Greek word for “gullible” is gunaikaria, which refers to women who are easily deceived or manipulated. Apparently, there were women in Ephesus who had been deceived and manipulated by false teachers because of their guilt and their lack of self-control (they are “burdened with the guilt of sin and controlled by various desires,” NLT).

Paul begins the third chapter of 2 Timothy with a description of false teachers in the last days (2 Timothy 3:1–9). In the last days, “people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of power, but denying its power” (verses 1–5, ESV). It is in this context that Paul mentions “gullible women” who are easily swayed by false teachers because of the burden of their sin.

The word gunaikaria, translated “gullible women” in the NKJV, is a diminutive word, literally meaning “little women” or “small women.” These women were “small” in their strength, “small” in their discernment, and “small” in their knowledge of and commitment to the truth. These women were targeted by false teachers who “worm their way into homes and gain control over” them (2 Timothy 3:6). The charlatans sought to secure the good graces of weak-willed women, promising relief from their guilt and taking advantage of their unchecked desires. In this way, the false teachers followed the example of Satan himself, who tempted Eve in the garden, rather than attack Adam directly. If they could get the women on their side, the false teachers had a foothold in the home.

Nothing in this passage suggests that all women are “gullible” or weak-willed. Paul is referring to a particular type of woman who was being victimized by false teachers. Generally, in Paul’s day, women were kept in isolation and were considered a lower social class than men. Most were uneducated, and few had much public interaction. It was among these women that the false teachers sought ways to finagle inroads. The unscrupulous religious frauds were preying on women and taking advantage of their problems.

All of us need spiritual maturity and discernment to protect ourselves from false teachers. The apostle John exhorts, “Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). Christians must stand firm on the truth. Other passages, such as Ephesians 4:14, emphasize the need for believers not to be “carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes” (ESV).

False teachers “creep into households” (2 Timothy 3:6, NKJV) to find their victims, exploiting gullible women for personal gain. The tactics of false teachers should be a warning for all believers to be vigilant. In Matthew 7:15, Jesus warns about “false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (ESV). Creeping into households is even easier today, with the prevalence of false teaching on broadcast television and streaming devices.

The mention of “gullible women” or “small women” in 2 Timothy 3:6 is significant for believers today. We dare not be “small” in strength, discernment, or knowledge. We must be strong-willed. We must grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord. We must remain rooted and grounded in Christ, who is the foundation of our faith. Moreover, we must not be weighed down by past guilt; instead, we should trust and believe that Christ covered our past, present, and future sins. “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9, ESV).

Church leaders must protect their congregation, especially the gullible, from the deceptive practices of false teachers. The primary way to do this is to teach sound doctrine. Paul urges Timothy to “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2, ESV). Leaders should teach sound doctrine, instruct, correct, and encourage. In doing so, they can protect gullible women and other believers from the influence of false teachers.
