My own mother abandoned me at the airport when I was just eight, leaving me with just a backpack, all to enjoy a luxurious vacation with her new husband and his kids. When I called crying, she coldly said, "You can figure it out. I'm not ruining my perfect family trip for your worthless drama." Her new husband added, "Some brats just need to learn real independence the hard way." His spoiled children laughed in the background. "Finally, a real vacation without the unwanted baggage." She added, "Stop being so pathetic and needy. Find your own way home." I did figure it out by calling my estranged father who arrived in a private jet. When she returned, she found my room empty and legal papers waiting.

My name is Leah, and when I was eight, my world revolved around my mom, Annette. She was everything to me after my parents divorced when I was 5. My father, Gordon, had essentially disappeared from our lives after the divorce. Mom always told me he was too busy with his business empire to care about us, that he'd chosen money over family. I believed her completely.

Mom remarried when I was seven to a man named Calvin, who came with two children of his own: Kylie, who was 10, and Noah, who was nine. From the beginning, it was clear that I was the outsider in this new family unit. Calvin made no effort to hide his preference for his biological children, and my mother seemed to go along with whatever made her new husband happy.

Kylie and Noah were everything I wasn't in Calvin's eyes. They were confident, demanding, and knew exactly how to manipulate situations to their advantage. Kylie had this way of smiling sweetly at adults while being absolutely vicious to me when they weren't looking. Noah was more direct in his cruelty, often "accidentally" breaking my toys or spilling things on my homework.

The problems started small. Family movie nights where I was told there wasn't enough room on the couch. Birthday parties where Kylie and Noah got elaborate celebrations while mine was forgotten or hastily thrown together. Vacation photos where I was consistently cropped out or positioned at the edges. I was too young to understand what was happening, but I felt the cold distance growing between my mother and me.

Everything came to a head during spring break of my second grade year. Calvin had planned an elaborate two-week vacation to Hawaii for "the family." I was so excited I could barely sleep for weeks beforehand. I had never been on a real vacation, and the thought of building sand castles with mom and maybe finally bonding with my new siblings filled me with hope.

The morning of departure, I woke up early and carefully packed my little purple backpack with my favorite stuffed animal, some books, and the new swimsuit mom had bought me. I was practically vibrating with excitement as we drove to the airport. Calvin seemed unusually quiet, and Kylie and Noah kept exchanging these knowing looks that made me uncomfortable, but I pushed those feelings aside.

At the airport, everything seemed normal at first. We checked in for our flight, and I held tightly to my boarding pass, reading "Honolulu" over and over again. Then Calvin said he needed to use the restroom and took Kylie and Noah with him. Mom said she was going to grab coffee and told me to wait by our gate.

I sat there for what felt like hours watching families board planes and wondering when my family would come back. Other children were running around with their parents, laughing and excited for their trips. I kept checking the big clock on the wall, noting that our departure time was getting closer.

Finally, I decided to call mom's cell phone. When she answered, there was loud music and laughter in the background. "Mom, where are you? Our plane is about to leave." There was a pause. Then her voice came through cold and distant in a way I'd never heard before.

"Leah, listen carefully. You're not coming with us." I didn't understand. "What do you mean? I have my ticket. I'm at the gate." "I mean, you're staying here. Calvin thinks it would be better if it was just our new family on this trip. You can figure it out. I'm not ruining my perfect family trip for your worthless drama."

I started crying, not understanding what was happening. "But mom, I don't know how to get home. I'm only eight." Calvin's voice came through the phone, harsh and dismissive. "Some brats just need to learn real independence the hard way. Maybe this will teach you some character." In the background, I could hear Kylie and Noah laughing. Kylie's voice carried clearly. "Finally, a real vacation without the unwanted baggage."

My mother's voice returned, and what she said next is burned into my memory forever. "Stop being so pathetic and needy, Leah. Find your own way home. You're smart enough to figure it out." The line went dead.

I stood there in the middle of Denver International Airport, 8 years old, clutching a phone and a backpack, completely alone. The reality of what had just happened hit me like a physical blow. My own mother had abandoned me. The woman who was supposed to protect me, love me unconditionally, had left me stranded hundreds of miles from home without a second thought.

Airport security found me about 20 minutes later, sobbing uncontrollably by the gate. They were kind, but clearly confused about how a child had ended up alone. When I tried to explain that my mom had left me, they initially thought there had been some kind of misunderstanding. They brought me to the airport's family services office, a small room with cheerful decorations that felt surreal given my situation.

A gentle woman named Mrs. Vega sat with me while they tried to figure out what to do. They called my mother's phone repeatedly, but it went straight to voicemail. As part of their standard protocol for unaccompanied minors, the airport security office recorded all phone conversations for legal protection.

"Sweetheart," Mrs. Vega said gently. "Is there anyone else we can call? Any other family members?" I thought hard. Mom had always said my father didn't want anything to do with us, but he was the only other person I could think of. I barely remembered him, just fragments of a tall man with kind eyes who used to read me bedtime stories. But I had secretly memorized his phone number years ago from mom's old address book when I was curious about him.

"My dad," I whispered, "but mom says he doesn't care about me." Mrs. Vega encouraged me to try anyway. With shaking fingers, I dialed the number I'd memorized and kept hidden in my heart for so long. The phone rang three times before a familiar voice answered.

"Gordon Cavendish speaking." "Daddy?" The word came out as barely a whisper. There was dead silence on the other end, then a sharp intake of breath. "Leah? Leah, is that you?" "Yes," I managed through my tears. "Daddy, I'm scared. Mom left me at the airport and I don't know what to do."

What happened next surprised everyone, including me. My father's voice changed completely, becoming urgent and focused. "Where are you exactly? Which airport?" "Denver. Mom was supposed to take me to Hawaii, but she said I couldn't come, and now I'm alone and I don't know how to get home."

"Listen to me very carefully, sweetheart. You're going to be okay. I want you to stay exactly where you are. Give the phone to the adult who's with you." I handed the phone to Mrs. Vega. I could only hear her side of the conversation, but her expressions shifted from skepticism to surprise to something like amazement. "Yes, sir. Yes, I understand. She's safe with us. How long will that take? A private jet? Yes, sir. We'll have her ready."

When she hung up, she looked at me with new eyes. "Honey, your father is coming to get you. He'll be here in 3 hours." I couldn't believe it. The father, who supposedly didn't care about me, was dropping everything to come get me...

Its inner lining is renewed every 2 to 4 days as old epithelial cells are shed and rapidly replaced by new ones generated from stem cells. Without this continuous regeneration, the stomach could begin digesting its own surface, leading to inflammation, ulcers, and serious injury. Pembagian Bid‘ah Menurut Ulama Mazhab Syafi‘i

Dalam khazanah keilmuan Islam, istilah bid‘ah tidak selalu bermakna sesat atau tercela. Ulama besar mazhab Syafi‘i, seperti Imam ‘Izzuddin bin ‘Abdis Salam (w. 660 H) dan dijelaskan pula oleh Imam an-Nawawi, membagi bid‘ah berdasarkan hukum syariat, bukan sekadar “ada atau tidak ada di zaman Nabi”.

Imam ‘Izzuddin bin ‘Abdis Salam berkata dalam Qawā‘id al-Aḥkām:

Bid‘ah terbagi menjadi lima: wajib, sunnah, haram, makruh, dan mubah.

Pembagian ini menunjukkan bahwa penilaian bid‘ah harus dikembalikan kepada kaidah hukum Islam, bukan emosi atau fanatisme.

1. Bid‘ah Wajib

Yaitu perkara baru yang wajib dilakukan karena tanpanya kewajiban agama tidak bisa terjaga.

Contoh:

Menyusun ilmu nahwu dan sharaf untuk menjaga pemahaman Al-Qur’an dan hadis.

Kodifikasi ilmu hadits (jarh wa ta‘dil, musthalah hadits).

Menulis mushaf Al-Qur’an dengan tanda baca dan titik.

➡ Semua ini tidak ada di zaman Nabi ﷺ, tetapi wajib hukumnya karena menjaga agama.

2. Bid‘ah Sunnah

Perkara baru yang dianjurkan karena membawa kebaikan dan tidak bertentangan dengan syariat.

Contoh:

Shalat tarawih berjamaah secara terus-menerus (dipelopori Umar bin Khattab).

Peringatan Maulid Nabi sebagai sarana menumbuhkan cinta kepada Rasulullah ﷺ.

Majelis dzikir dan shalawat bersama.

➡ Tidak dilakukan Nabi secara formal, tetapi sejalan dengan prinsip syariat.

3. Bid‘ah Mubah

Perkara baru yang boleh dilakukan atau ditinggalkan, tidak bernilai pahala atau dosa secara khusus.

Contoh:

Menggunakan mikrofon saat khutbah.

Membangun pesantren dengan sistem kelas modern.

Memakai pakaian tertentu saat pengajian.

➡ Murni urusan teknis dan kebiasaan.

4. Bid‘ah Makruh

Perkara baru yang tidak disukai, meskipun tidak sampai haram.

Contoh:

Menghias masjid secara berlebihan hingga mengganggu kekhusyukan.

Memanjangkan bacaan doa dengan berlebihan tanpa kebutuhan.

➡ Tidak berdosa besar, tapi lebih baik ditinggalkan.

5. Bid‘ah Haram

Perkara baru yang bertentangan dengan Al-Qur’an, Sunnah, dan ijma‘ ulama.

Contoh:

Menambah atau mengurangi rukun ibadah (misalnya menambah rakaat shalat wajib).

Keyakinan sesat dalam akidah, seperti menyamakan makhluk dengan Allah.

Ritual ibadah yang mengandung unsur syirik.

➡ Inilah bid‘ah yang tercela dan sesat.

Kesimpulan

Tidak semua bid‘ah itu haram. Menurut ulama mazhab Syafi‘i:

> Bid‘ah dinilai dari isinya, bukan semata-mata dari “ada atau tidak ada di zaman Nabi”.

Jika sesuai dengan kaidah syariat → bisa wajib, sunnah, atau mubah.
Jika bertentangan → bisa makruh atau haram.

Inilah pendekatan ilmiah Ahlussunnah wal Jama‘ah, bukan pendekatan hitam-putih yang menyederhanakan agama.

This profound insight from **Khalil Gibran**, the Lebanese-American poet, philosopher, and artist (best known for *The Prophet*, 1923), reframes the root of human anxiety in a deeply spiritual and psychological way.

Gibran suggests that worry about the future isn't primarily caused by contemplating what might happen—uncertainty itself isn't the villain. Instead, anxiety arises from our ego's desperate **attachment to control**: the illusion that we can (or should) dictate outcomes, shape events, or secure perfect safety in an ever-changing universe. Mere thinking about tomorrow can be neutral or even creative; it's the grasping, the "wanting to control it," that breeds fear, restlessness, and suffering.

This echoes Eastern wisdom (Taoism, Buddhism) that Gibran often wove into his work: true peace comes from surrender, trust in life's flow, and living fully in the present. When we release the need to orchestrate the uncontrollable, anxiety dissolves—not because the future becomes certain, but because we stop fighting its uncertainty.

Usman Khawaja, the elegant left-handed batsman who recently announced his retirement from international cricket on January 2, 2026, ahead of his farewell Test at the Sydney Cricket Ground, stands as one of the most significant figures in modern Australian sport. Born in Islamabad, Pakistan, and migrating to Australia at the age of four (some sources say five), he overcame immense barriers to become the first Muslim and the first player of Pakistani origin to represent Australia in Test cricket. His debut came in the 2010–11 Ashes series at the very SCG where his international journey will now conclude. Yet, despite his multifaceted life—as a husband, father, son, practicing Muslim, qualified pilot, and advocate for social causes—his **global identity** remains anchored firmly in one thing: he is an Australian cricketer.

This is not to diminish the other dimensions of who Usman Khawaja is. He is a devoted family man, married with two daughters, who has spoken openly about the support of his parents, Tariq and Fozia, in navigating life as an immigrant in a new country. He is a man of faith whose identity as a Muslim has shaped his worldview and, at times, brought him into the spotlight for principled stands on human rights and inclusivity. He is also a human being who has faced personal challenges, including injuries, repeated drops from the national side (seven times in his career), and moments of doubt. But the reality is undeniable: the world knows Usman Khawaja primarily because he plays cricket for Australia. People recognize his name, follow his innings, and celebrate his achievements due to the runs he has scored in the Baggy Green—over 6,200 Test runs at an average above 43, including 16 centuries—and the pivotal role he played in major victories, such as Australia’s World Test Championship triumph and dominant Ashes campaigns.

Khawaja’s breakthrough performances, like his twin centuries in the 2022 Ashes return or his 496 runs during the 2023 Ashes (the most in the series), silenced critics and cemented his place as one of Australia’s most reliable and stylish openers. He was named ICC Men’s Test Cricketer of the Year in 2023, the only batsman to score over 1,200 Test runs that year. These feats are what earned him worldwide recognition, from fans in Pakistan to admirers in England, India, and beyond. Without cricket, the story of a boy from Islamabad who became a trailblazer in Australian sport would not have reached the global stage. Cricket gave him the platform, the fame, and the voice.

Having said that, Australian cricket deserves credit for embracing him. The sport in Australia has historically been seen as predominantly white, and Khawaja himself has spoken candidly about early pressures to conform and the challenges of fitting into that culture, especially in the post-9/11 era. He has faced drops, criticism, and what he describes as differential treatment at times—including recent scrutiny over a back injury in the 2025–26 Ashes. Yet, the system ultimately supported him. Cricket Australia backed his selection through ups and downs, teammates like Steve Smith and captains like Pat Cummins stood by him, and he was given opportunities to prove himself repeatedly. Every player gets dropped, faces harsh criticism, or feels treated unfairly—even legends like Ricky Ponting, Shane Warne, or Steve Smith have endured it. This is the nature of elite sport worldwide, not unique to Australia. Khawaja’s persistence, talent, and eventual success highlight how the Australian setup, while imperfect, has been inclusive enough to allow a Pakistani-born Muslim to become a mainstay and even a symbol of progress.

In his emotional retirement speech, Khawaja reflected on inspiring “the next Usman Khawaja”—those who feel different or are told they don’t belong. He emphasized unity, stating he tried to bring people together where others divide. Australian cricket has evolved during his 15-year career, becoming more accessible and representative, thanks in part to pioneers like him. Through his Usman Khawaja Foundation, he has supported disadvantaged youth in pursuing cricket, further extending the game’s reach.

At the end of the day, Usman Khawaja’s towering global presence exists because of cricket—and specifically because of Australian cricket. He should never forget this, and he should remain deeply thankful. The game lifted him from a migrant background to international stardom, gave him a platform to express his values, and allowed him to represent a nation that welcomed his family decades ago. His story is a powerful reminder that while identities are layered and complex, sometimes the most defining one—the one that opens doors and touches the world—is the one earned through dedication on the field. Usman Khawaja, the Australian cricketer: thank you, and farewell.

Why I Use the Name “The Wounded Theologian”

I didn’t choose this name to be dramatic. I chose it because it’s true.

For a long time, I tried to do theology from a safe distance. I valued clear thinking, clean categories, and a faith that could be studied without being touched by it. I worked hard to be structured and systematic in both my approach and my conclusions, and for a while that felt like maturity.

It worked, until it didn’t.

In the process, I diminished my own humanity and the humanity of Christ in order to construct what I can now see was a kind of gnostic system. It was abstract, internally consistent, and self referential. It held together on paper, but it could not bear the weight of lived experience.

Growing up inside a complicated and often harmful family system taught me early how easily God language can be used to control, silence, or spiritualize pain. Some of the deepest wounds didn’t come from doubt or rebellion, but from loyalty and survival. From learning too young how to keep the peace and carry responsibility that was never meant to be mine.

Those experiences didn’t destroy faith, but they shattered a certain kind of innocence. I could no longer pretend that theology floats above real lives. Theology is forged inside them, often inside broken ones.

It wasn’t until I was challenged by William P. Young through The Shack that I began to see how sterile my beliefs had become. They were coherent, but emotionally unreachable. As parts of me began to heal, my old system started to fragment. It simply couldn’t accompany me into wholeness. Something more human was required.

That disruption opened the door to Trinitarian and relational theology, where God is not an isolated authority figure but a living communion of Father, Son, and Spirit. In that vision, relationship is not a secondary theme but the very life of God, and healing is not achieved through control or certainty, but through participation in love that makes room for weakness and truth.

I’m aware of the resonance with Henri Nouwen’s phrase The Wounded Healer. I’m not borrowing it or competing with it, only naming a similar posture from a different vocation, theology shaped not from distance, but from lived reality.

I use the name The Wounded Theologian because my thinking about God has been shaped as much by what harmed me as by what healed me. Some beliefs collapsed when they could no longer carry what I had placed on them. Others survived, but only after being stripped down to something truer.

This isn’t theology grounded in certainty or dominance. It’s theology shaped by scars. It knows how easily religious language can wound and how carefully it must be handled. It refuses easy answers, not because answers don’t matter, but because people do.

If God meets us anywhere, it isn’t after we’ve cleaned ourselves up. God meets us where truth finally catches up with us, where pretending stops, and where grace doesn’t explain the wound but stays present within it.
That’s where I write from. That’s why I use the name.

Rejecting Propaganda, Reclaiming Unity: A Call to All 64 Tribes

Our communities across all 64 tribes must understand their rights, autonomy, and power, and refuse to be manipulated by government propaganda. The government must stop deceiving our elders by claiming that the Nuer and Arabs are coming to attack them, a tactic used to mobilize young people into the military and fuel conflict against the Nuer.

Likewise, Nuer youth, especially the White Army, must recognize that the Dinka people are not their enemy. The real issue is the conduct and agenda of the South Sudan government. In the video, I urged our elders and villagers not to accept the government’s narrative that Arabs and Nuer are preparing to fight them. This falsehood is designed to provoke hostility between Nuer and Dinka communities. Instead, I called on all of us to stand together, reject division, and confront injustice as one people.

South Sudan’s government must choose peace and dialogue over mobilizing youth and the military to fight one another. Our future depends on unity, truth, and a shared commitment to justice.

⁦▪️⁩ ثَانِيًا : هُمْ يَفْعَلُونَ ذَلِكَ ، لِأَنَّهُمْ يَتَبَرَّكُونَ بِالأَطْفَالِ لِخُلُوِّهِمْ وَطَهَارَتِهِمْ مِنَ المَعْصِيَةِ وَالذُّنُوبِ وَالآثَامِ وَلِهَذَا يُعَبَّرُ عَنْهُمْ بِـ " المَلَائِكَةِ " لِطُهْرِهَا مِنَ الذَّنْبِ

فَتَكُونُ طَهَارَةُ الأَطْفَالِ مِنَ الذَّنْبِ سَبَبًا لِجَلْبِ البَرَكَةِ وَالخَيْرِ عَلَى الأَهْلِ وَالعَشِيرَةِ ، فَتَكُونُ #سَنَتُهُمُ_الفِلَاحِيَّةُ عَامِرَةً وَمَحَاصِيلُهُمْ مُبَارَكَةً تَحْمِلُ الخَيْرَاتِ .

وَحَثْوُ الحَلْوَى عَلَى رَأْسِ الطِّفْلِ لِتَكُونَ سَنَتُهُمْ وَسَنَةُ الطِّفْلِ حُلْوَةً فَهِيَ مِنْ #بَابِ_الفَأْلِ_الحَسَنِ حَسَبَ اِعْتِقَادِهِمُ البَاطِلِ

وَهَذَا التَّبَرُّكُ هُوَ مِنَ #الشِّرْكِ_الأَصْغَرِ وَقَدْ يُفْضِي إِلَى #الشِّرْكِ_الأَكْبَرِ 

🔴 #فَائِدَةٌ عَقَائِدِيَّةٌ مُهِمَّةٌ يَجِبُ مَعْرِفَتُهَا : فَإِنْ قِيلَ هَذَا الفِعْلُ مَتَى يَكُونُ #شِرْكًا_أَكْبَرَ وَمَتَى يَكُونُ #شِرْكًا_أَصْغَرَ

الجَوَابُ

⁦▪️⁩_ يَكُونُ #شِرْكًا_أَكْبَرَ إِذَا اِعْتُقِدَ أَنَّ هَذَا الطِّفْلَ هُوَ الَّذِي سَيَهَبُ البَرَكَةَ بِنَفْسِهِ، فَيُبَارِكُ فِي الحَرْثِ وَالزَّرْعِ وَغَيْرِهَا بِذَاتِهِ اِسْتِقْلَالًا مِنْ دُونِ اللّٰهِ حَيْثُ يُبَارِكُ تِلْكَ القَصْعَةَ لِتَكُونَ السَّنَةُ الفِلَاحِيَّةُ مُبَارَكَةً وَفِيرَةً .

فَالتَّبَرُّكُ الشِّرْكِيُّ ( شِرْكٌ أَكْبَرُ ) وَهُوَ مَا فِيهِ طَلَبُ الخَيْرِ وَالنَّمَاءِ مِنْ غَيْرِ اللّٰهِ ﷻ فِيمَا لَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا اللّٰهُ ﷻ كَأَنْ يَعْتَقِدَ المُتَبَرِّكُ فِي طِفْلٍ مَا ، أَوْ رَجُلٍ مَا أَوْ حَجَرٍ أَوْ شَجَرٍ أَوْ غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّنْ هُمْ مِنْ دُونِ اللّٰهِ القُدْرَةَ عَلَى إِعْطَاءِ الخَيْرِ وَالنَّمَاءِ فَوْقَ الأَسْبَابِ العَادِيَّةِ .

فَهَذَا التَّبَرُّكُ الشِّرْكِيُّ #شِرْكٌ_أَكْبَرُ بَلْ هُوَ #شِرْكٌ_فِي_الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ لِأَنَّهُ يَرْجِعُ إِلَى التَّصَرُّفِ فِي الكَوْنِ

⁦▪️⁩_ يَكُونُ #شِرْكًا_أَصْغَرَ وَهُوَ مَا يُسَمَّى بِـ ( التَّبَرُّكِ البِدْعِيِّ )

وَذَلِكَ يَكُونُ إِذَا اِعْتُقِدَ أَنَّ الَّذِي يَهَبُ البَرَكَةَ بِنَفْسِهِ عَلَى وَجْهِ الِاسْتِقْلَالِ هُوَ اللّٰهُ وَحْدَهُ ﷻ ، وَأَنَّ تَبَرُّكَهُمْ بِهَذَا الطِّفْلِ إِنَّمَا هُوَ مِنْ بَابِ الفَأْلِ فَقَطْ .

فَهُمْ يَطْلُبُونَ الخَيْرَ وَالبَرَكَةَ وَالنَّمَاءَ مِنَ اللّٰهِ وَحْدَهُ ﷻ وَلَا يَطْلُبُونَهَا مِنْ غَيْرِهِ ، لَكِنَّهُمْ جَعَلُوا فِي طَلَبِهِمْ لِلْخَيْرِ وَالنَّمَاءِ وَالبَرَكَةِ مِنَ اللّٰهِ ﷻ بِوَاسِطَةِ شَيْءٍ لَمْ يَرِدِ الشَّرْعُ بِهِ .

وَهَذِهِ الصُّوَرُ مِنَ التَّبَرُّكِ الشِّرْكِيِّ وَالبِدْعِيِّ مَوْجُودَانِ بِكَثْرَةٍ عِنْدَ #القُبُورِيَّةِ عُبَّادِ الأَضْرِحَةِ .

وَالحَاصِلُ : أَنَّ التَّبَرُّكَ بِشَيْءٍ لَمْ يَرِدْ بِهِ التَّبَرُّكُ بِهِ شَرْعًا فَهُوَ بَاطِلٌ مَمْنُوعٌ غَيْرُ مَشْرُوعٍ، لِأَنَّهُ إِمَّا شِرْكٌ ، أَوْ وَسِيلَةٌ إِلَى الشِّرْكِ ، وَكُلُّ ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَعْمَالِ الجَاهِلِيَّةِ .

🔴 فَائِدَةٌ عَزِيزَةٌ :

ذَكَرَ الإِمَامُ بْنُ القَيِّمِ رَحِمَهُ اللّٰهُ فِي [ إِغَاثَةِ اللَّهْفَانِ مِنْ مَصَائِدِ الشَّيْطَانِ (1/ 329) ] :

« أَنَّ قُبُورِيَّةَ دِمَشْقَ بِالشَّامِ كَانُوا يَتَبَرَّكُونَ بِالنُّصُبِ الَّذِي كَانَ تَحْتَ الطَّاحُونِ عِنْدَ مَقَابِرِ النَّصَارَى ، وَالنُّصُبِ الَّذِي كَانَ عِنْدَ الرَّحْبَةِ ، وَكَانَ هَؤُلَاءِ القُبُورِيَّةُ يَتَبَرَّكُونَ بِهِ، وَأَنْصَابٍ أُخْرَى أَيْضًا يُعَيِّدُهَا القُبُورِيَّةُ، فَكَسَرَهَا اللّٰهُ عَلَى يَدِ شَيْخِ الإِسْلَامِ ، وَأَيَّدَ حِزْبَ اللّٰهِ المُوَحِّدِينَ »

THEY MADE ME SIT ON THE FLOOR LIKE A DOG! Then the Chairman WALKED IN and bowed to ME.

The linoleum was freezing against my tailbone. Every time someone walked past, their shoes clicked inches from my head. "Get comfortable, mutt," Janet had sneered, adjusting her power suit. "Maybe you'll learn something by osmosis."

I wanted to disappear. I'd arrived early, prepped the conference room, even brewed a fresh pot of the good stuff – Kona blend, Janet's favorite. But none of it mattered. I was still the temp, the outsider, the one they could kick around without consequence. All because of the company merger. After the acquisition, the old guard at Sterling Dynamics made it clear they saw us from the smaller firm as nothing more than unwanted baggage.

I tried to focus on the presentation deck flickering on the screen, but Janet's words kept echoing in my head. Mutt. Osmosis. Like I wasn't even worth a real chair. Like my ideas, my experience, meant nothing. It wasn't just the humiliation, but the sheer, calculated cruelty of it all. I glanced around the room. Everyone avoided my gaze, pretending not to notice the woman sitting on the floor. Cowards.

My phone vibrated in my pocket. I ignored it. Probably another email from my landlord, reminding me rent was due. Or a message from Mom, asking if I'd heard back about any full-time positions. The irony wasn't lost on me: here I was, helping run a crucial strategy meeting for a multi-million dollar company, while simultaneously teetering on the edge of homelessness. I clenched my fists, digging my nails into my palms. I wouldn't cry. I wouldn't give them the satisfaction.

The door swung open, and a hush fell over the room. "Good morning, everyone," a voice boomed. It was Mr. Thompson, the CEO. Janet practically vibrated with excitement. This was her moment, her chance to shine in front of the boss. I sank lower, trying to become invisible. But then, something completely unexpected happened.

Mr. Thompson stopped just inside the doorway, his eyes scanning the room. He paused when he saw me, a flicker of… something… crossing his face. Disgust? Pity? I couldn't tell. And then, he did something that made my jaw drop. He bowed. A deep, respectful bow, right in my direction. The room erupted in a cacophony of whispers. Janet's face turned a shade of purple I didn't think was humanly possible. "Ms. Ramirez," Mr. Thompson said, his voice cutting through the noise like a laser. "Please, forgive our… oversight. There seems to be a distinct lack of hospitality in this room."

He gestured to one of the senior executives, a portly man named Mr. Peterson, who immediately jumped to his feet. "Peterson, give Ms. Ramirez your chair." Peterson sputtered, his face turning redder than Janet's. But he didn't argue. He scrambled to find another seat, while I hesitantly stood up, brushing off the wrinkles from my skirt. All eyes were on me. I could feel the heat of their stares, the mixture of confusion, resentment, and… fear? It was intoxicating.

"Thank you, Mr. Thompson," I said, trying to keep my voice steady. "But please, call me Sofia."

He smiled, a genuine, warm smile that reached his eyes. "Of course, Sofia. Now, shall we begin?"

As I settled into Mr. Peterson's ridiculously oversized chair, I couldn't help but feel a surge of vindication. But it was a hollow victory. I knew this was just the beginning. The old guard at Sterling Dynamics wouldn't let this go easily. They'd see me as a threat, an upstart who dared to challenge their authority. And they'd be right. Because after today, things were going to change.

I took a deep breath and opened my laptop. Time to show them what this 'mutt' was really made of. The presentation began, but inside, my mind was already racing. I had to figure out why Mr. Thompson had defended me so publicly. Was it genuine respect? Or was there something else at play? A power struggle, perhaps? Whatever the reason, I knew I had to be careful. Because in the corporate jungle, even a single act of kindness could be a trap.

The meeting droned on, filled with jargon and PowerPoint slides. But I couldn't shake the feeling that I was being watched. Every time I looked up, I caught Janet staring at me, her eyes filled with a cold, calculating rage. It was unnerving, to say the least. I’d known that corporate life could be a battlefield, but until today, I’d never felt the crosshairs aimed directly at me. I found myself reflecting on my career choices and recent life events, but always the central feeling was confusion. Who was I to be treated like this by someone I worked with? 

The hours crawled by. I presented my portion of the strategy deck, outlining a bold new plan for expanding into emerging markets. My voice was clear and confident, but inside, I was a mess of nerves. When I finished, Mr. Thompson was the first to applaud. Janet remained silent, her arms crossed tightly over her chest. The tension in the room was so thick you could cut it with a knife.

Finally, the meeting adjourned. As people filed out, Mr. Thompson approached me. "Sofia, could I have a word?" he asked, his voice low.

I nodded, my heart pounding in my chest. We walked to his office, a sprawling corner suite with panoramic views of the city. He closed the door behind us and turned to face me.

"I wanted to apologize again for what happened in there," he said, gesturing back towards the conference room. "It was unacceptable."

"Thank you, Mr. Thompson," I said. "I appreciate that."

"Please, call me Richard," he insisted. "And I want you to know that I value your contributions to this company. Your insights are invaluable."

I raised an eyebrow, skeptical. "Is that why I was sitting on the floor?"

He winced. "No, of course not. That was… a misunderstanding. A terrible lapse in judgment on Janet's part."

"A misunderstanding?" I repeated, my voice rising. "It felt like a deliberate act of humiliation."

He sighed. "I know. And I assure you, it won't happen again. I'll deal with Janet personally."

I looked him in the eye, trying to gauge his sincerity. Was he being genuine? Or was he just trying to smooth things over? I couldn't tell. But I knew one thing: I wasn't going to let this go. I deserved respect, just like everyone else. And I was going to fight for it, no matter what it took.

"Richard," I said, using his first name for the first time. "I appreciate your apology. But I need more than words. I need to see real change. I need to know that Sterling Dynamics is a place where everyone is treated with dignity and respect."

He nodded, his expression serious. "I understand. And I promise you, you will see change. I'm committed to creating a culture of inclusivity and respect here. And I need your help to do it."

I stared at him, surprised. "My help?"

"Yes," he said. "I want you to be my advisor on this issue. I want you to help me identify the problems and develop solutions. Will you do it?"

I hesitated for a moment. This was a huge opportunity. A chance to make a real difference. But it was also a huge risk. If I took on this role, I'd be making enemies. Powerful enemies. But I couldn't back down now. Not after everything that had happened. Not after the humiliation, the disrespect, the feeling of being less than human.

"Yes, Richard," I said, my voice firm. "I'll do it."

He smiled, relief washing over his face. "Thank you, Sofia. I knew I could count on you."

As I left his office, I felt a surge of determination. I was no longer just a temp, an outsider. I was an advisor, a change agent. And I was ready to fight for what was right, even if it meant taking on the entire corporate machine. As I stepped out of the glass doors, I noticed Janet at her desk, glaring in my direction. I straightened my back, held my head high, and walked past her without a word. The battle had just begun.

The rest of the day passed in a blur. I was bombarded with emails and phone calls, all related to my new role as Richard's advisor. It was overwhelming, but exhilarating. I felt like I was finally making a difference, finally using my skills and experience to create positive change. But beneath the surface, I was still wary. I knew that Janet and her allies wouldn't give up easily. They would fight back, using every dirty trick in the book. And I had to be prepared.

As I packed up my things to leave for the day, I received a text message from an unknown number. It read: "Watch your back, Sofia. You're playing with fire." I deleted the message and turned off my phone. It was time to go home, to rest, to prepare for the battles ahead. Because in the corporate jungle, survival of the fittest was the only rule that mattered. When I pulled up to my apartment complex, I noticed a black car parked across the street, its headlights off. I couldn't see who was inside, but I had a feeling I knew. I parked my car, grabbed my purse, and walked quickly towards my building, glancing over my shoulder every few steps. I unlocked the front door and slipped inside, breathing a sigh of relief. But I knew I wasn't safe yet. The corporate jungle had followed me home. And I had a feeling it was about to get a whole lot more dangerous. I turned on all the lights, double-locked the door, and peeked through the blinds. The black car was still there, its headlights still off. Waiting. Watching. I shivered, despite the warmth of the apartment. This wasn't just about a job anymore. It was about power, control, and survival. And I was caught in the middle.

As I settled in for the night, I tried to distract myself with a book, but my mind kept racing back to the events of the day. The humiliation, the apology, the new role, the threatening text message, the black car. It was all too much to process. I tossed and turned in bed, unable to sleep. Finally, I gave up and got out of bed. I poured myself a glass of water and walked over to the window. The black car was still there. Watching. Waiting. I closed the blinds and turned off the lights. I crawled back into bed, pulling the covers over my head. But I couldn't escape the feeling that I was being watched. That I was in danger. That my life was about to change forever.

«إني لواقف يوم بدر في الصف، فنظرت عن يميني وشمالي فإذا أنا بين غلامين من الأنصار حديثة أسنانهما، فتمنيت أن أكون بين رجلين أقوى منهما. فغمزني أحدهما وقال: يا عم، أتعرف أبا جهل؟

قال: أخبرتُ أنه يسب رسول الله ﷺ، والذي نفسي بيده لئن رأيته لا يفارق سوادي سواده حتى يموت الأعجل منا».
قال عبد الرحمن: فتعجبت لذلك، فغمزني الآخر فقال لي مثلها.

قال: «فلم أنشب أن رأيت أبا جهل يجول بين الناس، فقلت لهما: ألا تريان؟ هذا صاحبكما الذي تسألان عنه. فابتدراه بسيفيهما فضرباه حتى قتلاه. ثم انصرفا إلى النبي ﷺ فأخبراه، فقال: “أيُّكما قتـ.له؟”
قال كل واحد منهما: أنا قتـ.لته.
فقال: “هل مسحتما سيفيكما؟”
قالا: لا.
فنَظر النبي ﷺ في السيفين فقال: “كِلاكما قتـ.له”.»

وقال ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه:
«وجدتُه في آخر رمق فعرفته، فوضعت قدمي على عنقه».
وكان أبو جهل قد أمسك به مرة في مكة فآذاه. فقال أبو جهل وهو في سكرات الموت:
«لقد ارتقيتَ مرتقى صعبًا يا رويعي الغنم».
قال ابن مسعود: «ثم احتززتُ رأسه، وأتيتُ به رسول الله ﷺ فقلت: يا رسول الله، هذا رأس عـ.دو الله.
فقال ﷺ: “آلله الذي لا إله غيره؟”
فقلت: نعم والله الذي لا إله غيره، ثم ألقيتُ رأسه بين يدي النبي ﷺ فحمد الله.»

ووقف رسول الله ﷺ على مصرع ابني عفراء، فقال:
«رحم الله ابني عفراء، فهما شُركاء في قتـ.ل فرعون هذه الأمة ورأس أئمة الكـ..ـفر».
فقيل: يا رسول الله، ومن قتـ.له معهما؟
قال ﷺ: «الملائكة، وابن مسعود قد شَرِكَ في قتـ.له».

Crowdfunding for the Struggle - Turning Small Donations into Big Impact

By Comr. Preye V. Tambou, National President, Society for the Welfare of Unemployed Youths of Nigeria (SWUYN)

17th January, 2026

“The revolution will not be funded by billionaires. It will be built by the widow’s mite, the student’s last coin, and the worker’s one-day wage.” - Preye V. Tambou 

Every movement runs on courage, but courage without resources collapses. Placards cost money. Internet bundles cost money. Transport to rallies costs money. Medical bills for the injured cost money. Without funds, even the loudest voice grows silent.

Governments know this. That is why repression often begins by choking financial lifelines; freezing accounts, intimidating donors, and labeling activists as “terrorists” to cut off aid. The unspoken truth is this: whoever controls the purse controls the protest.

The solution? Crowdfunding. A people-powered treasury that no government can easily silence.

The Power of Many Small Gifts

In traditional politics, power is purchased by a few billionaires writing fat cheques. In people’s movements, power is built when millions contribute coins.

One student’s N500 becomes fuel for placards.

One market woman’s N1,000 becomes bottled water for marchers.

One diaspora youth’s $10 becomes a megaphone that shakes a city.

This is the math of movements: a thousand small sacrifices create one unstoppable struggle.

Example: #EndSARS (Nigeria, 2020)

The Feminist Coalition raised over N147 million in donations, largely from small givers. The money provided food, medical aid, legal support, and transport. With every transfer, donors were not just “supporters” - they became owners of the struggle.

When we give, we don’t just fund the fight - we join it.

Building Trust in the Treasury

The greatest barrier to crowdfunding is not poverty, but mistrust. Nigerians (and Africans at large) are skeptical because governments and NGOs have stolen donations before. For crowdfunding to work, trust must be greater than fear of theft.

Rules for Movement Crowdfunding:

1. Radical Transparency

Publish every donation received and every expense made.

Use live dashboards (Google Sheets, open-source trackers).

Example: The Feminist Coalition’s real-time financial updates built massive credibility.

2. Accountability Teams

Rotate treasurers to prevent corruption.

Separate fundraising from spending to avoid conflicts of interest.

3. Community Oversight

Allow donors to vote on how funds are spent.

Even small contributors deserve a voice.

4. Narrative Framing

Show impact: N1,000 = 10 placards. $10 = 5 meals for protesters.

People give when they see the story of their sacrifice.

Platforms and Tools

Crowdfunding does not need billion-dollar apps. It needs creativity.

* Local Transfers: Bank apps, mobile money (Opay, PalmPay, M-Pesa, MTN MoMo).

* Diaspora Support: GoFundMe, Patreon, PayPal.

* Crypto Donations: Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT (harder to freeze, useful in authoritarian crackdowns).

* Social Media Boosts: Instagram fundraisers, Twitter “tip jars,” TikTok live-gifting.

Each platform has its risks (fees, shutdowns, legal traps), but diversity protects movements. Never put all money in one basket.

Global Lessons in Crowdfunding Movements

1. Hong Kong Protests (2019):

Raised millions via online donations.

Funded ads in major international newspapers (“Dear World, Please Help Us”).

Lesson: Crowdfunding is not just survival - it’s diplomacy.

2. Occupy Wall Street (USA, 2011):

Relied on small contributions for food tents and sound systems.

Lesson: Sustained presence is possible only with continuous micro-donations.

3. Nepal Gen Z Revolution (2025):

Despite internet shutdowns, youth used QR codes, USDT wallets, and diaspora networks.

Lesson: Financial creativity is as important as street creativity.

Beyond Money: Crowdfunding as Participation

Each contribution is more than a transaction, it is a political act. A N200 airtime transfer says: “I belong to this fight.” Crowdfunding transforms the unemployed youth into investors in their own liberation.

Movements must emphasize this truth: giving is not charity - it is ownership.

Overcoming Barriers

1. Poverty

Even the poorest can give time, skills, or a single coin.

The psychology of giving is collective: “I may not have much, but together we have enough.”

2. Fear of Surveillance

Governments may track donations.

Solutions: anonymous crypto wallets, prepaid cards, or proxy accounts in friendly nations.

3. Donor Fatigue

People get tired.

Solutions: celebrate small wins, show impact regularly, rotate asks (one week for food, another for medicals).

The Multiplying Effect

Imagine 1,000 youths giving N500 weekly. That’s N500,000. In a month, N2 million. In a year, N24 million. With diaspora support doubling this, you have a war chest bigger than many government “youth empowerment schemes.”

Crowdfunding is not about one billionaire but building a billion drops into an ocean.

Money is not the root of all evil. In movements, money is the root of survival. Governments fear a funded struggle more than a loud struggle. Every coin is a bullet, every naira is a barricade.

From Funding to Freedom

The goal is not to hoard donations, but to weaponize them into:

* Food & logistics for protests.

* Legal defense for arrested comrades.

* Medical care for the injured.

* Media campaigns to shape global opinion.

* Skill-building programmes for long-term empowerment.

When crowdfunding is consistent, movements no longer beg for support. They build economic independence and economic independence is political power.

Voices from the Ground

“I gave my last N200 airtime, but when I saw ambulances at the protest, I knew my small seed had saved a life.” – Lagos student, #EndSARS

“We thought money would divide us but every time we donated, we felt like shareholders of the revolution.” – Kathmandu youth, #NepalRevolution 2025

“I cannot march - I am disabled but I can give. My donation became my feet in the street.” – South African pensioner during #FeesMustFall

Crowdfunding is more than finance. It is faith made visible. It is collective dignity turned into collective strength. It is proof that even the unemployed can fund their liberation, one coin at a time.

The State wants us to believe poverty makes us powerless but poverty cannot silence people who pool their hunger into hope.

If governments can loot billions, then millions of youths can unite billions of drops because the struggle is not only in the streets. It is in the wallets, in the apps, in the coins we refuse to waste on silence and when money flows from the people, power flows back to the people.

The revolution will not be televised. It will be crowdfunded.

Retro memories. Mattel Food Fighters (TV commercial from 1988).

Food Fighters was an action figure line released by Mattel in 1988. Proverbial for the concept of a food fight, the figures were all different types of anthropomorphic food dressed in military gear. Food Fighters consisted of ten figures, three vehicles, and an unproduced playset. The characters were divided into two armies: the protagonist Kitchen Commandos and the antagonist Refrigerator Rejects. Each figure was made of soft, rotocasted vinyl similar to a squeaky toy with hard plastic limbs. Each figure included a small hand weapon and removable backpack, resembling accessories from Hasbro's G.I. Joe line. The tagline on the figure' packaging read, "Combat At Its Kookiest!"

Due to the line's overall poor sales, Food Fighters were commonly sold at small discount store chains like Hills or Ben Franklin.

A lunchbox and thermos set, a jigsaw puzzle, and a single coloring book were some of the few pieces of merchandise to be released from 1988-1989 to support the line.

Collegeville Costumes also released three Food Fighters Halloween costumes in 1989, of the characters Burgerdier General, Private Pizza, and Fat Frenchy. These costumes have been proven to be extremely rare, and were generally unknown to collectors for many years.

"She Dragged the Crying Boy to the Revolving Doors, Screaming “Get This Trash Out of My Sight,” But When She Tried to Throw Him Into the Rain, She Didn't Realize the “Lowly” Security Guard Was the Only Thing Standing Between Her and the Destruction of Her Pristine Reputation—and He Was Done Being Silent.

Chapter 1

The rain in Chicago doesn’t just fall; it hammers against the glass like it’s trying to break in. From my post behind the concierge desk at The Obsidian, the most expensive residential tower in the Gold Coast, the weather was the only thing I couldn't control.

Everything else? I handled it.

I’m Marcus. I’ve been the head of security here for six years. Before that, I did twenty years in the Marines. I know how to read a room. I know that Mr. Henderson in 14B is cheating on his wife because he smells like cheap vanilla perfume on Tuesdays. I know Mrs. Gable in 6A is lonely because she calls down to report “suspicious noises” just to hear another human voice.

And I knew, the moment the gold-plated elevator doors slid open at 2:00 PM on a Tuesday, that Elena Sterling in the Penthouse was about to make a mistake she couldn't buy her way out of.

Elena was the kind of beautiful that felt sharp to the touch. Forty-two, widow of a tech mogul, and dressed in a cream-colored cashmere coat that probably cost more than my car. She usually walked through the lobby like she was floating above the marble, eyes fixed on a point in the distance that the rest of us couldn't see.

But today, she wasn't floating. She was storming.

And she was dragging something.

Or rather, someone.

""I said move!"" her voice cracked through the hushed, lavender-scented air of the lobby.

My head snapped up from the monitors.

Gripped tightly in her manicured hand was the wrist of a boy. He couldn't have been more than seven. He was stumbling, his sneakers squeaking desperately against the polished floor as he tried to find traction. He wasn't wearing Gold Coast clothes. He had on a faded navy hoodie that was two sizes too big, the cuffs frayed, and jeans with a grass stain on the knee. He was clutching a dirty canvas backpack like it contained the crown jewels.

""Please, Auntie El,"" the boy sobbed, the sound raw and wet. ""Please, I’ll be quiet. I promise.""

""Don't you call me that!"" Elena hissed, not even looking down at him. She was staring at the revolving doors, her destination clear. ""You are not my problem. I told them! I told the lawyers I wouldn't take a stray dog, let alone her mistake.""

I was already moving.

My hip bumped the edge of the desk as I rounded it, my boots hitting the floor with a heavy, rhythmic thud.

""Mrs. Sterling?"" I called out. My voice was practiced—firm, authoritative, but polite. The 'Customer Service' voice.

She ignored me. She yanked the boy harder. He tripped over his own feet, his knees hitting the marble with a sickening thack.

""Get up!"" she shrieked, looking around wildly. The lobby was fairly empty, but the doorman, struggling with a luggage cart near the entrance, had frozen. A couple waiting for an Uber near the fountain were staring, mouths open.

""Get up and get out! I am not turning my home into a shelter for unwanted baggage!""

The boy was crying silently now, the kind of crying that hurts to watch—mouth open, chest heaving, but no sound coming out because fear has choked it off. He scrambled to his feet, trembling.

""Mrs. Sterling!"" I barked, dropping the customer service act. I was ten feet away.

She finally acknowledged me, whipping her head around. Her eyes were manic, her mascara slightly smudged—a crack in the porcelain doll facade.

""Marcus! Good,"" she pointed a shaking finger at the revolving doors. ""Do your job. Get this... this trash out of my sight. He’s trespassing.""

I stopped three feet from them. I looked at the boy. He looked up at me, his eyes wide and brown, swimming with terror. He looked so much like my grandson, Toby, that I felt a physical phantom pain in my chest.

""He's a child, Mrs. Sterling,"" I said, my voice low. ""And it's pouring rain outside.""

""I don't care if it's a hurricane!"" she spat. ""He isn't on the lease. He isn't a guest. He is an intruder. If you don't remove him, I’ll have your badge by the end of the hour. Do you hear me? I pay the HOA fees that pay your salary. Move him!""

She turned back to the boy, her hand tightening on his arm until his skin turned white. She shoved him forward, hard. The boy stumbled toward the glass doors, toward the gray, unforgiving city.

""No!"" the boy wailed, reaching back for her. ""Don't leave me!""

She raised her hand, palm open, as if to shove him one last time, right through the exit.

Instinct took over. The Marine took over.

I didn't think about my pension. I didn't think about the rent I owed on my apartment in Bronzeville.

I stepped in.

I caught her wrist in mid-air.

The sound of the slap that didn't happen echoed in the silence of the room.

Elena froze. She looked at her wrist, wrapped in my large, dark hand, then up at my face. Her expression shifted from rage to pure, unadulterated shock. No one touched Elena Sterling. No one stopped Elena Sterling.

""Let go of me,"" she whispered, her voice dangerous.

""No,"" I said.

I gently but firmly pulled her hand away from the boy, breaking her grip on him. Then, I released her and immediately placed myself between her and the child. I felt the boy flinch behind me, and then I felt small hands grab the back of my uniform trousers.

He was hiding behind me.

""You're fired,"" she breathed, her face turning crimson. ""You are done. Do you know who I am?""

""I know exactly who you are, Mrs. Sterling,"" I said, and my voice carried to the back of the room. The couple by the fountain had their phones out now. Recording.

""You're a woman with a net worth of fifty million dollars,"" I continued, staring her down. ""You live in a penthouse that has a refrigerator for fur coats. You have more money than God.""

I reached back, blindly, until my hand found the boy’s trembling shoulder. I squeezed it gently.

""But right now?"" I looked her dead in the eye. ""You're showing everyone in this lobby that money can't buy you class. And it sure as hell can't buy you a conscience.""

The silence that followed was deafening.

""How dare you,"" she gasped, stepping back, clutching her pearls like a cliché villain. ""Security! Someone call the real police!""

""I already did,"" I lied. Or maybe I hadn't. I tapped my earpiece. ""But until they get here, this boy isn't going out in the rain. He's staying with me. And you? You can go back up to your ivory tower, or you can stand here and explain to the officers why you were assaulting a minor.""

Elena looked around. She saw the phones. She saw the doorman glaring at her. She saw the judgment.

She straightened her coat, pulling her dignity around her like armor, though it was already shattered.

""You've made a grave mistake, Marcus,"" she said, her voice icy again. ""Enjoy your last afternoon at The Obsidian.""

She spun on her heel and marched toward the elevators, the click-clack of her heels sounding like gunshots.

I didn't watch her go. I turned around and knelt on the cold marble floor, ignoring the creak in my bad knee. I was eye-level with the kid now.

He was shaking so hard his teeth were chattering.

""Hey there,"" I said, keeping my voice soft. ""I'm Marcus. You okay, son?""

He wiped his nose on his sleeve, looking at the elevators where the woman had disappeared, then back at me.

""She said... she said my mom is gone,"" he whispered. ""She said she's never coming back.""

My heart broke. Clean in two.

""What's your name?"" I asked.

""Leo,"" he said.

""Okay, Leo,"" I said, standing up and offering him my hand. It was rough and calloused, but steady. ""You don't have to worry about her right now. You’re with me. And nobody—I mean nobody—moves you unless I say so. You hungry?""

He nodded, a small, hesitant motion.

""Come on,"" I said, guiding him toward the security office behind the desk. ""I've got a stash of Oreos that I'm not supposed to have. Don't tell my doctor.""

As the glass door of the office clicked shut behind us, shielding us from the lobby, I knew two things for certain.

One: Leo was safe for the next hour. Two: My life, and the quiet existence I’d built, was about to go up in flames.

But looking at the kid holding that dirty backpack, I realized I didn't care. Let it burn.

Away from the bright lights of the ring and the scripted storylines, John Cena and Mickie James shared something real—a genuine connection during a time when both were climbing the ranks in WWE. For Mickie, it was meaningful. For Cena, the spark eventually faded.

When he ended things, Mickie was devastated. In the WWE machine, where everything revolves around protecting the top star, there was no room for messy emotions. Real heartbreak backstage wasn’t just unwelcome—it was treated as a liability.

Wrestlers from that era recall the shift as immediate. Mickie wasn’t punished for her work or misconduct; she was punished for feeling something. Her demeanor backstage changed, and instead of support, she faced subtle isolation. Her push stalled, her opportunities vanished, and she was shuffled between brands like unwanted baggage.

When management decided the situation had become too “inconvenient,” they took the easiest route: they released her. No storyline explanation. No farewell segment. Just a quiet erasure from the roster.

Those who were there at the time still say the same thing: Mickie James didn’t get fired because of her talent or work ethic. She got fired because her relationship with John Cena ended, and WWE didn’t want any turbulence around their chosen face of the company.

𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗞𝗔: 𝗔 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗔 𝗖𝗟𝗜𝗤𝗨𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗠𝗘

First and foremost, as we find ourselves amid recurring calamities that have kept our country trapped in poor governance and dictatorship, we must remain of sound mind and exercise accurate judgment.

South Sudan is composed of 64 tribes, with the Dinka being the largest ethnic group, present in nearly 70 percent of the 10 states and 3 administrative areas of the country. Because the President comes from this community, many South Sudanese have been led to believe that the Dinka are responsible for the nation’s suffering. This perception did not arise naturally; it was deliberately cultivated by the regime as a survival strategy—portraying the Dinka as dominant, evil, and responsible for state failure in the eyes of the other 63 communities.

At the same time, the regime propagated the idea among Dinka citizens that the government belongs to them, and that its failures are their collective burden. With no performance record to defend itself, the regime has relied on ethnic shielding as its last line of protection.

This raises a critical question:
Are the Dinka the real power behind the government?

The answer is simple: No.
What exists is propaganda—carefully designed to conceal the corruption and failures of a small ruling clique while dragging innocent citizens into conflicts they neither designed nor benefit from.

The Dinka represented in government account for less than 10 percent of the community. The majority of Dinka civilians receive no services, no protection, and no dividends of power. Instead, war, hunger, and preventable disease define daily life in their villages. Warrap State—particularly Kuajok, the President’s home area—records some of the highest deaths from treatable diseases, communal violence, and famine. The same reality exists in Lakes State, plagued by years of communal conflict, and Jonglei, where counter-insurgency tactics have repeatedly pitted communities against one another, especially involving the Murle.

The Rise and Fall of the Generals!

When South Sudan descended into conflict in 2013, the groundwork had already been laid. In 2012, a paramilitary force known as Mathiang Anyoor was formed under Gen. Paul Malong Awan. Its primary purpose was not national defense, but regime protection—ensuring that any perceived threat to President Salva Kiir could be neutralized.

The militia was indoctrinated with the belief that power belonged to them by ethnic right, and that whoever occupied the presidency was “their brother.” This ideology became lethal in 2013, when a political dispute was transformed into an ethnic war. What should have been a conflict between the government and opposition was reframed as Dinka versus Nuer. Thousands of lives were lost. Nearly 70 percent of Mathiang Anyoor fighters were killed by the White Army militia, which was later crushed with the intervention of the UPDF.

Gen. Paul Malong was subsequently appointed Chief of Defence Forces (CDF)—a political reward for the loss of youth from his community. During his tenure, he rose to immense prominence, arresting senior SPLM leaders on presidential directives. Figures such as Rebecca Nyandeng, Deng Alor, Pagan Amum, Chol Tong, and Majak Agot were detained and later branded “detainees,” despite no evidence linking them to the alleged coup attempt.

In 2016, after the revitalized peace agreement brought Dr. Riek Machar and SPLA-IO forces back to Juba, renewed fighting wiped out what remained of Mathiang Anyoor. With his militia destroyed and his political utility diminished, Gen. Malong—despite being Dinka—was arrested, humiliated, and accused of plotting against President Kiir.

Ironically, the instrument of his humiliation was Gen. Akol Koor, his own tribesman and Director-General of the National Security Service. Promised unimaginable power, Akol Koor grew more powerful than cabinet ministers and military commanders. Fear defined his reign.

Once Gen. Malong was neutralized, Gen. Akol was turned against his own community. He was used to eliminate Kerubino Wol, a youth figure known for job creation, on fabricated rebellion charges. He later moved against senior SPLM figure Nhial Deng Nhial, accusing him of anti-Kiir sentiments. After finishing these tasks, Gen. Akol himself became expendable and was placed under house arrest, accused of plotting a coup.

His downfall was engineered by Gen. Bol Mel, a businessman-general from the same Dinka community. Bol Mel was elevated beyond institutional limits—effectively becoming a state within a state. He allegedly masterminded the Nasir conflict, indiscriminate bombings, forced disarmament campaigns, and mass arrests, including that of the First Vice President Dr. Riek Machar, all to eliminate political obstacles to succession.

Eventually, Bol Mel too was discarded. President Kiir sidelined him and elevated his own daughter, once again proving that ethnicity offers no immunity in a regime governed by suspicion and self-preservation.

The Real Threat Today—and the Way Forward

Recently, the Bor community, which sacrificed immensely during the liberation struggle, was declared rebellious following a minor misunderstanding between a local defense group (the Red Belt) and security forces. The incident was exaggerated into a national security crisis. Heavy forces were deployed. Civilians were killed with impunity. Women and girls were harassed, and no accountability followed.

Despite this, the community remained calm and did not resist the state—until renewed conflict erupted in the Greater Lou region of Jonglei.
A division of 6,000 infantry, commanded by Maj. Gen. Bol Anuer, which defected from SPLA-IO, was deployed in a joint operation. The force was later overwhelmed, dismantled, and scattered by SPLA-IO fighters.

Now, the government is deploying the Agwelek forces, alongside sons of the defunct Greater Bor—commanded by Brig. Gen. Mawut Ajhok and Maj. Gen. Chol Gut-kom—to fight an opposition that is steadily gaining ground. This pattern is familiar: when war comes, Bor youth are mobilized first to fight wars rooted in ethnic manipulation rather than national interest.

As a proud son of Bor who has witnessed this regime’s failure—its harassment, killings, and betrayal of citizens—the question must be asked:
Why should anyone sacrifice their life for a dogfight among elites?
Those who died in past tribal wars were not honored. Gen. Abraham Jongroor and Gen. Ajak Yen, killed in 2013, left behind families who received neither recognition nor support. Their orphans struggle, as do the families of many fallen SSPDF officers.

To the sons and daughters of Greater Bahr el Ghazal: you have seen the humiliation of your leaders and the waste of your youth. This regime, falsely branded as “Dinka,” delivers nothing but death and division, while a small clique thrives. Many of the regime’s permanent beneficiaries—Tut Kew, Martin Elia, Wani Igga, Taban Deng Gai, among others—do not come from Dinka communities. They come from across South Sudan’s tribes, united only by betrayal of their people for personal survival.
Do not be deceived.

Do not protect a regime that survives by dividing tribes and destroying futures.

*Tribes are not enemies.
Opposition is not the enemy.
The regime is the enemy.**
~JBK

The people of South Sudan must awaken and critically examine the political invisibility of their elites.

Recap, 16 years down the line in South Sudan Politics.

During my undergraduate classes, when I was taking the classes of the comparative Political Systems under Professor Dr. Adel Khalil, Professor of Law and Comparative Political Systems, South Sudan was still a nascent state in the making. At the time, the country was heading toward the 2010 general elections and, shortly thereafter, the 2011 referendum that would eventually give birth to the Republic of South Sudan.

The academic atmosphere was charged with optimism and ideological curiosity. 

We examined the major systems of governance across the world, in his book, The comparative political system (Prof. Dr. Adel Khalid) unitary systems, federalism, confederations, liberal democracies, and authoritarian models. Against this intellectual backdrop, and considering the political realities of South Sudan, I developed a view that was unpopular to some but, in my assessment, realistically , South Sudan required a strong authoritarian system of governance, at least in its formative years.

This position was not formed in isolation. I vividly recall intense debates within the South Sudan diaspora political forums, including discussions in the the SPLM diaspora’s page. Two dominant schools of thought emerged. The liberalist camp, often driven by high political ambitions, mainly colleagues in the Western Hemisphere, I there than argued strongly and advocated for liberal democracy as the system of choice. 

On the other hand, the conservative camp argued for federalism or confederation, citing diversity and decentralization as safeguards against domination from some tribes such as Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk.

My position diverged from both camps. I supported authoritarian systems of governance as the best choice for the young country, and I did so deliberately, I also did not intend to copy paste the statement and perception from uncle Dr. Lem Akol Ajawin, then Minister of Foreign Affairs in the government of the National Unity then Republic of Sudan, who stated that Southerners were not going govern themselves should they succeed, Unquoted.

The tendency is that South Sudan is home to over 64 tribes and ethnic groups, each with distinct historical grievances, loyalties, and political expectations. My argument then, and now, was that no amount of procedural democracy alone could immediately win the trust, loyalty, or collective national consciousness of such deeply fragmented communities emerging from decades of war.

Nation building, particularly in post conflict societies, is not merely about elections or political freedoms. It is about order, authority, discipline, and the enforcement of a unifying national vision. Development requires stability; stability requires authority. 

Thus in my view, an effective state at such an early stage cannot rely solely on liberal democratic ideals that presuppose strong institutions, national cohesion, and political maturity, conditions that South Sudan did not yet possess.

This is not an argument against democracy per se. Rather, it is an argument for sequencing. 

For meaningful development to take root, South Sudan needed, and arguably still needs, a calibrated blend of democracy and dictatorship democratic aspirations guided and restrained by firm, centralized authority capable of enforcing the rule of law, managing diversity, and preventing fragmentation.

History offers numerous examples where states consolidated first through strong authority before transitioning into stable democracies. Ignoring this lesson in favor of idealism risks perpetuating instability, underdevelopment, and endless political contestation. Which is now the case.

In fragile states like South Sudan, governance should be judged not by ideological purity, but by its capacity to deliver unity, security, and development.  Sadly, I still hold the same views.

The Ideology of Domination: Why SPLA-IO Hardliners Reject the Republic Itself

South Sudan’s crisis is not governance, not reform, and not the existence of the state. The real problem is an ideology of domination entrenched within SPLA-IO hardliners, who believe that unless they dominate the system and others submit to their command, the government is illegitimate, unfair, and unacceptable

This is the unspoken doctrine of perpetual rebellion.

For these hardliners, legitimacy does not come from the Constitution, elections, peace agreements, or national institutions. Legitimacy exists only when they are on top, commanding the gun, controlling the ministries, and dictating the direction of the republic. Anything less is branded a “Dinka regime,” a “failed state,” or an “unfair government." This narrative is not grievance. It is political blackmail.

When Representation Betrays Its People: The Crisis of Nuer Leadership and the Absence of the State in South Sudan

BY JUOL NHOMNGEK DANIEL  

One of the most troubling dynamics in South Sudan’s prolonged crisis is not only the conduct of the ruling elite, but the role played by a segment of Nuer politicians who have traded the collective interests of their communities for personal access to government positions. These individuals present themselves as patriots and stabilizers, yet their political choices have deepened social fragmentation, legitimized repression, and aggravated the suffering of the very people they claim to represent.

The government has skillfully exploited their political vulnerability, rewarding loyalty with titles and seats while using them as instruments to neutralize popular dissent within Nuer communities. In doing so, it has elevated political compliance above public accountability. These politicians operate in open contradiction to the reality on the ground: Nuer communities across the country are rising against exclusion, militarization, and systemic injustice, while their supposed representatives collaborate with the very structures that perpetuate these conditions.

The Illusion of the State

At the heart of this crisis lies a more fundamental problem, the absence of a genuine state in South Sudan. What currently exists is not a modern, institutionalized state governed by law, but rather an informal association of power holders, largely rooted in liberation-era structures and sustained through coercion, patronage, and control of resources. Public property is treated as private loot, institutions function at the discretion of individuals, and governance is shaped more by personal loyalty than by constitutional order.

South Sudan lacks the defining characteristics of statehood as articulated in international law, including those outlined in the Montevideo Convention. Effective centralized authority, formal institutional organization, and predictable legal governance remain largely absent. Instead, the country continues to be administered through liberation structures inherited from the struggle period, whose legitimacy rested on popular trust rather than institutional design. That trust has since been exhausted, but the structures remain.

Communities therefore exist without formal mechanisms capable of representing, regulating, or accounting for political authority. In such an environment, power is exercised rather than governed, and internal regulation depends on the will of those who control the means of force.

Leadership, Trust, and the Question of Peace

In the Nuer context, peace and social stability cannot be imposed militarily. The only actors capable of restraining violence and mobilizing communities toward reconciliation are leaders who enjoy genuine social trust. Yet many Nuer politicians aligned with the SPLM-IG have chosen political convenience over communal responsibility. By endorsing coercion as a legitimate means of governance, they have widened the gap between the state and society.

A viable path forward requires these leaders to reassess their political alignment. Those within the government who claim to represent the Nuer must join hands with the SPLM-IO and other credible actors to demand genuine dialogue between communities and the state. Can the Nuer Tribe Reform or Overthrow the Government of South Sudan?
By Maxwell J.X
British Analyst, Newcastle - UK

Introduction

South Sudan remains one of the most ethnically divided nations in the world, with political power largely controlled by the Dinka tribe under President Salva Kiir. The Nuer, the second-largest ethnic group, have historically played a significant role in South Sudanese politics and armed conflicts. This article explores whether the Nuer can reform or overthrow the current regime and examines historical cases where tribes attempted to overthrow governments but ultimately failed, leading to their near extinction.

Can the Nuer Tribe Reform the Government?

Reforming a government requires structural changes, political will, and a coalition of different ethnic groups working together. While the Nuer have historically challenged Dinka dominance—most notably in the civil war (2013-2018)—true reform would require more than just Nuer leadership.

Challenges to Reform

1. Ethnic Fragmentation: South Sudanese politics is deeply tribal, making broad-based reform difficult.

2. Internal Divisions: The Nuer themselves are divided among different factions, including those loyal to Riek Machar and others aligned with the government.

3. Military Control: The government, backed by regional allies like Uganda and Sudan, has the military upper hand.

Reform is possible but would require a national movement that goes beyond a single ethnic group.

Can the Nuer Tribe Overthrow the Government?

Overthrowing a government is significantly more challenging than reforming it. Although the Nuer have been involved in armed rebellions—such as the 1991 split within the SPLA and the 2013-2018 conflict—these attempts have led to widespread suffering rather than lasting political control.

Key Obstacles to an Overthrow

Government Military Strength: The South Sudanese army (SSPDF) is well-equipped and has external support.

Lack of a Unified Front: Without alliances with other ethnic groups like the Equatorians and Shilluk, an armed Nuer uprising would likely be crushed.

International Influence: Neighboring countries and global powers have a vested interest in maintaining the current regime.

History has shown that no single ethnic group can successfully take power in a multi-ethnic state without facing overwhelming resistance.

Historical Cases of Failed Tribal Overthrows Leading to Near Extinction

Throughout history, various tribes have attempted to overthrow governments but faced brutal suppression, leading to near disappearance or severe marginalization.

1. The Herero and Nama Rebellion (1904-1907) – Namibia

Tribes Involved: Herero and Nama

Targeted Government: German colonial rule

Outcome: Massacre and near extermination

The Herero and Nama tribes of Namibia attempted to expel German colonial rulers. The Germans responded with a brutal extermination campaign, driving them into the desert to die of starvation. Today, these groups remain small and politically marginalized.

2. The Lakota and Sioux Resistance (1876-1890) – United States

Tribes Involved: Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho

Targeted Government: U.S. Government

Outcome: Defeat and loss of sovereignty

Despite a victory at the Battle of Little Bighorn, the Lakota Sioux were eventually crushed by U.S. forces. The Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) marked the end of their resistance, and their population was drastically reduced.

3. The Mau Mau Rebellion (1952-1960) – Kenya

Tribe Involved: Kikuyu (Mau Mau fighters)

Targeted Government: British colonial rule

Outcome: Military defeat and political sidelining

The Mau Mau, a Kikuyu-led movement, attempted to overthrow British rule but were violently suppressed. Many Kikuyu communities suffered, and their role in Kenya’s independence struggle was downplayed for decades.

4. The Zulu Kingdom’s Fall (1879) – South Africa

Tribe Involved: Zulu

Targeted Government: British Empire

Outcome: Defeat and collapse of Zulu dominance

The Zulu initially defeated the British at Isandlwana but were ultimately overpowered. Their kingdom was dismantled, and their influence in South Africa declined significantly.

5. The Kurdish Revolts (1920-Present) – Middle East

Tribe Involved: Kurds

Targeted Governments: Iraq, Turkey, Iran, Syria

Outcome: Repeated failures, massacres, and statelessness

Despite multiple uprisings, the Kurds remain stateless and continue to face repression across several countries. The Halabja massacre (1988) in Iraq saw thousands of Kurds killed with chemical weapons.

6. The Biafra Secession Attempt (1967-1970) – Nigeria

Tribe Involved: Igbo

Targeted Government: Nigerian Government

Outcome: Defeat and mass starvation

The Igbo tried to secede from Nigeria and form Biafra, but the Nigerian government imposed a blockade that led to over 1 million deaths from starvation. The Igbo remain politically marginalized in Nigeria.

Lessons for the Nuer Tribe

These historical cases illustrate the dangers of attempting to overthrow a government as a single ethnic group:

Mass killings and near-extermination events

Long-term political and economic marginalization

Loss of autonomy and cultural suppression

For the Nuer, a direct military overthrow is unlikely to succeed and could lead to devastating consequences. Instead, they should focus on:

1. Building Political Alliances – Working with other ethnic groups to form a united opposition.

2. Participating in Democratic Processes – Strengthening institutions rather than relying on armed rebellion.

3. Diplomatic Engagement – Seeking international support for inclusive governance.

Conclusion

While the Nuer are a powerful force in South Sudanese politics, history shows that single-tribe uprisings often result in heavy losses rather than long-term success. Instead of attempting an armed overthrow, the best path forward may be a coalition-based approach to governance, pushing for national unity and inclusive reforms.

I became a policewoman.

I was passionate, aggressive, and hungry for justice.

When our superintendent asked which officer would volunteer their phone number for people to call during home emergencies, I did not hesitate. I volunteered immediately.

Not because I enjoyed calls, but because I wanted men behind bars.

Any small disturbance, I was already at your doorstep. One or two questions, and I had already arrested the man. My operations were swift. I delivered with confidence and authority.

It did not take long before my rank was elevated. With it came more cases, more power, more opportunities to fight.

Then one day, a young lady ran into my office.

She was wailing, sobbing, groaning. I kept begging her to calm down and tell me what happened. Inside me, my ears were itching. I was already preparing to lock up another man.

When she finally spoke, my world shook.

A doctor at the hospital where she went for treatment had r@ped her. She said he injected her with something that made her drowsy. The last thing she remembered was him rubbing her head and telling her to sleep. When she woke up the next morning, she knew she had been vi0l@ted.

Everything blurred before my eyes.

How could a doctor do this to a patient under his care?

My blood boiled as I asked her questions and took her statement. I assured her the arrest would commence that same day. And if her story was true, we would not only charge him to court. I, Chinelo Uba, would personally ensure his medical license was revoked permanently.

We drove straight to the hospital.

He was not there.

We went to his house.

He was not around.

We tried calling him. His line was not connecting. The nurses we questioned said he usually set aside time for prayer and quiet reflection, and that we should come back later.

Inside my heart, I laughed bitterly.

Prayer my foot. That is how they are. Wicked set of people.

I assured the young lady that the arrest would commence the next day, as I had other matters to attend to.

When I got home, my blood was still boiling. I could hardly wait for morning.

My mother noticed.

She asked gently, “Chinelo, what happened? Which man do you want to arrest again?”

Then she continued, “Sometimes it hurts my heart. Not because you are a policewoman, but because you do this work with vengeance. You hate your father, but what your father did to us is what you are doing to men out there. Some cases can be settled amicably, but you arrest them and make them sleep in dirty cells before bail. Chinelo, take it easy.”

I did not reply her.

She would not understand.

This was not just about pain. It was about saving women like us. Women who had been crushed and silenced. And I told myself I would not stop until every careless man was punished.

I checked the time throughout the night until morning came.

I prayed. I bathed. I dressed.

I stood in front of the mirror and took one last look at myself.

Today is today.

I drove to the station, signed in for the day, then headed straight to the hospital. The young lady was already there, waiting.

I felt proud. Women were finally learning to speak up, not endure like my mother.

We waited.

Then a Prado drove in.

She grabbed my arm immediately and whispered, “That’s the doctor ma’am. He’s here.”
