Rebuttal: Against Ethnic Reductionism in Readings of South Sudan’s Conflict

By: Gatkuoth Lok Gatwich
A PhD Candidate in Social Transformation (Governance) at Tangaza University, Kenya. His research focuses on federalism, peacebuilding, and post-liberation governance in South Sudan, with particular attention to colonial legacies, political economy, and conflict transformation.

This rebuttal responds to the article “Can the Nuer Tribe Reform or Overthrow the Government of South Sudan?” Its central flaw is reducing South Sudan’s structural political crisis to an ethnic question, reproducing a colonial explanatory model that obscures power, political economy, and elite responsibility.
Ethnic groups do not challenge modern states; political movements, military coalitions, and elite networks in specific historical and institutional contexts contest them. Describing the SPLM/SPLA-IO or SSIM/SSIA as “Nuer” is therefore a misnomer. By the same logic, one could label the SPLA/SPLM a “Dinka” movement, which is equally inaccurate. These formations arose as political and revolutionary responses to exclusion and domination, not as ethnic collectives acting out of inherent hostility. Ethnicity in these conflicts appeared to have been instrumentally incentivized and mobilized, not as a causal driver of violence.
Historically, Sudan and South Sudan’s wars have been conflicts within and between revolutionary formations, not “tribal wars.” The SPLA/SPLM–SSIM/SSIA conflict of 1991–2002/3 was a rupture inside a liberation movement. The post-2013 conflict reflects the militarization of a failed post-liberation state captured by a few elite factions from multiple communities, including Nuer and Dinka. Political marginalization of the Nuer predates independence and stems from a colonial genealogy of domination, resistance, and containment.
During the Turko-Egyptian rule (1821–1885), the Upper Nile region endured slave raiding, forced labor, and resource plunder. The Nuer resisted these intrusions, defending communal autonomy and indigenous authority. Colonial administrators later dismissed this resistance as “anarchy,” transforming political agency into justification for repression. Under the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium (1899–1956), punitive pacification campaigns dismantled indigenous governance, suppressed local leaders, and imposed coercive administrative control. Resistance by communities such as the Aliab Dinka followed the same logic of anti-colonial opposition rather than ethnic antagonism. Colonial state-building relied on divide-and-rule, criminalizing autonomy and governing through force rather than consent.
Sudan’s independence in 1956 reproduced these structures. Political and economic marginalization persisted, reinforcing mistrust of the state. Between 1972 and 1983, many Nuer remained outside formal institutions, not from apathy but from historical memory of domination. This marginality did not preclude national engagement, as demonstrated by decisive Nuer support to the SPLA/SPLM at its formation in Bilpam in 1983.
Following the 2010 elections, armed resistance emerged in Jonglei led by Gen. George Athor Deng (Dinka) and Gen. David Yau Yau (Murle), both citing electoral fraud and political exclusion. These rebellions illustrate that opposition to the Southern Sudan state was driven by grievances over legitimacy and governance, not ethnic identity.
Independence in 2011 promised rupture but instead reproduced continuity. Nuer incorporation into the post-liberation state occurred largely through the security sector, producing an ambivalent inclusion that relied upon yet distrusted them. This contradiction culminated in purges and mass violence after December 2013, revealing a deeper constitutional failure: a state governing diversity through suspicion and militarized force rather than negotiation and law.
The article’s selective historical analogies, Herero, Mau Mau, Lakota, and Zulu, are misleading because they frame resistance as a warning against political transformation rather than interrogating structural and institutional dynamics. There is no serious analysis of the war economy: oil revenues, arms flows, regional militaries, and international interests. Elites across ethnic lines benefit from prolonged instability. By ethnicizing the conflict, responsibility is shifted away from ruling coalitions and external actors, fragmenting political consciousness and normalizing collective punishment.
A decolonial reading must reject ethnic reductionism. The core crisis is not Nuer power or Dinka dominance, but the failure of the post-liberation state, militarized politics, and the convergence of internal and external interests around managed instability. South Sudan requires a second liberation, peaceful, institutional, and constitutional, aimed at building a federal, plural, and negotiated state in which no community fears its government. Until then, South Sudan remains independent in form, but imperial in practice.

Rolandsen, Ø. H. (2005). Guerrilla Government: Political Changes in the Southern Sudan during the 1990s. Nordic Africa Institute.
Johnson, D. H. (2014). Briefing: The Crisis in South Sudan. African Affairs.

By Patrick Ali Malou 
 After the fighting in Pochalla, the four Pauls spit up; Paul Ruot, Paul Nyingori, Paul Adung and Paul Awel. It so happened that Paul Awel and Paul Adung went to a camp near Nasir, where with 800 men and 221 guns they fought against six companies of Northern Soldiers who attacked them on March 27th, 1964. Afterwards, Ruot and Nyingori rejoined Awel and Adung, and the four remained together for a month and constructed the general headquarters for Upper Nile province. This was the last meeting of the four Pauls. Paul Nyingori left in April to open a camp near Pibor, and Paul Adung left in June to begin operations in the region of Renk. Neither ever returned: Nyingori quarreled with Ruot and refused to come back, while Paul Adung was killed on his way back to the headquarters. The circumstances were these. The split between Ruot and Nyingori had led to Ruot’s resignation, but when the resignation was sent to the political wing of the movement in Ethiopia for ratification it was rejected, and Ruot was reinstated. Ruot then sent a letter to Adung that he was resuming command, and asked him to return to the headquarters. It was on his return that he met a force of Northern soldiers at Akoko, 50 miles north of Malakal. In the engagement, 15 Anya-Nya soldiers were killed; Adung was wounded and died of tetanus.

Following Adung’s death, Paul Awel was given command of Adung’s forces as well as his own. At the time there were three battalions in upper Nile, distributed as follows. The Northern battalion (formerly Adung’s) operated in the region of Renk and Kodok. After Adung’s death its operational commander was Daniel Owogo. The Western battalion (Awel’s) had as its area Malakal itself, Fangak, Bor and Bentiu districts. Second in command to Awel was Daniel Nyang Cuol. Finally, the Eastern battalion operated in Nasir and Akobo districts, under the command of Nyingori assisted by George Disol. The Pibor area was not included in the list. The reason is that at the time, the district commissioner was a Murle by the name of Hassan Nyingole, who persuaded the Murle people to be loyal to the Khartoum government and not to cooperate with the Anya-Nya soldiers.

In March 1965, the Anya-Nya soldiers suffered a severe loss with the death of Paul Ruot. He was proceeding to a meeting with Nyingori on the Ethiopian border, and on the way took some cattle from a small village between Akobo and Pibor. He then retreated, knowing that the Northern troops would follow him. The pursuing force was however larger than anticipated, coming up from Pibor in lorries along dry-season roads, and the ensuing battle was a grim one. Forty two Anya-Nya soldiers died, some of thirst as the defending force was cut off from water, and the number of Northern casualties was estimated to have been 85. Ruot himself was wounded in the shoulder and the right leg, each time returning to lead his men once more before being finally hit in the head. He was buried where he fell by his men.

Following the death of Ruot; Awel and Nyingori planned to meet, but Awel who was in the region of Malakal had 30 wounded men with him and could not make the journey to Nyingori’s camp. During the whole of 1965 there was constant fighting around Malakal, and to anyone who took note of the frequent ambushes and Anya-Nya raids, it must have been a mystery where they got their ammunition. The answer is simple; they purchased it in Malakal. It seems there was an Arab dealer there who had an officer friend who took the bullets from the armory and sold them. 

Suffice to say, the deaths resulting from the fighting in Upper Nile, and indeed throughout the Southern Sudan as a whole, were not confined to the Anya-Nya or Northern Sudan soldiers. The civilian population suffered a great deal. This is illustrated by the Abu Anga incident. In April 1965, the Nile steamer named Abu Anga, empty of passengers, was about to tie up to the bank at Warajwok, a few miles south of Malakal, in order to collect firewood. The Abu Anga was ambushed by a platoon of Anya-Nya soldiers led by Daniel Owogo. As soon as the captain of the steamer saw the attack he cut the connection between the second and third class barges, and the engine and the second-class departed, leaving the third-class behind. There had been 15 army troops guarding the second-class, but none on the third, which was promptly captured and sunk by Owogo. In retaliation, the Sudan army descended on Warajwok a few days later, when Owogo had left, and killed 89 people, all males.

The woman sitting in that chair isn't Elizabeth Bose's lion, the warm grandmother figure who would wave from balconies for another 50 years.

 That's Queen Mary, born Princess Victoria Mary of Tech on May 26th, 1867. widow of King George V, mother of two kings, grandmother of a third queen. She's 84 years old. She just buried her son.  an abdication that transferred the crushing weight of the crown onto shoulders that were never built to carry it. George V 6th reigned for 15 years. He steered Britain through the Second World War. Let that number sit for a moment because understanding what£10,000 meant in 1952 is the key to understanding everything contemptable about Edward VII's character. The average British worker in 1952 earned roughly £500 a year. A skilled industrial worker, someone with training, experience, someone who built things might see 600 lb to 700 if they were lucky.

 A physician or solicitor in established practice years into a career requiring extensive education might command 1,000 to 1,500 and consider themselves genuinely prosperous. To understand why this moment hit Queen Mary with such devastating force, you have to understand who she was and how she got there.

 Because Mary of Tech wasn't born to be queen. She wasn't even born to be comfortable. They called her family the popper princesses. Her father, the Duke of Tech, held a title that sounded impressive, but carried no income. By 1883, the situation had become untenable. The debts were too large to ignore. So, the Duke and Duchess of Tech did what disgraced aristocrats did in that era.

 They fled to Florence, where living was cheaper and creditors were farther away. Young Mary was 16 years old. She spent the next two years in Italian exile watching her parents attempt to maintain royal pretensions on a bankrupt budget. It was humiliating and it was formative. Mary became the family's fixer. While her mother organized elaborate dinners they couldn't afford and her father retreated into melancholy, Mary managed the household accounts.

 She negotiated with servants. She made economies where economies could be made. She learned at an age when most princesses learned nothing useful whatsoever. That dignity required discipline. That status meant nothing without the steel to maintain it. When the family finally returned to England in 1885, Mary carried that lesson with her.

 She was serious where the rest of her generation was frivolous. reserved where they were giddy. Queen Victoria noticed the old queen had spent decades watching the Wales family, her son Birdie, the future Edward IIIth, and his pleasure- seeeking children with mounting disapproval. They gambled. They scandalized.

 They treated royal status as license for indulgence rather than obligation for service. Mary was different. Victoria saw in her the same rigid sense of duty that characterized her own understanding of monarchy. When it came time to find a suitable bride for Prince Albert Victor, Eddie, the eldest grandson, second in line to the throne, Victoria's approval of Mary was decisive.

 The girl from the bankrupt family, the one who'd learned that appearances must be earned. In 1891, Mary became engaged to Prince Eddie. He was charming by most accounts. The day my own mother whispered, “We kept the better child,” something inside me went silent… and never came back.

I was born in America, a twin—but not an equal one. Chloe was the “angel.” Blonde hair, green eyes, dimples… the kind of kid strangers complimented like she was a miracle. Me? I was the extra. The spare twin. The one told to stand in the back of family photos so the lighting wouldn’t “ruin the picture.” The one who got socks while she got iPads. The one who carried bags, washed dishes, took the blame—then got sent away at 14 like unwanted luggage.

And they didn’t even pretend it was temporary.
My mom’s last words weren’t “we’ll miss you.” They were: “Don’t cause them as much trouble as you caused us.”

Uncle James and Aunt Laura saved me. They gave me a room, food, and something I’d never had—a place where I wasn’t competing for permission to exist. I grew up. I healed. I learned one brutal truth: if someone treats you like disposable, they’ll only come back when they need you.

Years later, Chloe calls out of nowhere—sweet voice, fake concern… then the punchline: “You should split your inheritance. We’re twins.”
And that’s when I realized… she didn’t just want money.

She wanted to erase what they did to me and rewrite the story like I owed her.
But I had receipts. Proof. Screenshots. Spreadsheets. Even the things they thought they’d buried forever.

And when Chloe tried to shame me publicly for refusing… I didn’t defend myself.
I didn’t argue.
I simply uploaded the truth where they couldn’t delete it.

The family chat went quiet. Then it exploded.
Because once the mask slips, it never goes back on the same way again.

But the most satisfying part? That came later… in a place she never expected to see me… when I saw her wearing something blue, holding a mop, and trying not to be recognized.

What did I post that made Chloe’s GoFundMe vanish overnight?
What did my parents do when the whole family finally saw the “spare twin” truth?
And why did Chloe’s last message prove she still hadn’t learned a single thing…?

CB College (Cantonment Board College) was the first all girls’ college established after the partition in Rawalpindi.

It was founded on February 26th, 1952, and started as a small school offering primary classes. It then upgraded to a degree college in 1963 and started offering post graduate classes in English and Urdu by 1966.

The founding principal of the school was Salma Masood, the wife of eminent educationist Prof Khawaja Masood. The couple played a significant role in promoting education in Islamabad and Rawalpindi.

The CB College was nationalised in 1972 and it was renamed the ‘Federal Government Postgraduate College for Women’.

The institution has been the alma mater of many distinguished women such as:
- Nadia Khan, well known actress and former TV host.
- Dr. Maleeha Lodhi, Pakistan’s representative to the UN 
- Tehmeena Janjua, Pakistan’s former foreign secretary

She was born in prison to a disgraced nobleman. At 16, she married an invalid poet. At 48, she secretly married the most powerful king in Europe. Then she walked away from it all.
November 27, 1635. Niort Prison, France.
While aristocratic babies entered the world in silk-draped chambers with midwives and wet nurses, Françoise d'Aubigné was born behind bars.
Her father, Constant d'Aubigné, was a minor nobleman who'd gambled away his fortune, conspired in political schemes, and ended up imprisoned for debt. Her mother, Jeanne de Cardilhac, could have abandoned him—returned to her family, saved herself the shame.
She chose to stay. In the prison. Raising her daughter among stone walls and the whispered judgment of a society that never forgave failure.
Françoise's first memories were of cold floors and her mother's quiet dignity. Of being the child people pitied or ignored. Of knowing, from the moment she could understand words, that her family name meant nothing.
When her father was finally released, the family drifted. Money was always scarce. Relatives took Françoise in—not out of love, but obligation. She was passed between households like unwanted luggage, always aware she was a burden.
At sixteen, a practical solution presented itself: marriage to Paul Scarron, a celebrated poet and wit who was forty-two years old, paralyzed, and grotesquely disfigured by illness.
It wasn't love. It was survival. Françoise would have a home. Scarron would have a young wife to manage his household and nurse him.
But something unexpected happened: Françoise discovered she had a gift.
Scarron hosted a literary salon—writers, philosophers, and artists gathering to debate and perform. Françoise, the silent young wife, listened. She absorbed everything. She learned that intelligence and charm could open doors that beauty and dowry never could.
She learned to speak thoughtfully. To listen carefully. To navigate social dynamics with grace.
When Scarron died in 1660, Françoise was twenty-four, widowed, and penniless again. But this time, she wasn't the helpless prison-born child. She was educated, poised, and quietly determined.
For years, she survived on the charity of friends from Scarron's salon. She took small positions. She waited for an opportunity.
In 1669, that opportunity arrived.
King Louis XIV—the Sun King, the most powerful monarch in Europe—needed a governess for his illegitimate children with his mistress, Madame de Montespan. The position required absolute discretion. The children's existence was a secret. Their governess would live in the shadows.
Françoise took the job.
She moved into rooms near Versailles with the King's hidden children. While the palace glittered with courtiers competing for attention, Françoise worked in silence—raising, educating, and loving children the court pretended didn't exist.
And the King noticed.
Louis XIV was surrounded by flattery. Every conversation was performance. Every person wanted something. But when he visited his children, he found their governess refreshingly different.
She didn't flirt. She didn't scheme. She didn't compete for his attention. She simply spoke to him honestly—about the children, about ideas, about things that mattered.
In a palace built on artifice, her sincerity was radical.
Their friendship deepened. Françoise became his confidante. While his mistresses provided passion and his courtiers provided entertainment, she provided something rarer: peace.
When Queen Marie-Thérèse died in 1683, Louis XIV was fifty-five years old. He'd had countless mistresses, fathered numerous illegitimate children, and lived a life of spectacular excess.
And he was tired.
He wanted something different. Something real.
In the autumn of 1683—most historians believe—Louis XIV secretly married Françoise d'Aubigné in a private ceremony witnessed by only a handful of people.
She was forty-eight. He was forty-five. She'd been born in prison. He was the most powerful king in the world.
The marriage was morganatic—she would never be publicly recognized as queen. No coronation. No title. Just a private partnership between a king exhausted by performance and a woman who'd learned grace through suffering.
For the next thirty-two years, Françoise lived as the King's secret wife. She had enormous influence but used it sparingly. She encouraged Louis XIV toward religious devotion. She advocated for the poor. She lived modestly by Versailles standards.
And she built something lasting.
In 1686, Françoise founded the Maison Royale de Saint-Louis at Saint-Cyr—a school for girls of noble birth but no fortune. Girls exactly like she'd been. Girls society had written off as unmarriageable, useless, doomed to dependence.
At Saint-Cyr, these girls received education. Real education—literature, mathematics, music, religion. They learned they had value beyond marriage prospects and dowries.
Françoise poured her heart into this school. She wrote its curriculum. She visited constantly. She knew hundreds of students by name.
This was her revenge on the world that had dismissed her: giving other forgotten girls the tools to rise.
When Louis XIV died in 1715, Françoise was eighty years old. She could have stayed at Versailles, living in luxury as the King's widow. Courtiers would have competed for her favor. She could have wielded power for years.
Instead, she walked away.
She returned to Saint-Cyr, to the school she'd founded, and lived there among the students and teachers. No palace. No servants. No performance.
Just a woman who'd been born in prison, married a king, and chose to spend her final years among girls learning to read.
She died at Saint-Cyr on April 15, 1719, at age eighty-three. Not surrounded by courtiers and nobles, but by the sound of young women's voices—reading, debating, becoming.
The legacy she built wasn't in gold or titles. It was in generations of educated women who might otherwise have been invisible.
Françoise d'Aubigné was never crowned queen. History books barely mention her. Tourists visiting Versailles don't learn her name.
But she proved something profound: power isn't about titles or recognition. It's about what you do with whatever influence you have.
She was born behind bars to a disgraced family. She married an invalid poet at sixteen to survive. She became governess to a king's secret children. She married that king in a ceremony no one acknowledged.
And then she used every ounce of influence to lift other forgotten girls out of the shadows.
Born in captivity. Loved by the Sun King. Remembered by the generations of girls she refused to let society discard.
Madame de Maintenon. The secret queen who understood that true power lies not in crowns, but in creating doors for those trapped outside.

Surah Al-Furqan (25:68–70) defines the qualities of true believers by forbidding three major sins—shirk (associating partners with Allah), unjust killing, and zina (fornication/adultery)—while also offering hope of forgiveness for those who sincerely repent, believe, and do righteous deeds. 

---

🌿 Text of the Verses
- 25:68 – “And those who do not invoke any other god besides Allah, nor kill a soul which Allah has made sacred except by right, nor commit fornication. And whoever does this shall meet a penalty.” 
- 25:69 – “The punishment will be doubled for them on the Day of Resurrection, and they will abide therein humiliated.” 
- 25:70 – “Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds—for them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good. And Allah is Ever Forgiving, Most Merciful.” 

---

📖 Definition & Tafsir

1. Major Sins Highlighted
- Shirk (polytheism): Worshipping other than Allah is the gravest sin. 
- Unjust killing: Human life is sacred; killing without just cause (like legal justice) is forbidden. 
- Zina (fornication/adultery): Immoral sexual relations destroy purity and social order. 

2. Consequence of These Sins
- Severe punishment in the Hereafter. 
- Multiplied torment and eternal disgrace for those who persist without repentance. 

3. Path to Redemption
- Repentance (Tawbah): Turning back to Allah sincerely. 
- Faith (Iman): Renewing belief in Allah and His guidance. 
- Good deeds (Amal Salih): Actively living righteously. 
- Transformation: Allah promises to replace sins with good deeds, showing His mercy and forgiveness. 

---

🌟 Key Lessons
- Balance of Justice and Mercy: These verses warn of grave consequences yet highlight Allah’s mercy for sincere repentance. 
- Hope for Sinners: Even those guilty of major sins can be forgiven if they reform. 
- Moral Framework: Protecting monotheism, life, and chastity are foundational to a just society.

One saddest things is that, South Sudan will not move forward until we confront one hard truth: we have confused politics with ethnicity, and that confusion is destroying our country.

So many times we have allowed leaders to hide behind tribes and turned political criticism into tribal warfare. When a leader comes from a certain community, we stop judging them as an individual and start defending or attacking them as a tribe. This is not patriotism. This is how accountability dies.

When individuals from other tribes such as Ezekiel Gathkouth (Nuer), Olony (Shilluk), or Lomuro (Pojulu) choose to support President Salva Kiir, they must not be called sellouts by their tribemates simply because they are supporting Kiir a  Dinka. At the same time, no Dinka is born with the duty to support Kiir, just as no Nuer is born to defend Machar, and no Pojulu is obligated to follow Lomuro. Political loyalty is not inherited through blood.

Similarly, when I say Kiir’s leadership is weak, no one from the Dinka tribe should hate me. When I say Machar is one of the reasons our country is not at peace, no Nuer including my good friend Lam should take it as an insult. And when I refuse to support Lomuro because I disagree with his actions, no one has the right to pressure me simply because he comes from my tribe. This is intellectual freedom. Criticizing leaders is not attacking tribes.

When we criticize leaders, we criticize their decisions, their competence, and their impact on the nation, not the communities they come from. Anyone who tells you otherwise is a “LAZY THINKER”

The young people of South Sudan, many of us spent more than 16 years in school. From nursery to university. We did not sacrifice our time, our families’ resources, and our futures just to come back and blindly pick up a gun and vow to die protecting leaders simply because they share our ethnicity. Education was meant to free our minds, not militarize our bodies.

No educated Dinka, Nuer, Shilluk, Pojulu, or Equatorian youth should accept being used as a tribal shield for failed leadership. Our responsibility is not to leaders it is to truth, justice, and the future of South Sudan.

Reject ethnic politics. Refuse to fight for politicians. Refuse to hate your fellow citizens. Demand accountability. Judge leaders as individuals. Organize, speak out, and think beyond tribe.

Politics is not ethnicity.
We are not tribal foot soldiers.
We are citizens and the future is ours to defend.

My father left my mother because she gave birth to seven girls.

She was in search of a boy, and that was why we got to seven.

After years of trying, the boy never came. Instead, my father chased us out of the house like unwanted luggage.

My father was a feared policeman. His rank alone could silence a room. He was huge, intimidating, and dreadful. I do not even want to begin to explain the kind of pain we endured under his roof. Living with that man was like living with fear itself.

Sometimes, I watch women talk about their fathers with softness in their voices. Some are closer to their fathers than their mothers. Each time I hear such stories, my mind tells me it must be an AI generated movie, because neither I nor my sisters ever experienced the beauty of having a father.

I was the fourth child. The one my father personally came to the hospital to see. When the nurse told him I was a girl, he walked out. He went on an assignment for one year and refused to pay the hospital bills.

From that moment, his resentment deepened.

Every scan and X ray he took my mother for confirmed I was a boy. Or so they told him. So when I arrived as a girl, something in him snapped. To him, I was proof that hope could betray.

All these things planted something ugly inside me. I did not just resent my father. I resented men as a whole. I wanted nothing to do with that gender.

Then life played its joke on me.

I became a policewoman.

One of the reasons I chose that path was to fight for my family and for women like my mother, women who had suffered under the hands of men and swallowed their pain in silence. I wanted to rescue women trapped under the grip of what I believed was an evil gender.

I was passionate, aggressive, and hungry for justice.

When our superintendent asked which officer would volunteer their phone number for people to call during home emergencies, I did not hesitate. I volunteered immediately.

Not because I enjoyed calls, but because I wanted men behind bars.

Any small disturbance, I was already at your doorstep. One or two questions, and I had already arrested the man. My operations were swift. I delivered with confidence and authority.

It did not take long before my rank was elevated. With it came more cases, more power, more opportunities to fight.

Then one day, a young lady ran into my office.

She was wailing, sobbing, groaning. I kept begging her to calm down and tell me what happened. Inside me, my ears were itching. I was already preparing to lock up another man.

When she finally spoke, my world shook.

A doctor at the hospital where she went for treatment had r@ped her. She said he injected her with something that made her drowsy. The last thing she remembered was him rubbing her head and telling her to sleep. When she woke up the next morning, she knew she had been vi0l@ted.

Everything blurred before my eyes.

How could a doctor do this to a patient under his care?

My blood boiled as I asked her questions and took her statement. I assured her the arrest would commence that same day. And if her story was true, we would not only charge him to court. I, Chinelo Uba, would personally ensure his medical license was revoked permanently.

We drove straight to the hospital.

He was not there.

We went to his house.

He was not around.

We tried calling him. His line was not connecting. The nurses we questioned said he usually set aside time for prayer and quiet reflection, and that we should come back later.

Inside my heart, I laughed bitterly.

Prayer my foot. That is how they are. Wicked set of people.

I assured the young lady that the arrest would commence the next day, as I had other matters to attend to.

When I got home, my blood was still boiling. I could hardly wait for morning.

My mother noticed.

She asked gently, “Chinelo, what happened? Which man do you want to arrest again?”

Then she continued, “Sometimes it hurts my heart. Not because you are a policewoman, but because you do this work with vengeance. You hate your father, but what your father did to us is what you are doing to men out there. Some cases can be settled amicably, but you arrest them and make them sleep in dirty cells before bail. Chinelo, take it easy.”

I did not reply her.

She would not understand.

This was not just about pain. It was about saving women like us. Women who had been crushed and silenced. And I told myself I would not stop until every careless man was punished.

I checked the time throughout the night until morning came.

I prayed. I bathed. I dressed.

I stood in front of the mirror and took one last look at myself.

Today is today.

I drove to the station, signed in for the day, then headed straight to the hospital. The young lady was already there, waiting.

I felt proud. Women were finally learning to speak up, not endure like my mother.

We waited.

Then a Prado drove in.

She grabbed my arm immediately and whispered, “That’s the doctor ma’am. He’s here.”

"My daughter-in-law dropped the kids off like they were unwanted luggage. 'Since you’re just rotting away in this cabin, do something useful,' she smirked. I just smiled, handing her the plane tickets. But as her car disappeared, my smile turned cold. 'You think my peace is a weakness? Enjoy your trip, darling, because you won't recognize your life when you get back.' The trap was set. Now, the real game begins."
The Audacity of Entitlement

I had spent thirty years as a high-stakes corporate litigator in Chicago, navigating boardrooms filled with sharks. When I finally retired to my secluded cabin in the Black Hills of South Dakota, I wasn't looking for a second career; I was looking for silence. My son, David, had married Sarah five years ago. Sarah was a woman who viewed everyone as a rung on her social ladder, including me. To her, my retirement wasn't a hard-earned rest; it was a "waste of productivity."

The peace shattered on a Tuesday morning when Sarah’s Range Rover pulled up the gravel driveway. She didn't even wait for me to invite her in. She stepped out, sunglasses perched on her head, looking at my cabin with undisguised disdain. "Evelyn, thank God you’re here," she said, her voice dripping with artificial urgency. "David and I desperately need a break. We’ve booked a ten-day luxury cruise through the Mediterranean. Since you’re just sitting here in the woods doing nothing anyway, you’re watching the twins."

I looked at my six-year-old grandsons, Leo and Max, who were already chasing a squirrel toward the lake. "Sarah, I have plans this week. I’m hosting a local conservation meeting and—"

She cut me off with a sharp laugh. "Plans? Evelyn, you’re a retiree. Your 'plans' involve birdwatching and knitting. We’ve already paid for the tickets. We leave tomorrow morning. Don't be selfish; it’s time you contributed something to this family instead of just hiding out here."

She handed me a folder of "instructions" that read more like a prison manifesto—organic-only meals, no television, and a strict 6:30 PM bedtime. Before I could even protest, she was back in her car. "The boys have their bags. See you in ten days!" As she sped away, kicking up dust, I looked at the folder. In it was a legal document she had accidentally included—a draft for a "Power of Attorney" over my estate, claiming I was becoming "mentally unfit" due to my isolation.

My blood turned to ice. She wasn't just using me as a babysitter; she was scouting my lifestyle to steal my autonomy. I looked at the boys, then at the dust trail of her car. I smiled, a cold, calculated expression that had once made CEOs tremble. "Sarah," I whispered to the empty air, "you should have remembered what I did for a living before you tried to play the predator."

Why Did Kuol Manyang Appear in Poktap, Panyagoor,and What Does It Really Mean?

When a senior elder, senior liberator, and senior presidential adviser like Kuol Manyang Juuk suddenly appears in a frontline zone such as Poktap, the question is not whether politics is involved, but whose politics and at what cost to ordinary people.

Was his presence a personal initiative, or was it a calculated deployment by Salva Kiir Mayardit to press communities of Duk County, Twic East County, and Bor County to rally behind the army? In South Sudan, such appearances are never neutral. They are messages, sometimes warnings delivered in high profile form.

This setups is familiar. When the state feels vulnerable, it reaches for history as a weapon. The tragedies of 1991 and 2013 are invoked not as lessons to prevent recurrence, but as emotional leverage used to frighten, shame, or pressure communities into compliance. It is an old tactic that reopen wounds to manufacture loyalty. But wounds that never healed do not respond to threats; they resist them.

Only weeks ago, Bor County was terrorised under the same flag now asking for unity and government support in fighting it war. Communities were levelled, civilians tortured, killed, and a whole county framed as sympathetic to rebellion because local youth organised protection against cattle raiders. Red Belt was not an insurgency; it was a desperate community response to insecurity, a failed government’s responsibility. Yet the government’s reaction treated it as treason. Today, sending Kuol Manyang to the frontline to “convince” Bor, Twi & Duk feels less like dialogue and more like coercion dressed in elder robes.

This is where humiliation enters the story, not Kuol Manyang’s humiliation by the people, but by the system that uses him. A liberation icon sent into an unwinnable moral terrain, asked to sell a war that many no longer believe in. When elders are deployed as shields for policy failure, their dignity becomes collateral damage. The people see it clearly; an adviser standing in a war zone does not equal consent; it signals desperation at the centre.

Meanwhile, the conflict is framed as a fight against an IO rebellion “dominated” by one community, specifically the Nuer as if war is a census category. This framing is dangerous. It reduces political disputes to ethnic arithmetic and invites collective punishment. Duk, Twic East, and Bor know where that road leads. They have walked it before, barefoot, carrying children.

What has changed is not the government’s script but the people’s reading of it. These communities have learned to recognise state weakness when they see it; rushed mobilisations, emotional blackmail, elders sent to the trenches, and history recycled as threat. They understand that when Juba feels unsafe, it asks the periphery to bleed first. This time, many are saying no, not loudly, not with slogans, but with refusal to be baited.

The claim that these communities must “protect the government seat” is particularly hollow. Governments protect citizens, not the other way around. When protection is reversed, when civilians are told to sacrifice themselves to secure a palace legitimacy collapses. Other constituencies can choose to defend that seat if they wish. Duk, Twic East, and Bor are choosing something else, the safety of their vulnerable civilians.

Evacuation over enlistment is not cowardice; it is clarity. Moving women, children, and elders out of harm’s way is a political statement louder than any rally. It says, we will not be conscripted into a senseless war; we will not be blackmailed by memories of massacres; we will not trade our children’s lives for speeches.

The tragedy is that figures like Kuol Manyang once stood for something better. Liberation was about dignity, choice, and the end of coercion. To see a liberator repurposed as a pressure instrument is to witness how far the project has drifted. Elders should mediate peace, not market war. Advisers should speak truth to power, not carry power’s anxieties to frightened villages.

South Sudan does not need more frontlines visited for optics. It needs accountability for terrorised counties, an honest reckoning with state violence, and a politics that stops gambling with history. Until then, communities will continue to read the signs and choose survival over symbolism.

If Poktap was meant to be a show of strength, it revealed the opposite. Strength does not arrive with tanks and elders under duress. It arrives when a government can persuade without fear, remember without manipulation, and protect without punishing. Duk, Twic East, and Bor have made their position clear. The question now is whether those in power are listening or merely sending another messenger into the dust like Kuoldit.

War is not a solution!

Can the Nuer Tribe Reform or Overthrow the Government of South Sudan?
By Maxwell J.X
British Analyst, Newcastle - UK

Introduction

South Sudan remains one of the most ethnically divided nations in the world, with political power largely controlled by the Dinka tribe under President Salva Kiir. The Nuer, the second-largest ethnic group, have historically played a significant role in South Sudanese politics and armed conflicts. This article explores whether the Nuer can reform or overthrow the current regime and examines historical cases where tribes attempted to overthrow governments but ultimately failed, leading to their near extinction.

Can the Nuer Tribe Reform the Government?

Reforming a government requires structural changes, political will, and a coalition of different ethnic groups working together. While the Nuer have historically challenged Dinka dominance—most notably in the civil war (2013-2018)—true reform would require more than just Nuer leadership.

Challenges to Reform

1. Ethnic Fragmentation: South Sudanese politics is deeply tribal, making broad-based reform difficult.

2. Internal Divisions: The Nuer themselves are divided among different factions, including those loyal to Riek Machar and others aligned with the government.

3. Military Control: The government, backed by regional allies like Uganda and Sudan, has the military upper hand.

Reform is possible but would require a national movement that goes beyond a single ethnic group.

Can the Nuer Tribe Overthrow the Government?

Overthrowing a government is significantly more challenging than reforming it. Although the Nuer have been involved in armed rebellions—such as the 1991 split within the SPLA and the 2013-2018 conflict—these attempts have led to widespread suffering rather than lasting political control.

Key Obstacles to an Overthrow

Government Military Strength: The South Sudanese army (SSPDF) is well-equipped and has external support.

Lack of a Unified Front: Without alliances with other ethnic groups like the Equatorians and Shilluk, an armed Nuer uprising would likely be crushed.

International Influence: Neighboring countries and global powers have a vested interest in maintaining the current regime.

History has shown that no single ethnic group can successfully take power in a multi-ethnic state without facing overwhelming resistance.

Historical Cases of Failed Tribal Overthrows Leading to Near Extinction

Throughout history, various tribes have attempted to overthrow governments but faced brutal suppression, leading to near disappearance or severe marginalization.

1. The Herero and Nama Rebellion (1904-1907) – Namibia

Tribes Involved: Herero and Nama

Targeted Government: German colonial rule

Outcome: Massacre and near extermination

The Herero and Nama tribes of Namibia attempted to expel German colonial rulers. The Germans responded with a brutal extermination campaign, driving them into the desert to die of starvation. Today, these groups remain small and politically marginalized.

2. The Lakota and Sioux Resistance (1876-1890) – United States

Tribes Involved: Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho

Targeted Government: U.S. Government

Outcome: Defeat and loss of sovereignty

Despite a victory at the Battle of Little Bighorn, the Lakota Sioux were eventually crushed by U.S. forces. The Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) marked the end of their resistance, and their population was drastically reduced.

3. The Mau Mau Rebellion (1952-1960) – Kenya

Tribe Involved: Kikuyu (Mau Mau fighters)

Targeted Government: British colonial rule

Outcome: Military defeat and political sidelining

The Mau Mau, a Kikuyu-led movement, attempted to overthrow British rule but were violently suppressed. Many Kikuyu communities suffered, and their role in Kenya’s independence struggle was downplayed for decades.

4. The Zulu Kingdom’s Fall (1879) – South Africa

Tribe Involved: Zulu

Targeted Government: British Empire

Outcome: Defeat and collapse of Zulu dominance

The Zulu initially defeated the British at Isandlwana but were ultimately overpowered. Their kingdom was dismantled, and their influence in South Africa declined significantly.

5. The Kurdish Revolts (1920-Present) – Middle East

Tribe Involved: Kurds

Targeted Governments: Iraq, Turkey, Iran, Syria

Outcome: Repeated failures, massacres, and statelessness

Despite multiple uprisings, the Kurds remain stateless and continue to face repression across several countries. The Halabja massacre (1988) in Iraq saw thousands of Kurds killed with chemical weapons.

6. The Biafra Secession Attempt (1967-1970) – Nigeria

Tribe Involved: Igbo

Targeted Government: Nigerian Government

Outcome: Defeat and mass starvation

The Igbo tried to secede from Nigeria and form Biafra, but the Nigerian government imposed a blockade that led to over 1 million deaths from starvation. The Igbo remain politically marginalized in Nigeria.

Lessons for the Nuer Tribe

These historical cases illustrate the dangers of attempting to overthrow a government as a single ethnic group:

Mass killings and near-extermination events

Long-term political and economic marginalization

Loss of autonomy and cultural suppression

For the Nuer, a direct military overthrow is unlikely to succeed and could lead to devastating consequences. Instead, they should focus on:

1. Building Political Alliances – Working with other ethnic groups to form a united opposition.

2. Participating in Democratic Processes – Strengthening institutions rather than relying on armed rebellion.

3. Diplomatic Engagement – Seeking international support for inclusive governance.

Conclusion

While the Nuer are a powerful force in South Sudanese politics, history shows that single-tribe uprisings often result in heavy losses rather than long-term success. Instead of attempting an armed overthrow, the best path forward may be a coalition-based approach to governance, pushing for national unity and inclusive reforms.

Maxwell J.X
British Analyst, Newcastle - UK

Why Did Kuol Manyang Appear in Poktap, Panyagoor,and What Does It Really Mean?

When a senior elder, senior liberator, and senior presidential adviser like Kuol Manyang Juuk suddenly appears in a frontline zone such as Poktap, the question is not whether politics is involved, but whose politics and at what cost to ordinary people.

Was his presence a personal initiative, or was it a calculated deployment by Salva Kiir Mayardit to press communities of Duk County, Twic East County, and Bor County to rally behind the army? In South Sudan, such appearances are never neutral. They are messages, sometimes warnings delivered in high profile form.

This setups is familiar. When the state feels vulnerable, it reaches for history as a weapon. The tragedies of 1991 and 2013 are invoked not as lessons to prevent recurrence, but as emotional leverage used to frighten, shame, or pressure communities into compliance. It is an old tactic that reopen wounds to manufacture loyalty. But wounds that never healed do not respond to threats; they resist them.

Only weeks ago, Bor County was terrorised under the same flag now asking for unity and government support in fighting it war. Communities were levelled, civilians tortured, killed, and a whole county framed as sympathetic to rebellion because local youth organised protection against cattle raiders. Red Belt was not an insurgency; it was a desperate community response to insecurity, a failed government’s responsibility. Yet the government’s reaction treated it as treason. Today, sending Kuol Manyang to the frontline to “convince” Bor, Twi & Duk feels less like dialogue and more like coercion dressed in elder robes.

This is where humiliation enters the story, not Kuol Manyang’s humiliation by the people, but by the system that uses him. A liberation icon sent into an unwinnable moral terrain, asked to sell a war that many no longer believe in. When elders are deployed as shields for policy failure, their dignity becomes collateral damage. The people see it clearly; an adviser standing in a war zone does not equal consent; it signals desperation at the centre.

Meanwhile, the conflict is framed as a fight against an IO rebellion “dominated” by one community, specifically the Nuer as if war is a census category. This framing is dangerous. It reduces political disputes to ethnic arithmetic and invites collective punishment. Duk, Twic East, and Bor know where that road leads. They have walked it before, barefoot, carrying children.

What has changed is not the government’s script but the people’s reading of it. These communities have learned to recognise state weakness when they see it; rushed mobilisations, emotional blackmail, elders sent to the trenches, and history recycled as threat. They understand that when Juba feels unsafe, it asks the periphery to bleed first. This time, many are saying no, not loudly, not with slogans, but with refusal to be baited.

The claim that these communities must “protect the government seat” is particularly hollow. Governments protect citizens, not the other way around. When protection is reversed, when civilians are told to sacrifice themselves to secure a palace legitimacy collapses. Other constituencies can choose to defend that seat if they wish. Duk, Twic East, and Bor are choosing something else, the safety of their vulnerable civilians.

Evacuation over enlistment is not cowardice; it is clarity. Moving women, children, and elders out of harm’s way is a political statement louder than any rally. It says, we will not be conscripted into a senseless war; we will not be blackmailed by memories of massacres; we will not trade our children’s lives for speeches.

The tragedy is that figures like Kuol Manyang once stood for something better. Liberation was about dignity, choice, and the end of coercion. To see a liberator repurposed as a pressure instrument is to witness how far the project has drifted. Elders should mediate peace, not market war. Advisers should speak truth to power, not carry power’s anxieties to frightened villages.

South Sudan does not need more frontlines visited for optics. It needs accountability for terrorised counties, an honest reckoning with state violence, and a politics that stops gambling with history. Until then, communities will continue to read the signs and choose survival over symbolism.

If Poktap was meant to be a show of strength, it revealed the opposite. Strength does not arrive with tanks and elders under duress. It arrives when a government can persuade without fear, remember without manipulation, and protect without punishing. Duk, Twic East, and Bor have made their position clear. The question now is whether those in power are listening or merely sending another messenger into the dust like Kuoldit.

Gen. Olony to Jonglei leaders: Stop dragging civilians into a war they didn’t choose

Years of fighting in Greater Upper Nile have left communities exhausted and increasingly exposed, with civilians now being drawn into a conflict they neither understand nor control, according to Lt. Gen. Johnson Olony, Deputy Army Chief for Disarmament and Mobilization.

Olony, who’s also the commander of the Agwelek forces, made the remarks on Friday while meeting Jonglei State Governor Riak Gai Kok in Poktap, Duk County, Jonglei State.

He warned that the growing involvement of civilians in the war risked catastrophic consequences for communities, particularly the Nuer.

Questioning why non-combatants were being mobilized, Olony said the conflict was fundamentally between the government and the Sudan People’s Liberation Army in Opposition (SPLA-IO), not civilians. 

He questioned why ordinary civilians were being pulled into battles that should be fought only by armed forces.

Drawing on his own experience as a rebel commander, Olony contrasted the current situation with earlier phases of the war, when fighting was limited to combatants. 

He said civilians did not follow commanders into battle and were spared the brunt of defeat or victory.

Speaking partly in the Nuer language, Olony cautioned Governor Riak Gai, saying the Nuer community risked being destroyed without fully understanding the implications of the conflict. 

He said people were being led into violence without clarity about its purpose or end.

The Agwelek commander also questioned the logic of the ongoing military campaign across Jonglei, listing a series of locations from Bor to Poktap, Duk Padiet, Pathai and Yuai, and asking what strategic objective justified such movements and fighting.

Rejecting the idea that the war could result in ethnic domination, Olony said no community could rule South Sudan as a tribe. 

He distinguished between ethnic rule and national leadership, saying individuals such as First Vice President Riek Machar or Governor Riak Gai Kok could govern the country as national leaders, but not on the basis of tribal identity.

Olony revived a controversial proposal he said he had raised before, arguing that lasting peace would only be possible if the Nuer community were given their own state or country to govern themselves.

The statement comes just a week after Olony issued hardline orders to troops preparing for a government offensive in Jonglei, telling them to “spare no lives,” including civilians. 

Those remarks triggered alarm among human rights groups and observers, who warned of the risk of mass abuses in a region with a history of ethnically driven violence.

Olony commands the Agwelek forces, a militia largely drawn from the Shilluk community that has fought on multiple sides of South Sudan’s conflicts and has not been fully integrated into the South Sudan People’s Defense Forces (SSPDF). 

His forces are currently operating alongside government troops against SPLA-IO fighters, whom authorities accuse of attempting to expand control toward central Jonglei and the national capital, Juba.

South Sudan has endured repeated cycles of violence since gaining independence in 2011, with conflicts frequently taking on ethnic dimensions involving Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk communities, leaving civilians bearing the heaviest cost.

So many times we have allowed leaders to hide behind tribes and turned political criticism into tribal warfare. When a leader comes from a certain community, we stop judging them as an individual and start defending or attacking them as a tribe. This is not patriotism. This is how accountability dies.

When individuals from other tribes such as Ezekiel Gathkouth (Nuer), Olony (Shilluk), or Lomuro (Pojulu) choose to support President Salva Kiir, they must not be called sellouts by their tribemates simply because they are supporting Kiir a  Dinka. Reject ethnic politics. Refuse to fight for politicians. Refuse to hate your fellow citizens. Demand accountability. Judge leaders as individuals. Organize, speak out, and think beyond tribe.

We are not tribal foot soldiers.

My father left my mother because she gave birth to seven girls.

She was in search of a boy, and that was why we got to seven.

After years of trying, the boy never came. Instead, my father chased us out of the house like unwanted luggage.

My father was a feared policeman. His rank alone could silence a room. He was huge, intimidating, and dreadful. I do not even want to begin to explain the kind of pain we endured under his roof. Living with that man was like living with fear itself.

Sometimes, I watch women talk about their fathers with softness in their voices. Some are closer to their fathers than their mothers. Each time I hear such stories, my mind tells me it must be an AI generated movie, because neither I nor my sisters ever experienced the beauty of having a father.

I was the fourth child. The one my father personally came to the hospital to see. When the nurse told him I was a girl, he walked out. He went on an assignment for one year and refused to pay the hospital bills.

From that moment, his resentment deepened.

Every scan and X ray he took my mother for confirmed I was a boy. Or so they told him. So when I arrived as a girl, something in him snapped. To him, I was proof that hope could betray.

All these things planted something ugly inside me. I did not just resent my father. I resented men as a whole. I wanted nothing to do with that gender.

Then life played its joke on me.

I became a policewoman.

One of the reasons I chose that path was to fight for my family and for women like my mother, women who had suffered under the hands of men and swallowed their pain in silence. I wanted to rescue women trapped under the grip of what I believed was an evil gender.

I was passionate, aggressive, and hungry for justice.

When our superintendent asked which officer would volunteer their phone number for people to call during home emergencies, I did not hesitate. I volunteered immediately.

Not because I enjoyed calls, but because I wanted men behind bars.

Any small disturbance, I was already at your doorstep. One or two questions, and I had already arrested the man. My operations were swift. I delivered with confidence and authority.

It did not take long before my rank was elevated. With it came more cases, more power, more opportunities to fight.

Then one day, a young lady ran into my office.

She was wailing, sobbing, groaning. I kept begging her to calm down and tell me what happened. Inside me, my ears were itching. I was already preparing to lock up another man.

When she finally spoke, my world shook.

A doctor at the hospital where she went for treatment had r@ped her. She said he injected her with something that made her drowsy. The last thing she remembered was him rubbing her head and telling her to sleep. When she woke up the next morning, she knew she had been vi0l@ted.

Everything blurred before my eyes.

How could a doctor do this to a patient under his care?

My blood boiled as I asked her questions and took her statement. I assured her the arrest would commence that same day. And if her story was true, we would not only charge him to court. I, Chinelo Uba, would personally ensure his medical license was revoked permanently.

We drove straight to the hospital.

He was not there.

We went to his house.

He was not around.

We tried calling him. His line was not connecting. The nurses we questioned said he usually set aside time for prayer and quiet reflection, and that we should come back later.

Inside my heart, I laughed bitterly.

Prayer my foot. That is how they are. Wicked set of people.

I assured the young lady that the arrest would commence the next day, as I had other matters to attend to.

When I got home, my blood was still boiling. I could hardly wait for morning.

My mother noticed.

She asked gently, “Chinelo, what happened? Which man do you want to arrest again?”

Then she continued, “Sometimes it hurts my heart. Not because you are a policewoman, but because you do this work with vengeance. You hate your father, but what your father did to us is what you are doing to men out there. Some cases can be settled amicably, but you arrest them and make them sleep in dirty cells before bail. Chinelo, take it easy.”

I did not reply her.

She would not understand.

This was not just about pain. It was about saving women like us. Women who had been crushed and silenced. And I told myself I would not stop until every careless man was punished.

I checked the time throughout the night until morning came.

I prayed. I bathed. I dressed.

I stood in front of the mirror and took one last look at myself.

Today is today.

I drove to the station, signed in for the day, then headed straight to the hospital. The young lady was already there, waiting.

I felt proud. Women were finally learning to speak up, not endure like my mother.

We waited.

Then a Prado drove in.

She grabbed my arm immediately and whispered, “That’s the doctor ma’am. He’s here.”

I Married an Omani Man — But His Family Didn’t Accept Me: A Housemaid’s Love Story in Oman

Her; Hi madam,

I don’t know if you still remember me. I was your client many years ago, around 2016. We were connected on your old account before. When I couldn’t find you anymore, I felt a little sad because you were one of the few people who listened to me during the hardest time of my life. Then recently, I found this account and gathered the courage to message you again.

Before, I even asked you for financial help because I truly had nothing. My employer didn’t treat me well and sometimes I didn’t even have proper food to eat. Life was very heavy for me back then.

Today, I want to share my story with you — not only the pain, but also how God slowly turned my tears into happiness.

This is my love story in Oman.

I am a college graduate with a degree in business. When I was studying, I had so many dreams. I imagined myself wearing office clothes, working in a company, helping my family, and building a good future. I studied hard because I believed education would change my life.

But reality is different.

Even though I finished college, finding a job was still very difficult. Every interview ended with rejection. Every day I felt like my diploma was just paper. I saw my parents getting older, still struggling with money, and I felt so helpless.

So I made a painful decision.

I decided to work abroad as a housemaid.

It wasn’t my dream job. It wasn’t what I studied for. But it was the fastest way to earn money. I told myself, “It’s okay. This is just temporary. I will sacrifice for two years, save money, then start a small business when I go home.”

I carried my dreams inside my luggage and left my country with hope in my heart.

But when I arrived in Oman, life became harder than I ever imagined.

My first employer treated me very badly.

I worked from early morning until late at night with almost no rest. Sometimes I was so tired my hands were shaking. My body hurt every day, but I had no choice but to continue.

The hardest part wasn’t the work.

It was the hunger.

There were days when I only ate bread and water. Sometimes just tea. I wasn’t allowed to cook for myself. I wasn’t allowed to take food without permission. Even when I was starving, I had to stay quiet.

I remember lying in bed at night with my stomach hurting from hunger, silently crying so nobody could hear me.

I felt like I wasn’t human.

I felt invisible.

I kept asking myself, “Is this really my life now? Is this what my future looks like?”

Many times, I wanted to give up. Many times, I wanted to go home. But I didn’t even have money for a ticket. I felt trapped.

So I prayed.

Every night, I prayed and cried to Allah.

“Please save me. Please change my life. Please send someone to help me.”

I didn’t know that my prayer was already on the way.

One day, while my employer was out, I secretly posted my number in a group chat, hoping someone might offer me another job. I was scared but also desperate. I just wanted to escape that house.

Then a message came.

It was from a man.

He said he was looking for staff.

My heart beat fast. I thought, “Maybe this is my chance. Maybe this is my freedom.”

We started talking. He sounded kind and respectful. For the first time in a long time, someone spoke to me gently.

But then, instead of offering me work, he said something unexpected.

He said he liked me.

He said he wanted to marry me.

I was shocked.

I didn’t know whether to laugh or cry.

Marriage? How could someone want to marry a poor housemaid like me?

At that time, my confidence was so low. I felt small and worthless because of how my employer treated me.

But he kept talking to me with sincerity. He didn’t care that I was a maid. He didn’t care about my past. He just cared about me.

Still, I was scared.

But I was also desperate to leave my situation.

So I told myself, “Maybe this is God’s answer. Maybe this man is the door out of my suffering. If he is good, then thank you, Allah. If not… then I will face it.”

I took the biggest risk of my life.

He transferred my visa under his name.

And then something happened that I will never forget.

Instead of hiding me or bringing me somewhere secret, he brought me straight to his family home.

I was shaking.

My hands were cold.

I felt so small standing at their door.

His family was shocked and angry. I could see it in their eyes. I heard their whispers.

“A housemaid?”
“Why her?”
“What will people say?”

Their words pierced my heart.

I wanted to disappear.

But my husband — that brave man — stood in front of me and said, “She will stay here. I will marry her. Whether you accept or not.”

Nobody had ever defended me like that before.

Nobody had ever chosen me like that.

I cried silently that night, not because I was hurt — but because for the first time, someone fought for me.

Still, life wasn’t easy in the beginning.

When he went to work, I stayed alone in the room. I felt like an outsider. His mother didn’t like me. Sometimes when I entered the kitchen, she would walk away. It broke my heart.

I felt unwanted again.

But this time, I didn’t run away.

I told myself, “I will win their hearts with kindness.”

So every day, I helped. I cleaned. I cooked. I respected them. Even if they ignored me, I stayed gentle.

Slowly… very slowly… things changed.

His mother started talking to me.

One day she asked me to help her cook.

Another day she asked about my family.

Then one day, she smiled at me.

That small smile meant everything.

From there, our relationship grew.

Now she treats me like her own daughter.

Sometimes when we talk about moving to another house, she says, “No. If you leave, I will go with you.”

When she says that, my heart feels so full I want to cry.

From being rejected… to being loved.

From being hungry… to cooking meals for my family.

From crying alone… to laughing with my children.

Now we have three beautiful kids, Alhamdulillah.

Every time I look at them, I remember the girl who ate only bread and cried herself to sleep.

If I could hug that girl, I would tell her, “Be strong. Your happiness is coming.”

Life truly changed in ways I never expected.

Sometimes the path is painful, but it leads to something beautiful.

If I didn’t suffer, I wouldn’t meet my husband.
If I didn’t cry, I wouldn’t appreciate my smiles now.
If I didn’t struggle, I wouldn’t be this strong.

Today, I am not ashamed of my past.

Because that housemaid…
that hungry girl…
that broken woman…

She became a strong wife, a loving mother, and a woman full of faith.

And my message to anyone who reads my story is this:

Never lose hope, even when life is unfair.
Never think you are worthless.
And never stop praying.

Because God hears every tear.

One day, your pain will turn into peace, and your story will become your greatest testimony.

Trust the process. Trust God. Your miracle might be closer than you think.

YOUR STOMACH IS NOT WEAK  IT’S BEEN UNDER ATTACK

That burning. The bloating. The nausea. The reflux that keeps you awake at night.

It didn’t start today.
Ulcers don’t just “happen.”
They are built silently by everyday habits we’ve normalized.

And no  it’s not just H. pylori.
Here’s what’s slowly destroying your stomach lining 👇🏾

 THE FOODS WE KEEP CALLING “NORMAL”
Refined carbs, sugar, junk oils, MSG, fizzy drinks.
Think of your stomach lining as a protective paint.

These foods peel it off layer by layer: 

• They feed bad bacteria
• Trigger inflammation
• Weaken the mucus barrier

Once that protection thins, stomach acid starts burning raw tissue.
That’s where pain, bloating and reflux begin.

 STRESS, TRAUMA & EATING LATE AT NIGHT
Stress is not just emotional  it is digestive poison.

Under stress: • Stomach acid drops
• Digestion slows
• Food ferments instead of breaking down

Late-night meals force your gut to work when it should be repairing.
Acid backs up. Nerves get irritated. Inflammation deepens.
This is how stress becomes gastritis.

 THE H. PYLORI TRUTH NOBODY TELLS YOU
This bacteria does NOT love strong acid.
It thrives when stomach acid is low.

Low acid allows H. pylori to: • Hide inside the stomach lining
• Damage protective mucus
• Cause ulcers that refuse to heal
That’s why some people treat ulcers repeatedly — and never fully recover.

 PAINKILLERS THAT QUIETLY ERODE THE STOMACH
Ibuprofen. Diclofenac. Aspirin.
They don’t just reduce pain.
They switch off your stomach’s defense system.
They block the chemicals that build protective mucus.
No shield = acid attacking your stomach wall directly.
Slow damage. Big consequences.

 BUT HERE’S THE PART YOU CAN CONTROL
Your stomach can heal.
But only when you stop attacking it and start rebuilding it.
Here’s what actually helps 👇🏾

 EAT FOR HEALING  NOT JUST FULLNESS
Choose foods that act like a natural bandage: • Soft meals, light soups
• Well-cooked vegetables (okra, ugu, pumpkin leaves)
• Boiled yam, ripe plantain, rice (small portions)
• Bone broth, pepper kept minimal
Avoid while healing: • Fried foods
• Alcohol & fizzy drinks
• Excess pepper and sugar

RESPECT REST, NOT CONSTANT EATING
Healing needs quiet time.
• Eat 2–3 proper meals
• Stop eating at least 3 hours before sleep
• Let night be for repair, not digestion

 SUPPORT STOMACH ACID THE RIGHT WAY
Acid is not the enemy.
Low acid invites bacteria and poor digestion.
Support gently with:

 • Bitter leaves (ugwu, scent leaf, bitter leaf)
• Adequate protein (eggs, fish, chicken)
• Lemon or apple cider vinegar — only if tolerated

 CALM THE BRAIN TO CALM THE GUT
Your stomach has nerves.
Slow down before meals. Breathe. Chew properly. Walk lightly in the evening.
A calm brain = a calmer stomach.

USE PAINKILLERS WITH RESPECT
Frequent pain is a message, not a deficiency.
Food, rest and timing should be first. Medication should be occasional, not daily.

Burning is not normal. Bloating is not normal. Constant discomfort is not “age” or “stress.”
Your stomach is asking for help  not silence.

ليلةُ النصفِ من شعبان
قال رسولُ الله ﷺ:
«إذا كانت ليلةُ النصفِ من شعبان فقوموا ليلَها وصوموا نهارَها…»
ودلّ رسولُ الرحمة ﷺ على عظيمِ منزلةِ هذه الليلة الشريفة بقوله:
«إنّ الله يطّلع على عباده في ليلةِ النصف من شعبان، فيغفر للمؤمنين، ويُمهل الكافرين، ويدعُ أهلَ الحقدِ بحقدهم حتى يدعوه…»
وقوله ﷺ:
«أتاني جبريلُ عليه السلام فقال: هذه ليلةُ النصف من شعبان، وللهِ فيها عتقاءُ من النار بعددِ شعورِ غنمِ بني كلب، لا ينظرُ الله فيها إلى مشرك، ولا إلى مشاحن، ولا إلى قاطعِ رحم، ولا إلى عاقٍّ لوالديه، ولا إلى مدمنِ خمر…»
وبهذه الليلةِ الشريفة، وبهذا القدرِ العظيم، أمر الإمامُ محمدُ الباقر عليه السلام بإحيائها فقال:
«فاجتهدوا في القُربة إلى الله فيها، فإنّها ليلةٌ آلى اللهُ تعالى على نفسِه أن لا يردّ سائلًا له فيها ما لم يسأل معصية، وهي الليلةُ التي جعلها الله لنا أهلَ البيت بإزاء ما جعل ليلةَ القدر لنبيّنا ﷺ، فاجتهدوا في الدعاء والثناء على الله عزّ وجلّ…»
شعبانُ شهرُ القداسة،
إعلانُ الأسرار، واستعلانُ النورين…
نورٌ يشرق في نصفه،
ونورٌ يُبشّر بقدومِ شهرِ الطهرِ والصيام…
ليلةٌ نوريّةٌ بقداستها،
فيها يُرتجى الدعاءُ عند الموقنين،
وتسيحُ الأرواح في سبحاتِ جلالها وجمالها…
عيدٌ تحتفي بقدره القلوبُ المؤمنة،
وتتلاقى على نوره الأرواح،
عيدُ القداسةِ الأرحب،
والنورِ الأشعب،
والسرِّ الأعجب…

وأن تفرغ على قلوبِ المفجوعين الصبرَ والسلوان،
وأن تُجيرنا من عذابِ النيران،
وأن تهدي نفوسَنا التقى والإيمان،
وترشدنا إلى سُبلِ الخيرِ والإحسان،
وتشملَنا برحمتك يا أرحمَ الراحمين،
يا رحمنُ يا رحيم…

Daka late goal sparks Nkana, Mines shock Eagles 

STRIKER Dave Daka netted a 94th minute winner to sink his former club Kansanshi Dynamos as Nkana FC won 1-0 to record their third consecutive victory.

This was in a MTN Super League week 17 encounter played this afternoon at Nkana Stadium, Kitwe.

The win pushes Nkana to 13th on the table with 19 points from 17 games while Kansanshi drop two places to 15th with 17 points from as many matches.

In Choma, Mines registered their second ever win in Super League history, stunning Green Eagles 1-0 at Independence Stadium. Patrick Simwinga grabbed the crucial goal in the 12th minute.

Despite winning, Mines remain bottom of the table with 12 points from 17 matches. Eagles are ninth after amassing 22 points.

At the Godfrey Ucar Chitalu Stadium, Kabwe Warriors got back to winning ways following a 1-0 win over FC MUZA. Former FC Leopards striker David Obashi was on target.

Warriors climb up two places to fifth on the log standings after garnering 26 points from 17 matches. For MUZA, they drop one place to seventh with 24 points.

Elsewhere, FC Leopards welcomed new coach Albert Kachinga in 'gloomy style' after losing 2-0 away to Nkwazi. The Edwin Imboela crowd frenzied with a brace from Carlos Kaoma who scored on either side of the half.

Nkwazi crawl out of the relegation zone to 14th on the table with 17 points from 17 matches while Leopards remain  rooted in 16th place with 12 points.

In Chingola, Stephen Mutama's 35th minute strike was enough to 'pierce' Nchanga Rangers as Konkola Blades emerged 1-0 victors.

 Blades occupy 10th position with 22 points. Nchanga maintain third place despite losing with 29 points from 17 games, just a point ahead of fourth-placed ZANACO who have a game in hand.

🖤 Between Sand and Skin: Arabization, African Identity, and the Hidden Color Lines of Africa
Introduction: An African Conflict Few Want to Name
Across North and Northeast Africa, identity has never been a simple question of geography. In countries like Sudan and Mauritania, a deep, unresolved struggle simmers beneath politics, religion, and culture—the conflict between Arabization and African identity.
This is not merely about language or dress. It is about power, race, history, and who gets to define what it means to belong. For centuries, Black African communities in these regions have been enslaved, marginalized, and erased, often by elites who identify as Arab or Arab-descended. Long before European colonialism, hierarchies already existed—colonialism simply hardened them.
This is the uncomfortable truth: racism in Africa did not begin with Europe, though Europe weaponized and globalized it.
1. Arabization: Culture, Power, and Erasure
Arabization refers to the spread of Arabic language, culture, and identity across North Africa and parts of the Sahel, largely through:
Early Islamic expansion
Trade routes across the Sahara
Intermarriage and elite dominance
Political and religious authority
In theory, Arabization was cultural and religious. In practice, it often became racialized.
Over time, “Arab” came to mean:
Lighter skin
Political dominance
Religious legitimacy
Social superiority
Meanwhile, Black African identity—even among Muslims—was framed as inferior, servile, or backward.
2. Sudan: Arab Identity vs Black African Reality
Sudan sits at a fault line between Arab North Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa. Its crisis is not new—it is centuries old.
a. The Myth of Arab Purity
Many northern Sudanese elites claim Arab ancestry, despite being ethnically mixed. Arab identity in Sudan became a status marker, not a genetic truth.
To be “Arab” meant:
Access to power
Land ownership
Military protection
Political voice
To be “Black” meant exclusion—even if you spoke Arabic and practiced Islam.
b. Enslavement of Black Sudanese
For centuries, Black African groups such as the Dinka, Nuba, Fur, and Nuer were:
Raided
Enslaved
Used as domestic servants and soldiers
Enslavement did not always disappear with modern laws—it mutated.
c. Darfur: Genocide with an Identity Core
The Darfur conflict was often framed as ethnic or tribal, but at its heart was a racial hierarchy:
Arab-identifying militias (Janjaweed)
Against Black African farming communities
Victims were not targeted for religion—they were Muslim—but for race and perceived inferiority.
Darfur exposed a brutal reality:
You can share faith, language, and nationality—and still be considered disposable.
3. Mauritania: Slavery That Refused to Die
Mauritania is one of the most disturbing examples of institutionalized racial hierarchy in Africa.
a. The Haratin: Black, Enslaved, and Invisible
The Haratin are Black Mauritanians, many descended from enslaved Africans. For generations, they were:
Owned by lighter-skinned Arab-Berber elites (Bidan)
Forced into domestic labor, herding, and farming
Denied education and property
Slavery was officially abolished multiple times:
1905
1981
Criminalized in 2007
Yet unofficial slavery persisted into the 21st century.
b. Slavery by Another Name
Even today, many Haratin remain trapped through:
Debt bondage
Inherited servitude
Social pressure and religious manipulation
Some are taught that serving Arab masters is God’s will.
Mauritania stands as proof that abolishing slavery on paper means nothing when society still believes in it.
4. Black Africans Enslaved by Other Africans: The Hard Truth
This history is deeply uncomfortable—but necessary.
Arab elites in Africa were not European colonizers.
They were Africans enslaving other Africans.
This does not absolve Europe. But it destroys the myth that:
“Africans only suffered slavery from outsiders.”
Pre-colonial Africa had:
Slave societies
Caste systems
Racialized labor
Colonialism did not invent racism in Africa—it institutionalized and globalized existing hierarchies.
5. Colonialism: The Accelerator, Not the Origin
European powers exploited these divisions masterfully:
Elevating Arab elites over Black Africans
Reinforcing racial hierarchies for easier control
Rewarding “Arab” identity with administrative power
Colonial borders froze these inequalities into modern states, ensuring that:
Old prejudices became national crises
Identity conflicts turned violent
What was once social became political and militarized.
6. Racism Within Africa: A Taboo Conversation
Many Africans resist this discussion, fearing it “divides us.”
But silence has cost millions of lives.
Racism within Africa manifests as:
Colorism
Ethnic supremacy
Language-based discrimination
Denial of Blackness in North Africa
Until Africa confronts internal hierarchies, Pan-African unity remains fragile.
7. Identity at War: What Is at Stake
The Arabization vs African identity conflict is not about rejecting Islam or Arabic language. It is about rejecting:
The idea that Blackness equals inferiority
The belief that African identity must be diluted to be respected
Historical lies used to justify oppression
True African liberation demands historical honesty.
Conclusion: Naming the Wound to Heal It
Sudan and Mauritania are not anomalies—they are mirrors. They reflect a continent struggling with its layered past.
Africa cannot heal by blaming only Europe.
Nor by denying its internal scars.
The path forward requires courage:
To admit Africans enslaved Africans
To dismantle racial hierarchies disguised as culture
To reclaim Black African identity without apology
Only then can Africa move from inherited division to chosen unity.
