My father left my mother because she gave birth to seven girls.

She was in search of a boy, and that was why we got to seven.

After years of trying, the boy never came. Instead, my father chased us out of the house like unwanted luggage.

My father was a feared policeman. His rank alone could silence a room. He was huge, intimidating, and dreadful. I do not even want to begin to explain the kind of pain we endured under his roof. Living with that man was like living with fear itself.

Sometimes, I watch women talk about their fathers with softness in their voices. Some are closer to their fathers than their mothers. Each time I hear such stories, my mind tells me it must be an AI generated movie, because neither I nor my sisters ever experienced the beauty of having a father.

I was the fourth child. The one my father personally came to the hospital to see. When the nurse told him I was a girl, he walked out. He went on an assignment for one year and refused to pay the hospital bills.

From that moment, his resentment deepened.

Every scan and X ray he took my mother for confirmed I was a boy. Or so they told him. So when I arrived as a girl, something in him snapped. To him, I was proof that hope could betray.

All these things planted something ugly inside me. I did not just resent my father. I resented men as a whole. I wanted nothing to do with that gender.

Then life played its joke on me.

I became a policewoman.

One of the reasons I chose that path was to fight for my family and for women like my mother, women who had suffered under the hands of men and swallowed their pain in silence. I wanted to rescue women trapped under the grip of what I believed was an evil gender.

I was passionate, aggressive, and hungry for justice.

When our superintendent asked which officer would volunteer their phone number for people to call during home emergencies, I did not hesitate. I volunteered immediately.

Not because I enjoyed calls, but because I wanted men behind bars.

Any small disturbance, I was already at your doorstep. One or two questions, and I had already arrested the man. My operations were swift. I delivered with confidence and authority.

It did not take long before my rank was elevated. With it came more cases, more power, more opportunities to fight.

Then one day, a young lady ran into my office.

She was wailing, sobbing, groaning. I kept begging her to calm down and tell me what happened. Inside me, my ears were itching. I was already preparing to lock up another man.

When she finally spoke, my world shook.

A doctor at the hospital where she went for treatment had r@ped her. She said he injected her with something that made her drowsy. The last thing she remembered was him rubbing her head and telling her to sleep. When she woke up the next morning, she knew she had been vi0l@ted.

Everything blurred before my eyes.

How could a doctor do this to a patient under his care?

My blood boiled as I asked her questions and took her statement. I assured her the arrest would commence that same day. And if her story was true, we would not only charge him to court. I, Chinelo Uba, would personally ensure his medical license was revoked permanently.

We drove straight to the hospital.

He was not there.

We went to his house.

He was not around.

We tried calling him. His line was not connecting. The nurses we questioned said he usually set aside time for prayer and quiet reflection, and that we should come back later.

Inside my heart, I laughed bitterly.

Prayer my foot. That is how they are. Wicked set of people.

I assured the young lady that the arrest would commence the next day, as I had other matters to attend to.

When I got home, my blood was still boiling. I could hardly wait for morning.

My mother noticed.

She asked gently, “Chinelo, what happened? Which man do you want to arrest again?”

Then she continued, “Sometimes it hurts my heart. Not because you are a policewoman, but because you do this work with vengeance. You hate your father, but what your father did to us is what you are doing to men out there. Some cases can be settled amicably, but you arrest them and make them sleep in dirty cells before bail. Chinelo, take it easy.”

I did not reply her.

She would not understand.

This was not just about pain. It was about saving women like us. Women who had been crushed and silenced. And I told myself I would not stop until every careless man was punished.

I checked the time throughout the night until morning came.

I prayed. I bathed. I dressed.

I stood in front of the mirror and took one last look at myself.

Today is today.

I drove to the station, signed in for the day, then headed straight to the hospital. The young lady was already there, waiting.

I felt proud. Women were finally learning to speak up, not endure like my mother.

We waited.

Then a Prado drove in.

She grabbed my arm immediately and whispered, “That’s the doctor ma’am. He’s here.

At fifteen, my mother left me at the airport like unwanted luggage, choosing champagne and first-class comfort over her own child.
“Handle it,” she said coldly.
So I made one call—to the father she’d kept distant for years.
He came for me in a private plane.
When my mother returned from her perfect trip, she found my bedroom stripped bare…
and a legal document sitting quietly on the dresser.
Her vacation was over.
The consequences had arrived.

I was fifteen the first time I understood that my mother didn’t see me as her child.

She saw me as inconvenience.

The airport was crowded that morning, full of rolling suitcases, families hugging goodbye, business travelers rushing toward their gates. I stood beside my mother near the check-in counter, holding my backpack, half-awake and confused.

“Why are we here so early?” I asked.

She didn’t even look at me.

“Because my flight boards in an hour,” she said, scrolling through her phone.

I frowned. “Your flight?”

She sighed, finally glancing up with irritation.

“Yes. Paris. Remember? I told you.”

My stomach tightened. “But… what about me?”

That’s when she turned fully toward me, her lipstick perfect, her sunglasses expensive, her voice colder than the air-conditioning.

“You’re old enough to figure it out,” she said.

I stared at her. “Figure what out?”

She leaned closer, lowering her voice like she was embarrassed to be seen speaking to me.

“I’m not dragging a teenager around Europe,” she said sharply. “Handle it.”

My throat went dry.

“You’re leaving me here?”

She shrugged, as if she were leaving behind a forgotten coat.

“I paid for your ticket back home. Go to the gate later. Or call someone. Just don’t make this dramatic.”

Then she picked up her designer bag, adjusted her scarf, and walked toward security without another glance.

I stood there, frozen.

People moved around me like I was invisible.

I wanted to cry. I wanted to scream.

But mostly, I felt something worse.

Abandoned.

I sat on a cold metal bench for nearly an hour, staring at the departures board, listening to announcements echo through the terminal.

Then I did the only thing I could think of.

I made one call.

To the father she’d kept distant for years.

The man she never spoke about except with bitterness.

My hands shook as I dialed the number I’d secretly saved.

He answered on the second ring.

“Hello?”

My voice cracked.

“Dad… it’s me. She left me at the airport.”

Silence.

Then his voice changed completely.

“Stay where you are,” he said. “I’m coming.”

I didn’t believe him until three hours later, when a private plane landed.

And my father walked into the terminal like a storm.

When my mother returned from her perfect trip days later, expecting everything unchanged…

She found my bedroom stripped bare.

And a legal document sitting quietly on the dresser.

Her vacation was over.

Rapport d'investigation : La Sécession du Soudan du Sud - De la Guerre d'indépendance à la Guerre Civile

Introduction : Un État Né dans la Douleur

Le Soudan du Sud, devenu le 193e État membre des Nations Unies le 9 juillet 2011, incarne à la fois la réalisation la plus aboutie d'un mouvement sécessionniste en Afrique post-coloniale et l'un de ses échecs les plus tragiques. Cette enquête retrace la genèse de ce mouvement, analyse les fractures ethniques et religieuses qui l'ont structuré, dresse le bilan humain catastrophique des conflits et examine son inscription dans un schéma régional récurrent : celui de régions principalement chrétiennes et anglophones cherchant à se séparer d'un pouvoir central perçu comme arabo-musulman .

1. Genèse Historique : Un Siècle de Marginalisation

La revendication sud-soudanaise plonge ses racines dans la période coloniale. Le condominium anglo-égyptien (1899-1956) a administré le Nord et le Sud selon des logiques distinctes, creusant un fossé économique, culturel et religieux. À l'indépendance du Soudan en 1956, le pouvoir à Khartoum, détenu par une élite se revendiquant arabe et musulmane, a rapidement imposé l'arabe comme langue officielle et envisagé l'application de la charia, niant l'identité distincte du Sud .

Cette marginalisation a déclenché la Première Guerre civile soudanaise (1955-1972), suivie d'une brève autonomie. La révocation de cette autonomie et l'intensification des politiques d'islamisation ont provoqué la Seconde Guerre civile (1983-2005), l'un des conflits les plus meurtriers de la fin du XXe siècle, opposant principalement l'Armée de libération du peuple soudanais (SPLA) au gouvernement de Khartoum .

L'accord de paix global de 2005 a instauré une période d'autonomie et prévu un référendum d'autodétermination. En janvier 2011, près de 99% des votants ont choisi l'indépendance, officialisant une partition longtemps considérée comme impossible .

Principales Revendications du Mouvement Sécessionniste :

· Identitaire et Culturelle : Préservation des cultures nilotiques et des langues locales face à l'arabisation forcée.
· Religieuse : Liberté de culte et refus de la charia, dans un Sud majoritairement chrétien et animiste.
· Politique : Autodétermination et gouvernance propre, mettant fin à la domination perpétuelle de l'élite du Nord.
· Économique : Contrôle équitable des ressources, notamment les importants gisements de pétrole situés dans le Sud.

2. Fractures Internes : Ethnicité et Religion, des Forces Centrifuges

Contrairement à une vision simpliste d'un Sud uni face au Nord, la société sud-soudanaise est traversée de profondes fractures qui ont condamné l'État post-indépendance.

Une Mosaïque Ethnique Complexe
Le Soudan du Sud compteplus de 60 groupes ethniques distincts, classés principalement comme nilotiques .

· Dinka : Environ 35.8% de la population. Groupe le plus nombreux, ayant fourni la majorité des leaders historiques de la SPLA, dont le président Salva Kiir.
· Nuer : Environ 15.6% de la population. Deuxième groupe en importance, ayant également fourni une élite militaire et politique rivale, comme Riek Machar.
· Autres groupes : Shilluk, Bari, Azande, Murle, entre autres, composent le reste de cette diversité extrême .

Le Clivage Religieux Fondateur
La différence religieuse a été un moteur essentiel de la sécession.

· Soudan (Nord) : Identité nationale construite autour de l'arabité et de l'islamité. L'appartenance à l'islam conditionnait l'accès plein à la citoyenneté et aux ressources .
· Soudan du Sud : Christianisme majoritaire (introduit pendant l'ère coloniale) mélangé à des croyances animistes traditionnelles. Cette différence a servi de marqueur identitaire central contre le projet étatique de Khartoum .

3. Bilan Humain : Le Prix Exorbitant d'une Indépendance Fragile

Le coût de la création du Soudan du Sud est astronomique, couvrant des décennies de conflit.

Avant l'Indépendance (Guerres Civiles Soudanaises) :

· La seconde guerre civile (1983-2005) a causé la mort d'environ 2 millions de personnes, principalement des civils victimes de la famine et des maladies .

Après l'Indépendance (Guerre Civile Sud-Soudanaise, 2013-2020) :
Ironiquement,l'indépendance a rapidement débouché sur une guerre interne atroce, opposant les partisans du président Kiir (principalement Dinka) à ceux de l'ancien vice-président Machar (principalement Nuer).

· Morts violentes : Environ 190,000 .
· Morts indirectes (famine, maladies) : Environ 193,000 .
· Total des morts (estimations avril 2018) : 383,000 personnes .
· Déplacés : Plus de 4 millions de personnes, dont 2.1 millions de déplacés internes et plus de 2.3 millions de réfugiés dans les pays voisins .

Cette guerre a été marquée par des massacres ethniques ciblés, comme le massacre de Nuer à Juba en 2013 ou celui de Bentiu en 2014, montrant comment les anciennes solidarités de la libération se sont effondrées au profit de lignes de fracture ethniques locales .

4. Analyse Comparative : Le Schéma Récurrent des Sécessions Chrétiennes et Anglophones en Afrique

Le cas sud-soudanais n'est pas isolé. Il s'inscrit dans un schéma géopolitique observable en Afrique centrale et orientale, où des régions périphériques, souvent christianisées et administrées par les Britanniques, contestent l'autorité d'un État central perçu comme héritier d'une domination arabo-musulmane ou francophone.

Pour illustrer ces points communs et différences, voici une comparaison des trois principaux mouvements :

Soudan du Sud

· Puissance coloniale : Britannique (condominium anglo-égyptien)
· Clivage central : Nord (Arabo-musulman) vs. Sud (Nilotique-chrétien/animiste)
· Résultat : Indépendance acquise en 2011 (reconnue)
· Conflit post-sécession : Guerre civile majeure (2013-2020), fractures ethniques (Dinka/Nuer)

Biafra (Nigeria)

· Puissance coloniale : Britannique
· Clivage central : Nord (majoritairement haoussa-fulani musulman) vs. Sud-Est (majoritairement igbo chrétien)
· Résultat : Sécession échouée (1967-1970)
· Conflit post-sécession : Réintégration, méfiance persistante, ressentiment

Ambazonie (Cameroun)

· Puissance coloniale : Britannique (Sud) vs. Française (Nord)
· Clivage central : Régions francophones vs. Régions anglophones (Nord-Ouest/Sud-Ouest)
· Résultat : Conflit sécessionniste en cours (depuis 2017), non reconnu
· Conflit post-sécession : Conflit asymétrique en cours, répression et crise humanitaire

Points Communs Structurants :

1. Héritage Colonial : Dans chaque cas, la frontière du conflit recoupe d'anciennes frontières administratives coloniales, où les Britanniques ont laissé une empreinte durable (système juridique de common law, langue anglaise, éducation) .
2. Clivage Linguistique et Culturel : L'anglais sert de marqueur identitaire et de langue de résistance contre la langue du pouvoir central (arabe au Soudan, français au Cameroun).
3. Clivage Religieux : La religion chrétienne (ou son syncrétisme avec les croyances traditionnelles) est un pilier de l'identité sécessionniste, opposée à un État souvent perçu comme promouvant l'islam (Soudan, Nord Nigeria) ou dominé par une majorité culturellement différente (Cameroun francophone).
4. Revendication de Ressources : La contestation porte aussi sur le contrôle des richesses (pétrole au Soudan du Sud et au Biafra, terres agricoles et potentiel pétrolier en Ambazonie).

5. Conclusion : L'Échec de la Construction Nationale Post-Sécession

L'histoire du Soudan du Sud démontre avec une cruelle clarté que l'indépendance ne suffit pas à construire une nation. Si la lutte contre un ennemi commun (Khartoum) a pu unifier temporairement les Sud-Soudanais, les élites du mouvement de libération n'ont pas su ou pas voulu transcender les loyautés ethniques pour forger une identité nationale inclusive .

La guerre civile de 2013-2020 a révélé que les fractures ethniques (Dinka/Nuer) étaient plus puissantes que le projet national. Le pays, classé dernier en termes d'indice de développement humain, reste un État fragile, où la paix est précaire et où la logique du partage du pouvoir entre élites rivales prime sur la construction d'institutions pour tous .

En définitive, le Soudan du Sud offre une leçon géopolitique majeure : les mouvements sécessionnistes fondés sur le rejet d'une domination peuvent réussir à obtenir l'indépendance, mais ils échouent souvent à résoudre en leur sein les mêmes dynamiques d'exclusion et de compétition pour le pouvoir et les ressources qui ont justifié leur combat initial. Ce schéma, visible aussi dans les douloureuses histoires du Biafra et de l'Ambazonie, interroge la viabilité à long terme des États nés de la partition dans l'Afrique contemporaine.

My Mother-In-Law Dumped My Daughter And Me On An Empty Island & Burned My Passport So I’d Be Trapped During What Was Supposed To Be A Family Trip. My Husband Stood With Her, Not Me. But When They Arrived Home, They Were Shocked To See The Stranger Waiting For Them…

My name is Emily Carter, I am a 32-year-old nurse from Dallas, Texas, and I truly believed the trip to Harbor Key would finally melt the ice between me and my mother-in-law. My husband, Jason, called it “a family reset.” His mother, Linda, called it “her treat,” which should have been my first red flag.

From the moment we got off the plane, Linda treated me like unwanted luggage. She rolled her eyes when I asked about Lily’s sunscreen, mocked my “cheap” sandals, and complained loudly to Jason that I was “too dramatic” for wanting our four-year-old to nap. Jason brushed it off with a tight smile. “She’s just old-school,” he whispered that night while I lay awake, listening to the waves and my racing heartbeat.

On the second day, Linda announced a surprise. “I rented a small boat,” she said, waving the keys. “We’re going to go explore a private island. Just us. No crowds, no noise, no annoying tourists.” She glanced at me when she said “annoying,” her lips curling.

The island really was beautiful—white sand, turquoise water, a ring of palm trees whispering in the breeze. The captain dropped anchor offshore and let us take the small dinghy to the beach. Lily squealed, chasing gulls along the waterline, while I spread out towels and the cooler. I noticed Linda had brought my passport and wallet in her bag instead of leaving them in the hotel safe, but she brushed off my question with a clipped, “You worry too much.”

After an hour, I realized the dinghy was gone.

“Jason?” I called, squinting toward the boat. It was now several hundred yards away, engine idling. Jason stood beside his mother, both of them just watching us. A cold knot formed in my stomach.

“Very funny,” I shouted, waving my arms. “Bring the dinghy back. Lily’s getting tired.”

Linda cupped her hands around her mouth. “This is what you wanted, isn’t it? Peace and quiet? You and your precious daughter can have all the alone time you want.”

She pulled something small and navy from her bag. It took me a second to recognize the gold crest of my passport. Then I saw the orange flicker of the lighter in her other hand.

“Linda, don’t you dare!” I screamed.

Jason didn’t move. He didn’t even look at me. He only stared at the deck as Linda touched the flame to the corner of my passport. The Systemic Weaknesses of the SPLM-IG: Power, Plausible Deniability, and the Erosion of the South Sudanese State 

BY JUOL NHOMNGEK DANIEL

Introduction

More than a decade after South Sudan’s independence, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Government (SPLM-IG) alleges that it remains the dominant political force in the country. Yet its continued hold on power has increasingly been accompanied by accusations of authoritarianism, systemic corruption, ethnic favoritism, and the hollowing out of state institutions. Rather than consolidating a post-liberation democratic order, the SPLM-IG is widely perceived to have transformed the state into an instrument of regime survival. This article analyzes the systemic weaknesses of the SPLM-IG, focusing on its governance practices, use of plausible deniability, manipulation of identity politics, and the progressive erosion of institutional legitimacy.

From Liberation Movement to Personalized Power

The SPLM was founded as a liberation movement grounded in collective leadership, ideological cohesion, and mass mobilization. Under the SPLM-IG, however, this legacy has been steadily dismantled. Party organs such as the National Liberation Council, the Political Bureau, and the National Convention were dissolved or sidelined between 2013 and 2015, effectively eliminating internal checks on executive authority. Decision-making has since become centralized around the presidency, transforming the party into a personalized political vehicle rather than a functioning institution.

This personalization of power has weakened governance at both party and state levels. Ministries operate without autonomy, the Council of Ministers is frequently paralyzed by mistrust and boycotts, and coalition governance under the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity (R-TGoNU) remains largely symbolic. The result is a “hollowed-out” state in which authority exists without accountability and power without institutional restraint.

Plausible Deniability as a Governing Strategy

One of the most distinctive features of SPLM-IG rule is the systematic use of plausible deniability. Senior officials and military commanders have repeatedly issued inflammatory statements or carried out coercive actions, only for the government to later deny responsibility once domestic or international backlash emerges. This pattern has been evident in cases ranging from alleged “spare no one” orders in Jonglei, to the categorization of entire counties as “hostile,” to the denial of well-documented atrocities during the 2013–2014 violence.

Such denials are rarely accompanied by credible investigations or accountability measures. Instead, responsibility is deflected onto “rogue commanders,” opposition provocation, or vague security threats. This strategy allows the SPLM-IG to benefit from intimidation and coercion while maintaining a façade of legality and restraint. Over time, plausible deniability has evolved from an ad hoc tactic into a structural mode of governance.

Human Rights, Misinformation, and the Control of Narrative

The SPLM-IG has consistently framed its actions as necessary for national security and stability, even when confronted with credible allegations of human rights violations. Reports of ethnic targeting, suppression of opposition rallies, arbitrary detention, and the blocking of humanitarian aid have been dismissed as misinformation or opposition propaganda. Violence involving state-aligned militias is often ignored or reframed as intercommunal conflict beyond government control.

This manipulation of narrative serves two purposes. First, it shields the regime from accountability by obscuring chains of responsibility. Second, it delegitimizes opposition actors, particularly the SPLM-IO, by portraying them as the sole source of instability. The result is a political environment in which truth becomes contested, and governance is reduced to narrative dominance rather than policy performance.

Ethnicization of Power and the Politics of Exclusion

Perhaps the most corrosive systemic weakness of the SPLM-IG is its reliance on ethnic and identity politics as a mechanism of power retention. The party is widely perceived as Dinka-dominated, with key security and political positions concentrated within a narrow ethnic elite. Access to state resources, employment, and protection is often tied to political loyalty and tribal affiliation rather than merit or citizenship.

This ethnicization of governance has transformed political competition into existential communal conflict. Security forces have been accused of targeting communities perceived as opposition-aligned, particularly the Nuer, under the guise of disarmament or counterinsurgency operations. Land disputes and administrative boundary changes have been politicized, further inflaming local tensions. Instead of fostering a shared national identity, the SPLM-IG has presided over the fragmentation of the South Sudanese polity into rival ethnic constituencies.

Militarization and the Weaponization of State Institutions

The SPLM-IG’s dependence on security forces to manage political dissent has undermined civilian governance. The South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF) are frequently deployed not as a neutral national army, but as a partisan instrument against perceived political threats. Allegations of forced defections, recruitment of child soldiers, and the suppression of opposition activities point to a broader militarization of politics.

Peace agreements, particularly the R-ARCSS, have been accused of being selectively implemented or “weaponized” to entrench the status quo. Unilateral appointments, removal of opposition officials, and delays in security sector reform have eroded trust and stalled the transition process. In this context, peace becomes procedural rather than transformative, serving regime continuity rather than national reconciliation.

Corruption, Economic Mismanagement, and State Capture

Systemic corruption represents another foundational weakness of the SPLM-IG system. Oil revenues and public lands have been repeatedly implicated in allegations of misappropriation and elite enrichment. While the government often attributes economic collapse to war and sanctions, critics argue that corruption is not a by-product of conflict but a central feature of governance.

The fusion of party, state, and private interests has resulted in state capture by a narrow political elite. Public service delivery has collapsed, education and healthcare systems remain underfunded, and over two-thirds of the population depends on humanitarian assistance. Economic mismanagement thus reinforces political dependency, making citizens more vulnerable to coercion and patronage.

Conclusion: A Crisis of Legitimacy and Statehood

The SPLM-IG’s systemic weaknesses are not merely technical failures of governance; they reflect a deeper crisis of political vision and legitimacy. By prioritizing regime survival over institutional development, ethnic loyalty over citizenship, and plausible deniability over accountability, the party has undermined the very foundations of the South Sudanese state.

While the SPLM-IG continues to exercise formal power, its authority is increasingly disconnected from popular consent and institutional credibility. Without genuine reforms, restoring internal party democracy, depoliticizing state institutions, addressing ethnic exclusion, and implementing peace agreements in good faith, the current system risks perpetuating a cycle of instability, fragmentation, and violence. In this sense, the greatest weakness of the SPLM-IG is not opposition pressure, but its own transformation from a liberation movement into an instrument of permanent crisis management.

Aria fell fully to her knees.

“Mum, please listen to me,” she begged through tears. “I have backing. The father of my child is happy—”
“I said shut up!” Anita screamed, cutting her off.
She pointed violently at Aria’s stomach.
“That bastard inside you will destroy your life!”

Aria stood her ground, "My child isn't a bastard... My baby has both mother and father." Anita's face twisted, "I SAID SHUT UP YOUR MOUTH!" she screamed, spinning away from Aria.

Her gaze fell on the oranges, and she picked one up, knife in hand. She began peeling it, her movements deliberate and calm. "Aria, I want to tell you a story..." she said, her voice icy. "A story about your father... Your father isn't dead. He's somewhere I don't care to know. I only told you he was dead so you'd stop asking about him." 

What? 

Anita continued.
“Your father…” she began, then stopped.
“There are things I have never told you about myself.”
She turned away briefly, wiping her eyes angrily, then faced Aria again.
“Aria, I became an orphan when I was just one year old,” she said coldly.
“No parents. No relatives. No village that wanted me.”
Her voice sharpened.
“I was dumped in an orphanage like unwanted luggage.”
Aria froze.

“Nobody wanted me,” Anita continued. “Not a single soul. I grew up learning how to survive, not how to live.”
Her eyes burned red.

“At seven years old, I started begging for food,” she said.
“They didn’t feed us enough. Hunger was normal. Pain was normal.”
She scoffed.
“I suffered.”
She took a deep breath.
“Then I realized something—education was my only escape.”
She straightened.
“I studied in that orphanage. I fought. I prayed. I earned a scholarship that carried me through high school.”
Her voice lowered.

“At nineteen,” she said, “I gained admission into the university.”
She laughed bitterly.
“I was just in year one when I met someone I thought was family.”
She looked Aria straight in the eyes.
“That man… was your father.”
Silence filled the room.
“He promised me everything,” Anita continued.
“Love. Marriage. A home.”
Her lips trembled.
“He spent money on me. He fed me. He made me feel wanted for the first time in my life.”
Her voice cracked slightly.
“He made me believe I finally belonged somewhere.”

Her expression darkened suddenly.
“And then I got pregnant.”
Aria’s breath hitched.
“I was nineteen,” Anita said. “Scared. Confused. Alone.”
She clenched her fists.
“I decided to surprise him. I went to his place unannounced—to tell him about the pregnancy.”
Her eyes hardened.
“What I heard that day…” she shook her head, “…is a story for another lifetime.”
Her voice turned sharp.
“I found out everything was a game. A bet. A lie.”
She laughed bitterly.
“He never loved me.”
Her voice broke now.

“I went back to my hostel. Packed my things. I couldn’t stay another day.”
She swallowed.
“As I was leaving campus, a couple hit me with their car.”

Aria gasped.

“They rushed me to the hospital,” Anita said.
“You survived. I survived.”
She wiped her tears angrily.
“They offered to help me—on one condition.”
Her jaw tightened.
“That I give you to them after delivery so they could send me back to school.”
She shook her head fiercely.

“I refused.”
Her voice shook with emotion.
“I told them you were my only family. And I would never give you away.”
She exhaled deeply.
“I worked,” she said.
“I cleaned houses. I washed clothes. I swept compounds. I scrubbed toilets.”
Her eyes burned with pride and pain.
“There was no dirty job I did not do.”

She paused.
“When you were almost eight months in my womb,” she continued, “I was working as a hotel cleaner.”
She looked at Aria.
“One day, a guest forgot a huge bag of money.”
Her voice softened briefly.
“I ran after them. I returned it.”
She smiled sadly.

“They were moved by my honesty. They gave me half of the money.”
Her eyes filled again.
“They told me to stop cleaning. To take care of myself. To start something small. To go back to school if I wanted.”
Her face hardened.
“That money was my foundation.”
She stepped closer.
“I started a business. I went to school. I took care of you.”
Her voice rose.
“I built everything you enjoy today with pain and blood.”

She pointed at Aria’s stomach.
“And now history is repeating itself.”
She shook her head slowly.

“I never wanted you to suffer what I suffered.”
She picked up the small knife from the table—the orange-peeling knife—and held it loosely.
“Aria,” she said calmly, dangerously, “you must make a choice today.”
Aria trembled.
“If you keep that child,” Anita continued, “the bastard you are carrying—”
Aria sobbed.
“I will kil! myself today,” Anita said flatly.
She raised the knife slightly.
“But if you ab*rt that pregnancy,” she added, “we will go home and pretend nothing ever happened.”

Silence crashed over the room.
That was emotional blackmail.
Pure. Cold. Calculated.

Only then did Aria speak.
She fell to her knees.
“Mum…” she cried. “I am so sorry for what my father did to you.”
Anita scoffed.
“I’m sorry you suffered all your life,” Aria continued through tears.
“I’m sorry he broke you.”
She looked up.
“But my situation is different.”

Anita laughed sharply.
“No man is different!”

“Henry is,” Aria insisted softly.
“He loves me. He has shown me to his family.”
She cried harder.
“He is nice and kind to me. He has the means to take care of me.”
She shook her head.
“Please don’t call my baby a bastard, Mum.”
She crawled closer.
“All you did in this life was for me,” she said.
“To make me better than you.”
Her voice trembled.
“You didn’t succeed in love,” she whispered, “but that doesn’t mean I won’t.”
She lifted her face.
“Mum… when you were pregnant with me at nineteen, you kept me.”
She sobbed.
“You weren’t even a graduate then—and today, I am.”
She held her stomach.
“My baby and you mean everything to me.”
She shook her head desperately.
“I can’t choose. I can’t choose between my child and my mother.”
She cried uncontrollably.
“I cannot choose.”. 

Aria lifted her head again, tears still falling, but her eyes were clear now.
“Mum,” she said softly, “you taught me something very important growing up.”

Anita didn’t respond.

“You taught me that pain can either make us wiser… or make us bitter.”
She swallowed hard.
“And you warned me never to let one person’s wickedness define my whole world.”

Anita’s fingers tightened.

“Please don’t categorize all men as bad,” Aria continued carefully. “Not because my father was bad… not because he betrayed you.”

She shook her head slowly.

“If we judge everyone by the wounds one person gave us, then we allow that person to keep controlling our lives—long after they are gone.”
Her voice broke slightly.
“My father hurt you. Deeply. And you are allowed to be angry about that.”
She looked at her mother with compassion.
“But Mum… you don’t deserve to live your whole life imprisoned by what he did.”

Anita scoffed weakly. “You think healing is that simple?”

“No,” Aria replied immediately. “Healing is not simple. It is painful. It is slow. And sometimes… it is terrifying.”
She moved her knees closer on the floor.
“But it is still necessary.”
She placed her hand gently on her chest.
“You survived,” she said. “But surviving is not the same as healing.”

Anita flinched.

“You survived the orphanage. You survived betrayal. You survived pregnancy alone.”
Her voice softened.
“But Mum… you don’t have to keep fighting ghosts.”

She raised her eyes.
“You can heal now.”
The room went quiet.
“You told me education saved you,” Aria continued. “Strength saved you. Courage saved you.”
She smiled faintly through tears.
“But healing will save you too.”

Anita turned her face away.

“I am not asking you to forget what you went through,” Aria said quickly. “I am asking you not to let it destroy the future you built with so much sacrifice.”
She looked down at her stomach.
“This child is not your past,” she whispered. “This child is my present… and my hope and your future.”

She lifted her head again.
“And Henry is not my father.”
Her voice was firm now.
“You didn’t raise me to be blind. You raised me to observe. To question. To choose wisely.”
She inhaled deeply.
“If Henry ever becomes what my father was… I will walk away.”
She met Anita’s eyes.
“Because I know my worth—you taught me that.”

Anita’s lips trembled slightly.
“Mum,” Aria said gently, “you gave me life when the world told you to give me away.”
She smiled weakly.
“Let me give my child a chance too.”

Anita bowed her head again.

“And please… heal from what you went through.”
Her voice broke fully.
“So you can see life differently.”
So you can see me differently.
So you can see this child, your grand child… not as a repetition of your pain—but as proof that pain does not always have the final word.”
“Please, Mum.”

The silence that followed was heavy—
not with anger,
but with a battle inside a woman who had never learned how to stop fighting.

Aria’s words settled deep into Anita’s chest.
Her hand began to shake.
The knife trembled.
Then—
it slipped from her fingers and fell to the table.
Anita sank into the chair and broke down completely.
Not anger.
Not shouting.
Crying.
“I tried…” she sobbed. “I only wanted to protect you. I was afraid history would repeat itself.”
Aria rushed forward, picked up the knife, and placed it far away. Then she knelt before her mother and held her tightly.
“Mum,” she whispered, “you don’t have to fight anymore. I’m not your past. I’m your healing.”
Anita cried harder and wrapped her arms around her daughter.
“I’m sorry,” she cried.
“I forgive you,” Aria replied softly.
The door opened.
The doctor stepped in. “We’re ready for the procedure.”
Anita lifted her head immediately.
“There will be no procedure,” she said firmly.
“My daughter is keeping my grand baby.”
She stood up, holding Aria’s hand.
“We’re going home.”
And together, mother and daughter walked out
not broken,
but finally free.

Date: Tuesday Feb 3rd, 2026-History and values speak louder than noise in Greater Jonglei.

When Hon. Aguer Panyang served as Governor of Jonglei State, he mentored and politically developed leaders such as Atong Kuol Manyang and Amuor Pach and many others young men and women from Bor County and Duk and none from Twi East. His approach demonstrated the importance of leadership grooming, transparency, Fairness and inclusion.

My question is this: which young leaders from Twi East have been mentored or politically developed by Gen. Kuol Manyang or Hon. Michael Makuei?
This is not an attack, but a call for honest reflection on political mentorship, inclusion, and leadership development among Twi youth.Since July 30, 2005, following the death of Dr. John Garang De Mabior, many Twi Dinka especially the younger generation have observed patterns of political exclusion, marginalization, and mistreatment within South Sudan’s governance structures. These experiences are not theoretical; they have been witnessed firsthand.

There is also a widely shared account among elders that during his 2004 visit to Twi Dinka land, Dr. John Garang warned community leaders that if anything happened to him, Twi Dinka might face hardship and cruelty. Whether remembered as history or cautionary wisdom, this message reflects the deep sense of vulnerability and neglect felt by the community over the years.This statement is not meant to inflame division, but to demand accountability, fairness, and inclusion. Sustainable peace in Greater Jonglei and South Sudan as a whole requires truth, mentorship of all communities, and equal political opportunity, not silence or denial.

Many Buor youth view Twi elders and politicians as mentors and protectors who help guide and support their political growth.

In contrast, many Twi East youth perceive certain Buor political leaders not as allies, but as covert actors who work against their interests.

From the Twi East perspective, these leaders are seen as being involved directly or indirectly in actions that cause political exclusion, economic marginalization, psychological intimidation, and even physical insecurity. This perception, shaped by lived experience, has deeply damaged trust between the two communities.Bridging this divide requires honest acknowledgment, accountability, and a complete change in political behavior, not denial or silence.

Conclusion:

Honestly speaking, from our lived experience, the only thing many Twi East young political voices see being offered by certain Buor political leaders is harm in one form or another political obstruction, economic exclusion, psychological intimidation, or physical insecurity rather than genuine support to help us climb the political ladder. This difference highlights a clear contrast in political values and leadership culture.

Our values speak louder than words. Political brutality, greed, and manufactured insecurity must stop, as they are not only harming others but also damaging the image and moral standing of Bor leadership itself. This culture of greed and domination must end. We are looking toward leveling up toward a better future built on fairness, mentorship, regional peace, and reconciliation within Greater Jonglei, Greater Upper Nile, and South Sudan at large.

🌿 Who was Ngundeng Bong

Ngundeng belonged to the Nuer people. His father (Bong Chan) was from the Bul-Nuer, while his mother (Nyayiel Malual) came from the Lou-Nuer. 

According to Nuer oral tradition, his birth was considered miraculous (his mother was believed to be barren for a long time), and because of the unusual circumstances, he was named “Ngundeng” meaning “God-given” or “Gift of Deng.” 

From around the 1850s–1860s, he began to prophesy and act as a spiritual leader. Many among the Nuer came to believe he was possessed by the divinity of Deng (the sky-god of Nuer religion), and that he served as Deng’s earthly representative. 

---

🔮 His Role and Prophecies

Ngundeng built a spiritual and political centre at a place called Wec Deng in present-day Jonglei State. There he gathered followers, gave prophecies through songs and trance-induced pronouncements, and ruled (in spiritual / moral terms) over many Nuer. 

He preached against internal Nuer feuds, cattle-raids, and inter-communal violence; he emphasized peace among Nilotic peoples and co-existence. 

His prophecies reportedly included predictions about major upheavals: division of Sudan, civil war, and future suffering for his people — warnings and promises delivered decades before modern conflicts. 

Importantly: Ngundeng did not claim to be God. Rather, he claimed to be a prophet or vessel of divine spirit — a mediator between his people and Deng. 

---

🛕 The Monument: Ngundeng Pyramid & What It Symbolized

Under Ngundeng’s guidance, between the 1870s and early 1880s, his followers built a large cone-shaped earth mound/shrine at Wec Deng. This mound — called the “Ngundeng Pyramid” — was about 300 feet in circumference and 50–60 feet high. It was surrounded by elephant tusks and served as a sacred and political centre. 

The pyramid was a symbol of spiritual authority, Nuer unity, and resistance against outside domination (colonial intrusion).

 "Saifuddeen  magana kake son kayi ne?."
 cikin tsananin kukan ya rink'a gyad'awa Nuruddeen  kai.
 Duk da k'arfin hali irin na Ummi  tuni kuka takeyi dan tausayin d'an nata wanda yaci sunan babanta.
shi kuwa Nuruddeen cikin mamaki ya kalli k'anin nashi cikin kad'uwa yace.
"Kana ji nane idan nayi Mgna kana gane me nake cewa ne?."
 kanshi ya jujjuya kana ya zame hannunwan Nuruddeen daga rik'on da ya mishi sannan ya tsuguna a gaban Nuruddeen d'in tafin hannunshi yasa ya lailaiye yashin tsakiyar gidan nasu kana yasa yatsarshi ma nuniya ya fara rubutu da harshen fullanci yace.
"Ya Nuruddeen bana jin kuma naji na kasa yin mgna, cikin mak'ok'orona kamar an cusheshi kunnuwana sunyi dim bana jin komai, 
Amman da ina ganin bakinku ina gane abunda kuke fad'a."
sai ya kuma d'ago kanshi ya kalli Nuruddeen daya rusuna yana karantar rubutun yana kuka tamkar an musu mutuwa, 
hannu yasa ya share hawayen fuskar Nuruddeen d'in kana yaci gaba da rubutu da harshen hausa yace.
"Ya Nuruddeen ku nema min mgni mana, insamu irink'a Magna kamar kowa, ku kaini a bud'e min kunnena mana in rink'a jin muryar Ummi na da naku ku rink'a hira dani."
Ruggumoshi Nuruddeen yayi tare da sakin kuka murya na rawa yace.
"In sha Allah zan nema maka mgni Saifuddeen zan tattare dukkan buk'atun rayuwata zan jinginesu zan gina taka rayuwar, don gobenka tayi kyau."
Sai ya kuma tsaidashi tare da matsawa baya suna fuskatar juna yace.
"Saifuddeen kana gane abinda nike fad'i maka?."
 kai ya gyad'a mishi, da sauri alamun eh yana ganewa, ganin haka Nuruddeen yayi wani murmushi da yafi kuka ciwo a zuciya tare da cewa.
"Saifuddeen kayi murmushi kamar yadda nayi."
 ba musu yayi murmushin da har saida dimples enshi duka uku suka lotsa biyu na kumatun gefe dama da gefe hagu d'aya kuma na tsakiyar d'an gemunshi, 
murmushin ya kuma fad'ad'awa ganin itama Ummi tana murmushi still su duka hawaye na kwaranya a idanunsu,
Abba kuwa tuni ya mik'e bisa taburmar dake tsakiyar gidan da yake konciyan zafine, kwanan woje akeyi,
kuma har yayi baccin da ya kwana bayiba.
Shi kuwa Nuruddeen hannunshi ya d'aura kan k'ahon zuciyarshi kana ya fara mgna yana murmushi still hawaye na zuba yake cewa.
"Saifuddeen *Babu nakasasshe sai rago*, kasa a ranka ita. Nakasa ba kasawa bace, 
in sha Allah ni d'an uwanka Nuruddeen zan baka dukkan kulawa zaka rayu kamar ko wanne mai ji da gani da mgna, kada ka kareya shi nakasa baiwace ta Allah wonda yakewa wanda yakeso, 
lokuta da dama bahaushe na karin mgnar da kan zama izina misali inda suke cewa, wani hanin ga Allah baiwane."
sai ya kuma sharte hawayenshi kana yaci gaba da cewa.
"Zan nema maka mgni iya raina da mutuwa, amman kasa a ranka mgni baya canza k'addarar mutun,
kasa aranka wani hanin ga Allah baiwace.
Kasa a ranka Allah yayi maka rahamar tsare maka harshenka daga sobon Allah ne kasa aranka Allah ya tsare maka kunnenka daga jin zantuka na haram ne da aikata sabon Allah, kamar yadda haka abin yake ga makaho Allah ya tsare mishi idanunshi daga ganin Haram, 
Saifuddeen zan yi iya iyiwana kan ciwonka dana mahaifinmu har sai dai in yafi k'arfina."
 tuni Rahma da Raihana suketa kuka, Hayatuddeen ma dake gefen Ummi kuka yakeyi ganin yayunshi na kukan.
Kuka sosai Ummi takeyi dan tausayin Nuruddeen yaro k'arami Allah ya jarab ceshi ya d'ora mishi nauyin jinyar uba da k'ani bugu da k'ari shike ciyar dasu, 
domin sam Abba baya iya noma makaranshi sai su murdeshi haka yasa shima Nuruddeen baima iya nomanba, 
kasan cewar su Abba sun gaji tarin filaye a wurin babansu wanda shima babansu a wurin babanshi ya gada,
to nauyin rayuwarsu ya ta'allaqa da su bada jinginan filayen ana noma ana basu yan wasu kud'ad'e da zasu iya ciyar dasu. 
To amman da yake larurar jinya ta shiga sai ya zama kud'in basu isarsu, 
wasuma in sun karb'i gonakin basa basu kud'in jinginar wasu kuma suyi ta bayarwa har kud'in yafi k'arfin yadda zasu iya maida musu su bare su amshi gonarsu dole sunaji suna gani gonakinsu suke fin k'arfinsu, 
uwa uba ga Bappa Ali k'anin Abba irin mutanennan masu saude-saide.
Shiyasa tun bayan rasuwan iyayensu  motsi kadan sai ya saida gona. 
Yaje yayi tabin masu magani wai zai nemawa Abba mgnin jikinshi wai ko Allah  zaisa ya rabu da makaranshi,
 kwana kad'an abu yayi sanyi in ya sake tashi sai yafi na baya.
bud'e ido Ummi tayi jin abinda Nuruddeen yake fad'i, rubutun gaban Saifuddeen ta zubawa ido inda yake cewa.
"Ya Nurudeen makaranta nafa ya zanyi inyi karatu? banaji bana iya Magna, gashi next week zamu fara exams, isilamiya ma an kusa ayi musabak'a Ya Nuruddeen ta ina zanyi karatu ta yaya zan bada hadda?."
wannan tambayar tashi itace tasa kukan Nuruddeen k'aruwa yana kuka yake cewa.
"Zakayi karatu Saifuddeen, in sha Allah zakayi karatu boko da Arabic, in Allah ya yarda nakasarka bazata zama tawaya ba." 
kai ya gyad'a alamun gamsuwa kana ya koma bayan Abbanshi ya konta time to time hawaye na zubo mishi yana sharewa, a haka yayi bacci kasan cewar basuyi bacci ba daren jiya yawo suka kwana sunayi. 

Allah sarki Nuruddeen daga wannan ranar, 
ya fara fafutukar nemawa Saifudddeen mgni amman ina, 
k'addara ta rigayi fata, domin wannan abune da muka sani a k'asar hausa, some times k'enda tana sanadin makanta, kuramta gurguntaka, koma tab'uwar hankali gaba d'aya wa Al'ummarmu musamman in lokacin zafi akayishi. Kamar dai yadda ta kasance akan Saifuddeen.

Haka dai rayuwa tai ta tafiya yau fari gobe summa, 
a cikin wannan yanayin aka aura da Rahma tunda ta gama Secondary school inta, 
inda aka aura mata Sadik dan abokin abbansu Hamisu.

Shi kuwa Saifuddeen, ya bar zuwa makaranta dan ko yaje malaman basu wani meda hankali kanshi,
 kuma gashi babu makarantar nakasassu a Dukkun,
sai dai yana zuwa islamiya,
kuma  Alhamdulillahi malam suna matuk'ar kula dashi, 
a wannan lokacin akwai wani babban malami su abokin Malam Ashiru ne wanda shida kanshi yake ware Saifuddeen ya koyar dashi, yakan bashi hadda ya kuma, iya in yazo sai ya zauna dashi ya bashi takardu ya rubuta mishi abinda ya koyar dashi kuma Alhamdulillahi da kai yake kawo komai yadda ya kamata, 
wasu lokutanma har shike karb'ar haddan na k'asa dashi kuma duk k'ank'antar batan da akayi Saifuddeen  zai gane har yayiwa yaran gyara ta hanyar rubuta musu komai.

kusan shekara biyu da faruwar abun kenan wanda tuni Saifuddeen yana da haddan izu 37 a kanshi yana kuma karanta littatafai na addini sosai kamar Hadisai, tauhit, Nahawa, kulasatul nurul yak'in, da kuma tajweed  dan yama fi maida hankali kan tajwweed a cewar shine zai taimakawa karatunshi ya gane kurenshi da kanshi ya gyarawa kanshi, kana sosai yake bibiyar littafan koyan larabci.
Zuwa wanna lokacin ya saba da kuramtarshi, Nuruddeen kuwa har yau yana nema mishi mgnin.

Adianes Cortes Oyala, 23 years old, South Tower 82nd floor

Adianes Cortes Oyala was born on August 9, 1978 and lived in Brooklyn, NY. She had a sister, Yasmine, and a younger brother, Antonio. attended and graduated from John Dewey High School in 1996. Adianes met her sweetheart, Felipe Oyola, when they were teenagers working at a fast food restaurant in Brooklyn. She was working as a cashier while she was working as a cook. Adianes and Felipe got married in 2000 and had dreams of children together, although they wanted to raise them in Florida, where Adianes’s parents and 13 year old brother lived. They were saving money for the move and for their own house together. Felipe said, “We wanted to give them things we never had. We’ve always lived in apartments, never having control. We wanted something of our own.” Adianes was a loving daughter to her parents, a caring sibling, and was very close to her cousins who she’d grown up with. Adianes was described by her friends and family as warm, caring, sweet, and determined.

Adianes worked in human resources and payroll for Fuji Bank on the 82nd floor of the World Trade Center’s South Tower. Working one floor below her was her husband, Felipe, who was supervisor of mail services for the bank. On the morning of September 11, 2001, Adianes was working on the 82nd floor of the South Tower when Flight 11 struck the North Tower. She went down to the sky lobby on the 78th floor, where she found her husband also waiting for the elevators. Adianes was very upset by the situation, and the pair exchanged a comforting hug while Felipe told her that everything would be alright before the loud speakers told them it was safe to return to their offices. Felipe returned to his office first, and Adianes followed. When Flight 175 struck the South Tower, both Adianes and Felipe were still inside the building. Felipe was just barely able to escape before the towers collapse, while Adianes sadly did not. Adianes’s life was taken on September 11th, but the love, accomplishments, and memories made throughout her life can never be taken. She will never be forgotten.

In the video below showing SSPDF soldiers reading the Bible in the Dinka language, then dancing to their cultural dance while burning a Nuer cultural symbol, have deeply shocked and wounded many within the Nuer community.😓
To the Nuer people, this act is not just offensive it represents one of the greatest humiliations inflicted on their identity, culture, and dignity.

Dancing proudly while a Nuer symbol burns adds another layer of insult. It transforms destruction into celebration and suffering into spectacle. For the Nuer people, this moment revives painful memories of marginalization, cultural erasure, and ethnic targeting. It reinforces the fear that diversity is not being protected, but mocked.
The SSPDF is meant to be a national institution one that belongs equally to all South Sudanese, regardless of tribe or language. Any behavior that appears to elevate one culture while degrading another undermines trust in the army and weakens the idea of a shared national identity.
This incident is not only about the Nuer. It is about the future of coexistence in South Sudan. A nation cannot be built on humiliation. Unity cannot grow where cultural disrespect is tolerated or ignored.
True peace requires accountability, empathy, and respect for all communities. Recognizing the pain caused by such actions is the first step toward healing. Ignoring it only deepens the wounds.

Respect for culture is respect for humanity. Without it, reconciliation remains impossible.

My sister, who has never cared about anything except her gifted son, called me so casually it chilled my blood: “I dropped my disabled daughter off at your place.” Shock slammed into me as I raced home, only to find the little girl trembling and sobbing on my doorstep. That moment cracked something open—fear, anger, and a strange determination tangling inside me. I had no idea what three months would bring, but the truth unfolded with a force that none of us could escape.....When my sister, Laura, called me that Tuesday afternoon, I expected another long monologue about her son’s violin competitions. Instead, her voice was strangely casual—almost careless.
“I dropped Emily off at your place,” she said.
I froze. “What do you mean you dropped her off?”
“She’ll be safer with you. I’m busy.”
Then she hung up.
I sped home, my chest tight with confusion and rising dread. Emily, nine years old, born with cerebral palsy, had always been treated like an afterthought in Laura’s household. Her twin brother, Evan, the gifted prodigy, absorbed all attention, all praise, all affection. Emily existed in the margins, quiet and unnoticed.
When I reached my apartment building, I found her curled up on my doorstep, her backpack beside her, her cheeks streaked with tears.
“Aunt Maggie…” She reached for me with trembling arms. “Mom left.”
I took her inside, wrapped her in a blanket, and heated soup while she clung to my sleeve as if I might vanish too. Over the next days, I tried contacting Laura. My calls went unanswered; my texts left on “Read.” She had simply off-loaded her daughter like unwanted luggage.
Weeks passed, then months. I managed doctor visits, therapy sessions, school enrollment, and sleepless nights when her muscles seized in pain. But slowly, something changed. Emily began to smile more. She learned to trust that someone would come when she called. She decorated her new bedroom with drawings—messy, uneven, but bursting with color.
Three months later, everything seemed almost stable… until the letter arrived.
It came in a thin white envelope bearing Laura’s handwriting. I opened it at the kitchen table while Emily colored beside me.
“I’m coming to take her back,” the letter read.
“My life is finally settling down. Be ready.”
My stomach clenched. After abandoning her child without warning or support, now she wanted her back? I looked at Emily—laughing softly at her scribbled cat drawing—and something in the room shifted. I realized that regardless of DNA or titles, I had become her stability. I had become her home.
That night, as rain hammered the windows, a sharp knock echoed through the hallway.
Emily flinched.
I stood up slowly, pulse pounding.
On the other side of the door, a shadow moved.
Laura had come early.
And she wasn’t alone.

Someone Should Tell Dinka and Nuer Communities: Peace Cannot Be Bought by War

Concerned: Equatoria Leader from Western Equatoria State 
Victor Benneth Keliopas
Tel:0923536467

Someone should tell the Dinka and Nuer communities a hard but necessary truth: peace cannot be bought through war confrontations driven by national power interests. The continued cycles of violence among our communities threaten not only lives but the very foundation of the nation we struggled to create. The vision that sustained the SPLM through 21 years of liberation struggle for our independence was never about division, tribal dominance, or endless confrontation. It was about freedom, justice, unity, and dignity for all.

During the long years of struggle, Dinka, Nuer, Equatorians, and all South Sudanese shed blood together with a shared dream. That sacrifice must not be broken apart by internal conflicts fueled by competition for power. When communities are mobilized against each other, it weakens the nation and betrays the ideals of the SPLM vision that united us against oppression. Independence was not achieved so that we replace one form of suffering with another.

War confrontations do not serve the people; they serve narrow interests. They destroy trust, displace families, collapse economies, and rob the younger generation of hope. No community can claim victory when schools are closed, cattle are lost, and graves multiply. Power gained through violence is temporary, but the damage left behind lasts for generations.

Peace is not merely an agreement among political elites; it is a responsibility of communities. It requires rejecting hatred, resisting manipulation, and choosing dialogue over revenge. Most importantly, it requires love—love for neighbors, love for the nation, and respect for human life. Without love, reconciliation becomes impossible, and without reconciliation, the country remains fragile.

The SPLM vision of the 21-year struggle calls on us to protect our independence by strengthening unity, not tearing it apart. Dinka and Nuer communities must see each other not as enemies, but as partners in nation-building. Our independence will only have meaning if it delivers peace. The time has come to honor our struggle by choosing coexistence, healing, and a shared future for all South Sudanese.

The major problem with opposition political movements in South Sudan is that most of them are formed on the basis of tribal identity, and their missions and objectives are fundamentally driven by tribal competition for dominance in government, rather than a national vision.
For example, the Real SPLM, under the leadership of Lt Gen. Pagan Amum, draws the majority of its supporters and fighters from the Chollo (Shilluk) community, which makes it largely an ethnic-based movement.
Second, the National Salvation Front (NAS), led by Lt. Gen. Thomas Cirillo, is predominantly supported by Bari-speaking communities. Its political and military objectives are largely confined to the Equatoria region, making it difficult for people from Upper Nile or Bahr el Ghazal to join. Anyone from those regions who attempts to do so risks being viewed as a traitor or as someone responsible for the suffering of Equatorians.
Third, the South Sudan United Front (SSUF) under Gen. Paul Malong is overwhelmingly Dinka-dominated, with very few non-Dinka members, mostly from Upper Nile. This further reinforces the perception of the movement as ethnically exclusive.
Fourth, the SPLM-IO faction led by Gen. Simon Gatwech Dual is dominated by the Nuer Lou, limiting its appeal and legitimacy among other Nuer sections and non-Nuer communities.
Overall, these movements lack inclusive national character, and as long as opposition politics remain tribalized, they are unlikely to offer a genuine alternative to the current system or bring lasting peace to South Sudan.

Looking beyond the lie, the term “Nuer Weu” serves as a mockery of choosing nationalism over tribalism!

By Dr. Sunday de John
 
When it comes to sharing my unsolicited opinions on South Sudan, I find myself getting involved uninvited. This is my home; it is my country, and I cannot remain passive while its affairs are discussed, especially when I believe I can help address the challenges we face.

The Nuer community has coined the term “Nuer-Weu,” which has become a potent weapon. This term targets national leaders of Nuer descent who have chosen to serve in the government of the Republic of South Sudan rather than participate in the widespread and destructive rebellion. It is used to shame leaders such as H.E. Taban Deng Gai, Ambassador Lol Gatkuoth, Gen. Hoth Mai, Hon. Tut Gatluak Manime, H.E. Nguen Monytuil, Gen. Makal Kuol, Gen. Bouy Rolnyang, Gen. Matthew Puljang, and many others. These people face this unrealistic labeling for rejecting chaos and ethnic conflict.
 
These people are not traitors; they are principled citizens exercising their constitutional right to participate in the government. They have prioritized the nation over chaos. Therefore, the mockery directed at them must cease. Those who mock them need to reconsider their stance, as no tribe can convincingly install a president. No amount of weaponry can surpass the power of the ballot.
 
H.E. President Salva Kiir Mayardit holds his office today because he was elected, not due to Dinka military dominance. He is supported by all citizens of South Sudan, as a constitutional order cannot be overthrown through unconstitutional means. Likewise, Dr. Riek Machar Teny will attain the presidency of South Sudan only through democratic processes and sound policy, it will not happen through Nuer bloodshed. This is the reality, not merely my opinion.
 
The dangerous illusion of establishing a separate tribal government for the Nuer or Dinka is poisoning the future of our country. There is no Nuer government, nor will there ever be one. Equally, there is no Dinka government, and there will not be one either. What exists is solely the Government of the Republic of South Sudan.
 
While we continue to mock those who prioritize nationalism over tribalism, our children are left to study under trees. Our sick loved ones suffer and die without access to medicine. Our roads are reduced to muddy paths.
 
This mindset may appear courageous, but it is misguided. We must recognize and contemplate, before it is too late, that wars do not construct schools. Conflicts do not create roads, and the persistent underdevelopment afflicting Nuer lands and the entire country stems directly from Nuer’s highest affinity for violence.
 
We have been misled or, more accurately, we have misled ourselves into believing that rejecting government jobs demonstrates loyalty. But loyalty to what? Is it loyalty to a life of poverty? Is it loyalty to witnessing the development of other regions while ours remains stagnant? Winning wars is meaningless if the victories lack a just cause. The Nuer have fought for Dr. Riek Machar Teny, and it is time for them to confront the reality that fighting for one man's claim to power while our people lack basic necessities is not heroism. It is an act of unnecessary self-destruction.
 
Ask yourselves what "Nuer Weu" truly means in a realistic context. Nuer Weu encompasses having a stable income. It includes the ability to send your children to school. It signifies access to essential services. It means not living in refugee camps or Protection of Civilian Sites (PoCs). It represents active participation in the governance and affairs of your country.
 
Those of us in rebellion have sacrificed our futures for a fantasy that will never come to fruition. We will never establish a government that exclusively represents our community. No tribe, be it Nuer, Dinka, Bari, Madi, Shilluk, Taposo, Kuku, Kakwa, Baka, etc.; will ever install a president by force in South Sudan. Tanks do not create legitimacy; elections do. Recognizing this truth is not a sign of cowardice; it is a mark of wisdom.
 
It is time to abandon the notion of Nuer Weu. Those who bear that label are not misguided; they are wise. They have opted for stability, adherence to the law, and a commitment to the national purpose. Consequently, they are also leading more fulfilling lives.
 
The Dinka-Nuer rivalry must be resolved timely. It must end, or it will finally lead to our destruction. This rivalry should be transformed into constructive competition. Compete in building hospitals and constructing roads and schools. Compete in graduating skilled doctors, lawyers, and engineers. Compete in lifting your people out of poverty.
 
Stop fostering false beliefs, such as the misguided notion of Nuer Weu, while inciting younger generations to adopt tribal loyalty. Such loyalty demeans others, undermines the nation, and perpetuates injustices. Every South Sudanese citizen has the right to live and work anywhere in the country.
 
A rational citizen should never forfeit their rights to escape a nickname, whether it be Nuer Weu or any other derogatory term. A choice like that signifies a preference for chains over freedom.
 
South Sudanese must reflect on their actions and cease the self-destruction driven by one person's ambition. There is no honor in this; it is sheer foolishness. Our children will never forgive us for prioritizing war over their education, rebellion over their healthcare, and ethnic fantasies over their future. South Sudan belongs to all of us, or it belongs to none of us.
 
Till then, yours truly, Mr. Teetotaler!

WHY SOUTH SUDAN NATIONAL ARMY ARE PRAYERS BY DINKA LANGUAGES AND THEY CALL THEMSELVES AS ARMY OF SOUTH SUDAN. 
WHAT DO YOU THINK ABOUT THAT 🤔
​Political Dominance: Critics often point out that because many high-ranking officials and commanders are Dinka, the language becomes the "prestige" language of the institution, sometimes unintentionally (or intentionally) overshadowing others.

​Logistics vs. Identity: In a perfect world, a national army would use a neutral language like English (the official language) or Juba Arabic (the street language of the people)to ensure everyone feels included. When one tribal language dominates, it can make soldiers from the other 63 tribes feel like "guests" in their own army.

​THE 64 TRIBES REALITY 
​The strength of South Sudan is supposed to be its diversity. When the SSPDF conducts prayers or parades primarily in one language, it misses an opportunity to reinforce national identity over tribal identity.

For a national army to truly be "national," it needs to look and sound like the whole country. Using English or Juba Arabic during official prayers is usually the best way to ensure a Nuer soldier, a Lotuko soldier, and a Dinka soldier are all praying as one.
​

​I think that for South Sudan to move toward lasting peace and professionalize its military, the "64 tribes" concept needs to be more than just a slogan. If the SSPDF wants to build deep trust across the country, making sure that no single culture dominates the others especially in spiritual or official ceremonies is a massive step toward true unity.
​Language is power. Sharing that language space is a way of sharing power.

„15 Zentimeter“: Eine demütigende Tortur, die französischen Gefangenen zweimal täglich zugefügt wurde.

Dies ist die persönliche Erzählung von Zinaï Voronin, aufgezeichnet nach Jahrzehnten eines erstickenden Schweigens, das unzerbrechlich schien. Mehr als ein halbes Jahrhundert lang vermied sie es, das zu offenbaren, was sie in den Arbeitslagern Deutschlands erlebt hatte, und trug eine Last mit sich, die ihre Seele bei jedem Atemzug verbrannte. Heute, in ihrem hohen Alter, hat sie sich endlich dazu entschlossen, den Mund zu öffnen, damit die Wahrheit nicht mit ihr in der kalten Erde des Vergessens verschwindet. Dies ist nicht nur eine Kriegsgeschichte; es ist der Bericht darüber, wie ein so einfacher und schulischer Gegenstand wie ein fünfzehn Zentimeter langes Lineal in ein Instrument zur Zerstörung der weiblichen Würde und in eine Waffe der absoluten Kontrolle verwandelt werden konnte.

Bevor die Welt in Asche, Rauch und Stacheldraht versank, war Zinaï eine 19-jährige junge Frau, die in einem ruhigen Dorf in der Nähe von Limoges, im Herzen Frankreichs, lebte. Sie hatte lange blonde Zöpfe, Augen voller Hoffnung und träumte davon, Grundschullehrerin zu werden, indem sie ihre Nachmittage damit verbrachte, den einheimischen Kindern Gedichte vorzulesen. Im letzten Sommer vor dem Chaos kaufte sie ein hellblaues Kleid mit einem zarten weißen Kragen, das sie mit einer Mischung aus Stolz und Bescheidenheit trug. Damals war das Maß ihrer Kleidung nur eine Frage jugendlicher Eitelkeit; sie hätte sich niemals vorstellen können, dass in kurzer Zeit jeder Zentimeter Stoff auf ihrem Körper von grausamen Männern überwacht werden würde, die die Geometrie benutzten, um den Geist zu entmenschlichen.

Die Besatzung kam mit dem metallischen Klang der Stiefel und dem süßlichen Geruch von billigem Tabak. Im Jahr 1942 begann die deutsche Kriegsmaschinerie, junge Menschen gewaltsam für die Arbeit in ihren Fabriken zu rekrutieren. Zinaï wurde an einem grauen Morgen aus den Armen ihrer Mutter gerissen und in Güterwaggons gepfercht, die für den Viehtransport bestimmt waren. Zehn Tage dauerte die Reise in absoluter Dunkelheit, umgeben vom Geruch der Angst, des Schweißes und des rostigen Metalls. Als sie am Ziel ankam, war die Luft geschwängert von Kohle und einer chemischen Säure, die in den Nasenlöchern brannte. Dort lernte sie Hans kennen, den für die Disziplin zuständigen Aufseher, einen Mann, der selten schrie, aber immer ein poliertes Holzlineal bei sich trug. Jener Gegenstand, der an jedem anderen Ort ein Symbol der Bildung gewesen wäre, wurde dort zum Emblem des Terrors.

PhD candidate Gatkuoth Lok Gatwich from Tangaza University, Nairobi, warns against oversimplifying South Sudan’s conflict along ethnic lines. Speaking on Radio Tamazuj, he criticized the framing of the crisis as a “Nuer vs. Dinka” struggle, calling it a colonial reductionist view that obscures power, political economy, and elite responsibility.

According to Gatkuoth Lok Gatwich:

▪️ Political movements, elite networks, and revolutionary formations—not ethnic groups—drive conflict.
▪️ Historical grievances, colonial domination, and post-liberation state failures underpin resistance, not inherent ethnic hostility.
▪️ Selective comparisons to other global conflicts mislead by ignoring the war economy, oil revenues, arms flows, and elite interests.

He emphasizes that ethnic reductionism shifts responsibility away from ruling coalitions and external actors, normalizes collective punishment, and prevents meaningful political transformation.

Gatkuoth calls for a “second liberation” for South Sudan—peaceful, constitutional, and institutional—to build a federal, plural, and negotiated state where no community fears its government.

Until then, he warns, South Sudan remains independent in form but imperial in practice.

The major problem with opposition political movements in South Sudan is that most of them are formed on the basis of tribal identity, and their missions and objectives are fundamentally driven by tribal competition for dominance in government, rather than a national vision.
For example, the Real SPLM, under the leadership of Lt Gen. Pagan Amum, draws the majority of its supporters and fighters from the Chollo (Shilluk) community, which makes it largely an ethnic-based movement.
Second, the National Salvation Front (NAS), led by Lt. Gen. Thomas Cirillo, is predominantly supported by Bari-speaking communities. Its political and military objectives are largely confined to the Equatoria region, making it difficult for people from Upper Nile or Bahr el Ghazal to join. Anyone from those regions who attempts to do so risks being viewed as a traitor or as someone responsible for the suffering of Equatorians.
Third, the South Sudan United Front (SSUF) under Gen. Paul Malong is overwhelmingly Dinka-dominated, with very few non-Dinka members, mostly from Upper Nile. This further reinforces the perception of the movement as ethnically exclusive.
Fourth, the SPLM-IO faction led by Gen. Simon Gatwech Dual is dominated by the Nuer Lou, limiting its appeal and legitimacy among other Nuer sections and non-Nuer communities.
Overall, these movements lack inclusive national character, and as long as opposition politics remain tribalized, they are unlikely to offer a genuine alternative to the current system or bring lasting peace to South Sudan.

Die vergessenen Lager „Lusthäuser“: Wozu wurden Frauen gezwungen?

In den tiefsten und dunkelsten Winkeln der Geschichte des Dritten Reiches existiert ein Kapitel, das so abscheulich ist, dass es selbst Jahrzehnte nach dem Zusammenbruch des Regimes kaum gewagt wurde, darüber zu sprechen. Es ist die Geschichte der Lagerbordelle, einer grausamen Erfindung der SS-Bürokratie, die unter dem Deckmantel der „Leistungssteigerung“ und „Disziplinierung“ eine Form der systematischen sexuellen Versklavung schuf, die in ihrer Kaltblütigkeit kaum zu übertreffen ist. Während die Welt heute die Namen der großen Vernichtungslager kennt, blieb das Schicksal der Frauen, die in den sogenannten „Sonderbauten“ zur Prostitution gezwungen wurden, lange Zeit im Verborgenen, begraben unter einer Schicht aus Scham, Stigma und dem bewussten Verschweigen der Täter und Mitwisser.

Alles begann in den Köpfen von Männern wie Oswald Pohl, dem Chef des SS-Wirtschafts- und Verwaltungshauptamtes. Für ihn waren die Häftlinge in den Konzentrationslagern keine Menschen, sondern lediglich Einheiten von Arbeitskraft, die es mit maximaler Effizienz auszubeuten galt. Im Jahr 1942, als der Krieg an allen Fronten tobte und die deutsche Rüstungsindustrie verzweifelt nach mehr Produktion verlangte, suchte die SS nach Wegen, die Moral der Funktionshäftlinge – jener Kapos und Vorarbeiter, die für die Ordnung in den Lagern zuständig waren – zu stärken. Die Idee war ebenso simpel wie pervers: Man wollte ein Belohnungssystem einführen. Wer hart arbeitete und loyal gegenüber der SS war, sollte Zugang zu einem Bordell erhalten. Heinrich Himmler, der Reichsführer SS, gab persönlich die Zustimmung zu diesem Vorhaben, das nicht nur die Arbeitsproduktivität steigern, sondern auch die „unnatürliche Unzucht“, wie er Homosexualität unter Häftlingen nannte, bekämpfen sollte.

Das erste dieser Bordelle wurde im Juni 1942 im KZ Mauthausen eröffnet. Es war ein Gebäude, das sich äußerlich kaum von den anderen Baracken unterschied, doch im Inneren war es ein Ort des organisierten Grauens. Zehn Frauen wurden aus dem Frauenkonzentrationslager Ravensbrück dorthin deportiert. Man hatte ihnen versprochen, dass sie nach sechs Monaten Dienst freigelassen würden – ein Versprechen, das fast nie eingehalten wurde. Diese Frauen wurden nicht zufällig ausgewählt. Es waren meist junge Frauen, die von der SS als „asozial“ eingestuft worden waren – ein vager Begriff, der alles von Obdachlosigkeit über Prostitution bis hin zu unangepasstem Verhalten abdeckte. Auch politische Häftlinge oder Frauen aus den besetzten Gebieten Osteuropas fanden sich in diesen Todesfallen wieder. Sie wurden vor ihrem Einsatz einer demütigenden Prozedur unterzogen: Sie erhielten bessere Rationen, medizinische Versorgung und sogar Kosmetika, aber nur, um sie für die männlichen Besucher „attraktiv“ zu machen. Es war eine rein funktionale Verschönerung, vergleichbar mit dem Polieren einer Maschine vor dem Einsatz.

Warum? Siehe unten.
