The words came from a terrified patient inside the Women's Lunatic Asylum on Blackwell's Island. She was begging the doctors, the nurses—anyone who would listen.
She was talking about the new patient. The one who seemed too calm. Too aware. Too sane.
That patient was Nellie Bly.
And she was exactly where she wanted to be.
New York City, 1887.
The city's asylums were shrouded in mystery. Rumors swirled about horrific conditions, abuse, and women disappearing behind locked doors, never to be seen again.
But they were just rumors. No proof. No witnesses willing to speak. No way to know the truth.
Nellie Bly, a 23-year-old journalist for the New York World, decided to find out for herself.
Her editor, Joseph Pulitzer, supported her plan: Get yourself committed to the asylum, document everything, and expose the truth.
It was dangerous. It was unprecedented.
If something went wrong, Nellie could be trapped there indefinitely—declared insane with no way out.
She did it anyway.
THE PLAN
Nellie checked into a women's boarding house and began acting erratically.
She stayed up all night, pacing the halls. She spoke incoherently. She stared at nothing. She claimed not to know who she was or where she came from.
The landlady called the police. A judge examined her and declared her insane.
And on September 25, 1887, Nellie Bly was committed to the Women's Lunatic Asylum on Blackwell's Island.
The moment she arrived, Nellie dropped the act.
She behaved completely normally. She spoke clearly. She answered questions rationally.
It didn't matter.
Once you were inside, you were insane. No amount of sanity would set you free.
What Nellie discovered inside was worse than anyone had imagined.
INSIDE THE ASYLUM
The asylum held over 1,600 women.
Many of them weren't mentally ill at all.
They were poor. They were immigrants who didn't speak English. They were women whose husbands wanted to be rid of them. They were girls who'd been raped and were considered "damaged." They were inconvenient, unwanted, and discarded by society.
And once inside, they were tortured.
The "treatment" was barbaric.
Patients were forced to sit in freezing cold baths for hours—punishment disguised as therapy. The food was rotten, inedible. Rats roamed freely. The halls were filthy and freezing.
Nurses beat patients with sticks. They tied women to chairs and left them for days. They mocked them, starved them, and ignored their desperate pleas for help.
Nellie watched women scream for help and be silenced with violence.
She saw patients beg for warm clothing and be denied.
She witnessed daily cruelty designed not to heal, but to break.
And she documented everything.
In her mind. Memorizing every detail. Because she couldn't write anything down.
For ten days, Nellie endured the same treatment as everyone else.
She froze in the ice baths. She choked down spoiled food. She slept on a hard bench in a freezing room with no blankets.
She didn't complain. She didn't fight back.
She documented.
THE ESCAPE
October 4, 1887.
After ten days inside, an attorney hired by her newspaper finally secured her release.
She walked out of Blackwell's Island and immediately began writing.
On October 9, 1887, the New York World published "Ten Days in a Mad-House"—Nellie Bly's firsthand account of life inside the asylum.
The article was explosive.
Nellie described everything in vivid, horrifying detail:
The ice baths that left women shivering for hours.
The rotten food crawling with insects.
The rats that ran freely through the wards.
The beatings administered by nurses.
The women who didn't belong there.
She wrote about a woman who spoke only German and was declared insane because doctors couldn't understand her.
She wrote about girls as young as sixteen locked away for being "difficult."
She wrote about wives whose husbands wanted new families.
She wrote about women who begged to be released and were told they'd never leave.
The public was horrified. Outraged. Demanding answers.
THE AFTERMATH
A grand jury was immediately convened to investigate.
They toured Blackwell's Island. They interviewed patients and staff.
They confirmed everything Nellie had written.
The city of New York immediately allocated an additional $1 million to the Department of Public Charities and Corrections to reform asylum conditions.
Staff were retrained or fired. Oversight increased dramatically. Patients gained new rights and protections.
Some of the women Nellie had met were released. Others received proper care for the first time in years.
"Ten Days in a Mad-House" became a national sensation. It was published as a book. It was read across the country. It sparked a conversation about mental health, women's rights, and institutional abuse.
Nellie Bly became famous overnight.
But she didn't stop.
THE LEGACY
In 1889, at 25 years old, Nellie set out to break the fictional record set in Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days.
She traveled around the globe in 72 days, 6 hours, and 11 minutes—by steamship, train, rickshaw, and sheer determination.
She became an international celebrity.
But it was "Ten Days in a Mad-House" that cemented her legacy as the mother of investigative journalism.
Before Nellie, undercover journalism didn't exist.
She invented it.
After Nellie, investigative reporters followed her lead—going undercover in factories, prisons, sweatshops, and more to expose injustice.
Nellie Bly died in 1922 at age 57.
By then, she had revolutionized journalism, traveled the world, and advocated for women's rights and workers' protections.
But her asylum exposé remains her most enduring achievement.
Because of Nellie, over 1,600 women were seen.
Because of Nellie, their suffering was acknowledged.
Because of Nellie, the system that imprisoned them was forced to change.
Because of Nellie, mental health reform began in America.
Because of Nellie, journalists learned that sometimes the most important stories require more than a notebook—they require courage.
THE REAL STORY
Think about what she risked.
At 23 years old, she voluntarily got herself declared insane.
She knew that once inside, there might be no way out. Women had disappeared into asylums and never been seen again.
She knew she'd be subjected to the same abuse as everyone else. The freezing baths. The beatings. The starvation.
She knew that if her newspaper abandoned her, if the plan failed, she could spend the rest of her life locked away.
And she did it anyway.
For ten days, she endured torture. She watched women suffer. She memorized every detail because she couldn't write anything down.
And when she got out, she didn't write a sensationalist story for clicks.
She wrote the truth.
She named the abuses. She described the women who shouldn't be there. She forced the world to see what it had been ignoring.
1,600 women. Many of them perfectly sane.
German immigrants declared insane because they didn't speak English.
Teenage girls locked away for being "difficult."
Wives whose husbands wanted them gone.
Women who'd been raped and were considered "damaged goods."
Poor women who had nowhere else to go.
All of them abandoned. All of them tortured under the guise of "treatment."
Until Nellie Bly spent ten days in hell and told the truth.
Her story sparked a grand jury investigation. Led to $1 million in immediate reforms. Changed how America treated mental illness.
But more than that—she invented a new kind of journalism.
Before Nellie, reporters just reported facts. They interviewed people in power. They wrote what they were told.
After Nellie, journalists went undercover. They exposed hidden truths. They gave voice to people society ignored.
Every investigative journalist working today—every undercover report, every hidden camera exposé, every story that risks everything to reveal injustice—follows in Nellie Bly's footsteps.
She was 23 years old when she faked insanity and walked into hell.
She was 23 years old when she changed journalism forever.
She was 23 years old when she proved that one person, willing to risk everything, can force the world to change.
Her name was Nellie Bly.
And every woman who was released from that asylum, every patient who received better treatment, every journalist who went undercover to expose injustice—they all owe her a debt.
She didn't just write the story.
She lived it.

O dia 7 de fevereiro marca o Dia Nacional de Luta dos Povos Indígenas. A data foi estabelecida pela lei nº 11.696 de 2008, conquista dos movimentos sociais e de direitos humanos de grupos minoritários. O dia rememora o falecimento de Sepé Tiaraju, índio guarani, que foi uma das lideranças indígenas de uma das muitas revoltas contra portugueses e espanhóis, ocorrida em 1756, contra as determinações do Tratado de Madrid, que redesenhou as fronteiras das Américas Portuguesa e Espanhola.
A data remete a conscientização e a importância dos debates ligados às pautas dos povos originários, tais como a luta pelo direito à terra e contra a destruição da natureza, assim como questões ligadas à saúde e a educação nas aldeias, além do reconhecimento dos saberes tradicionais, entre outros pontos.
 
Há 266 anos, o guarani mbya Djekupe Aju (ou Sepé Tiaraju, nome aportuguesado) proferiu uma frase que ficou cunhada na história dos mais de 300 povos originários que vivem hoje no Brasil: “Ko yvy ha jara”. Numa tradução não tão literal do guarani para o português, a frase significa “esta terra tem dono”, porque, segundo explica o antropólogo Iberê do Povo Guarani Mbya, “jara” não significa exatamente “dono”, mas sim “guardião”.
“Quando a gente falava isso, os europeus não entendiam porque não compreendem a nossa relação com a terra. Não consideramos ninguém dono da Terra e, sim, guardiões”, tanto que nos nossos idiomas não existe uma palavra que expresse o conceito de “dono” do mundo capitalista”, afirma. É essa frase que marca o dia 7 de fevereiro na memória dos povos originários brasileiros e sua luta pelos seus territórios e direitos cidadãos.
Que este 7 de fevereiro seja um momento de revigoramento de nossa memória coletiva, das forças e resistências para as próximas lutas – que sejamos todos Guarani, Kayapó, Mundukuru, Araweté, Avá-Canoeiro, Bororó, Cinta Larga, Huni Kuin, Ticuna, Sateré Mawé, Xavante, Yanomani, Pataxó Hã-Hã-Hãe!

I summarize my story and my message as the testimony of someone whose entire life has been shaped by sacrifice for South Sudan and whose conscience now forces me to question the direction my country has taken. I fought in the civil war as a child soldier, long before I understood the full meaning of politics or power. I experienced violence and hardship at an age when I should have been in school. After the war, I survived years in a refugee camp as one of the Lost Boys of South Sudan, living with uncertainty and struggle, holding onto the hope that all of that suffering would someday produce a free and just nation. Later, I came to the United States of America and spent more than two decades rebuilding my life and eventually becoming an American citizen, but my heart and my identity have always remained tied to South Sudan and to the dream we fought for in our youth.

That dream was independence, dignity, and equality. When South Sudan became a nation, I believed we were breaking away not only from Sudan geographically, but also from the systems of oppression and marginalization that had hurt our people for generations. Today, however, I find myself deeply troubled. When I see a South Sudanese activist arrested while traveling and handed over to military intelligence for allegedly insulting or defaming the president, I see more than a single incident. I see a warning sign of a government that is uncomfortable with criticism and willing to criminalize dissent. In political terms, this reflects the treatment of speech as a political offense, where criticizing authority becomes dangerous. This reality forces me to ask painful questions: Is this the South Sudan we sacrificed our childhoods for? Is this the freedom we promised ourselves?

I feel deep frustration and pain when I look at how President Salva Kiir Mayardit and many leaders from different tribes are governing South Sudan. Sometimes it feels as if those in power rule the country like outsiders disconnected from the suffering of their own people. This feeling is especially painful for me when I think about the Dinka community, because a large number of Dinka sons and daughters sacrificed their lives during the long liberation struggle against Turkish, Egyptian, and Arab domination in Sudan. Our communities paid a heavy price for freedom.

Today, I cannot ignore the painful contradiction I see. Many ordinary South Sudanese citizens are suffering in ways that remind me of the hardships our ancestors endured under previous regimes. I am not saying this to attack an entire ethnic group, but to question a system of leadership that seems distant from the daily reality of its people. Independence was meant to end oppression, not reproduce it in another form. When citizens feel neglected, silenced, or mistreated, it raises serious moral and political questions about whether our leaders are honoring the sacrifices that created this nation.

I cannot ignore the similarities between the repression we once resisted and the patterns I now observe within my own country. The struggle for independence was justified by claims of mistreatment and injustice under the old Sudan. Yet today, I feel that many citizens experience fear and unfair treatment under our own leadership. This realization is heartbreaking. It feels like a betrayal of the ideals that motivated an entire generation to fight and endure unimaginable suffering. Independence was supposed to create space for open voices, accountability, and democratic culture. Instead, I sometimes see restrictions that echo the past we tried to escape.

I speak openly and strongly about the failures I see within my own community because honesty is a form of loyalty to the truth. As someone from the Dinka community, I feel shame and disappointment when leaders associated with my people are perceived as mistreating their own citizens or failing to deliver equal justice. My criticism is not hatred toward my people; it comes from love and a desire for improvement. I refuse to accept a situation where ordinary citizens feel neglected or treated as less important than armed groups or political interests. Leadership should protect and uplift all citizens equally, without favoritism or discrimination. When that responsibility is neglected, it is my duty as a citizen and as an activist to say so clearly.

My life experiences have shaped my commitment to advocacy. I see myself as an activist for the voiceless in Ruweng, Padang, Badan, and across South Sudan. I understand that speaking out can carry risks, especially in an environment where criticism is sensitive. But I believe that silence allows injustice to grow. Having lived through war, displacement, and exile, I feel a moral obligation to use my voice to challenge oppression and demand accountability. My activism is rooted in the belief that true nation-building requires open dialogue, courage, and the willingness to confront uncomfortable truths.

I emphasize that real independence is not only about sovereignty or borders. It is about creating a society where citizens can question their leaders without fear, where institutions serve the people, and where dignity is guaranteed regardless of ethnicity or political alignment. I want a South Sudan where leaders are accountable to the public, where criticism is seen as a contribution to improvement rather than a crime, and where every citizen feels equally protected by the state. Ethnic divisions and political rivalries should never override our shared humanity or our shared responsibility to build a peaceful nation.

Despite my frustration and disappointment, I still carry hope. My message is not one of surrender but of determination. I believe South Sudan can rise above its current challenges if its people and leaders commit to justice, equality, and genuine reform. By questioning, criticizing, and engaging in honest reflection, I aim to contribute to a future where the sacrifices of my generation were not in vain. I want the next generation to inherit a country defined not by fear or repression, but by fairness, opportunity, and respect for every voice.

My journey from child soldier to the Lost Boy of Sudan, and become an American citizen has taught me resilience and responsibility. I continue to fight for South Sudan, not with weapons, but with words, ideas, and advocacy. I remain committed to the vision of a nation where freedom is real, accountability is normal, and every person is treated with dignity. This is the South Sudan I still believe in and continue to work toward.

MY MOTHER LOCKED ME IN A DOG CRATE IN THE FREEZING RAIN SO HER NEW BOYFRIEND WOULDN'T HEAR ME BREATHE, BUT WHEN A SCARRED PITBULL CRAWLED IN TO KEEP ME WARM, THE MONSTERS INSIDE REALIZED THEY WERE NO LONGER IN CHARGE.

The glass of the patio door was double-paned and expensive, the kind that turned the world outside into a silent movie. That was the point, I supposed. Inside, the fireplace was roaring, casting a golden, flickering glow over the Persian rug and the leather armchairs. Inside, the air smelled like rosemary roasted lamb and expensive red wine. Outside, where I was, the air smelled like wet concrete and impending snow. The temperature was dropping fast, hovering just above freezing, and the condensation from my own breath was starting to frost on the metal wires pressing against my cheek.

I was twelve years old, and I was curled into a ball inside a large wire dog crate on the back deck of a three-million-dollar home in Connecticut. 

My knees were pulled up to my chest, my arms wrapped tight around my shins to conserve whatever heat I had left in my thin windbreaker. The metal tray at the bottom of the crate was freezing, sucking the warmth right out of my jeans. I tried to shift, but the crate—technically size Extra Large, meant for the Great Dane Gary had promised to buy but never did—was just small enough that I couldn't fully straighten my neck. So I sat hunched, shivering violently, watching the scene play out inside like a ghost haunting his own life.

Gary was standing by the fireplace, swirling a glass of Cabernet. He was wearing that cashmere sweater my mother had bought him with his own credit card, the one she said made him look distinguished. He was laughing at something she said, his head thrown back, teeth gleaming in the firelight. He looked like a man who had everything under control. A man who didn't have to worry about 'baggage.'

That’s what he called me. Baggage. 

My mother, Elena, was sitting on the sofa, her legs tucked under her. She was wearing a silk dress that was too thin for the season, but inside that house, it was always summer. She held her wine glass with both hands, looking at him with an expression I used to know—adoration. But there was something else in her eyes now, something brittle. Desperation. She laughed when he laughed. She nodded when he spoke. And every few minutes, her eyes would dart toward the patio door, toward the darkness where I was caged.

Whenever she looked, I held my breath, hoping she would see me shivering. Hoping she would remember that I was her son, not a dog. But every time her eyes met the glass, she looked right through me, or maybe she just looked past me, fixing her gaze on the reflection of the beautiful life she was so terrified of losing.

"He needs to learn structure," Gary had said two hours ago, as he dragged me by the collar of my shirt through the kitchen. I hadn't even done anything wrong. I had just walked into the living room while he was on a conference call. I had forgotten the rule: *Invisible after 6:00 PM.*

"He’s undisciplined, Elena," Gary had told her, his voice calm, terrifyingly level. "He interrupts. He takes up space. If he wants to act like an animal, let him sleep like one. It’s the only way the lesson sticks."

And my mother, my beautiful, soft-spoken mother who used to sing me to sleep when we lived in that drafty apartment in Queens, had just stood there. She had wrung her hands, looked at the floor, and whispered, "Maybe you're right, Gary. He has been... difficult lately."

She let him push me out the door. She let him latch the metal bolt. She watched him put the padlock on, just to be sure.

It had been raining then. Now, the rain was turning into sleet, tapping a rhythmic, icy code against the plastic tarp Gary had thrown halfway over the crate—not to keep me warm, but to keep the crate from rusting. The wind whipped around the corner of the house, cutting through the wires, biting into my skin. My teeth were chattering so hard my jaw ached. I squeezed my eyes shut, trying to disappear. If I disappeared, maybe it wouldn't hurt. 

I tried to remember the apartment in Queens. It was small and smelled like old onions, but it was warm. It was ours. Now we lived in a palace, and I was the prisoner in the dungeon.

A noise from the yard made my eyes snap open. 

The backyard was massive, a sprawling acre of manicured lawn that bordered a dense, dark woodland. The motion sensor lights hadn't triggered, which meant whatever was out there was low to the ground. I held perfectly still. Gary had told me there were coyotes in the woods. 

*Crunch. Crunch.* 

Footsteps on the frozen leaves. Heavy. deliberate.

I stopped shivering out of pure fear. I pressed myself against the back corner of the crate, the wire digging into my spine. A shadow detached itself from the gloom of the rhododendron bushes. It was massive. Broad-shouldered. 

It wasn't a coyote.

It moved into the faint light spilling from the patio door, and my breath hitched. It was a dog. A Pitbull, slate gray and built like a tank, with a head the size of a cinder block. One of its ears was tattered, looking like it had been chewed off in a fight long ago. Ribs showed faintly beneath a coat that was scarred and patchy. It looked like a monster. It looked like something Gary would describe as "trash."

The dog stopped five feet from the crate. It lowered its heavy head, sniffing the air. I could see the muscles in its shoulders bunching. 

*Please go away,* I begged silently. *Please don't eat me.* I had nowhere to run. I was boxed meat.

The dog took a step closer. It let out a low huff, steam rising from its snout. Its eyes, amber and intelligent, locked onto mine. It didn't look aggressive. It looked... curious. And cold. It was shivering, too. Its back leg trembled with a spasm that mirrored my own.

Inside the house, Gary stood up to pour another glass of wine. The movement caught the dog’s attention. The animal flinched, dropping low to the ground, ears pinned back. It watched Gary with a distinct, recognizable emotion: wariness. This dog knew what men like Gary were. It knew about hand gestures that meant pain.

The dog looked back at me. I was small. I was on the ground. I was trapped. 

Slowly, agonizingly slowly, the dog crept forward. It sniffed the wire mesh. I smelled its wet fur, the scent of pine needles and old dirt. I didn't move. I slowly uncurled one hand and pressed my fingers against the wire.

The dog licked my fingers. One rough, warm swipe.

Then, it did something impossible. The crate had a secondary door on the side, one Gary hadn't padlocked because the latch was rusted stuck. Or so he thought. The dog nosed at the side panel. The latch was loose. With a surprising amount of dexterity, the dog used its nose to nudge the metal pin upward. It rattled. I froze, looking at the house. Elena was laughing again, oblivious.

The dog pushed. The side door creaked open just enough. 

I thought it was coming in to attack me. I braced myself. But the massive gray head pushed in, followed by the broad shoulders. The dog crawled into the cramped space with me. It didn't growl. It didn't bite. It circled once, struggling in the tight confines, and then flopped down heavily right on top of my freezing legs.

It was like a heater being turned on. 

The dog’s body heat was immense. It laid its heavy head on my chest, letting out a long, weary sigh. I could feel its heart beating against my stomach—slow, steady, strong. Instinctively, my frozen hands found their way into its thick neck fur. I buried my face in its flank, sobbing silently. The dog didn't mind. It just pressed closer, a solid wall of muscle and warmth between me and the freezing wind.

For the first time in hours, the shivering stopped. I wasn't trash anymore. I was a pack member.

We lay there for what felt like an hour. Me and the stray. Two unwanted things keeping each other alive in the dark. I watched the house through the dog’s ears. 

Then, the patio door handle turned.

My blood ran cold. The dog felt my tension instantly. Its head lifted off my chest. The muscles under my hands turned to steel.

"Just going to have a smoke, babe," Gary’s voice boomed as the sliding door opened. A gust of warm air rushed out, followed by the smell of expensive tobacco.

Gary stepped onto the patio, humming to himself. He didn't look at the crate immediately. He lit his cigar, took a puff, and then turned, a smirk playing on his lips. "Hey, baggage," he called out, walking toward the crate. "You learned your lesson yet? Or do you need another hour to—"

He stopped. He squinted. 

He saw the shape inside the crate. It was too big to be just me.

"What the hell?" Gary muttered. He took a step closer, reaching for the latch. "What did you bring in there, you little freak?"

That was when the low rumble started. 

It wasn't a bark. It was a vibration that shook the entire crate. A sound dredged up from the deepest, most primal part of the earth. 

The dog shifted. It didn't abandon me. It moved *in front* of me. It placed itself directly between me and the door Gary was reaching for. 

Gary froze, his hand inches from the wire. 

The dog snarled. It was a terrifying sound, a wet, guttural warning that promised absolute violence. I saw Gary’s face go pale in the porch light. He stumbled back, dropping his cigar.

"Elena!" he screamed, his voice cracking, losing all that smooth, rich authority. "Elena, get out here!"

My mother came running to the door, glass in hand. "Gary? What is it?"

"He’s got a... there’s a beast in there!" Gary pointed, his hand shaking. 

The dog let out a sharp, explosive bark that rattled the wire mesh. It stood its ground, shielding me completely. I peered around its shoulder, looking at the two of them. My mother looked terrified. Gary looked small. 

For the first time in my life, looking at the man who owned the house and the woman who owned me, I didn't feel afraid of them. They were just people. And they were scared.

The dog looked back at me for a split second, a quick check-in, before turning its amber gaze back to Gary. The message was clear: *Open this door, and I will end you.*

Gary backed up all the way to the glass door. "Call the police," he hissed at my mother. "Call the cops and get animal control. I want that thing shot."

But as he reached for his phone, the neighbors' floodlights flicked on. The barking had carried. And I knew, as I wrapped my arms tighter around the dog’s neck, that tonight wasn't going to end the way Gary thought it would. The dog wasn't the only one who had been heard.

South Sudan today functions without a truly national army; instead, power is exercised through tribal civilian armies such as Agwelek for the Shilluk, Abushok for the Dinka padang of upper nile,  Mathiang Anyoor for the Dinka of Greater Bahr el Ghazal, and Red Belt for the Bor Dinka. These forces are armed using national resources mainly to purchase weapons, while basic needs are completely neglected, no regular salaries, no food rations, no schools for soldiers’ children, and no welfare support. Fighters are left to survive by killing animals for food, yet are still mobilized and sent to invade Nuer areas under the false label of “national army operations.” This reality exposes a system where the state funds violence but abandons the very people carrying it out.
The routine use of Dinka local language during so-called national duties, instead of a neutral official language like Arabic, reveals that these forces do not represent the nation but a single ethnic dominance. Language becomes a tool of exclusion and intimidation rather than unity. In this context, tribal conflict is deliberately sustained, not resolved used as a political weapon to divide communities, weaken national identity, and maintain control. President Kiir is widely seen as relying on this ethnic militarization and perpetual insecurity to stay in power, at the cost of national cohesion, justice, and the future of South Sudan.

Unclaimed Luggage

The daughter stands
with her weight forward,
as if bracing against a wind
no one else feels.

Concern has made a home in her muscles.
Not fear—
duty.
The quiet ache of watching the adults
drop what they cannot carry
and instinctively bending
to lift it.

She cannot let go into life.
How could she?
Her hands are already full
of bags that are not hers.

Unclaimed luggage circles endlessly—
grief without owner,
rage rerouted,
secrets wrapped in politeness,
responsibility disguised as love.

She learned early:
if I don’t hold this,
it will spill everywhere.

So she holds.
Jaw tight.
Chest forward.
Eyes scanning for the next impact.

She does not know yet
that life is not entered
by vigilance,
but by trust in ground.

She does not know
that suitcases left long enough
are eventually opened by someone else—
or discarded—
or returned to the one who packed them.

For now,
she stands at the threshold,
heavy with concern,
mistaking endurance for safety,
care for control.

What she needs
is not reassurance
but permission.

Permission to put the bags down.
Permission to disappoint the system.
Permission to feel the weight
fall through her feet
into something older
that can take it.

Gravity is waiting.
Not to crush her—
to relieve her.

One day
she will step forward
empty-handed
and feel how little she was ever required
to carry alone.

For now,
she stands.
And even that
is understandable.

Edel Serenya Luthariel ♡

Four arrested over drug trafficking in Abyei

February 8, 2026 ABYEI

Authorities in the disputed Abyei region said on Friday they had arrested four suspected drug dealers and seized narcotics during a security operation in Abyei town.

Yohana Akol, spokesperson for the Abyei Area administration, told Radio Tamazuj that police confiscated 56 rolls of cannabis, locally known as bangi, and an unspecified quantity of tramadol tablets during the arrests.

He said security forces were continuing searches for other suspected dealers in the town and surrounding counties, citing growing concern over drug abuse among young people.

“The main challenge is the increasing involvement of youth in the drug trade,” Akol said, adding that the administration had ordered intensified searches to curb related crimes.

Last year, Abyei authorities imposed restrictions on the use of illegal substances, including a ban on alcohol consumption in shops and public places, following a surge in crime, officials said.

Akol said investigations were underway and would be opened against the suspects, stressing that the administration was determined to prevent crime linked to drug abuse.

Bulabek Deng Kuol, the paramount chief of the Ngok Dinka in Abyei, welcomed the arrests but blamed economic hardship for pushing some young people into the drug trade.

“Abyei is congested with refugees, returnees, and traders, and job opportunities are limited,” Deng said. “But drug trafficking is destructive, and we support the government’s action to stop it.”

He said community leaders would work with authorities to monitor and report drug-related activities in the area.

Ateny Wek Ateny

The use of the term "Khartoumers" is essentially a false and misleading propaganda. I've heard this description many times whenever something unpleasant happens involving someone who speaks Arabic. A friend might visit you for the first time and find you listening to the news in Arabic, and they look confused, asking in surprise, "Are you a Khartoumian?" I always reply, "No, I just speak Arabic as a second language." It's as if English speakers are called "Londoners" just because they speak English, even if some don't know where London is on the map!

Just as there are young men and women proficient in English without ever setting foot in England, Arabic is also a language that can be learned, even in China.

The generation that continued the liberation struggle—Dr. John Garang De Mabior, Kerubino Kwanyin Bol, William Nyuon, Salva Kiir Mayardit, and Arok Thon Arok—these founders of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM) were all "Khartoumians" in the sense that they studied in Sudanese institutions like Wadi Seidna Military College, were fluent in Arabic, and served in the Sudanese army.

Finally, it's grossly unfair to view Arabic speakers as less patriotic. All those who led the liberation and independence of South Sudan were Arabic speakers. So, let's stop boasting about ignorance and recognize that language isn't a measure of patriotism, but a means of understanding, communication, and progress.
Therefore, I always proudly respect you, someone who knows the truth and must be respected. 🙏

Our name is inspired by the Japanese term kokoro, alternately translated as “mind,” “heart,” or “spirit.” 

In our interpretation, there is no separation between these words, only a deep weaving — a unity that we see mirrored in the natural world. Kokora invites us to honor the oneness of nature and the vast web of connections that make us whole

At Kokora, we seek to regenerate the vitality within by forging an alliance with nature, the source of nourishment for all life.

Our journey begins on our Regenerative Organic Certified farm in Costa Rica’s Enchanted Valley, where we embrace cultivation practices that honor the land while imbuing our herbs with vibrant activity. From this starting point, our work ripples outward, enhancing the ecosystems around our farm, uplifting the communities we touch, and harmonizing the health of our customers.

Every step of the Kokora process — from soil management, seed selection, cultivation, and harvest, to drying, extraction, concentration, and production — supports the awakening of nature’s full potential.

“Daughter, be ready tomorrow. We’re bringing Grandma to you—you’ll take care of her. After all, she left her apartment and dacha to your brother, and they…”

DAUGHTER, TOMORROW—BE READY FOR GRANDMA.

The call came on a Sunday evening, just as Sveta was pulling on her cozy reindeer pajamas and looking forward to tea and a book. The caller ID read: Dad. She blinked in surprise. They usually called on Saturdays at midday—like clockwork. A stiff five-minute check-in: “health, weather, everything fine.”

“Dad, what happened?”

She heard him breathe into the receiver before he spoke.

“Sveta, hello. Clear your day tomorrow. Be home by lunchtime. We’re bringing Mom to you.” He paused, as if to make sure she’d heard. “Your grandmother, I mean.”

Sveta’s first thought was a visit? But Grandma Anna Petrovna hadn’t really gotten out of bed for nearly two years after her stroke. She could barely speak. Why would they haul her three hundred kilometers just to “stop by”?

“You’re bringing her… permanently?” Sveta asked, not believing her own words.

“Permanently. There’s nowhere else for her to go, Sveta.”

“Dad, wait. How is there nowhere? She has her own three-room place downtown, a dacha… She lives with you, but it’s all hers. And my brother—Kolya! He’s in the same city!”

That’s when another voice cut in—sharp and piercing, unmistakably her mother. Her mother always insisted on speakerphone, as if supervising the conversation.

“Sveta, don’t make this difficult. Grandma left the apartment and the dacha to your brother. Officially. The papers were signed a month ago. And your brother,” her tone turned syrupy and cruel, “is renovating that very apartment right now. Turning it into ‘European style,’ you know. Dust, mess, workers in and out. Kolya has a young family and a small child. They’ve temporarily moved in with us. And the bedridden old woman goes to you.”

Sveta felt the floor tilt under her. She lowered herself slowly onto the edge of the bed.

“So… you’re saying Grandma gave everything to Kolya, but the responsibility of caring for her goes to me?” Sveta managed.

“Well, you’ve always been our helpful one,” her mother continued, without a hint of embarrassment. “And you’re alone—no family of your own. You have your own one-room apartment. It’s not big, but it’ll be enough for you and Grandma. Kolya needs support now more than ever—his own place, his future. He’s a man, the one who carries the family name. And Grandma decided that herself. Maybe she thinks you deserve attention more than… some piece of property.”

“Some piece of property,” Sveta echoed. “Mom—do you hear yourself?”

“Sveta, enough!” her father exploded, apparently snatching the phone away. “It’s decided. We already left—we’re spending the night on the road. We’ll be there by two tomorrow. Set up a couch or a bed. That’s it. Be ready.”

Click. Dial tone.

Sveta sat with the phone clenched in her hand, staring at the wall. Her jaw literally hung open—shock, confusion, and a raw, burning humiliation all at once. Scenes from her childhood flashed in her mind.

Grandma Anna Petrovna: strong, strict, smelling of pies and lavender—an unquestioned matriarch. Sveta, the first grandchild, spent every summer at her dacha. They weeded the garden together, cooked jam, Grandma taught her cross-stitch and told endless stories about the war and her youth. Grandma would say, “You’re my golden girl, Sveta—patient and kind.” Kolya, five years younger, was the spoiled favorite. He came to the dacha in short visits, broke things, complained he was bored, rushed back to friends. Grandma would shake her head: “What do you do with a boy like that… modern times.” But there was always a special softness in her voice for him—the “carrier of the name.”

Then came university, work, and Sveta’s move to another city. She called Grandma every week. She came for holidays, brought medicine, warm blankets, good tea. Kolya called rarely—but every birthday he showed up with grand, flashy gifts: an expensive phone Grandma didn’t know how to use, a spa certificate she never redeemed. Grandma would brag to the neighbors: “My grandson doesn’t forget me!”

And this was the result: She left everything to my brother. Why would Grandma do that to her? The thought battered Sveta’s mind like a trapped bird. What had she done wrong? Loved not enough? Cared the wrong way? Or was it not Grandma at all… but her parents? Sveta knew how her mother worshipped Kolya, how she’d always repeated the same lines: “It’s easier for you—you’re a girl,” “Kolya needs help—he’s a man, it’s harder for him,” “The apartment matters more for Kolya—he’ll have a family.” Maybe years of that mantra had seeped into Anna Petrovna’s weakened mind. Or maybe her parents had “helped” Grandma make that decision when she was vulnerable after the stroke. The idea was disgusting, but Sveta couldn’t shake it.

She cried—out of hurt at Grandma, helpless rage at her parents and brother, and fear of what was coming. Tomorrow, her quiet, organized life would be invaded by someone else’s decisions, problems, and her grandmother’s helpless body. Her life would end. She would become a caregiver—with no right to gratitude because “Kolya got the apartment.” She’d been chosen because she was the most convenient. The most agreeable. The easiest to use.

The next day, around three, the doorbell rang. In the hallway stood her father, her mother—and a small, hunched figure in a wheelchair, which they struggled to roll out of the cramped elevator. Anna Petrovna. She looked even smaller and more fragile than Sveta remembered. The eyes that had once been sharp and alive were now dull and frightened. She recognized Sveta—her lips trembled as she tried to form a smile, but it came out as a weak, painful grimace.

“There,” her mother said, unloading bags of medicines and adult diapers. “Settle her in. We’ll write everything out for you: the pill schedule, meals. Here.” She shoved a paper into Sveta’s hand. “We have to go—long drive back, and we need to help Kolya at the renovation.”

They stayed less than an hour. Kissed Grandma on the forehead. Gave Sveta a dry, perfunctory hug. Her father wouldn’t look her in the eyes. Her mother pressed an envelope into her hand. “This is for the first expenses.”

And then they left—as if they’d dropped off unwanted luggage at a storage locker.

A hollow silence filled the apartment, broken only by Anna Petrovna’s heavy, rasping breathing. Sveta approached the wheelchair. She wanted to scream, “Why?!”—but she saw a tear slide slowly down the old woman’s wrinkled cheek. The scream lodged in Sveta’s throat.

Life split into “before” and “after.” Days became a never-ending loop: morning care, porridge, pills, changing linens, a short wheel out to the bench in the courtyard, lunch, reading aloud, television, dinner, waking up at night. Sveta quit her job and switched to remote work, losing a huge portion of her salary. Her personal life—already sparse—disappeared completely.

Sometimes Kolya called. “How’s it going? Managing? Thanks, sis—you’re our hero. Oh—sorry, the crew’s calling me!” And he’d hang up, cheerful and busy.

Anna Petrovna barely spoke. She mostly watched. Her gaze often settled on Sveta when Sveta, exhausted, dozed in an armchair with a book, or mopped the floors, or made a pureed soup. In that stare were pain, shame, and something else Sveta couldn’t decipher.

One late autumn day, with cold rain streaming down the windows, the crisis hit. Grandma spiked a fever; her breathing turned wheezy and broken. The ambulance crew looked grim.

“Double pneumonia. In her condition… prepare yourself.”

They took her to the hospital.

In intensive care—where the air smelled of antiseptic and death—Sveta stayed day and night. Her parents called once a day. Kolya came once, for ten minutes, said, “Hang in there,” and vanished.

And then, during one of those endless nights, when the monitors beeped softly and Grandma seemed half gone already, Sveta laid her head against the edge of the bed and whispered through tears:

“Grandma, I’m so tired. And it hurts so much. Why did you love him more? Why did you do this to me?”

She didn’t expect an answer. But she felt a faint movement. Grandma opened her eyes—clear ones. The sharp eyes from Sveta’s childhood. With immense effort she shifted her hand. Sveta took it—cold and weightless like a fallen autumn leaf—and leaned close.

Grandma’s lips moved. Sveta bent lower.

“Not… I…” Grandma exhaled, tears spilling from her eyes. “Couldn’t… otherwise… They… would take… everything… and you… throw you out… You… kind… He… will take… but… won’t give… even… to you…”

She stopped, drained. Sveta froze, trying to piece together the fragments.

Couldn’t otherwise… They would take… He will take, but won’t give…

And suddenly—like a flash—it all fit.

Grandma hadn’t preferred Kolya. She had been… afraid. Afraid of his greed, afraid of her parents enabling him. She’d known that if she left her inheritance to Sveta, Kolya and Sveta’s parents would make Sveta’s life hell—contest the will, crush her, tear apart the apartment, the dacha, and Sveta herself.

But this way…

They got what they wanted. And Grandma got a quiet corner, care, and peace beside the one she truly loved—at the cost of a monstrous injustice and unbearable pain for that very person. It was a sacrifice—twisted and cruel, but maybe the only move Anna Petrovna could make in her helpless state to protect someone, at least a little. To be near someone.

“Grandma…” Sveta whispered, pressing the old hand to her cheek. “I understand. I understand everything. Forgive me for not seeing it sooner.”

Anna Petrovna closed her eyes. A strange, deep relief softened her face. Two days later she was gone. She died quietly in her sleep, holding Sveta’s hand.

After the funeral, the family gathered in Sveta’s now-emptier-than-ever apartment. Her mother asked the first thing that mattered to her:

“So? Did Grandma say anything at the end? Did she pass on something?”

Sveta looked at them—at her mother, consumed only by Kolya’s inheritance; at her father, eyes lowered; at Kolya, already on the phone discussing possible redevelopment plans for Grandma’s apartment…

Breaking News: Suspected Murle Raiders Steal Over 1,350 Cattle in Baidit, Jonglei State.

Bor,10th February 2026(JT)  Suspected Murle armed youth reportedly raided more than 1,350 head of cattle in Baidit Payam of Bor County, Jonglei State, early today, 10 February 2026, at approximately 1:15 a.m. local time.

A local resident, Alier Kuol, said the attackers stormed a cattle camp around midnight. He stated that local youth are currently pursuing the raiders in an effort to recover the stolen animals.

This incident follows a similar attack about two weeks ago, during which more than 600 cattle were reportedly taken from Pakawau by suspected Murle criminals.

Bor County Commissioner Hon. Ateny Pech confirmed that Baidit Payam has suffered repeated attacks attributed to Murle raiders. He vowed that this latest incident would not go unpunished and said local youth are already on the ground tracking the attackers.

Meanwhile, in a related peace effort, Chief Administrator Hon. Gola of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area arrived yesterday in Bor, Jonglei State, following an invitation from Governor Dr. Riek Kok. The delegation includes Gen. David Yau Yau, the Speaker, and religious leaders.

The visit aims to conclude a peace conference initiated last year between Jonglei State and the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, intended to address recurring intercommunal violence and cattle raids.

This hadith warns Muslims against wearing amulets, charms, or taweez for protection.

1️⃣ Meaning of Tameemah (تميمة)
A tameemah is anything worn or hung (on the neck, arm, car, house, etc.) to:
 • Avoid evil
 • Prevent sickness
 • Bring luck
 • Protect from harm

People often believe these objects can save them from problems.

2️⃣ Why Is It Called Shirk?
Shirk means giving Allah’s power to something else.

If a person believes:

“This amulet will protect me,”
then he is giving Allah’s power to an object.

This is major shirk, because:
 • Only Allah controls harm and benefit.
 • No object has power by itself.

3️⃣ If Someone Says: “It’s Just a Means”
Some people say:

“I don’t believe it has power, it’s just a reason.”

Even then, most scholars say it is haram, because:
 • The Prophet ﷺ did not allow it.
 • It weakens trust in Allah.
 • It leads people towards shirk.

4️⃣ Correct Islamic Way of Protection
Islam teaches us to seek protection through:

✔️ Dua
✔️ Qur’an (like Ayat-ul-Kursi, Surah Falaq, Naas)
✔️ Dhikr
✔️ Tawakkul (full trust in Allah)

These are the real shields for a believer.

To: H.E. Salva Kiir Mayardit, President of the Republic of South Sudan
CC: Minister of National Security, Minister of Interior, Governor of Jonglei/GPAA, UNMISS Special Representative

Subject: URGENT: Appeal to Stop Frequent Armed Attacks by Armed Elements from Pibor Region

Your Excellency,

I am writing to you as a deeply concerned advocate regarding the escalating, violent, and frequent attacks launched by armed youth from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area against the neighboring communities in Jonglei State. 

The continued, unchecked raids on our communities have resulted in loss of innocent lives, abduction of women and children, destruction of homes, and theft of cattle. These incidents are destroying the fabric of our society and preventing the peaceful coexistence necessary for development. 

We urgently request your administration to take the following actions:

Immediate Security Deployment: Deploy neutral and disciplined SSPDF forces to the hotspot areas to create buffer zones and stop further bloodshed.

Disarmament Campaign: Initiate a comprehensive, fair, and transparent disarmament targeting armed gangs and cattle raiders.

Accountability for Perpetrators: Identify, arrest, and prosecute the individuals, including ringleaders and local politicians, who are inciting violence or engaging in abductions and looting.

Dialogue and Reconciliation: Facilitate a genuine, government-led peace dialogue between the leaders of the Murle, Nuer, and Dinka communities to address the root causes of conflict, including cattle rustling and resource competition. 

The people in the affected areas cannot continue to live in fear. We believe in your commitment to unity and protecting all citizens of South Sudan, regardless of their ethnic background. 

We trust that you will treat this matter with the urgency it deserves.

Sincerely,

Dr. Elijah Abuoi Arok

My mother-in-law gave me an hour to leave the house or she would throw my luggage out. Confused, I asked, "why?" she replied, "my daughter doesn't like you, so you need to go." I left quietly, but a week later, she called me saying, "why haven't you paid the rent yet?" I had been waiting for this moment. My answer left them both in complete shock

The first suitcase hit the hallway floor like a gunshot. Not mine. She threw it there.

It was a gray Tuesday in Columbus, Ohio, the kind of day where the air feels heavy even before someone breaks your life in half. My mother-in-law stood at the top of the stairs, arms crossed, lips pinched like she’d been rehearsing this moment.

“You have one hour,” she said, voice calm but cruel. “If you’re still here, I’ll throw the rest of your luggage onto the lawn.”

I blinked, still holding a dish towel in my hand like a ridiculous shield. “Why?” I whispered, because there had to be a reason—an explanation, a misunderstanding, something.

She didn’t even hesitate. “My daughter doesn’t like you,” she replied. “So you need to go.” And just like that… I was no longer family. I was furniture being removed.

I walked out without screaming. Without begging. I took only what fit in my bag, keeping my face steady while my heart cracked quietly. I didn’t want to give them the satisfaction of watching me fall apart. I didn’t argue. I didn’t defend myself. I just left… because sometimes leaving is the only way to survive with dignity intact.

A week later, my phone rang while I was sitting in a small rented room, staring at the ceiling like it might answer the questions my life couldn’t.

Her name flashed across the screen. The same woman who kicked me out. The same voice that said I was unwanted “Why haven’t you paid the rent yet?” she snapped, like I was a tenant who forgot her obligation.

I inhaled slowly. Because this… was the moment I’d been waiting for. I didn’t raise my voice. I didn’t insult her. I didn’t cry. I gave her one sentence—one clean, sharp sentence—that made the line go silent.

And then… her daughter grabbed the phone. And her voice? It wasn’t smug anymore. It was terrified.

  What did I say that made them realize they’d just made the worst mistake of their lives?  Why did my husband suddenly drive back in the middle of the night after hearing it?  And what was the secret behind that “rent”… that they never expected me to know?

Ana auna shi daga 0 zuwa 100.

0 yana nufin Extreme Fear wato matsanancin tsoro
100 yana nufin Extreme Greed wato matsanancin kwaɗayi

Idan index ya yi ƙasa sosai, kasuwa cike take da tsoro.
Idan ya yi sama sosai, kasuwa cike take da FOMO da kwaɗayi.

Tayaya yake aiki?

Index ɗin ba ya kallo farashi kaɗai.
Yana tattara bayanai daga abubuwa daban daban sannan ya haɗa su wuri guda domin ya bada lamba guda ɗaya.

Yanayin zuciyar masu investing a wannan lokacin.

Idan Bitcoin yana faɗuwa da sauri kuma mutane suna panic selling, index zai sauka zuwa Fear.

Idan Bitcoin yana hawa da ƙarfi kuma social media ya cika da hype, index zai tashi zuwa Greed.

Yaya ake lissafa shi?

Ana haɗa abubuwa kamar:
 1. Volatility
Idan kasuwa tana da tashin hankali sosai, hakan na nuna tsoro.

Idan volume ya ƙaruwa sosai yayin pump, yana nuna greed. Idan volume ya karu yayin dump, yana nuna fear.

Ana duba ko farashi yana hawa ko faɗuwa cikin ƙarfi.
 4. Social Media Activity
Yawan maganganu, hashtags, hype a Twitter da sauransu.

Yawan binciken kalmomi kamar Bitcoin crash ko Buy Bitcoin.

Yadda kuɗi ke motsi tsakanin Bitcoin da altcoins.

Yawanci mutane suna tsoro sosai. Wasu lokuta wannan na iya zama damar shiga idan kasuwa tana kusa da bottom.

Lokacin da yake a Extreme Greed:
Yawanci mutane suna shiga saboda FOMO. Sau da yawa kasuwa na iya yin correction.

 “BENUE IS BLEEDING”

Once upon a time,
Benue was not a battlefield.
It was a blessing.

They called her the Food Basket of the Nation,
where yam stood like kings in the soil,
where rivers sang to farmlands,
where children gathered in compounds
to listen to moonlight stories
from wrinkled lips and wise hearts.

We had peace.
We had culture.
We had tomorrow.

But one night…
tomorrow was murdered.

They came in disguise.
With smiles and sticks.
With cows and guns.
They called themselves herders,
but they brought herds of death.

It started in Tyoshin.
And we laughed.
We mocked.
We accused our own brothers.
We blamed victims without evidence.
Even government closed its eyes
because silence was cheaper than justice.

From Gwer…
to Guma…
to Sankera…

Fire followed them like a shadow.

Sankera....
the home of the biggest yam market in West Africa
now begs for a single tuber.
The land of abundance
now borrows hunger.

Kwande...
our ancestral heartbeat
is under siege.
People no longer sleep in their homes.
They sleep in fear.
They sleep in exile.
They sleep on borrowed floors.

Instead of ranching cattle,
they are ranching human beings.
Packing us in camps.
Like forgotten luggage.
Like unwanted memories.

Children are born in tents
and think nylon roofs are heritage.
Maidens are married in camps,
not in their father’s courtyards.
Our traditions are now refugees.

IDP camps have become our villages.
Our villages have become homes for the invaders.

The bellies of vultures
are now our cemeteries.

And our leaders?

Busy polishing their ambitions
with our blood.

Busy campaigning
on corpses.

Busy negotiating power
while widows negotiate survival.

We are killed by guns,
and buried by silence.

We are slaughtered by herders,
and forgotten by government.

They tell us,
“Don’t mention names.”
“Don’t talk.”
“Don’t protest.”

Because votes are more important than lives.
Because politics is sweeter than justice.

Our blood is traded
for political careers.

Oh Benue…
you are bleeding.

Oh Tiv Nation…
you are fading.

Not because we are weak.
Not because we are cowards.

But because we were sold.

Sold by those we trusted.
Sold by those we elected.
Sold by those who swore to protect us.

But hear me, leaders—

When the poor are finished,
they will come for you.

When the masses are gone,
there will be no shield left for you.

We are all surrounded.

God…
heal our land.

Heal our tears.
Heal our graves.
Heal our stolen future.

Let Benue live again.
Let Tiv breathe again.

Before we become
a memory…
in somebody else’s history.
MC Hyula Twalegh

"For everything, there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven" Ecclesiastes 3:1

Growing up in rural Michigan, I had my first job as a "rock picker." A farmer would round up a bunch of kids to come to his farm and "pick rocks." Now that I think of it, it was a funny phrase because we didn't pick just one rock. There were hundreds. If left in the fields, stones can damage farming equipment. You may wonder how rocks keep emerging. There isn't some "rock fairy" dropping stones onto fields to annoy farmers. Instead, stones are heaved forth in the frost/thaw cycle of the earth. This is winter's way of "healing the land." The land can't heal without winter.

I think the same is true of us. We all need winter seasons to heal us — and to unearth rock-like burdens embedded in the soil of our hearts. Solomon writes in Ecclesiastes 3 that life is a passage through various times: a time to be born and to die, to weep and to laugh, to keep silent, and to speak. Yet there's little doubt we will go through all seasons — including winter.

Perhaps that is a good thing. If a field needs winter to heal, people do, too. Winter seasons compel us to slow down, reflect, and give God room to "pick the rocks" in our hearts. We all have rocks — the unseen burdens we haul around in our hearts like unwanted baggage. I am good at keeping old stones buried by putting my hand on the plow, so I don't have to deal with them. But hidden rocks still cut our insides and weigh us down. 

Think of your heart as a field. If Jesus were standing with you on the edge of that field, I imagine He would leave no stone unturned. What a beautiful image — Jesus gathering stones to make your heart-field new again. There is no rock too big for Jesus. He specializes in rolling stones away, including the one in front of His tomb.

So what stones are wounding your soul? Please slow down, my friends, and allow winter to do its work. Jesus has come to rid the field of your life of the rocks that lie there.

Dear God, part of me resists winter's slow, healing work. But I know that there are rocks in the field of my heart, and You are the One who can roll them away. So please come and "pick rocks" in my heart right now, showing me the rugged places I may not even be aware of, and till the soil so that You can grow something new and beautiful in me. Thank You for being with me for every step of my healing. In Jesus' Name, Amen.

What a difference a year makes…

Last year at this time, I was in the middle of the worst week of my life. The betrayal I experienced is one that I still think about and shake my head in wonder. No one who is a good person should ever feel the pain I felt. But I did. And it ALMOST broke me. 

This morning I woke up next to the love of my life and the dog that healed a major part of me. MY house is full of only the people I KNOW are on my side. My circle is SIGNIFICANTLY smaller and it will always remain that way. But those people with stand with me 10 times out of 10. They WILL stand up in a room full of peers and say “Hey!! What you are doing to Jen is wrong!!!”

Drama… gone. Worrying if I’m valued at all… gone. Feelings of being unworthy and stupid… gone. 

As cheesy as it sounds, I am the Phoenix. I have risen above everyone that ever put my name in their mouth with lies and deceit attached and dripping off of it. The truth is out there, it’s just that no one can shake off the embarrassment and shame of how they treated me to get it. 

That’s ok. I know now what you thought of me all along. 🤷‍♀️ And I have mourned the part of me that ever thought you cared for and respected me. 

Thank you for the lessons. Thank you all for the reminder that you must protect your home and your peace at all costs. 

What a difference a year makes…

First-time buyer? Do these 3 things first...

If you’re buying your first home, don’t start with Zillow.

Start with this:
✔️ Have real lender approval: Get fully underwritten, not just pre-qualified.
A pre-qualification is a conversation. A fully underwritten pre-approval means your lender has verified income, assets, and credit. In competitive markets, this makes your offer stronger and prevents last-minute financing surprises. Nothing kills excitement like a loan falling apart three days before closing.

✔️ Know your true monthly budget... it's about your real monthly number — not just the price.
Mortgage payment is only part of it. Taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance, HOA, and future repairs all matter. If the payment stretches you thin, homeownership stops feeling exciting and starts feeling stressful. The goal is stability, not just keys.

✔️ Build a strategy before you start touring homes. Having a Real Estate Professional guiding and advocating for you can make all the difference! What’s negotiable? What’s non-negotiable? What’s your walk-away number? What happens if there are multiple offers? 

Buyers who “figure it out as they go” overpay or panic. Buyers with a plan stay calm and win smart.

Confidence doesn’t come from scrolling Zillow. It comes from preparation.

If you’re thinking about buying your first home this year, let’s make sure you do it the right way.😉

Baal is mentioned directly in the Qur’an in Surah As-Saffat (37:125), when Prophet Ilyas (عليه السلام) said to his people:

“Do you call upon Baal and abandon the Best of creators?”
(Qur’an 37:125)

Baal was an idol worshipped by ancient Levantine civilizations. It represented power, fertility, and false authority. The Qur’an presents it as a symbol of shirk — placing devotion in created things instead of the Creator.

Islam’s message has always been consistent:
Power belongs only to Allah.
Authority belongs only to Allah.
Worship belongs only to Allah.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ warned that the greatest injustice is shirk. He said:
“The greatest sin is that you associate partners with Allah while He created you.”
(Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim)

Throughout history, idols change names. Sometimes they are statues. Sometimes ideologies. Sometimes systems of power. But the Qur’anic principle remains the same — anything elevated to the level of ultimate loyalty, fear, or devotion besides Allah becomes a form of modern “Baal.”

Surah An-Nur (24:3) — Asal Matlab aur Tafseer (simple samajh)
📖 Ayat ka matlab:
Allah Ta’ala farmate hain:
“Zina karne wala mard sirf zina karne wali ya mushrik aurat se nikah karega,
aur zina karne wali aurat sirf zina karne wale ya mushrik mard se nikah karegi.
Aur ye baat mominon par haraam kar di gayi hai.”
📌 Tafseer (scholarly explanation)
⭐️ 1) Iska asli maqsad kya hai?
Ulama (Ibn Kathir, Maududi, Qurtubi) kehte hain:
🔹 Ye ayat zina ki burai ko bayan karti hai
🔹 Jo banda zina ko normal bana leta hai, uska rujhan aksar waise hi logon ki taraf hota hai
🔹 Mominon ko aisi zindagi se roka gaya hai
👉 Yani ye overall warning hai: paak aur halal zindagi choose karo.
⭐️ 2) Kya zaani kabhi nek se shaadi nahi kar sakta?
❗ Nahi — Islam me ye permanent rule nahi.
🔹 Ye ayat un logon par apply hoti hai jo zina ko lifestyle bana lete hain
🔹 Agar koi sincere tauba kar le aur zindagi sudhar le:
➡️ Allah usko paak kar dete hain
➡️ Uska nikah nek insaan se bhi jaiz hai
⭐️ 3) Legal perspective (hukm)
🔹 Ye ayat moral prohibition hai — mominon ko zina se door rehne ka hukm
🔹 Ye automatic legal ban nahi banati ke gunaah karne wala hamesha zaani hi rahe
🔹 Qur’an ka principle: Tauba se insan paak ho jata hai
⭐️ 4) Context samajhna zaroori
Scholars batate hain:
👉 Zina sirf personal gunaah nahi
👉 Ye social harm hai
👉 Is se rishte aur communities par bura asar padta hai
✨ Simple Quote
“Islam morality aur social purity ko promote karta hai — gunaah se door rehna momin ki pehchan hai.”
📌 Key Points (aam samajh ke liye)
✅ Ayat zina se sakht nafrat aur warning hai
✅ Ye un par apply hoti hai jo baar-baar gunaah karte hain
✅ Tauba se insan paak ho jata hai
✅ Nikah nek Muslim se bhi jaiz ho sakta hai
✅ Maqsad paak rishte promote karna hai
🤍 Agar ye ilm faida de, share zaroor karein — shayad kisi ki zindagi badal jaye.

The jungle was alive with screaming. Not animal screaming. Not the howl of wind through the canopy. Human screaming. Hundreds of voices rising together in a sound that had frozen the blood of American soldiers across the Pacific for 3 years. Sergeant William Miller pressed his eye to the darkness and felt his stomach drop through the floor of the halftrack. The treeine was moving.

 It wasn't shadows. It wasn't his imagination. The entire edge of the jungle was surging forward like a wave made of bayonets and rage. Banzai, the word traveled down the defensive line in horse whispers. Men checked their ammunition. Men said prayers they hadn't spoken since childhood. The foxholes that had seemed deep enough an hour ago now felt like shallow graves waiting to be filled. This wasn't a probing attack.

This wasn't harassment fire. And this was a full regimental charge. Hundreds of Japanese infantry pouring out of the darkness with fixed bayonets and the absolute intention of dying on American steel. Miller looked at the four Browning M2 machine guns mounted above his head and made a decision that would have gotten him court marshaled 24 hours earlier.

 He grabbed the canvas bag from under his seat and started feeding a belt of ammunition into the first gun. The loader next to him stared at the brass casings and his face went pale. Sarge, that's the forbidden mix. I know exactly what it is. Command said anyone caught loading that ratio would be command isn't here. Load the guns. What Miller was feeding into those weapons was technically against regulations.

 It was dangerous to the crew. It was destructive to the equipment. A and in approximately 90 seconds, it was going to turn a desperate last stand into a massacre that the Japanese survivors would describe in horrified whispers for the rest of their lives. The M16 multiple gun motor carriage had spent 6 months being the most mocked vehicle in the Pacific theater.

 The infantry called it the bird watcher because that's all it ever did. Watch birds, watch clouds, watch empty sky while real soldiers fought and died in the mud below. It was designed to shoot down Japanese aircraft. But the Japanese aircraft were already gone. The American fighters had swept them from the sky like dust from a shelf.

NAKALABAS na kami ng gate at namangha ako sa aking nakita. Hindi ko inaasahan na sa labas pala ng malaking gate ay may mga nakatayong kubo. Hindi ko mabilang kung ilang kubo ang nakatayo sa gilid ng kalsada. Hindi lang ito mukhang ordinaryong bahay kubo, dahil may sarili itong malaking tent na kapag uulan ay puwedeng gamitin bilang pantakip. Malaki talaga ito, at automatic na titiklop kapag parating na ang ulan. May kaniya-kaniya rin itong mga bangko at mesa sa labas. Nakakamangha lang talaga itong tingnan. Hindi ko inaasahan na may ganito pala rito sa lugar nila. Para itong hideout.

 “Gulat ka ba?” Narinig kong tanong ni Rowan. Sino ba ang hindi magugulat sa lugar na ‘to? 

Parang tagong-tago nga ang lugar na ‘to. Naalala ko rin kanina na may nagbabantay sa daan, kung saan kami dumaan, at may kinausap si Lindsay bago kami tuluyang nakapasok.

 “Ikaw ba ang may pakana ng lahat ng ito?” tanong ko sa kaniya. 
Tumango siya, sabay napahawak sa kaniyang panga at minasahe ito.

 “Yeah. Hindi rin madali ang paggawa ng mga kubo na ‘to. Mukha lang mga tuyong halaman ang pantabon sa mga kubo na ‘yan, pero gawa ‘yan sa bakal. Pati ‘yang tent na automatic na tatabon sa kubo, gawa rin ‘yan sa bakal.”

  “Talaga? Paano n’yo naisip ang bagay na ‘yan? Ang galing naman,” na-e-excite kong sabi habang pumapalakpak. Natutuwa ako at namangha talaga ng sobra. 

  “Yeah. Ilang taon din namin ginawa ang mga ‘to  5-6 years, probably. Matagal talaga, dahil gusto namin na safe ang mga tauhan namin, kung sakaling may kalaban na bigla na lang darating. Bulletproof at soundproof din ang mga ‘yan.”

  “Wow. Ang galing. Napaka-talino naman ng ideas n’yo. Puwede ba tayong pumasok? Or baka lahat ng mga nakatayong Kubo ay may nag-mamay-ari na?” usal ko. Tumingin ako sa kaniya at ngumisi nang napakalaki. 

  “Yup. For couples kasi ‘tong ginawa namin. Pero mayro’n isa na walang nakatira, kaso lalakarin pa natin ‘e. Gusto mo ba makita?” pabulong niyang tanong sa aking tainga. 

  Bigla naman nagtaasan ang balahibo ko sa katawan. Lumakas bigla ang kabog sa dibdib ko, at nag-iinit ang mukha ko ng dumapo sa leeg ko ang mainit na hininga ni Rowan. 

  “Y-yes, g-gusto kong makita,” tugon ko na lang kahit medyo nauutal. 

  “Okay, let’s go. Bawal kang sumigaw roon, o kahit kaunting ungol mo lang. Bawal!” ani Rowan na parang nagpapaalala. Pero bakit naman sinali ang ungol, titingnan lang naman namin ang sinabi niyang kubo. 

  Hinawakan niya ang kamay ko nang mahigpit at nagsimula na kaming lumakad. Para kaming magkasintahan na nag-night walk, habang magkahawak kamay. Magaan na ang pakiramdam ko ngayon, at parang gusto ko na lang magpa-baby sa kaniya. Kinikilig lang talaga ako ng sobra. 

  Habang naglalakad ay napansin ko na parang malayo na kami sa mansyon. At hindi ko na rin nakita ang mga kubo sa paligid. Bigla akong nakaramdam ng takot at napakapit kay Rowan ng mahigpit. 

  “Malapit na tayo, kaya huwag kang matakot,” mahinang sabi ni Rowan at tumawa pa. 

  “Pinagtatawanan mo ba ako?” nakangusong wika ko. 

  “Hindi naman. Halata kasing natatakot ka ‘e. Nandito naman ako,” bulong niya at biglang huminto. 

  “O, bakit ka huminto?” tanong ko at napatingin sa paligid na sobrang dilim. 

  “Nandito na tayo,” tugon niya. 

  “Ha? Sigurado kang nandito na tayo?” gulat kong sambit at nagpalinga-linga sa paligid. Wala naman aking nakitang bahay kubo, o ilaw man lang. Madilim pa rito sa gawi namin kaya mas lalong wala akong makita. 

  “Hoy, pinagloloko mo ba ako? Takot ako sa dilim, Rowan,” mahinang sambit ko habang mas kumapit sa kaniya. 

  “Hawak ka lang, hindi naman kita bibitawan,” saad niya. 
Maya-maya pa ay bigla na lang umilaw ang taas ng malaking puno. 

  “Oh my god! A tree house?” gulat kong usal. 

“Oh gosh, ang ganda.” Ang kaninang kaba at takot n naramdaman ko ay biglang napalitan ng pagkamangha. 

  “Ang ganda rito. OMG!” Hindi ko mapigilan sambit. 

  “Akyat tayo?” ani Rowan. Mabilis naman kong umo-o. Hinawakan niya ulit ang kamay ako at dinala ako sa isang maliit na hagdanan. 

  “Be careful ha, watch your steps,” paalala ni Rowan habang nakasunod sa akin. 

  Namangha talaga ako nang sobra na hindi ko na alam kung ano ang sasabihin. A tree house. Hindi pa ako nakaakyat sa tree house. Wala kasing puwedeng gumawa ng tree house para sa akin eh. May malaking puno sana sa likod ng bahay namin. 

  Nakaakyat na ako, at kung kaninag pagkamangha ko ay mas nadagdagan. Para akong hihimatayin sa aking nakita. 

  “A tree house, with this kind of view? Rowan, Love, are you seriously want to surprise me or what?” I said. And couldn't bring myself back. 

  Para akong nasa loob ng isang book. A fantasy book. Sobrang laki ng puno, at nakagawa ng bahay. Ang ganda pa ng sahig nila, at may mga furniture pang nakasabit na para bang isa talaga itong bahay. May mga gamit pa. At kumpleto talaga. 

  Napako talaga ang mata ko sa view. Kitang-kita ko ang Manila mula rito. Ang ganda tingnan. Mga makukulay na mga ilaw. Mga building na magkakaiba ang laki. Sobrang lapad ng nakikita ko, at nakakalula. 

  “Hindi ako makapaniwala sa nakita ko, Love. Ang ganda talaga.” Bigla akong naging emotional at hindi napigilan ang luha ko. 

  “Woah. Bakit ka umiiyak? Tears of joy na ‘yan, Love? If so, masaya ako, Love. Masaya ako na nagustuhan mo rito,” he said and face me. 

  I immediately hugged him. And buried my face on his chest, “Sobrang ganda. Marami ka na sigurong nadala rito ‘no?” wala sa sarili kong tanong. 

  “Ikaw lang dinala ko rito, Love,” tugon naman niya. Napatingala ako at tiningnan ang mukha niya. He is serious. 

  “Weh!”

  “Totoo nga, kahit tanungin mo pa lahat ng tao rito.”

“Kasabwat mo sila, kaya kaya ka nilang pagtakpan,” anas ko. Tumawa siya at marahan na hinaplos ang pisngi ko. 

  “Ikaw pa lang ang dinala ko rito, aside sa ibang babae tulad ni Lindsay na nakakabatang kapatid ng sekretarya ko. Ay wala na, pero dito sa loob mismo ng tree house na ‘to ay ikaw pa lang talaga,” malambing at kalmado niyang sambit. 

  “Maniniwala na ba ako?”

  “Yes, love. Believe me, ikaw lang ang mahal ko.” Susugal na muna ako sa ngayon, kapag naulit na naman na masaktan. Katapusan ko na. 

  “Promise me, Love. Na kapag wala ka na maramdaman na pagmamahal sa akin. Please, let me know. Para handa akong pakawalan ka.” Takot na kasi akong masaktan.

  Limang taon ang nasayang dahil lang sa isang babae na bago lang nakilala. May pagmamahal na rin naman akong naramdaman may Rowan, pero hindi gaano kalalim tulad kay Drake. 

  “Hindi mangyayari ‘yan, Love. Baliktarin man ang mundo, hindi mawawala ang pagmamahal ko sa ‘yo.”

…..

Ngumiti ako nang matamis sa kaniya at dahan-dahang sumandal ang ulo ko sa dibdib niya. Sana nga ikaw na ang binigay sa akin. Hindi kita papakawalan, kahit ano pa ang mangyari. Gusto kong tumanda kasama ka. Gusto kong magkaroon tayo ng masaya at kumpletong pamilya. At kapag nangyari ‘yon, hindi ko bibiguin ang mga magiging anak natin, lalo na ang magiging asawa ko na nasa harapan ko ngayon. Hindi ko ipaparanas sa mga anak ko ang naranasan ko sa pamilya ko noon. Ang pamilya ang palaging uunahin ko.

 Alam kong masyado lang namin minamadali ang mga bagay-bagay. Gusto ko pa siyang lubos na makilala. Mas lalo kong idiniin ang aking tainga sa kaniyang dibdib upang marinig ang kabog ng puso niya—nakakarelaks at nakakawala ng anumang alalahanin. Pero puwede naman siguro na magkasama kaming kilalanin ang isa’t isa, hindi ba?

 “Gusto kong iparanas sa ‘yo ang tamang pagtrato. Gusto kong ibigay lahat nang mayro’n ako. Ang akin ay sa ‘yo rin, Mahal. Sulitin natin ang bawat araw na magkasama tayo,” pabulong niyang sinabi.

 Tumingala ako at sinalubong ang kaniyang mga matang puno ng pagmamahal. Seryoso siya. Galing sa kaibuturan ng puso niya ang kaniyang mga salita, at ramdam kong espesyal ako sa kaniya. 

 “Salamat, Mahal. Salamat at nakilala kita. Salamat sa pagmamahal at pagtanggap mo sa akin. Sobrang nagpapasalamat ako na palagi kang nasa tabi ko. Mahal kita,” sabi ko nang naiiyak, sabay yakap sa kaniya nang mahigpit.

 Sinubsub niya ang mukha niya sa aking leeg, kaya nakiliti ako at natawa. “Baka nagugutom ka na. Puwede kitang ipaghanda ng hapunan, may mga pagkain naman dito,” sabi niya. 

“Hintayin mo na lang ako sa kuwarto habang naghahanda ako, okay?” nakangiti niyang wika bago niya ako hinalikan sa noo.

 “Sige, Mahal,” tugon ko naman. Hinila niya ako at dinala sa isang kuwarto.

 Malaki pala ang loob ng treehouse. May station rin at mga CCTV kung saan makikita ang buong mansyon, labas at loob.

 “Wow, ang gara naman dito. Kumpleto talaga,” namamanghang wika ko. Binuksan niya ang pinto at bumungad sa akin ang mabangong amoy ng pabango.

 “Bakit amoy pabango?” tanong ko na may pagtataka.

 “Favorite kong pabango ang Lavender Scent kaya bumili ako para rito sa kuwarto. Rito kasi ako tumatambay kapag bumibisita rito,” sagot naman niya.

 “Wow, nakahanda talaga ah. Nakaka-impress ka naman,” masaya kong wika.

 “Magpahinga ka muna. Puwede mong buksan ang TV kung gusto mo. May mga pagkain din diyan sa mini fridge, kaya kumain ka lang kung gusto mo. Pasok na.”

 “Okay, wala ka naman tinatago rito, ‘di ba?” tanong ko nang pabiro.

 He chuckled. “Silly. Wala naman, Love. Bukod sa mga miyembro, ikaw pa lang ang unang babaeng nakapasok dito,” sagot niya. Ngumiti naman ako dahil sa kilig.

 “Sige, Love. Luto ka na,” ani ko at tinulak siya palabas. Tumawa naman siya at iniwan na ako sa kuwarto.

 Maganda, malinis, at malaki ang kuwarto ni Rowan. Tiningnan ko ang bawat sulok nito; simple lang ang datingan. Plain lang ang kulay ng mga dingding, walang nakasabit na dekorasyon. Tanging malaking kama, isang mini fridge, at 36-inch na TV lang ang nandoon.

Naramdaman ko ang pagod sa mga paa ko kaya minabuti kong umupo muna sa kama at hinubad ang suot kong sapatos. Nakasuot lang ako ng dress at blazer—hindi pa ako nakapagpalit ng damit mula nang dalhin ako dito ni Lindsay kanina. Hindi na rin ako nag-abala na manghiram ng damit sa kanya.

 Humiga ako upang magpahinga, hanggang sa muling sumagi sa isip ko ang babaeng kasama ni Rowan kanina. Sino kaya siya sa buhay ni Rowan? Nasaktan talaga ako kanina dahil sobrang close nila sa isa’t isa. Pero siniguro naman sa akin ni Rowan na ako lang at ako ang mahal niya.

 Wala nang makakaagaw sa taong mahal ko, at hindi ako papayag na may mang-agaw pa sa kaniya. Si Rowan na ang huling lalaking mamahalin ko, at lalaban ako kahit kamatayan pa ang katapat.

 Tumayo ako at, walang pagdadalawang-isip, tinungo ang mini fridge at binuksan ito. Walang masyadong laman—tanging chocolate bar at ilang inumin lang ang nandoon. Dahil bigla akong natakam sa chocolate bar, kinuha ko ito at agad na binuksan. Parang matagal-tagal na rin mula nang huli akong kumain ng chocolate, kaya siguro natakam ako nang makita ko ito.

 Bumalik ako sa kama at umupo habang ninanamnam ang chocolate na kinakain ko. Ang sarap talaga ng chocolate; nakaka-adik. Dahan-dahan ko lang itong kinakain para hindi agad maubos. Maya-maya, biglang nag-iiba ang pakiramdam ko at nag-iinit ang katawan ko. May naramdaman akong kakaiba sa loob ko, and I like I am getting wet. 

 “Bakit ako naho-h*rny ng wala sa oras?” tanong ko sa sarili ko nang nakahiga ako. Hindi ko na talaga maintindihan ang sarili ko. It feels so strange.

 “Parang gusto kong galawin ang sarili ko at l***san. Hindi ko alam kung bakit bigla na lang akong naging ganito.”

 “Ugh…” wala sa sariling ungol ko. Napapikit ako at itinaas ang suot kong dress hanggang sa panty ko.
