WHO IS DR. JOSEPH NGUEN MANYTUIL?

Dr. Joseph Nguen Manytuil is a prominent South Sudanese politician and medical doctor who served as the Governor of Unity State for over a decade. Born into the Bul-Nuer community, he is the son of the late Manytuil Wichjang, a highly respected traditional chief known for his leadership in the Mayom region. Manytuil’s career is defined by his transition from the medical field to the volatile political landscape of Sudan and later independent South Sudan, where he became a central figure in the power struggles within the Greater Upper Nile region.

•EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION.

Joseph Nguen Manytuil was raised in a large traditional family in Mayom County. His father, Chief Manytuil Wichjang, was a significant figure in Bul-Nuer society, known for his bravery and judicial wisdom.Manytuil pursued higher education in medicine, eventually traveling to Egypt to attend university. He successfully obtained a medical degree, specializing in surgery. His academic studies period, he was supported by the late General Paulino Matip Nhial, a powerful Nuer military leader in the history of South Sudan 🇸🇸 and Sudan 🇸🇩 by then.

•MEDICAL CAREER AND TRANSITION TO POLITICS.

Following his graduation, Dr. Manytuil practiced medicine in both Khartoum and Bentiu.He contested the governorship of Unity State in 1998 but lost to Taban Deng Gai, a defeat that fueled a long-standing political rivalry.

•POLITICAL LEADERSHIP AND GOVERNORSHIP.

Manytuil’s political fortunes shifted significantly after the independence of South Sudan. On July 7, 2013, President Salva Kiir Mayardit appointed him as the Caretaker Governor of Unity State, replacing his rival Taban Deng Gai. When President Kiir expanded the number of states in 2015, Monytuil became the first governor of Northern Liech State.

His tenure was characterized by intense conflict, particularly during the South Sudanese Civil War (2013–2018). He remained a staunch ally of President Kiir, leading to his label as a "Nuer-Wew" (a term used for Nuer leaders loyal to the government of South Sudan 🇸🇸) by his detractors.

•RECENT DEVELOPMENTS AND REMOVAL.

In recent years, Dr. Manytuil was a vocal advocate for the dredging of the Naam River to mitigate the catastrophic flooding that has plagued Unity State since 2019. This stance led to a public and heated confrontation with academic figures,Professor John Akech of the University of Juba, who opposed the project on environmental grounds. On May 20, 2024, President Salva Kiir relieved Dr. Manytuil of his position as Governor of Unity State, replacing him with Justice Riek Bim Top.

The only sect that will be safe is Ahlus-Sunnah wal-Jama’ah, who adhere to the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ, and hold fast to what he and his Companions were upon

#Question: Who is that sect? And will the (72) seventy-two sects live forever in Fire, as the Mushrik will or not? And does the term Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ apply to those who follow him as well as to those who do not, or is it to the former only? 
The Meaning of the Prophet’s Statement: “…All of them will be in the Fire, except one.” 

#Answer: What is meant by the term Ummah in this Hadith is the Ummah of response which shall be divided into seventy-three sects; seventy-two of which are deviant who practice innovated religious practices that do not constitute apostasy. Each shall be tortured in accordance to its innovations, and deviation, except for those whom Allāh pardons, and forgives. Their final abode will be Paradise. The only sect that will be safe is Ahlus-Sunnah wal-Jama’ah, who adhere to the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ,  and hold fast to what he and his Companionship, [may Allāh be pleased with them], were holding. It is they about whom the Prophet ﷺ said: “ “A group of my Ummah shall remain steadfast, on the truth, victorious, unharmed by those who oppose them, and do not support them, until death or until the Day of Resurrection.”
[Al-Bukhaari nos.71, 3641 no.1920] 

As for those whose innovation casts them out of Islaam, they belong to the Ummah of invitation (mankind at large) not the Ummah of response. They shall remain in Hell-Fire forever, and this is the most valid opinion. 

It is also said that the term ‘Ummah’ in this Hadith means the Ummah of invitation, which is a general term including all those to whom the Prophet ﷺ was sent (i.e. mankind) those who believe and those who do not believe. Whereas the term ‘the safe sect’ is the Ummah of response, which strictly applies to those who believe in the Prophet ﷺ, trustfully, and die on this condition. This is the sect that will be safe from Fire; either by prior punishment or without prior punishment and their final abode will be Paradise. 

As for the seventy-two sects (in the second opinion) they are all, excluding the saved sect, disbelievers who will live forever in Fire. Hence, it is clear that the Ummah of Da’wah, is more general in connotation than the Ummah of response. That is to say, whoever belongs to the Ummah of response, belongs to the Ummah of invitation, while not everyone of the Ummah of invitation belongs to the Ummah of response. 
 
Permanent Committee for Research and Verdicts
 
Fatawa Islamiyah, vol.1, p.20.

Success

Squeezed between the sea and the mountains, Rio de Janeiro is a city fragmented into several regions with their own characteristics and cultures. The birthplace of some of the most traditional samba schools, a cradle of brilliant artists, a factory of tenacious workers, the setting of a famous and democratic dance held beneath a viaduct, whose trademark is irresistible choreographies synchronized with pulsating Charme music, Madureira, a place of simple and honourable people, shelters some of the most incredible individuals I have ever known: Aunt Francisca, the folk healer. A Black woman, short in stature, very thin, with completely white hair, the same colour as her dresses, also known for her elegant, almost poetic conversation. Ever since I have known her, she has lived in a very humble and tidy house. In the living room, perfumed by the herbs of the fumigator, rosemary, benzoin, and lavender are her favourites, there is an altar with images of Master Jesus, Mother Mary, and Saint George, the warrior saint. She receives everyone seated in a faded blue armchair, “the colour of Our Lady’s mantle”. With naturally gentle gestures, she is always available to those in need of a strong prayer to ease the afflictions of the soul. Using sprigs of rue, which she passes over the bodies of the supplicants, eyes closed, she utters words that come from the depths of the heart. Regardless of the magnitude of the suffering, I have never seen anyone leave that house without a sliver of hope on their lips or a light in their eyes that had not existed before. To those who wish to pay for the service, the old woman merely smiles and says, “Kneel before the altar and give thanks to Our Lord Jesus Christ. To Him, all honour and glory. To me, nothing is owed”.
Her age is a mystery. Her appearance has always been the same since I first knew her, still a child, led by my father’s hand, worried about that distracted boy who could spend hours enchanted by unimportant things. I liked Aunt Francisca as much as I liked her house. It was as if we entered a temple set apart from time and the world. The silence and stillness of that place flooded my heart with peace. The prayer did me good, but the brief conversation we had afterward was even better. Followed by a welcoming embrace, her gentle, sweet, and wise words revealed the good side of the worst situations. They not only soothed my heart but also clarified my gaze. The folk healer always showed sincere affection for me. No matter how long I went without visiting, when I did return, she asked about my terrible grades in Mathematics, a subject I hated, and my good grades in History, a topic that fascinated me. Then she let out a mischievous laugh and whispered so my father would not hear, “We must not like something just because someone else likes it or believes everyone should like it. There are no two people alike. Each one has their own way, with their beauty, charm, and power. To flee from this is to deny the magic that was granted to us”.
As an adult, I continued to frequent the good old woman’s house. However, many years had passed since my last visit. Through distraction and carelessness, we remove from our routines tasks that are fundamental to the exercise of happiness. Nothing is worse for distancing us from who we are and from who we can become. Then happiness withers. Only through routine is it possible to trace the route toward the Light. Given the time that had elapsed, I believed she might have departed for the High Lands. As Aunt Francisca was averse to telephones, social networks, and other modernities, there was only one way to find out: it was necessary to go to Madureira.
To my joy, everything was exactly as it had been the last time. Both Aunt Francisca and her house. I did not dare delve into the mysteries of time. I carried with me other, more urgent concerns. Because of serious financial difficulties the publishing house had gone through, I had sold half of the company’s shares. The honeymoon with the new partner was brief. He soon implemented a series of changes that he believed were necessary to reverse the negative cash flow. I agreed with some of them. I did not merely agree, I applauded them. They were not only indispensable but also intelligent and creative. However, others I did not like. One of them, in fact, bothered me greatly. They would begin publishing shallow works, written by opportunistic authors, such as instant celebrities, yanked into fame due to scandals, media crimes, or launched into the stratosphere of popularity by social networks, without having performed any action of justifiable value. Despite their undeniable commercial appeal, they were empty of artistic, pedagogical, or philosophical content. In a few months, the face of the company I had taken years to sculpt would be disfigured. It was not a matter of criticism or prejudice against those who explored that niche; I simply did not want it for my publishing house. I was accused of intransigence, purism, and naivety.
After listening to me without saying a word, Aunt Francisca prayed over me. Then she embraced me for interminable minutes, as if she could hear the sensitive words of the heart, unpronounceable by hurried and afflicted lips. She offered me some water taken from a pitcher that rested on the altar: “It has been energized; it serves to bring calm to the soul”. She waited for me to empty the glass and asked, “How do you understand success?” Although I had not grasped the reason for the question, I replied that success happens when an individual achieves desired goals or surpasses their own expectations. The good old woman continued, “What happens if what was achieved is lost for any reason?” Still without understanding where she was leading me with those questions, I said that in such cases, from success comes failure. She went on, “How can we ascertain a person’s success?” I explained that the most common criteria were fortune, fame, or political and social power. Aunt Francisca curved her lips into a slight smile and asked, “What happens when, for some reason contrary to our desire, money disappears, fame frays, or power is usurped?” I answered that from achievement comes the fall. And the fall is the cruellest of failures. It is better not to reach the top than to plunge from it. The folk healer frowned and commented, “Success is frightening. It scares me. I do not want it for myself”.
I tried to correct the reasoning. I clarified that fame, fortune, and power were common parameters, not necessarily mine. For me, success was being happy, dignified, and free; loving deeply and living in peace. The good old woman looked at me with compassion and reflected, “Universal truths are indisputable and impressive in the beauty of their idea. However, almost no one turns them into action. It requires effort, self-denial, and courage to apply them to daily life. Very few are willing to change. Change hurts. One must admit mistakes, deconstruct false truths, and accept the effort of personal reconstruction. Leaving behind ways of being and living that, because they are so intimate, we believed immutable to our personality, is not easy”. I asked her to explain further. She exemplified, “Everyone claims to desire peace in the world. I believe they are sincere. However, they cannot maintain it even in their own homes. They demand that others act according to their taste, do not tolerate differences, fight when contradicted, and curse uncomfortable truths. They consider these behaviours an inevitable part of who they are. No one reaches the right destination by traveling the wrong road”.
She sipped a gulp of coffee contained in a small enamelled iron mug that rested on the floor beside the faded blue armchair and commented, “Everything that can be taken, lost, or disappear by the action of time or of someone else is with me, but it is not mine. It is a loan or a concession. In either case, it is a transient experience whose greater purpose is my evolution. What is mine, nothing and no one can steal, because it neither ages nor rusts. It does not depend on laws, political systems, or economic policies. It does not fit into accounting or frames, nor can it be kept in safes or serve as currency in the market. The origin of most suffering arises from the anxieties over achievements that unravel according to the variations of days and the world, without our being able to prevent it. These do not fit in the luggage toward the High Lands. We know this, yet we continue to attribute them as fundamental to success”. She looked at me gently and whispered as if telling a secret, “To a person belong the virtues they have added to the soul. No more, no less. An inner construction emanated in serenity, balance, and strength of movement”.
She furrowed her brows and warned: “Bankruptcies, layoffs, illnesses, betrayals, slanders, unwanted separations through divorce or the death of loved ones are just a few examples of situations that make the world collapse for many people. Success is the foundation that keeps us standing when everything around us falls apart”. She shrugged and concluded: “If we have not built these inner pillars, we still do not know success. If we already have them strong, we are free to move forward without depending on any external circumstances such as fortune, fame, privileges, favours, or positions of any kind. Nothing and no one will be able to prevent us from flowing through the adversities of days. Intrinsic success stabilizes, protects, illuminates, propels, and guides. Extrinsic ones, although they shine brightly, often lack light”.
I asked how to achieve this kind of success. The folk healer explained to me: “Contrary to common belief, it is not protagonism in extraordinary events, stages filled with spotlights, plump bank accounts, happiness fabricated through perfect photographs, trips to paradisiacal places, positions of authority, or attendance at luxurious ceremonies that determine a life full of achievements. Success is an inner construction that allows us to live with joy, serenity and clarity, balance and strength of movement, regardless of the events around us”. I commented that, judging by the old woman’s words, it was a very valuable power and within everyone’s reach, since it depended solely on each person’s will. I asked why we were so far from this important conquest. Aunt Francisca smiled and recalled: “To find and enjoy something, it is necessary to understand the search and the purpose. Whatever it may be. As for deep success, what prevents it are the small undue permissions we grant ourselves day by day, driven by the impulse of unbridled desires and senseless interests. This makes us choose brilliance over light, going against truth and virtues. Without realizing it, every day we move a little farther away from who we could become”.
She furrowed her brows again as she increased the tone of seriousness and commented: “Forget the idea that we are in a bad place because of someone else or bad luck. Each person is where they placed themselves. The fall does not come from the bad influence of some friends or the neighbourhood. We listen to the words that flatter our affinities. Each one is responsible for themselves and for the consequences they have caused. No one has a cursed destiny. We are the exact product of our incessant factory of choices”.
She took another sip of coffee before concluding: “Nor would it be fair to attribute failure to great and sudden catastrophes. No one trips over mountains, my child. Life collapses outwardly only after it has crumbled inwardly. This takes time. The waste of an existence happens little by little, in the small daily concessions we authorize out of dubious interests, comfort, or lack of courage. It is necessary to reverse the routine of the relationship each one maintains with themselves. There is no other path to success”.
She paused briefly so I could connect the reasoning and suggested: “At every moment, bring to the surface of consciousness the hidden feelings that drive your choices, for they speak of the genuine intentions behind each decision. We do not always decide for the reasons we like to justify and believe”. Then she asked a simple rhetorical question: “Do you understand what distances us from true success?”
Seeing that no answer was necessary, she added: “The sincere analysis of the feelings that propel or restrain reason is an indispensable part of a good routine. Recognize them, accept them, and transmute them when necessary. Thus we define choices and destinies. Choices serve to craft routes that, in turn, bring us closer to or farther from genuine success. Feelings reveal the habitual behaviours that lead us to walk in circles. All feelings have a name. Until we decode them precisely, we will continue without understanding the gears of reason. We will continue without understanding the authentic foundations of our own decisions and the reason we cannot move forward, even after so much effort. No one understands where they are going before knowing themselves more and better. Deep success will always lie offshore from those who refuse to make the movement toward their own core. To find the essence is to understand the genuine feelings that move thoughts, for they are essential in the process of expansion or contraction of existential advances. Success occurs as a natural consequence of this understanding, as well as of the transformations indispensable to refining the inner foundations, indispensable to facing the adversities inherent in life”.
She looked at me seriously and concluded: “Without understanding the Path, in the frantic search for positions and privileges of apparent success, we will not know personal magic”. I asked what that magic consisted of. She explained by example: “Peace is not the absence of storms. Peace is feeling serene, balanced, and strong during storms. This is success. There is no more powerful magic”.
Aunt Francisca was right. Genuine victory will never be about permissions and authorizations. Any conquest whose maintenance does not require merit, but depends on the variations of the world, can become a prize in reverse. In truth, success would be like a ship, although small ,  or even invisible to the belief of many ,  it was very well built, proving itself capable of safely and autonomously navigating the uncertain and treacherous seas of existence. It involves a set of conquests of the soul. The idea of dignified, free, and firm inner movements, strong enough to sustain external displacements according to one’s own gaze, taste, and will, possessed irresistible arguments and charms.
However, I still had not understood how that conversation applied to the problem that tormented me at the publishing house. Aunt Francisca explained: “The model of apparent success manifests itself in various ways. It is not always in the unbridled desire for fame, money, or prominent positions invested with power. The exercise of control and dominance among family members, friends, or in the work environment reveals nuances of this surface power. There is nothing wrong with wanting things our way. What is wrong is entering into conflict when contradicted. We have the right and the responsibility to conduct our lives in our own way, driven by interests and flavours that are akin to us. For this, it is necessary to understand the limit of action. Both desire and freedom have insurmountable boundaries. No one is obliged to agree with or accompany anyone. This rule applies both to us and to others. If the matter concerns intimate issues, we have the right to stay or leave, say yes or no, do or undo. When it intersects with another’s right, dialogue and sensibleness become necessary, knowing that others have interests and desires not always equal to ours. We may agree or disagree; however, accepting the choice that belongs to the other by right is an act of respect. Welcoming differences of opinion and taste without resentment or rancour is an even nobler act, whether for the dignity contained in it or for the freedom self-granted”.
She sipped a little more coffee and argued: “The conflict of ideas requires dialogue for a healthy solution. The difference in perspectives is not about who is right or wrong. Clear, gentle, and sincere communication serves to find a point of light in the relationship, where those involved can yield and coexist without betraying their own essence. Without vanity and pride, with humility and honesty. In relationships like this, driven by goodwill, there can never be a loser or a winner. We win or lose together. These are the basic rules for winning a game called success”.
I argued that this point of communion is not always possible in relationships. Concessions need limits so they do not become abusive. Some people do not understand this. The good old woman reflected: “When one of those involved prioritizes surface success over deep success, driven by feelings they cannot understand or do not wish to change, they will act driven by illegitimate intentions or impulses devoid of any virtue. By not knowing the inestimable value of unmonetized wealth and truth detached from obligation, whatever the result, they will make themselves a loser, without anyone having pushed them toward defeat”. She looked at the image of the warrior saint on the altar, as if seeking inspiration, and commented: “One may head toward bad conflict or choose the good fight. To defeat the other or oneself. Genuine love for the world requires detachment from the things of the world. With each choice we define the type of success we seek and, consequently, the destiny that awaits us”.
Once again, the good old woman was right. My publishing house was not mine alone. The new partner was a good man, full of virtues, and had found excellent solutions to serious problems. He simply had a different view from mine in some business aspects. Something natural and not necessarily bad. I needed to dialogue with myself to understand the boundary between what was inadmissible and what was mere captiousness, between intolerance and respect, between pride and humility. I needed to understand whether the problem lay with me, with him, or with both. Then I would invite him to a frank yet gentle conversation. Something within me told me we would find the point of light: a place in the heart where we could coexist well and in peace, despite inevitable differences. I only thought this, without saying anything to Aunt Francisca.
The folk healer smiled and, as if guessing my thoughts, asked me for a hug. She wanted to listen to my heart just to confirm what she already knew. Then she said: “Vanity grants the illusion of success. That is why it is so difficult to overcome it. Among other traits, vanity manifests itself in the exaggerated desire to be right about everything and every subject. A futile attempt to fill an existential void that will continue to distort behaviours and choices as long as it is not understood. You will go on believing that applause, subservience, and reverence will make up for the lack of something that, no matter how much you search, you will never find in the world. What fills the inner void is an ever more refined understanding of oneself, wrapped in good feelings. Nothing else will suffice”.
She held my hands tenderly and brought the conversation to a close: “Genuine power lies in the richness of the elements that build consciousness. When you discover them and bring them to the surface of life in the form of virtues, in the way you treat yourself and everyone else, you will gain access to personal magic. A way of crossing through the days with authenticity and originality, but also with lightness and gentleness. In other words, without giving up your values and directions, you will be able to move without conflicts, resentments, guilt, or fear. Even if belittled or misunderstood, only these will know success”.
The prayer had ended. I thanked Aunt Francisca for the blessing with a loud kiss on her cheek and left. Like the others, that visit had done me a great deal of good. I left carrying with me the enchantment of finding joy and beauty where before there had been only agony and sadness. Along with two certainties. One is that when conflict is imminent, it almost always means there is a route available that has not yet been perceived. It is the path to success, or, if you prefer, the route of light. If success and light are not aligned, the road is wrong. The other certainty is that I needed to return to Madureira more often.

Mae Geri (前蹴り) – The Power of the Front Kick
Mae Geri is one of the most fundamental and powerful kicks in Karate.
It is simple in appearance, but extremely effective when performed with proper technique.
In full-contact styles like Kyokushin, Mae Geri is a devastating weapon for body attacks and fight control.
Meaning of Mae Geri
Mae (前) = Front
Geri (蹴り) = Kick
So, Mae Geri means “Front Kick.”
It is a direct, straight-line attack — fast, sharp, and powerful.
Historical Background
Mae Geri comes from traditional Okinawan and Japanese Karate.
It became especially powerful and practical in full-contact fighting through Masutatsu Oyama, the founder of Kyokushin.
In Kyokushin, fighters train Mae Geri not only for speed — but for knockout-level body impact.
Types of Mae Geri
1️⃣ Mae Geri Keage – Snapping front kick (quick and sharp)
2️⃣ Mae Geri Kekomi – Thrusting front kick (deep and powerful)
Keage = Speed
Kekomi = Penetrating Power
Both are important in training.
 Technique Breakdown (Step-by-Step)
Start in fighting stance
Lift the knee straight up (high chamber position)
Pull toes back
Extend the leg forward
Strike with the ball of the foot (Kosshi)
Snap back quickly to guard position
Key points:
Keep your back straight
Push hips forward for power
Hands must protect the face
Do not drop your guard
🔹 Target Areas
✔ Solar plexus
✔ Lower ribs
✔ Stomach
✔ Chin (Jodan level)
✔ Thigh (in some situations)
In Kyokushin tournaments, Mae Geri to the body can knock the wind out of the opponent instantly.
🔹 Benefits of Mae Geri Training
✅ Strengthens quadriceps and hip flexors
✅ Improves balance and coordination
✅ Develops core stability
✅ Builds explosive power
✅ Improves flexibility
✅ Enhances timing and distance control
It is one of the best kicks to develop strong basics.
🔹 Training Methods
✔ Shadow practice
✔ Heavy bag training
✔ Pad work
✔ Slow control training
✔ Combination drills
✔ Conditioning exercises
✔ Core strengthening
Many traditional masters, including Masutatsu Oyama, emphasized repetition and conditioning to perfect this kick.
🔹 Common Mistakes
❌ Leaning too far back
❌ Not lifting knee high enough
❌ Not pulling toes back
❌ Dropping hands
❌ Weak hip thrust
Technique is more important than speed.
🔹 Mae Geri in Competition
In Kyokushin:
Mae Geri controls distance
Stops opponent’s forward movement
Creates openings for combinations
Can finish the fight with a strong body shot
A perfectly timed Mae Geri can change the entire match.
🔹 Mental Discipline
Mae Geri teaches:
Precision
Focus
Control
Discipline
Timing
A true karateka does not kick wildly.
He kicks with purpose, control, and spirit.
 Conclusion
Mae Geri may look simple —
but in the hands of a trained fighter, it becomes a powerful weapon.
Strong basics create strong champions.
Train hard.
Perfect the chamber.
Drive the hips.
Strike with focus.

" They Loaded Forbidden Ammo—And Turned Night Into a Beam of Red Death..........."

The jungle was alive with screaming. Not animal screaming. Not the howl of wind through the canopy. Human screaming. Hundreds of voices rising together in a sound that had frozen the blood of American soldiers across the Pacific for 3 years. Sergeant William Miller pressed his eye to the darkness and felt his stomach drop through the floor of the halftrack. The treeine was moving.

 It wasn't shadows. It wasn't his imagination. The entire edge of the jungle was surging forward like a wave made of bayonets and rage. Banzai, the word traveled down the defensive line in horse whispers. Men checked their ammunition. Men said prayers they hadn't spoken since childhood. The foxholes that had seemed deep enough an hour ago now felt like shallow graves waiting to be filled. This wasn't a probing attack.

This wasn't harassment fire. And this was a full regimental charge. Hundreds of Japanese infantry pouring out of the darkness with fixed bayonets and the absolute intention of dying on American steel. Miller looked at the four Browning M2 machine guns mounted above his head and made a decision that would have gotten him court marshaled 24 hours earlier.

 He grabbed the canvas bag from under his seat and started feeding a belt of ammunition into the first gun. The loader next to him stared at the brass casings and his face went pale. Sarge, that's the forbidden mix. I know exactly what it is. Command said anyone caught loading that ratio would be command isn't here. Load the guns. What Miller was feeding into those weapons was technically against regulations.

 It was dangerous to the crew. It was destructive to the equipment. A and in approximately 90 seconds, it was going to turn a desperate last stand into a massacre that the Japanese survivors would describe in horrified whispers for the rest of their lives. The M16 multiple gun motor carriage had spent 6 months being the most mocked vehicle in the Pacific theater.

 The infantry called it the bird watcher because that's all it ever did. Watch birds, watch clouds, watch empty sky while real soldiers fought and died in the mud below. It was designed to shoot down Japanese aircraft. But the Japanese aircraft were already gone. The American fighters had swept them from the sky like dust from a shelf.

 What remained of the Imperial Japanese Air Force was being hoarded for kamicazi attacks against the Navy. They weren't wasting precious planes on ground support. And so the M16 crews sat in their vehicles day after day, scanning for threats that never came. They became a joke. The riflemen would walk past and ask if they had spotted any dangerous sparrows.

 The tank crews would radio mock air raid warnings just to watch the flack wagons spin their turrets toward empty clouds. The logistics officers complained constantly about the fuel consumption and the specialized ammunition. The halftrack burned gasoline at an alarming rate for a vehicle that never fired a shot in anger.

 But the crulest insult was the nickname that infantry commanders used when they thought the crews couldn't hear. Target magnet. The M16 had armor that could stop rifle rounds, but it was thin by any real standard. The open turret design meant the gunner stood exposed from the chest up during operation. And the vehicle was tall and visible. It drew attention.

 And in a war where Japanese anti-tank teams hunted anything larger than a jeep, attention was the last thing you wanted. Miller had listened to these insults for months, he had watched his crews morale crumble under the weight of being called useless. He had filed requests to be reassigned to literally any other duty. The requests were denied.

 High command had shipped thousands of M16s to the Pacific, and they weren't going to admit the deployment was a mistake. So, the bird watchers stayed in their halftracks and watched the war happen around them. But Miller was not the kind of man who accepted uselessness. He was a mechanic before the war, a man who understood machines on an intuitive level.

 He spent the long empty hours studying the Maxin turret, learning its capabilities by testing its limits. And he discovered something that the training manuals never mentioned. The four M2 Browning machine guns could depress to fire horizontally. They weren't locked to anti-aircraft angles. Just before he was scheduled to die by lethal injection, a death row inmate made one final request: to see his young daughter, whom he hadn’t held in three years.

What she whispered in his ear would unravel a five-year-old conviction, expose corruption at the highest levels of the justice system, and reveal a secret no one was prepared for.

The clock on the wall read 6:00 a.m. when the guards opened the cell of Daniel Foster, who had spent the last five years on death row at the Huntsville Unit in Texas.

For five years, Daniel had shouted his innocence into concrete walls that never answered back. Now, with only hours left before his scheduled execution, he had just one request.

“I want to see my daughter,” he said, his voice hoarse. “Just once. Please let me see Emily before it’s over.”

One guard looked at him with sympathy. Another shook his head.

But the request reached the desk of Warden Robert Mitchell, a 60-year-old veteran who had overseen more executions than he cared to remember. Something about Daniel’s case had always unsettled him. The evidence had seemed airtight—his fingerprints on the weapon, blood on his clothes, a neighbor claiming to see him leaving the house that night.

Yet Daniel’s eyes never looked like those of a killer.

After a long pause, Mitchell gave the order. “Bring the child.”

Three hours later, a white state vehicle pulled into the prison lot. A social worker stepped out, holding the hand of an eight-year-old girl with blonde hair and solemn blue eyes.

Emily Foster walked through the prison corridor without crying. Without trembling. Inmates fell silent as she passed.

When she entered the visitation room, Daniel was shackled to the table, thinner than she remembered, wearing a faded orange jumpsuit.

“My baby girl…” he whispered, tears filling his eyes.

Emily stepped forward slowly. She didn’t run. She didn’t cry.

Title: “The Merchant of War: Zubayr Rahma Mansur and the Shadows of Sudan”
Zubayr Rahma Mansur, born around 1830 in the Bahr el-Ghazal region of what is today South Sudan, remains one of the most controversial and enigmatic figures in 19th-century African history. Often remembered as both a warlord and a merchant, Zubayr’s life exemplified the tumultuous intersection of local African power dynamics, the expansionist ambitions of Egypt under Khedive Ismail, and the creeping influence of the British Empire along the Nile.
Rise from Humble Beginnings
Zubayr Rahma Mansur began his career not as a soldier, but as a trader. He came from a modest family but quickly understood the immense wealth that lay in controlling trade along the vast, sparsely governed regions of Sudan. By the 1850s, he had established himself as a dominant figure in the ivory and slave trade, a path that would define his fortune and his notoriety. His trading caravans, often protected by armed followers, extended deep into the interior, reaching into the lands of the Dinka, Shilluk, and other indigenous groups.
The Warlord Emerges
By the 1860s, Zubayr’s wealth allowed him to raise a private army, sometimes reported as numbering thousands. This force gave him both economic leverage and political clout. He challenged local chieftains, imposed his own taxation system, and created a quasi-state in Bahr el-Ghazal, effectively functioning independently of Egyptian oversight. His autonomy, however, made him a target for the Egyptian administration, which sought to consolidate control over Sudanese territories.
Conflict with Egypt and Britain
Zubayr’s growing power was a direct threat to the ambitions of Khedive Ismail of Egypt, who was trying to extend authority over Sudanese lands as part of a larger vision of modernization and resource extraction. The Egyptians attempted multiple military campaigns to subdue him, but Zubayr’s knowledge of the terrain, combined with loyalty from his forces, allowed him to resist. His campaigns became legendary: he was ruthless, strategic, and fiercely independent.
The British, too, watched Zubayr closely. While not directly involved at first, they recognized that his semi-independent power represented both an opportunity and a challenge to their regional interests along the Nile. His story intersects with the broader history of colonial competition in Africa, where local leaders like Zubayr could leverage European rivalries to their own advantage, at least temporarily.
Legacy of Controversy
Zubayr Rahma Mansur’s life is fraught with moral ambiguity. On one hand, he was a skilled leader, a shrewd strategist, and an astute merchant who carved out a kingdom in an era of external domination. On the other, he was heavily involved in the slave trade, which brought immense suffering to thousands. This duality makes him a figure both reviled and admired in Sudanese history.
After years of conflict, Zubayr was eventually captured and taken to Cairo, where he was imprisoned. Despite his downfall, his legend endured: he represented the power of local agency against imperial forces, a reminder that African leaders were not merely passive victims of European or Egyptian expansion.
Conclusion: A Complex Shadow
Zubayr Rahma Mansur’s story is more than a tale of war and trade; it is a reflection of Sudan in the 19th century—fragmented, contested, and caught between local ambitions and foreign domination. He is remembered as the “Merchant of War,” a man whose wealth and ruthlessness challenged empires, leaving a legacy that still sparks debate among historians today. His life invites reflection on the fine line between leadership and exploitation, autonomy and complicity, making him one of the most fascinating—and polarizing—figures in African history.

The Power Broker: Why William Nyuon Was Vital.
The powerful statement from Hon. James Kok Rueh, and it touches on one of the most critical, yet often overlooked, chapters of the South Sudanese liberation struggle.
​To understand why Kok Rueh would make such a definitive claim, we have to look at the 1983 Bor Mutiny and the internal dynamics of the nascent SPLA/M.

​The Power Broker: Why William Nyuon Was Vital
​William Nyuon Bany wasn't just another officer; he was a bridge. Here is why his support for Dr. John Garang was a "make or break" moment for the movement:
​The Anyanya II Connection: Before the SPLA fully formed, many South Sudanese fighters were part of Anyanya II. William Nyuon had significant influence within these ranks. His decision to align with Garang—rather than rival factions—brought a massive amount of "boots on the ground" and legitimacy to Garang's leadership.

​Military Credibility: While Dr. John Garang was the intellectual and strategic visionary (the PhD soldier), William Nyuon was a grassroots, battle-hardened commander. In the early days, soldiers followed men they knew in the trenches. Nyuon provided the military backbone that allowed Garang to consolidate political power.

​Ethnic and Regional Unity: At a time when the movement could have easily fractured along ethnic lines, Nyuon (a Nuer) throwing his weight behind Garang (a Dinka) was the primary signal that the SPLA was a national movement, not a tribal one.

​The Weight of the Statement
​When a politician like James Kok Rueh says Garang "would not have led" without Nyuon, he is highlighting a historical truth: Leadership is a coalition. Garang had the vision for "New Sudan," but Nyuon had the keys to the soldiers' loyalty in the bush. Without Nyuon’s initial backing, Garang might have remained an intellectual in exile rather than the leader of a revolutionary army.

​A Complex Legacy
​Of course, history is rarely a straight line. The relationship between the two men eventually fractured during the internal splits of the 1990s, which makes Kok Rueh’s retrospective comment even more poignant. It serves as a reminder that the foundation of South Sudan’s independence was built on these high-stakes personal alliances.

The Lion of the Dinka, son of Kuethpiny’s proud lineage, drinks nothing but milk and water. A man of iron skin but a gentle soul, he stands as a peerless fighter through every season.

While others sought safety in exile on distant shores or in foreign universities, Salva Kiir remained anchored to the unforgiving Sudanese terrain, holding the ground for his people in every war that broke out  - for five decades! He chose to stay💪. 

Should we mock a decorated sentinel committed to defending his people to the very hilt, just because of frailty?  No!

Though the world of academic ink and heavy books remains foreign to him, he speaks the language of the brave men in tangled thorny bush with absolute fluency.

He became a master of the unseen path, after many years of moving his men with a silence more profound than a serpent’s glide. To him, the scrubland holds no secrets; he is a tactician of the wild who understands the rhythm of the field better than any scholar would understand a page. 

This journey began in the heat of his youth - at only fifteen years old, he claimed his first rifle and his file number, marking the start of a five-decade march through the weary miles of war. He saw blood and tears of his people flowing for decades until they won their freedom.

Now, as the light begins to change, he reflects the inevitable truth of the horizon: for even the fiercest warrior, when the golden disc finally descends, it sets for every man alike.

Ver o interesse dos animais não significa querer ou fazer com que esse interesse prevaleça, mas reconhecer esse interesse é reconhecer também um conflito de interesses.

Mesmo que o interesse deles não prevaleça, dizer que não há um interesse conflitante não faz sentido, embora seja comum porque gostamos de promover a ideia de que os animais experimentam e vivem o que devem experimentar e viver, e como se suas vidas não pudessem (pelo imperativo do não dever) ser outra coisa que não resultado desse interesse.

Mas, mesmo impondo limitações aos animais com base no interesse humano, o animal não cabe dentro do interesse humano, porque ele transborda, e transborda o que não é interesse humano - ele sempre ultrapassa esse interesse, independentemente de onde veio e para onde vai, e porque o animal não humano não pode reconhecer-se como na medida do interesse humano. Como pode uma vida senciente ser medida do interesse utilitário de outra vida?

Há sempre algo no animal não humano que não pode ser compatibilizado com nosso interesse deslocado do interesse dele. Quem pode dizer que um animal vive dentro da medida perfeita de nossa vontade e porque ele é a medida perfeita de nossa vontade? E que fora de nossa vontade, esgota-se o animal porque nada há nele além disso. Isso só seria possível se o animal não fosse animal, se fosse vazio em vontades e interesses.

Não importa se pensamos em animais criados nas piores condições ou em condições consideradas aceitáveis aos objetivos que definimos. Qualquer ideia de que um animal pode ser resumido a uma vivência que é vivência em forma da realização de um desejo humano equivoca-se se conclui que o animal “é o que é” porque ele não pode ser nada além de limite ou extensão do que queremos.

É pelo transbordamento de si, não humano, que impomos os limites que destroem os animais para que não sejam quem são, para que não possam ser quem são, porque é na mistura contraditória do “quem” e do “que”, que sobre eles decidimos o que queremos, como o tempo de viver e o tempo de morrer. Assim o animal é vida para o que queremos a partir da vida (o que é permitido como vida) e morte para o que queremos a partir da morte.

My brother Kamran khawaja

After my boyfriend died in a crash, I was already shattered—then life slammed another blow. I was pregnant, carrying twins. The stress strangled my body, forcing strict bed rest and 24‑hour monitoring; I couldn’t even be alone. With nowhere else to go, I slipped into my dad’s house. My mom had left us years before, and my dad had remarried a younger, impeccably polished woman named Veronica. I hoped we could coexist, that the babies could find stability in his home.

At first, it was bearable. Yet I always felt like an intruder, watched by Veronica as if I were a temporary guest. Dad tried to keep the peace, never siding with her, never confronting her. Then cancer struck—swift, brutal. We counted days instead of plans.

Dad passed away. I barely had a moment to grieve before Veronica’s cruelty revealed itself. Less than 36 hours after the funeral, she declared the house hers. I was the unwanted baggage. My pregnancy mattered not.

“Pack your stuff. You have 36 hours. I don’t want babies in my home!” she barked. I froze. “I’m due in two weeks. Where am I supposed to go?”

She shrugged. “A motel. A shelter. Not my problem.”

My legs gave out. “Dad would never—”

“Dad’s not here,” she snapped. “I am.” She smirked, calling the boyfriend she’d been hiding. “Throw her out.” “She doesn’t belong here!”

She grabbed my arm and tried to shove me out into the pouring rain. But it was too late. Within eight hours, she herself found herself without a roof over her head.

Everyone Crossed The Street To Avoid The 'Monster' Bleeding In The Alley, But When I Saw What They Did To His Teeth, I Realized He Wasn't The Killer—He Was The Victim Used To Train Them.

The rain in Chicago cuts right through you in November.

It’s a bone-deep cold that settles in your marrow and refuses to leave.

But I wasn't shivering because of the weather.

I was shivering because of the text message flashing on my phone screen at 11:42 PM.

"Big gray pit. South side, behind the old auto plant. Bleeding out. Looks vicious. Don't get close, he looks like a fighter."

I’ve been doing animal rescue for ten years.

I’ve seen things that would make a grown man drop to his knees and weep.

But the words "looks like a fighter" always trigger a specific kind of dread in the pit of my stomach.

It means danger.

It means a dog that has been programmed to kill, a dog that associates humans with pain and other dogs with death.

It usually means a one-way trip to the vet for a final injection, because nobody can rehab the demons out of a true fighting dog.

Or so I thought.

I grabbed my catch pole—the heavy-duty one—and my thickest bite gloves.

I threw them into the back of my Jeep and drove south.

The city changes when you cross into the industrial district.

The streetlights burn out and don't get replaced.

The potholes get deeper.

The shadows get longer.

I parked the Jeep at the mouth of the alley.

The rain was coming down in sheets now, drumming against the metal roof of the car like bullets.

I took a breath.

"Okay," I whispered to myself. "Just assess the situation. Do not be a hero."

I stepped out.

The smell hit me instantly.

Wet cardboard. Old grease. And underneath it all, that unmistakable, metallic tang of fresh blood.

I clicked on my tactical flashlight.

The beam cut through the rain, sweeping over overflowing dumpsters and piles of discarded tires.

And then I saw him.

He was massive.

A gray hulk of muscle, huddled in the corner where two brick walls met.

The text wasn't lying.

He looked like a nightmare.

His ears were cropped short—a jagged, amateur job done with kitchen scissors, likely years ago.

His face was a roadmap of scars, old white lines crossing over fresh, weeping wounds.

He was covered in mud and blood, his breathing ragged and heavy.

As the light hit his face, he stiffened.

A low rumble started in his chest.

It was a sound so deep I could feel it vibrating in the soles of my boots.

"Easy, big boy," I said, my voice trembling.

I kept the catch pole ready, the loop open.

I needed to get that loop over his head before he could launch at me.

If this was a fighting dog, he could cover the ten feet between us in a fraction of a second.

He lifted his head.

His eyes were swollen shut on the left side, but the right eye fixed on me.

It wasn't the look of a killer, though.

It was the look of something broken.

But I couldn't trust that.

I took a step forward.

He flinched, pulling his lips back in a snarl.

This was it. The strike zone.

I braced myself for the lunge.

I watched his mouth open, expecting to see the flash of ivory daggers that could crush bone.

But when his lips pulled back... I froze.

I dropped the catch pole.

It clattered loudly on the wet pavement, but I didn't care.

I felt the air leave my lungs in a sharp gasp.

"Oh my god," I whispered.

There were no fangs.

There were no teeth.

His mouth was a ruin of inflamed, purple gum tissue.

Every single tooth had been filed down.

Not broken. Filed.

Sawed down to the gum line with a rasp, likely while he was tied down and screaming.

The realization hit me like a freight train.

He wasn't a fighter.

He wasn't a champion in the ring.

He was the bait.

He was the practice dummy.

They had stripped him of his only weapon so the other dogs—the "real" fighters—could tear him apart without fear of getting hurt themselves.

He had been thrown into a ring, defenseless, to be chewed on for sport.

And when he finally couldn't stand up anymore, they had dumped him here like garbage.

The anger that flared in my chest was so hot it almost blinded me.

I fell to my knees in the mud.

I didn't care about the protocols anymore.

I didn't care about the bite gloves.

"I'm so sorry," I choked out, tears mixing with the rain on my face. "I am so, so sorry."

The dog watched me, confused.

He was waiting for the blow.

He was waiting for the pain.

I reached out my hand.

My bare hand.

It was the most dangerous thing you could do, even with a toothless dog. The pressure of those jaws could still break my wrist.

But I needed him to know.

I needed him to know that this hand wasn't going to hit him.

He flinched again, pressing his head back against the brick wall.

"It's okay," I whispered. "I've got you."

Slowly, agonizingly slowly, he stretched his neck forward.

He sniffed my fingers.

He smelled the scent of my own dogs on my skin.

And then, he did the last thing I expected.

He didn't snap.

He didn't growl.

He leaned forward and dragged his rough, warm tongue across my palm.

One lick. Then another.

He let out a long, shuddering sigh and collapsed his heavy head into my hand.

He was surrendering.

Not to death, but to me.

I scooped my arms under his bloody, shivering body.

He weighed at least eighty pounds, dead weight, but adrenaline gave me strength I didn't know I had.

I lifted him up, his blood soaking immediately into my jacket.

"I'm taking you home," I promised him, walking as fast as I could back to the Jeep. "And nobody is ever going to hurt you again."

But as I laid him in the back seat and saw the extent of the damage under the dome light, I realized that saving him from the alley was just the beginning.

The real fight was just starting.

And I wasn't sure if he had enough life left in him to win it.

SEBELUM RESI TERBIT
​Panggilan dari Frekuensi Terlarang
​Sebelum badai Januari menerjang, Kenzo duduk di atas motornya yang terparkir di pinggir tebing dimensi. iPod tuanya berderit, mengeluarkan suara statis yang menyakitkan telinga. Itu bukan lagu, melainkan frekuensi dari Sektor Terlupakan.
​Kenzo melihat bayangan Laras di permukaan air yang tenang—Laras yang asli, yang jiwanya sedang memudar. Di saat yang sama, ia menerima notifikasi di layar retaknya: “Permintaan Pengiriman Jiwa: Alamat Toko Buku Elias.”
​Ia tahu ini adalah paket terlarang. Di dunia kurir dimensi, mengirimkan memori ke tubuh yang sudah kosong adalah dosa besar. Tapi Kenzo melihat sesuatu yang lain; ia melihat kesempatan untuk "menghidupkan" Laras kembali, meski harus meminjam raga wanita lain bernama Clara.

​Perjalanan Melintasi Badai
​Kenzo memacu motornya menembus dinding ruang dan waktu. Tubuhnya mulai mengalami glitch—tangannya sesekali berubah menjadi kode digital biru yang transparan. Setiap kilometer yang ia tempuh menuju dunia Elias, satu bagian dari ingatan Kenzo tentang dirinya sendiri terhapus.
​"Jika aku memberikan memori ini pada Clara," bisik Kenzo pada kegelapan, "maka Laras akan hidup di sana, tapi aku akan mati di sini."
​Saat ia tiba di depan Toko Buku Elias, badai Januari 2026 sedang di puncaknya. Ia melihat Elias dari balik kaca jendela, pria yang sudah kehilangan segalanya. Di situlah Kenzo sadar: Dia bukan sedang menolong Elias, dia sedang mengantar kematian bagi dirinya sendiri.

***************************
​NEGOSIASI DENGAN MAUT
Di Persimpangan Sektor Terlupakan
​Sebelum sampai ke toko buku, Kenzo harus menarik jiwa Laras dari jurang dimensi. Di sana, Laras berdiri di sebuah jembatan yang runtuh, dikelilingi kabut putih yang mematikan.
​Kenzo: "Laras! Ikut aku! Aku punya jalan keluar. Kau bisa kembali ke dunia nyata."
​Laras: (Menoleh dengan mata redup) "Ke dunia nyata? Bagaimana bisa, Kenzo? Tubuhku sudah menjadi abu setahun yang lalu."
​Kenzo: "Ada seorang wanita... Clara. Pikirannya kosong karena trauma. Aku akan menyisipkan jiwamu ke sana. Kau akan hidup lagi. Kau bisa merasakan hangatnya matahari lagi!"
​Laras: (Mendekat, menyentuh wajah Kenzo yang mulai retak digital) "Lalu bagaimana denganmu? Apa yang kau berikan pada penjaga dimensi sebagai gantinya?"
​Kenzo: (Tersenyum getir) "Hanya sebuah nama, Laras. Nama yang tidak akan ada gunanya lagi jika kau tidak ada di dunia itu. Aku akan menjadi bayanganmu. Aku akan menjagamu dari balik tabir."
​Laras: "Jangan lakukan ini, Kenzo! Itu bukan hidup! Itu adalah penjara abadi di mana kau bisa melihat tapi tidak bisa memiliki!"
​Kenzo: "Aku lebih memilih dipenjara sambil melihatmu tersenyum, daripada bebas di dunia yang tidak memiliki jejakmu sama sekali. Sekarang, masuklah ke kotak ini. Jangan menoleh ke belakang."

​Dialog Terakhir di Sudut Toko Buku
​Kembali ke badai Januari 2026. Kenzo berdiri di depan Elias yang sudah gila karena duka. Sebelum Elias membuka kotak itu, Kenzo mencengkeram bahunya keras-keras.
​Kenzo: "Dengarkan aku, Elias! Sekali kau membuka kotak ini, tidak ada jalan kembali. Wanita yang akan berdiri di depanmu nanti memiliki wajah Clara, tapi jiwanya adalah Laras—wanitaku."
​Elias: (Tersenyum gila) "Aku tidak peduli! Aku tidak peduli siapa yang ada di dalam sana, asalkan dia tidak menatapku dengan ketakutan! Aku butuh seseorang untuk mencintaiku, Kenzo!"
​Kenzo: "Kau egois! Kau membunuh identitas Clarumu demi ambisimu sendiri! Dan kau tahu apa yang paling lucu? Dia akan mengingat namamu, tapi dia akan memimpikan aku setiap malam. Kau akan memeluk tubuhnya, tapi hatinya akan menangis memanggil pria yang bahkan tidak bisa kau ingat namanya."
​Elias: "Biarkan saja! Biarkan kami saling menyiksa dalam kepalsuan ini, daripada aku mati dalam kesepian! Cepat berikan kotaknya!"
​Kenzo: (Melepaskan kotak itu dengan tangan gemetar) "Satu menit dari sekarang, namaku akan hilang dari ingatanmu. Kau akan melihatku sebagai debu di udara. Selamat atas kebahagiaan palsumu, Elias."

DETIK-DETIK PENGIRIMAN 
​Clara: (Tiba-tiba berhenti menjerit, matanya berubah menjadi biru terang saat kotak itu terbuka) "Kenzo...?"
​Elias: (Mencoba memeluknya) "Clara! Ini aku, Elias! Kau sudah kembali!"
​Clara (Laras): (Melihat menembus Elias, matanya terpaku pada Kenzo yang mulai memudar) "Kenzo, jangan pergi! Kenapa tanganmu menghilang?! tuan, bantu dia! Kenapa kau diam saja?!"
​Elias: (Bingung, melihat ke arah Kenzo tapi matanya tidak bisa fokus) "Bantu siapa, sayang? Tidak ada siapa-siapa di sini. Hanya ada kita berdua. Kau hanya berhalusinasi karena kelelahan."
​Kenzo: (Berbisik di telinga Elias untuk terakhir kalinya) "Selamat datang di neraka yang kau buat sendiri, kawan."
​
RESI AIR MATA: PENGIRIMAN YANG MENGHANCURKAN JIWA
​Perjanjian Berdarah di Toko Buku
​Di tengah badai Januari 2026, toko buku Elias bukan lagi tempat bernaung, melainkan peti mati bagi kenangan. Elias bersimpuh di kaki Clara, meraung sambil memegangi ujung gaun wanita itu.
​"Siapa Anda? Tolong lepaskan saya, Tuan!" teriak Clara dengan wajah ketakutan. Ia memandang Elias seolah pria itu adalah orang asing yang mengerikan.
​Kenzo berdiri di pintu, menyaksikan kehancuran itu. Hatinya yang sudah retak sejak kehilangan Laila, kini pecah berkeping-keping. "Elias, hentikan," suara Kenzo bergetar. "Dia tidak ada lagi di sana. Kau hanya menyakitinya."

​Elias menoleh, wajahnya basah oleh air mata dan ingus, matanya hancur. "Kau kurir dimensi, kan?! Ambilkan dia kembali! Ambil jiwanya dari neraka mana pun! Aku akan memberikan apa saja! Ambil nyawaku, Kenzo! Ambil!"
Kenzo berjalan mendekat, mengeluarkan sebuah kotak hitam kecil yang berdenyut seperti detak jantung. "Harganya bukan nyawamu, Elias," kata Kenzo dingin, sementara tubuhnya sendiri mulai transparan terkena cahaya lampu toko. "Harganya adalah namaku. Saat paket ini terbuka, kau akan mendapatkan 'dia', tapi kau—dan seluruh dunia—akan melupakan bahwa aku pernah ada. Aku akan menjadi hantu di antara kalian."
​Elias tidak peduli. Ia merampas kotak itu. "Lakukan! Kirimkan sekarang!"

​Dialog yang Menyayat Hati
​Kenzo menarik kerah jaket Elias, membawanya ke sudut ruangan. "Kau tahu apa harganya? Aku harus pergi ke Sektor Terlupakan. Aku harus menemui Laras. Dan jika aku membawa memori Clara kembali, aku tidak akan pernah bisa pulang. Aku akan terjebak di sana, melihat Laras setiap detik tanpa pernah bisa memeluknya. Aku akan menjadi hantu yang kelaparan akan sentuhan!"​Elias tertawa histeris di tengah tangisnya. "Setidaknya kau bisa melihatnya! Aku? Aku melihat Clara setiap hari tapi dia menatapku seperti sampah! Itu lebih sakit dari kematian, Kenzo! Tolong aku..."​Kenzo melepaskan cengkeramannya. Ia memandang foto Laras di dompetnya yang sudah usang. "Baik. Jika ini satu-satunya cara agar tidak ada lagi pria yang menangis seperti pecundang di depan wanita yang ia cintai... aku akan pergi."

​Pertemuan yang Menyakitkan di Halte Biru
​Di dimensi sunyi, Kenzo bertemu Laras. Namun, pertemuan ini bukan reuni yang indah. Laras menangis tersedu-sedu saat melihat Kenzo datang membawa kotak memori itu.
​"Jangan lakukan ini, Kenzo! Jika kau menyerahkan detak jantungmu untuk kotak ini, kau akan merasakannya... rasa sakit saat tubuhmu hancur namun jiwamu dipaksa tetap sadar," tangis Laras pecah.
​"Aku lebih baik hancur bersamamu di sini, daripada hidup di atas sana tanpa arti, Laras," Kenzo berteriak, air matanya jatuh ke tanah dimensi yang hampa, menguap sebelum menyentuh bumi.
​Mereka mencoba berpelukan untuk terakhir kalinya, namun tubuh Kenzo mulai berubah menjadi partikel cahaya kebiruan. Rasanya seperti ribuan jarum menusuk setiap sarafnya. Kenzo melolong kesakitan, sebuah teriakan yang mengguncang dimensi sunyi itu. "AAAAAAKHH! SAKIIIT, LARAS! SAKIIIT!"

​Puncak Tragedi: Sakura yang Berdarah
​Di dunia nyata, bunga sakura pertama gugur. Elias membuka kotak itu di depan Clara. Seketika, memori membanjiri otak Clara seperti tsunami.
​"Elias..." Clara berbisik. Ia mengingat semuanya. Tapi di saat yang sama, ia melihat bayangan Kenzo yang sedang hancur di depan matanya. Clara menjerit, menutupi telinganya. "Siapa pria itu?! Kenapa dia berteriak?! Kenapa dia hancur demi aku?!"
​Elias memeluk Clara, namun hatinya dihantam kenyataan pahit. Ia mendapatkan cintanya kembali, tapi ia harus menyaksikan seorang pria asing mati dengan cara yang paling mengerikan untuk mewujudkannya. Elias menangis sejadi-jadinya, meraung di bahu Clara.
​"Maafkan aku, Kenzo! Maafkan keegoisanku!" teriak Elias ke arah udara kosong.

​Penjara Tanpa Dinding
​Kenzo kini berada di sisi Laras. Tapi tragisnya, karena ia adalah "Kurir Abadi", ia dihukum untuk tetap membawa beban perasaan semua orang yang pernah ia antar paketnya.​Ia berdiri di tengah taman, tepat di samping Elias dan Clara yang sedang berpelukan. Kenzo mencoba menyentuh pipi Laras yang ada di sampingnya, tapi tangannya kini benar-benar hanya udara. Ia bisa merasakan kehangatan air mata Laras, tapi tidak bisa menghapusnya.​Kenzo melihat ke arah iPod di tangannya. Layarnya retak, mengeluarkan darah digital yang kental. Sebuah pesan terakhir muncul, sebuah pesan yang paling menyakitkan dari semua.

​"Kau telah mengantar paket terakhir. Harganya adalah: Kau akan mencintai mereka selamanya, tapi mereka akan melupakan namamu dalam satu jam ke depan. Kau akan sendirian dalam keramaian, Kenzo. Selamanya."​Kenzo jatuh berlutut di aspal taman yang ramai. Orang-orang berjalan menembus dadanya. Ia berteriak memanggil nama Laras, memanggil nama Elias, tapi tidak ada yang menoleh. Hanya kesunyian yang menjawab tawanya yang pecah menjadi tangisan pilu.​Di bawah pohon sakura yang indah, Kenzo hancur. Ia sukses mengirimkan kebahagiaan, namun ia adalah satu-satunya orang yang tertinggal dalam kegelapan yang tak berujung.

​THE TRAGIC LOVE STORY OF AN INTERDIMENSIONAL COURIER 🛵
​BEFORE THE TRACKING NUMBER WAS ISSUED
​A Call from the Forbidden Frequency
Before the storms of January struck, Kenzo sat on his motorcycle parked at the edge of a dimensional cliff. His old iPod crackled, emitting a static sound that pained the ears. It wasn't a song; it was a frequency from the Forgotten Sector.
​Kenzo saw Laras’s reflection in the still water—the real Laras, whose soul was fading away. Simultaneously, a notification appeared on his cracked screen: "Soul Delivery Request: Elias Bookstore Address."
​He knew this was a forbidden package. In the world of dimensional couriers, delivering a memory into an empty body is a cardinal sin. But Kenzo saw something else; he saw a chance to "revive" Laras, even if it meant borrowing the body of another woman named Clara.
​A Journey Through the Storm
Kenzo accelerated his bike, piercing through the walls of space and time. His body began to glitch—his hands occasionally turning into transparent blue digital code. For every kilometer he traveled toward Elias’s world, a piece of Kenzo’s own memory of himself was erased.
​"If I give this memory to Clara," Kenzo whispered into the darkness, "then Laras will live there, but I will die here."
​When he arrived at Elias Bookstore, the January 2026 storm was at its peak. He saw Elias through the glass window—a man who had lost everything. It was then Kenzo realized: He wasn't helping Elias; he was delivering his own death.
​NEGOTIATING WITH DEATH
​At the Crossroads of the Forgotten Sector
Before reaching the bookstore, Kenzo had to pull Laras's soul from the dimensional abyss. There, Laras stood on a collapsing bridge, surrounded by lethal white mist.
​Kenzo: "Laras! Come with me! I have a way out. You can return to the real world."
Laras: (Turning with dim eyes) "To the real world? How, Kenzo? My body turned to ash a year ago."
Kenzo: "There is a woman... Clara. Her mind is empty due to trauma. I will insert your soul there. You will live again. You can feel the warmth of the sun again!"
Laras: (Approaching, touching Kenzo’s digitally cracking face) "And what about you? What are you giving the Dimensional Gatekeeper in exchange?"
Kenzo: (With a bitter smile) "Just a name, Laras. A name that will be useless if you aren't in that world. I will become your shadow. I will watch over you from behind the veil."
Laras: "Don’t do this, Kenzo! That isn't living! That is an eternal prison where you can see but never possess!"
Kenzo: "I would rather be imprisoned while watching you smile than be free in a world that holds no trace of you. Now, get into this box. Do not look back."
​The Final Dialogue in the Corner of the Bookstore
Back to the storm of January 2026. Kenzo stood before Elias, who was driven mad by grief. Before Elias could open the box, Kenzo gripped his shoulder tightly.
​Kenzo: "Listen to me, Elias! Once you open this box, there is no going back. The woman who will stand before you will have Clara's face, but her soul belongs to Laras—my woman."
Elias: (Smiling insanely) "I don't care! I don't care who is inside, as long as she doesn't look at me with fear! I need someone to love me, Kenzo!"
Kenzo: "You are selfish! You are killing Clara’s identity for your own ambition! And you know what’s funniest? She will remember your name, but she will dream of me every night. You will hold her body, but her heart will cry out for a man whose name you won't even be able to remember."
Elias: "So be it! Let us torture each other in this falsehood, rather than me dying in loneliness! Give me the box, now!"
Kenzo: (Releasing the box with trembling hands) "One minute from now, my name will vanish from your memory. You will see me as mere dust in the air. Congratulations on your fake happiness, Elias."
​The Moment of Delivery
Clara: (Suddenly stops screaming, her eyes turning bright blue as the box opens) "Kenzo...?"
Elias: (Trying to hug her) "Clara! It’s me, Elias! You’re back!"
Clara (Laras): (Looking right through Elias, her eyes fixed on Kenzo who is starting to fade) "Kenzo, don’t go! Why is your hand disappearing?! Sir, help him! Why are you just standing there?!"
Elias: (Confused, looking toward Kenzo but unable to focus his eyes) "Help who, darling? There’s no one here. It’s just the two of us. You’re just hallucinating from exhaustion."
Kenzo: (Whispering into Elias's ear for the last time) "Welcome to the hell you created for yourself, my friend."
​RECEIPT OF TEARS: A SOUL-CRUSHING DELIVERY
​A Bloody Covenant
In the midst of the January 2026 storm, Elias’s bookstore was no longer a shelter, but a coffin for memories. Elias knelt at Clara's feet, wailing while clutching the hem of her dress.
​"Who are you? Please let me go, Sir!" Clara screamed in terror, looking at Elias as if he were a terrifying stranger. Kenzo stood at the door, witnessing the devastation. His heart, already cracked since losing Laila, now shattered into pieces. "Elias, stop," Kenzo’s voice trembled. "She is no longer there. You are only hurting her."
​Elias turned, his face wet with tears and snot, his eyes broken. "You’re a dimensional courier, right?! Bring her back! Take her soul from whatever hell it’s in! I’ll give you anything! Take my life, Kenzo! Take it!"
​Kenzo walked closer, pulling out a small black box that throbbed like a heartbeat. "The price isn't your life, Elias," Kenzo said coldly, while his own body began to turn transparent under the shop lights. "The price is my name. When this package opens, you will get 'her', but you—and the entire world—will forget I ever existed. I will become a ghost among you."
​Elias didn't care. He snatched the box. "Do it! Send it now!"
​The Heart-Wrenching Exchange
Kenzo grabbed Elias’s jacket collar, pulling him to the corner of the room. "Do you know the cost? I have to go to the Forgotten Sector. I have to meet Laras. And if I bring Clara’s memory back, I can never go home. I will be trapped there, seeing Laras every second without ever being able to hold her. I will be a ghost hungry for touch!"
​Elias laughed hysterically through his tears. "At least you can see her! Me? I see Clara every day but she looks at me like trash! That is more painful than death, Kenzo! Help me..."
​Kenzo released his grip. He looked at the photo of Laras in his worn-out wallet. "Fine. If this is the only way so that no more men cry like losers in front of the woman they love... I will go."
​THE PUNISHMENT OF THE RECIPIENT: HOLLOW HAPPINESS
​Three months after Elias threw away the receipt, the miracle began to rot. Elias had his Clara back, but he realized something was wrong. Clara remembered his name and his poems, but she no longer had a "soul" behind those memories.
​"Elias, why are you looking at me like that?" Clara asked with a flat smile at the dinner table. Elias went silent. Clara's smile felt like a computer program—perfect but cold. He realized the memories Kenzo delivered were just data. The feelings that accompanied them had burned away when Kenzo shattered in the other dimension.
​The Shadow's Terror
Every night, inside the bookstore that now felt like a tomb, Elias began to hear the sound of paper rustling. He saw the shadow of a man in a courier jacket in the corner of his eye, but when he turned, no one was there.
​Clara began to draw something obsessively. Elias approached, and his heart nearly stopped. Clara was no longer painting Elias's face, but thousands of sketches of a crumpled delivery receipt and a shattered iPod.
​"Who is this, Clara?" Elias asked, his voice shaking violently.
Clara turned with empty eyes that began to leak black tears. "I don't know his name, Elias. But he screams inside my head every time you kiss me. He says... 'I have delivered it, now pay the price.'"
​THE END: A CIRCLE OF REGRET
​Elias finally broke. He ran to the trash can in the city park, clawing through filth and waste, searching for the receipt he threw away months ago. He sobbed, his fingernails bleeding from scratching the earth.
​"Kenzo! Come back! Take these memories back! I don’t want this happiness!" Elias wailed under the cherry blossom tree, which was now barren and dead.
​But there was no answer. In another dimension, Kenzo just stood still, watching Elias who was now mad with regret. Kenzo felt no satisfaction in seeing Elias suffer; he only felt hollow.
​The punishment was complete:
​Kenzo: Forgotten and unable to touch.
​Elias: Possesses the physical body of the one he loves, but has lost her soul forever.
​Clara: Trapped in memories that aren't hers, haunted by the screams of the man who sacrificed his life for her.
​"True love never asks for a sacrifice," the wind whispered in the bookstore, "but selfishness demands everything."
