MOD _ CRTF special task force in Hpasawng

Part One

A few days ago, after crossing mountains and streams, I arrived in the Hpasawng area of Kayah (Karenni) State, where the Central Region Task Force (CRTF), also known as 'Lel-Htoo' and designated as Battalion 9918 under the Ministry of Defence (MOD) of the National Unity Government (NUG), is currently operating. Once you cross the Salween River, you have arrived in Hpasawng.
Along with Lel-Htoo (CRTF) and its alliance armed forces, including KNSA (Karenni National Solidarity Army), also known as 'Kyel-Phyu' (White Star), the Karenni Army (KA), KNPLF (Karenni Nationalities People's Liberation Front), known by the abbreviation 'Ka-La-La-Ta,' KPLA (Karenni People's Liberation Army), KNDF (Karenni Nationalities Defense Force), Hpasawng PDF, Baw Lakhe PDF, and other associated groups formed the combined revolutionary forces and have been blockading and attacking Senior General Min Aung Hlaing's Light Infantry Battalion (LIB) 135 in Hpasawng town for many months. 

On the way, while passing through Mese Township, which is administered by the KNPLF (Ka-La-La-Ta), I witnessed buildings, including the KNPLF headquarters, that had been crumbled and destroyed by bombings from Min Aung Hlaing's air force.
Civilian places, which are completely unrelated to combat, such as Buddhist monasteries, Christian churches, hospitals, and schools, were brutally destroyed. In reality, the revolutionary troops do not station in such public places because they are concerned about harming the public. They live under trees, bamboo clumps, and in residential houses within ruined towns and villages.
Since local informants (Dalans) are everywhere, Min Aung Hlaing's military knows perfectly well that there are no revolutionaries in those hospitals and religious buildings. But these attacks are done on purpose to make people lose faith in the revolution and see the revolutionaries as enemies.

Traveling in the liberated area is truly delightful. Even the simple act of breathing feels free. When I filled up 100,000 kyats' worth of fuel at a gas station, they gave me bottled water as a gift. Haha... just take a look at the writing on the water bottle. It says, 'Let's participate in the revolution by drinking [this] support water. ' Of course, I drank it all!

The camp of the CRTF special task force where I arrived was temporarily stationed in a ruined village near Hpasawng town. They do not stay in one place for long. In this ruined village where the villagers have fled, some stay in about 10 remaining houses, while others stay in makeshift tents hidden in the forest. I observed that they never remain in one place for long stretches of time and are typically stationed at least 100 to 200 feet apart. They have dug bomb shelters (trenches/bunkers) beneath every hut and house that are about ten feet long and deep enough for a person to stand in, and they place a high level of security awareness on the fact that Min Aung Hlaing's planes are hovering constantly and that drones patrol every day.

As soon as I arrived at the camp, they showed me these bunkers and told me to jump in immediately if there was an emergency. We frequently hear the humming sound of aircraft.
When that happens, they shout out, 'Nget-Soe (Bad Bird)!... No, wait... it's Chay-Par-Koung (The Pooper)!... No, it's actually A-Paw-Koung (The Thing Above)!' 'Nget-Soe' (Bad Bird) refers to Jet fighters. 'Chay-Par-Koung' (The Pooper) is the nickname for the Y-12 transport planes, because they drop bombs out of the rear cargo door like they are defecating. 'A-Paw-Koung' (The Thing Above) refers to Unmanned Aerial Vehicle VTOL drones. UAV VTOL can make vertical take-off and landing. 

There was a time when I wasn't sure if I should laugh or cry. We were in a thick forest where big snakes were free to move around. Someone walked in front of me one time and said, "Uncle, I saw a snake about the size of your wrist. Come into this bunker! It crawled right inside! It has stripes; I'm not sure if it’s a poisonous one. I looked into the bunker, but there was nothing there. "It has holes inside," he said.

While we were talking, the sound of an aircraft suddenly appeared. He shouted, 'Into the bunker, quick! Get down!' and pointed to the very bunker the snake had entered. I yelled, 'Hey! That's the hole the snake just went into!' He replied, 'Then let's go to the bunker under the house! Come quick!' and dragged me along. While we ran, the sound of the plane slowly faded away. Phew... nothing happened in the end!

In reality, there is no time to be afraid in a situation where one could encounter enemy attacks at any moment. Since we are already deep within the danger zone, no one can stay inside a bunker all the time, nor would there be any point in doing so.

As for the youths, they are passing their time happily for the sake of the country, rotating between patrolling duties and going to the frontline camps. 

"Arloo Kyaw" is the nickname of a sniper who just got back from the front lines. He has been a part of the revolution since the beginning, so he has now served for over 4 years.
The Ruger Precision Rifle .338 Lapua sniper rifle he holds can penetrate a bulletproof vest from a distance of 3,000 feet, and skilled shooters can successfully hit a target from about one mile away.

Manufactured in the United States, this sniper rifle is renowned worldwide for its accuracy and long-range capabilities. They are far more sophisticated sniper rifles than those in Min Aung Hlaing's military today, according to Arloo Kyaw.

Question: So then, if you were to compare your rifles with the rifles currently used by the snipers in Min Aung Hlaing's ('Ma Ah La') military, what would it be?
Answer: Their rifles are less effective than ours. Ours are much more effective.
Question: So, can we say that your sniper rifles are not outdated when compared to those of military soldiers? 

Answer: Absolutely, ours are advanced ones. I have eliminated around 30 enemies with this rifle; some of my comrades did more than me. 

The code name of the officer in charge of military operations is 'Khway Bee Loo'. He is busy working with communication equipment inside a bunker beneath the house where he is currently staying. He stated that they have initiated preparations as a result of intelligence that Min Aung Hlaing's military is dispatching reinforcement columns to disrupt the siege on the Hpasawng region, which the revolutionary groups have been obstructing.

(He stated, "Last year, when we were blocking the Hpasawng, they sent many reinforcement columns.") However, the entire column was wiped out. It will be the same; our defending columns will fight here, while a separate group tasked with cutting them off will ambush them along the route. So, we don't have to be concerned about their coming.') 

Khway Bee Loo is a pleasant guy. When I asked him to describe one of his encounters..."
"If I have to talk about combat experiences, there are many. However, one recent and remarkable instance occurred during a hill capture mission. The enemy knew we were about to take that hill. 
Our radio frequencies coincided, and they intercepted our channel. Once they gained access, they turned on the radio and said, 'Aren't you guys coming up yet? Are you not coming up? We're waiting for you! That's what they said.  At the time, we were still at the bottom of the hill. The enemy had intercepted our radio frequency and spoken to us; our information had been compromised. However, once we were prepared and began the assault, it only took five minutes. It wasn't a very big hill, but we got it. We instantly moved on to the next hill after capturing the previous one. We also seized firearms and ammo there. Regarding the hill, it was a mutual challenge. They sought to provoke and test us, so we answered by demonstrating our capabilities. That's how we caught it.”

Question: So, in terms of the folks who challenged your men, what happened during the actual fighting?

Answer: They all fled. To be honest, I led the charge up that hill. When my men opened fire and we seized their trenches and shelters, those guys simply fled, especially the one with the '79' (grenade launcher/gear). Later, we learned that he was a 'Bo Lay' (Lieutenant). His soldiers told us that he was the first one to flee. He was the highest-ranking individual on the hill. We assumed the person with the 79 grenade launcher was a Sergeant, but it turns out he was a Lieutenant. He was the first to challenge us, and the first to flee. We did chase and shoot them. But then I told them to protect the area first and then follow them cautiously, so they were able to escape in the end.

Question: Were there any casualties on their side?
Answer: They definitely suffered significant casualties. There were around five or six killed and wounded. Although there were injuries, the person [who was left behind] bled out and died; we were unable to save him. We asked him why he wasn't running like the others. He said, 'When your soldiers arrived, the lieutenant had already fled before I could. I'd been shot in the stomach, so I couldn't flee and was left behind.

'Khway Bee Loo's' left chest bears tattoos of dates and names of deceased comrades, indicating "My Fallen Comrades." 
He pointed at the tattoos and recounted their stories. "This is 'Oo Htun', the first to fall. This is 'Ah Maung Kar' from Nyaung Done, this is 'Shan Gyi', a buddy from Northern Shan State. This is 'Ar Loo', the column commander. He is regarded as our older brother. This one's Ar Too. When he added that he was considering tattooing the names of 5 additional friends who had died in recent conflicts beneath the current ones, I could sense his profound connection to his troops. 

Many members of their organization have tattoos done by a comrade known as "Swe Khant." He was an art teacher before the coup. Because he has artistic abilities, one of the group leaders purchased tattoo equipment for him. Many of his colleagues wish to be his canvas. 

The leader of this CRTF group is Ko Kyaw Zay Ya. He was formerly a member of the ABSDF (All Burma Students' Democratic Front) and was involved with the VBSW (Vigorous Burmese Student Warriors). Those who follow Myanmar politics will likely remember the VBSW group for their involvement in the 1999 siege of the Myanmar Embassy in Bangkok.

Ko Kyaw Zay Ya had received US military Ranger training. In the late 1990s, he pursued further education and studied at a university in the United States. After the coup, he joined the revolution. Initially, the NUG Ministry of Defence (MOD) assigned Ko Kyaw Zay Ya the duty of Commander for the Central Region.

However, Ko Kyaw Zay Ya later resigned from that position and currently serves as a Military Advisor for this specific battalion. He has extensive combat experience, and is focused purely on military operations and has no interest in politics. Although he no longer serves as the Regional Commander, he still serves under the MOD. He emphasized the importance of the central Command and Control system in the revolution on the phone. I couldn’t meet him in person. He said that although their group faces shortages (needs) just like many others, they will survive by whatever means available. 

"The CRTF, like other revolutionary movements, operates in a resource-constrained environment. In times like these, it's not important to focus on basic needs like food and shelter. Instead, what's needed are new technologies, steady military supply support, and more weapons. "But no matter how pressing the needs are or how tough the situation is, we will have to keep doing the best we can with the resources we have right now," he said.

In the "Lel-Htoo" (CRTF) group led by Ko Kyaw Zay Ya, almost all of the commanders are from Generation Z. I only went to the camp in the Hpasawng area, but they have members in other places of Myanmar as well. 

I went to where the CRTF frontline unit was stationed in the morning. This unit is part of the united forces that are blocking Light Infantry Battalion (LIB) 135 in Hpasawng. The CRTF members made me wear a bulletproof vest and a ballistic helmet. However, they don't have enough gear for everyone. I feel bad about this. I truly wished that all of them had helmets and jackets that would protect them. We left the car at a certain spot and kept walking. The Operations Officer, Khway Bee Loo, led the way, followed by Jauk Jak and me.  La Pyae was walking behind me.

The forest got thicker as we walked further. "Uncle, be careful," Jauk Jak warned. Do not talk loudly. There is less space between us and the enemy now. Since I was tired, I slowed down, and they stopped to wait for me. I walked as much as I could without stopping because I didn't want them to be in danger. It got so bad that I had to push against my knees with my hands sometimes. Making a video with my phone in one hand at the same time. I had to tell myself, "These teens could die at any time." Why should I take a break? There was no easy way to get there. It looked like people had pushed through the bushes to make tracks that we had to follow.

When I looked up, the trees were so thick that I couldn't always see "Jauk Jak" in front of me. Out of nowhere, a tunnel they had dug showed up among the banana trees and weeds. It was hard to walk along the edge of the ditch. From the ledge, which was only about the width of my palm, I almost fell into the ditch several times. Sometimes, I had to walk with one leg on the left bank and the other on the right.

Although this situation is routine for them, for me, it was the experience of a lifetime. In this way, we reached a bunker. Jauk Jak told me to get down inside the bunker. The bunker was about chest-deep. There, we met other members of their group.

JJ said that the enemy was only about 60 meters away. He showed me the bullet cases from yesterday's battle. I collected some of the casings as souvenirs. He also mentioned that two heavy artillery shells fired by the enemy had landed near this location. 'Yesterday, a 79 (grenade) round landed over there. Another one landed right near here,' he said.

Actually, I had planned to visit this location yesterday. However, because of the emergency hospitalization of a comrade yesterday, we only ended up going to the front line today. Jauk Jak arranged for me to speak with the squad leader of the group. 

Since we were worried the enemy might hear us if we spoke loudly, we had to ask questions and answer in whispered tones. For me, this was my very first experience conducting an 'interview in whispers. The squad leader mentioned that there was a battle yesterday, after which the enemy retreated.

Question: "Comrade Phoe Htaung, what was the situation of the battle like? When did the fighting happen?"
Answer: "Yesterday evening, just past 4:00 PM, the junta soldiers launched a column offensive against us. They used snipers. We returned fire with small arms. The battle lasted only about 15 minutes to half an hour. They retreated after that. When we cleared the area [after they left], we didn't find any traces."

Question: Does the fighting happen every day?
Answer: It doesn't happen every day. There are times when the enemy probes and advances little by little. Similarly, when we push forward to test them, battles tend to occur.

Then, we continued our journey. We arrived at a place that was even closer to the enemy. I asked Jauk Jak to help film a video so that I would be included in the shot. That was the real front line. I was so exhausted that I was struggling to catch my breath. There, I interviewed another comrade. His name is Comrade Wunna.

Question: Has anyone among your fellow soldiers been hurt or killed in battle? 
Answer: Yes, there are. When we were capturing the Buddhist monastery, we had to sacrifice about three of our brothers."
Question: Were they killed right in front of you?
Answer: Yes, right beside me.
Question: What killed them? Was it airstrikes or gunfire?
Answer: Yes, it was the airstrikes.
Question: with what?
Answer: with Y-12 
Question: How do you feel in your heart about the loss of your comrades?
Answer: In my heart, I feel that our brothers are still fighting together with us in every battle. Of course, I feel sad. But we must continue doing what needs to be done. To ensure the fall of the military dictatorship, we will continue fighting forward, honoring the promise we made to our fallen brothers.
Question: I have heard that some revolutionaries get discouraged and leave the movement. Is that true? What do you think about that? How do you feel about it? What is your stance?
Answer: As the revolution drags on, some people do leave for various reasons, such as family difficulties and so on. In reality, things aren't easy for anyone. But the main thing is one's conviction. From the moment I left home, I came out with the mindset that I must defeat this dictator. Therefore, we will never give up.

Just as we finished the interview, I heard the sound of an MG-42 machine gun, which they call Nga-Gyin-Mee (Fish Tail), ring out four or five times from the enemy's side. They told me to get into the trench immediately. Since I am older, I couldn't jump down like them. I had to hold their hands to climb down. Then I walked as fast as I could, almost running. There were foxholes along the top of the trench. They ordered me to get into one quickly. I had to slide down into it. Inside the hole, it was pitch black and damp. As I had kept my phone camera recording continuously, I captured everything up until I was inside the hole looking back out. At that moment, no one knew what would happen, whether heavy artillery would fall, or if the enemy troops themselves would appear, as we were so close to them. After about five minutes, although there was no further gunfire, they decided it was best not to stay and that I should return. Khway Bee Loo asked Jauk Jak and me to go ahead first. He said he and La Pyae would stay behind for cover and follow later. So, we headed back.

No battle occurred on that specific day. However, I was told that a major battle broke out in that very spot the following day, with the enemy using fighter jets and dropping bombs from Y-12 aircraft. Jauk Jak said to me, "Uncle, was it good luck or bad luck? I really can't say. He was referring to the fact that we missed the battle. I really couldn't say either. 

Some analysts assume that Min Aung Hlaing's military might launch an offensive with superior force in the Hpasawng region before Armed Forces Day on March 27th. While the revolutionary forces can conduct intercept attacks, I do not know to what extent they will be able to stop them.

A Call for National Transformation: An Appeal to the Dinka Community
By General Mun Both Jock, Leader for Political Revolution in South Sudan

This communication serves as a formal appeal and a personal reflection from your brother, Mun Both Jock, a visionary committed to the fundamental restructuring of South Sudan.

 This message is issued through our international media platforms to engage the Dinka community in a critical dialogue regarding the future of our nation.

The Question of Political Tribalism.

We must confront a difficult inquiry: Is the Dinka community bound by a brand of tribalism that precludes support for visionaries from other ethnic backgrounds? 

If the spirit of South Sudan is truly inclusive, we must ask why the Dinka  community has historically hesitated to rally behind non-Dinka leaders who offer viable alternatives.

For instance, Dr. Riek Machar has repeatedly advocated for federalism and democratic reform as a superior alternative to the status quo. However, despite the merit of these visions, a broad segment of the Dinka community has remained distant, seemingly due to ethnic affiliation rather than policy disagreement.

The Current Crisis of Leadership
We must look at our reality with unclouded eyes. The administration of President Salva Kiir has reached a point of absolute stagnation. The presidency is no longer defined by governance or progress, but by physical decline and a tragic inability to deliver anything to the people except conflict and mourning though out the country. 

• Economic Collapse: Widespread poverty and hunger.
• Social Trauma: Years of displacement and systemic violence.
• Infrastructure Deficit: A total absence of development projects.

The President’s tenure has devolved into the promotion of "Konkoch" (eternal rule)—a philosophy that prioritizes ethnic ego over the survival of the state. This is an unacceptable path for a modern nation.

 You cannot use Konkoch to support a President who cannot bring peace, freedom and prosperity fot all.
Now, it’s time for Dinka community to support a non dinka visionary who can bring change, Freedom and prosperity for all.

A Historical Imbalance of Support 
History demonstrates that other South Sudanese communities have shown immense loyalty to Dinka leadership for decades:

1. Abel Alier (Anyanya I): Supported by all, yet his tenure concluded with corruption and the divisive regionalization of the country which led to the creation of three South Sudan regions such as, Upper Nile, Equatoria and Bar el ghzel. 

2. Dr. John Garang (1983–2005): While he successfully led us toward independence, we must acknowledge that the pivotal concept of self-determination was pioneered by Dr. Riek Machar—the very man currently marginalized by the regime in Juba .

3. Salva Kiir (2005–Present): For over twenty years, the nation has endured a leadership that is leading South Sudan into an abyss.

This is what we need to change today and not tomorrow.
All of us as South Sudanese let’s say enough is enough for the leadership of Salva Kiir.
The Path Forward: A Vision for Prosperity
If you reject the label of tribalism, then the time has come to demonstrate national unity by supporting leadership based on merit and vision rather than lineage.

I, Mun Both Jock, offer a blueprint for a Federal, Democratic, and Prosperous South Sudan. My mission is defined by:
• Infrastructural Revolution: The construction of modern roads, bridges, and power grids.
• Industrialization: Creating factories and jobs to end the cycle of poverty.
• True Liberty: Establishing a state where freedom is a reality for every citizen, not a slogan.

The tragedies of the current regime affect us all—the Dinka community included. It is time to move beyond the "Konkoch" mentality and embrace the "visionary of the people."
Mark my words: True freedom is within our reach.

I have the blue print of New South Sudan . Trust me. I know how to build this Nation.
I wish you peace, liberty, and prosperity.
General Mun Both Jock Leader for Political Revolution in South Sudan

At 18, my parents left me at my grandparents' farm so their “golden daughter” could shine, then drove away as if I were a burden they could finally get rid of. Years later, after I had built an empire they never imagined, they returned asking for help only to find there was no place for them at my wedding.
I stood there in my custom-designed wedding dress, silk as soft as water, and checked the seating chart one last time as my wedding planner, Grace, approached with her tablet.
“Where should we seat your parents and sister?” she asked softly. I didn’t blink. I didn’t even lift my eyes from the invitation.
“There are no seats for them,” I said, as calm as a breeze. “They weren’t invited.”
Grace’s face changed color as if she’d misheard. She didn't know why because the reason began ten years earlier, long before flowers, champagne, and string lights transformed my grandparents' estate into a wedding venue.
I was eighteen then, living with hope as fragile as a sheet of paper. College guidebooks piled high on the kitchen table. An acceptance letter to State University. A small scholarship I'd earned through sleepless nights. For the first time, I believed I could step out of the shadow that had clung to me throughout my childhood.
Then Madison walked in with a tennis racket slung over her shoulder, and the room seemed to be rearranged around her, as if she were the sun. Ice. Towels. Compliments. My parents' eyes fixed on her future as if it were a prize they'd finally won.
That evening, my father announced a “short trip” to visit my grandparents in rural Nebraska. Two days, he said. A simple visit. I believed him because I didn't want to imagine that parents could lie to their children so easily.
Halfway across the state border, my mother turned back and said we needed to “sacrifice” so Madison could train full-time. And the first sacrifice was my education tuition, living expenses, my start. They said I could “take a year off” at the farm, help Mrs. Rose and Mr. Frank, and be useful while they built Madison’s career.
The cornfields flashed past the window as if my life was being erased in each moment.
At the farm, my grandparents hugged me, their hands smelling faintly of lavender soap, their eyes shining with worry. Over iced tea and cookies, my parents smiled and explained that I had volunteered to stay. That I was noble. That I had always been thoughtful.
My grandparents looked at me as if they wanted to argue  but they were old, my parents were very persuasive, and I was too stunned to resist.
The next morning, the SUV rolled away with its empty suitcases and absolute certainty. I stood on the porch in my pajamas, watching the dust settle, and understood that I had been left behind like an unwanted piece of luggage.
I learned farm life the hard way: the 4 a.m. alarm clock, the cold air in the barn, the blisters turning into calluses. I learned to work without praise. I learned what love looked like when it wasn't fake my grandmother's ointment on my hands, my grandfather's steady voice saying, "You can do it," when my body wanted to give up.
Years passed. The farm changed. And so did I.
Now the grounds were draped in white tents and sunflowers, and my grandparents sat in the front row because they were the sole reason I was standing here. Those in the back were people who had come during dreary seasons—not people who remembered you when there was something glittering to photograph.
Grace swallowed and nodded, still trying to understand. “Okay,” she said carefully. “So… there’s no family area.”
Before I could reply, her earpiece crackled. Her eyes darted toward the hallway.
“Teresa,” she whispered, “the security guard said a car just pulled up at the gate. They’re asking for your name.”
I smoothed the silk dress around my waist, took one last look in the mirror, and felt something settle in my chest quiet and steady.

Feedback, Criticism, demarketing and Victoria Travels.
Part 1... 

In every business, and indeed, any human endeavour, feedback mechanisms are indispensable instruments of growth. 
Constructive criticism is equally vital. No individual, institution, or enterprise evolves in the absence of honest appraisal. 

Both feedback and criticism, when responsibly deployed, are catalysts for institutional refinement. 
However, we must delineate clear  boundaries.

There is feedback, which is measured, specific, and improvement-oriented.
There is criticism, which may be constructive or, at times, negatively framed but still issue-based.
And then there is demarketing, which is a deliberate or reckless attempt to devalue, malign, or commercially sabotage a brand in public space.
These three are not interchangeable. 

To mount social media space and categorically brand a company like Victoria Travels as “the worst transport company in the world” transcends feedback and criticism, and descends into reputational assault. This is premium "Tsav" and wickedness from high heavens. 

And, sadly, to imagine that such sweeping indictments often emanate from individuals with zero entrepreneurial exposure. People who have never successfully operated even an okada business! 

A troubling pattern is emerging. Sometime ago, this same posture was adopted toward SUDOPEE Supermarket. The question I keep asking... Why is the hatred always to publicly vilify indigenous Benue-owned businesses? Are supermarkets or transport companies owned by non-indigenes infallible? 
Or is there a subtle disposition to cannibalize our own?

Markets and businesses thrive on choice. If a service provider does not meet your expectations, move to the next! Patronize an alternative without embarking on a devilish campaign against the former.

We must also appreciate the legal implications of reckless digital demarketing. There are precedents, including the case involving Erica-Foods, where careless reputational attacks on social media attracted serious legal consequences. 

Finally, If public transportation proves intolerable, go and buy your car. If that too does not suffice, you may as well opt for a private jet, after all, we do have an airport.

Attention, vidage de sac.

Si je me suis quasi installé à l'est de l'Allemagne, c'est parce que j'y ai retrouvé des choses qui sont devenues rares chez nous: des magasins sans vigile, des centre-villes sûrs et propres, de la sécurité au quotidien... 🤩

Mais c'est clairement en train de changer. Je l'ai ressenti par exemple quand les supermarchés ont commencé à installer des caméras. Et aujourd'hui une lettre d'une voisine affichée dans le hall a confirmé mon impression.

Pour la seconde fois en quelques mois, une paire de baskets a été volée sur le perron d'une porte. Et en prime, l'ascenseur a été taggé 😤 Les gens d'ici découvrent qu'il faut désormais bien fermer la porte de l'immeuble pour éviter les problèmes, et c'est nouveau pour eux. Elle a même conclu sa lettre par "Es wird immer schlimmer" (ça devient de pire en pire) 🙄

Pour moi par contre ce n'est pas si surprenant. Avec une adolescence entre Trappes et Marseille, j'avais déjà expérimenté un car-jacking quand la plupart des français ne connaissaient pas encore le terme 😅 J'ai pu voir comment l'insécurité et les incivilités ont gagné du terrain année après année, comment de grandes villes sont devenues des endroits à éviter à la tombée de la nuit.

Alors voir la même tendance prendre forme sous mes yeux ici, ça me met les boules. Parce que j'avais commencé à envisager de poser mes valises pour de bon... mais si c'est pour me retrouver dans la même chienlit qu'en France dans quelques années, ça ne vaut peut-être pas le coup de continuer à me passer de bon fromage 😂

Peut-être qu'il faudrait que je reparte plus loin vers l'est. Voire même changer de continent. Mais est-ce qu'il y a encore des coins où on peut être préservé de cette "évolution", je commence à en douter.

Tout ça ne va pas arranger ma misanthropie... 🙄😅

December 1943, Dant, Belgium. Sister Mariah Clare Bulma stood in the convent kitchen and watched three Nazi officers walk through her door. The tallest one, a Gustapo captain with cold blue eyes, pointed at the large copper cauldron hanging over the fireplace. He spoke in German, then in broken French. The Sisters of Mercy Convent would prepare Christmas lunch for 45 Nazi officers tomorrow.
They would arrive at noon. The soup must be ready by 2:00. Sister Marie Clare nodded slowly, her hands folded inside her greywolf habit. She was 34 years old, born in Montreal, Canada, and she had been running this convent since the German invasion began 3 years ago. The captain turned and left, his boots echoing on the stone floor.
Sister Marie Clare walked to the window. Outside in the courtyard, 23 orphan children played in the December cold. Their breath made white clouds in the air. Beyond the convent wall, she could see the town of Dinant stretching down to the river. The medieval church tower rose above the old buildings. Everything looked peaceful, but peace was a lie.
That morning, the Gestapo had nailed a new poster to every door in town. Sister Marie Clare had read it three times. her stomach twisting with each word. For every German soldier killed by resistance fighters, 10 Belgian civilians would be executed. The resistance had killed 12 German soldiers last week. 127 names were on the execution list.
The killings would happen on Christmas Day at dawn. The people would die in the town square while church bells rang. Inside the convent, 47 elderly refugees huddled in the chapel, praying for miracles that never came. They had fled here when the Germans destroyed their villages. Now they would watch their neighbors die from the convent windows.
Sister Marie Clare closed her eyes. The smell of woodm smoke filled the kitchen. The copper cauldron needed cleaning. The pantry needed counting. The children needed feeding. Everything needed to continue as normal, even though nothing was normal anymore. That night, three resistance fighters came to the convent through the secret door in the cellar.
Sister Marie Clare knew them all. Pierre was a baker. Jeanluke was a school teacher. Marie was a farmer's daughter. They sat at the wooden table in the dark kitchen speaking in whispers. Pierre wanted to attack the German headquarters. Jeanluke wanted to blow up the bridge. Marie wanted to ambush the execution squad.
Sister Marie Clare listened to their plans and shook her head at each one. The Germans would kill 50 more civilians for any attack. The cycle of death would never end. Then she spoke, her voice barely louder than the crackling fire. What if there was another way? What if the Nazi officers never made it to Christmas morning? Pierre laughed, a bitter sound.
The SS tested all food served to officers. Special inspectors tasted every dish. Any hint of poison. And the Germans would burn the entire town. It was impossible. Jeanluke agreed. They had tried poisoning before in other towns. It always failed. The Nazis were too careful. Their security was too strong. Sister Marie Clare stood and lit a candle.
The small flame cast dancing shadows on the stone walls. She had not told anyone in Belgium about her life before the convent. Before she took her vows 9 years ago, before she devoted herself to God, she had been someone else. In Montreal, she had worked in a laboratory. She had studied chemistry at the university. Her specialty was agricultural pesticides.
She knew poisons the way other people knew prayers. She understood how chemicals moved through the body, how they hid their presence, how they mimicked natural diseases. She explained her idea slowly using simple words. The SS inspector only tasted the first bowl of soup. He never tested the whole pot.
If someone added poison after the inspection, during a moment of confusion, it could work. But the poison had to be special. It could not kill immediately. It had to wait to hide to make the deaths look like sickness from bad food. White arsenic could do this. 2 g would cause terrible illness. 3 g would kill, but not for 24 hours.

THEY CALLED HIM A MONSTER AND DEMANDED HE BE EUTHANIZED. THEN I SAW HIS TEETH, AND I REALIZED WE WERE THE MONSTERS.

CHAPTER 1: THE DEATH ROW WALK

The smell of the shelter always hits you before the noise does.

It’s a specific cocktail of scents that you never truly scrub out of your clothes.

Industrial bleach. Wet concrete. Cheap kibble. And underneath it all, the sharp, metallic tang of pure adrenaline and terror.

I parked my truck in the lot of the county shelter, just like I do every Tuesday and Thursday. It was raining in Detroit, a cold, miserable drizzle that turned the sky the color of a bruised lung.

I sat in the cab for a minute, gripping the steering wheel, taking a deep breath.

"Just walk the dogs, Mike," I told myself. "Just walk them. Don't get attached. Not today."

That’s the mantra. That’s the lie we all tell ourselves.

I grabbed my lanyard and headed inside.

The intake board was full. It’s always full. This is a high-kill facility. We don't call it that in the brochures, but that’s the reality. Space is finite. Mercy is expensive.

When a new dog comes in, an old one usually goes out the back door in a black plastic bag.

I walked past the front desk, nodding to Sarah, the intake coordinator. She looked tired. Her eyes were red-rimmed.

"Bad day?" I asked.

She didn't look up. "Row C. Kennel 42. He’s a Code Red, Mike. Don't even bother walking him. He’s scheduled for the needle at 5:00 PM."

I froze.

Code Red means aggressive. Irredeemable. Dangerous to staff.

"What did he do?"

"Police drop-off," Sarah sighed, finally looking at me. "Raided a trap house on the East Side. They found him chained in the basement. He’s torn up, Mike. And he’s... he’s scary looking. He growled at the vet tech. Just leave him be. Let him go in peace."

I nodded, but my stomach twisted.

I walked down the long concrete hallway. The cacophony of barking started.

A hundred dogs, jumping against chain-link fences, begging to be seen.

Pick me. Pick me. I’m a good boy. I sit. I shake.

I walked past the labs, the shepherds, the mutts. I gave treats, I took a few notes for the adoption website, but my feet kept moving toward Row C.

Kennel 42.

It was at the far end, near the drainage chaotic. The lights were dimmer back there.

I stopped in front of the cage.

At first, I didn't see anything. Just a gray wool blanket bunched up in the corner.

Then, the blanket moved.

A head popped up.

I involuntarily took a step back.

Sarah wasn't lying. He was a nightmare.

It was a Pitbull, or what was left of one. He was slate gray, thick-necked, and built like a tank. But his face...

It was a roadmap of violence.

Jagged, pink scars ran across his muzzle. Part of his left ear was missing, looking like it had been sheared off with dull scissors. His eyes were wide, bloodshot, and frantic.

He stood up, his legs shaking so hard I could hear his claws clicking against the concrete floor.

Click-click-click-click.

He let out a low sound. It wasn't a bark. It was a guttural rumble that vibrated in his chest.

A couple of potential adopters, a young couple looking for a "starter dog," walked up behind me.

They looked into Kennel 42.

"Oh my god," the woman whispered, covering her mouth. "Look at that thing. It looks like a killer."

The man pulled her away, sneering. "That’s why I hate those dogs. Look at him. He’s probably killed someone's cat. They should just put him down and save everyone the trouble."

They walked away, heading toward the puppies in the front lobby.

I looked back at the dog.

He had heard them. I swear he understood.

He pressed himself tighter into the corner, making himself as small as his seventy-pound frame would allow.

On the front of his cage, the red laminated card glared at me.

NAME: UNKNOWN
ID: #8940-C
CAUTION: BITE RISK. EXTREME AGGRESSION. DO NOT HANDLE.

I looked at my watch. It was 3:45 PM.

He had an hour and fifteen minutes left to live.

I stared at him. He stared at me.

And that’s when I noticed something.

Most aggressive dogs, the ones who really want to hurt you, they come to the front of the cage. They lunge. They snap. They defend their territory. They want you to know they are the boss.

This dog wasn't doing that.

He was trembling.

Not shaking from adrenaline—shaking from fear.

He was looking at me sideways, showing the whites of his eyes—what trainers call "whale eye." But he wasn't posturing. He was cowering.

"Hey, buddy," I whispered.

The dog flinched as if I’d thrown a rock at him.

"It's okay. I'm not gonna hurt you."

I reached into my pocket and pulled out a piece of high-value treat—dried liver.

I tossed it through the chain link.

It landed near his paws.

He didn't look at the food. He kept his eyes locked on my face, waiting for the blow. Waiting for the pain.

"You're not a killer, are you?" I murmured.

Something in my gut told me the sign was wrong.

I’ve been working with shelter dogs for ten years. I’ve been bitten. I’ve had stitches. I know what a dangerous dog looks like.

This dog looked like a victim.

I looked around. The hallway was empty.

If Sarah saw me do what I was about to do, I’d be banned from the shelter. Insurance liability. Instant termination of my volunteer contract.

But 5:00 PM was coming.

I took the keys off my belt.

My hands were sweating.

Don't do it, Mike. He’s a Code Red.

I slid the key into the lock.

Click.

The sound echoed like a gunshot in the hallway.

The dog scrambled backward, hitting the back wall with a thud. He let out a sharp yelp.

I slowly opened the heavy gate.

"Easy," I said, keeping my voice flat and calm. "Easy now."

I stepped inside the kennel.

The smell of fear was overwhelming in here.

I closed the gate behind me but didn't latch it. Just in case I needed to run.

I sank down to my knees, sitting on my heels. I made myself small. I averted my eyes, looking at the floor, showing him I wasn't a threat.

"I'm right here," I whispered. "Come say hi."

Silence.

Then, the clicking sound again.

Click-click-click.

He was moving.

I didn't move a muscle. I held my breath.

I could feel his heat. He was close.

I felt a wet nose touch my ear.

He sniffed my neck. He sniffed my shoulder.

I slowly, very slowly, turned my head.

He was inches from my face. Up close, the scars were even worse. Old wounds, new wounds, burns.

He opened his mouth.

My heart hammered against my ribs. This was it. The bite. The locking of the jaws.

He lunged forward.

I flinched.

But teeth didn't sink into my flesh.

A giant, wet, slobbery tongue dragged across my cheek.

He let out a whimper and collapsed into my lap, burying his heavy blocky head into my chest. He was shaking so hard he was vibrating my entire body.

"Oh, buddy," I exhaled, wrapping my arms around him. "You're just a big baby."

I started to pet him, running my hands down his back to soothe him.

He yelped when I touched his ribs.

I stopped.

I looked closer at his paws. They were splayed out at odd angles. His front paws looked... flattened.

I gently lifted one. He pulled back, whining, but let me look.

My stomach dropped.

His toes had been smashed. Repeatedly. Broken and healed wrong.

Why would someone do that?

Then I looked at his face again. He was panting now, relieved to have human contact.

I needed to check his age. I needed to see his teeth to estimate how old he was. Maybe that would help me plead his case to Sarah.

"Let me see those chompers, pal," I said softly.

I gently lifted his scarred upper lip.

I stopped breathing.

The world seemed to tilt on its axis.

There were no teeth.

Not just missing a few.

They were gone.

His canines had been filed down to the gum line. His front teeth were pulled out. The gums were a mess of jagged scar tissue and old, healed abscesses.

I sat back on my heels, the realization hitting me like a physical punch to the gut.

He wasn't a fighter.

Fighters need teeth. Fighters need weapons.

He was the practice dummy.

He was a bait dog.

They had smashed his paws so he couldn't run away. They had pulled his teeth so he couldn't fight back.

And then they threw him into a ring with monsters and let them tear him apart so they could learn how to kill.

He had never hurt anyone in his life. He couldn't hurt anyone.

He had spent his entire life being chewed on, defenseless, terrified, and in pain.

And now, because he looked scary, because he had the scars of his torture written on his face, we were going to kill him.

We were going to finish the job the dog fighters started.

Tears blurred my vision. Hot, angry tears.

"No," I whispered, my voice shaking. "No way in hell."

I looked down at him. He was licking my hand with his toothless mouth, his tail giving a tiny, hesitant thump against the floor.

He had every right to hate me. He had every right to hate every human being on this planet.

But he didn't. He just wanted to be held.

I checked my watch.

4:15 PM.

Forty-five minutes.

I stood up. The dog scrambled up with me, pressing against my leg, looking up at me with those desperate, soulful eyes.

"You're not staying here," I told him.

I clipped the leash onto his collar.

I kicked the gate open.

I wasn't a volunteer anymore. I was a man on a mission.

But as I walked him out of the kennel, Sarah appeared at the end of the hallway.

She stopped. Her eyes went wide when she saw me with the Code Red dog on a leash.

"Mike!" she shouted. "What are you doing? Put that dog back! He's dangerous!"

"He's not dangerous!" I yelled back, my voice echoing off the concrete walls. "He doesn't even have teeth, Sarah! Look at him!"

"It doesn't matter!" she snapped, marching toward me. "He's property of the county. He's on the Euthanasia List. You cannot take him."

"Watch me," I growled.

"Mike, if you walk out those doors with that dog, I have to call the police. That's theft. And you'll be barred from the shelter forever."

I looked at Sarah. I looked at the dog, who was cowering behind my legs, peeing on the floor in fear because of the raised voices.

I looked at the exit door. It was fifty feet away.

"Call them," I said.

And I started running.

Er nahm seine Geliebte mit zu einer Diamantengala — ohne zu wissen, dass seine Ehefrau die Erbin hinter all dem war …

Die Einladung kam in einem dicken elfenbeinfarbenen Umschlag an, mit silbernem Wachs versiegelt und mit einem Wappen geprägt, das die meisten Menschen in New York sofort erkannten.

Die jährliche Diamantengala der Aurelius Foundation

Ausgerichtet im Astoria Crown Ballroom

Black Tie.

Nur auf Einladung.

Nathaniel „Nate“ Caldwell drehte die Karte langsam in seinen Händen, ein ruhiges Lächeln breitete sich auf seinem Gesicht aus.

„Das ist es“, murmelte er.

Auf der anderen Seite seines Manhattan-Penthouses richtete Lila Monroe ihre Diamantohrringe vor dem Spiegel.

Sie war umwerfend — blonde Wellen fielen über ihre Schultern, ein rotes Kleid schmiegte sich an jede Kurve.

„Die Aurelius-Gala?“, sagte sie mit geweiteten Augen.

„Das ist das Ereignis des Jahres.

Milliardäre.

Senatoren.

Altes Geld, Adel.

“

Nate nickte.

Als Seniorpartner bei Caldwell & Pierce Investments hatte er ein Jahrzehnt damit verbracht, sich in die elitärsten Finanzkreise vorzuarbeiten.

Die Aurelius Foundation war nicht nur eine Wohltätigkeitsorganisation — sie war Macht.

Wer der geheimnisvollen Erbin nahe stand, stand auch einer der größten privaten Vermögen Amerikas nahe.

Gerüchten zufolge konnte das Vermögen der Familie Aurelius mit dem von Tech-Giganten mithalten.

Die Erbin selbst jedoch war praktisch unsichtbar.

Keine öffentlichen Interviews.

Keine auffälligen Social-Media-Auftritte.

Keine Boulevardberichte.

Nur Einfluss.

Und heute Abend wollte Nate gesehen werden.

Er blickte auf seine Uhr.

„Wir sollten gehen“, sagte er glatt.

Lila hakte sich bei ihm unter.

„Und deine Frau?“, fragte sie mit einem verspielten Grinsen.

Nates Gesicht verhärtete sich für den Bruchteil einer Sekunde.

„Sie besucht solche Veranstaltungen nicht.“

Auf der anderen Seite der Stadt, in einem ruhigen Stadthaus an der Upper East Side, stand Eleanor Caldwell vor ihrem eigenen Spiegel.

Ihr schwarzes Kleid war schlicht, elegant, fast zurückhaltend — bis das Licht auf die Kette an ihrem Schlüsselbein fiel.

Eine Kaskade seltener blauer Diamanten, unverkennbar unbezahlbar.

Hinter ihr richtete ihre Assistentin den Verschluss vorsichtig.

„Ms. Aurelius“, sagte die Assistentin leise, „der Wagen ist bereit.“

Eleanor nickte leicht.

Für die Welt war sie Eleanor Caldwell — Kunstberaterin, sanftmütig, verheiratet mit einem ehrgeizigen Finanzmann.

Doch von Geburt an war sie Eleanor Aurelius — die alleinige Erbin der Aurelius Foundation und ihrer gewaltigen Besitzungen in Luxusdiamanten, dem Abbau seltener Erden und globaler Philanthropie.

Ihre Familie hatte ihr Imperium über drei Generationen hinweg leise aufgebaut.

Sie schätzten Diskretion mehr als Spektakel.

Genau deshalb hatte sie Nate glauben lassen, sie sei lediglich „wohlhabend“.

Als sie sich vor acht Jahren kennengelernt hatten, hatte sie sich in seinen Ehrgeiz, seinen Charme, seinen Hunger nach Erfolg verliebt.

Erst später erkannte sie, dass dieser Hunger zu etwas anderem werden konnte.

Im vergangenen Jahr war Nate zunehmend distanziert geworden.

Späte Nächte.

Private Anrufe.

Ein veränderter Tonfall, sobald sie über Werte statt über Profite sprach.

Und dann, vor drei Monaten, hatte sie die Wahrheit erfahren.

Lila Monroe.

Ein Model, das zur Society-Dame geworden war und sich mühelos durch die höchsten Kreise bewegte.

Eleanor hatte ihn nicht zur Rede gestellt.

Noch nicht.

Stattdessen wartete sie.

Und heute Abend würde sie nicht länger warten.

Der Astoria Crown Ballroom funkelte wie ein auf die Erde gefallenes Sternbild.

Kristalllüster brachen das Licht über Marmorböden.

Diamanteninstallationen — jede einzelne Millionen wert — standen entlang des Randes hinter Glas.

Ein Live-Orchester erfüllte den Raum mit sanften, schwebenden Streichern.

Nate trat mit Lila an seiner Seite ein, sein Selbstvertrauen stieg ins Unermessliche.

I was talking to some folks the other day at work. We got into the discussion about what would happen if there was a big power outage. What is the first thing people would be concerned about?
Social media, cell phones, things on the internet. 
How many people would actually have their first thought be having running water, food preservation, sources of heat?
Now, I know I'm in a very unique position with my job, and I am very confident I could manage well without the modern luxuries - but how many people could? How many people can start a fire? Raise animals? Sew? Process fibers? Dig a well? Grow crops? Build shelter?
Half kidding with this - but if anyone wants to start a self-sufficient funny farm (obviously with modern luxuries) I think we should. Let's get back to basics, let's know where our food is coming from, let's put in the work to feel like we earned it. I think this world would be a much better place.

The Canadian Nun Who Poisoned 45 Nazi Officers With Soup During Christmas Lunch....."
December 1943, Dant, Belgium. Sister Mariah Clare Bulma stood in the convent kitchen and watched three Nazi officers walk through her door. The tallest one, a Gustapo captain with cold blue eyes, pointed at the large copper cauldron hanging over the fireplace. He spoke in German, then in broken French. The Sisters of Mercy Convent would prepare Christmas lunch for 45 Nazi officers tomorrow.
They would arrive at noon. The soup must be ready by 2:00. Sister Marie Clare nodded slowly, her hands folded inside her greywolf habit. She was 34 years old, born in Montreal, Canada, and she had been running this convent since the German invasion began 3 years ago. The captain turned and left, his boots echoing on the stone floor.
Sister Marie Clare walked to the window. Outside in the courtyard, 23 orphan children played in the December cold. Their breath made white clouds in the air. Beyond the convent wall, she could see the town of Dinant stretching down to the river. The medieval church tower rose above the old buildings. Everything looked peaceful, but peace was a lie.
That morning, the Gestapo had nailed a new poster to every door in town. Sister Marie Clare had read it three times. her stomach twisting with each word. For every German soldier killed by resistance fighters, 10 Belgian civilians would be executed. The resistance had killed 12 German soldiers last week. 127 names were on the execution list.
The killings would happen on Christmas Day at dawn. The people would die in the town square while church bells rang. Inside the convent, 47 elderly refugees huddled in the chapel, praying for miracles that never came. They had fled here when the Germans destroyed their villages. Now they would watch their neighbors die from the convent windows.
Sister Marie Clare closed her eyes. The smell of woodm smoke filled the kitchen. The copper cauldron needed cleaning. The pantry needed counting. The children needed feeding. Everything needed to continue as normal, even though nothing was normal anymore. That night, three resistance fighters came to the convent through the secret door in the cellar.
Sister Marie Clare knew them all. Pierre was a baker. Jeanluke was a school teacher. Marie was a farmer's daughter. They sat at the wooden table in the dark kitchen speaking in whispers. Pierre wanted to attack the German headquarters. Jeanluke wanted to blow up the bridge. Marie wanted to ambush the execution squad.
Sister Marie Clare listened to their plans and shook her head at each one. The Germans would kill 50 more civilians for any attack. The cycle of death would never end. Then she spoke, her voice barely louder than the crackling fire. What if there was another way? What if the Nazi officers never made it to Christmas morning? Pierre laughed, a bitter sound.
The SS tested all food served to officers. Special inspectors tasted every dish. Any hint of poison. And the Germans would burn the entire town. It was impossible. Jeanluke agreed. They had tried poisoning before in other towns. It always failed. The Nazis were too careful. Their security was too strong. Sister Marie Clare stood and lit a candle.
The small flame cast dancing shadows on the stone walls. She had not told anyone in Belgium about her life before the convent. Before she took her vows 9 years ago, before she devoted herself to God, she had been someone else. In Montreal, she had worked in a laboratory. She had studied chemistry at the university. Her specialty was agricultural pesticides.
She knew poisons the way other people knew prayers. She understood how chemicals moved through the body, how they hid their presence, how they mimicked natural diseases. She explained her idea slowly using simple words. The SS inspector only tasted the first bowl of soup. He never tested the whole pot.
If someone added poison after the inspection, during a moment of confusion, it could work. But the poison had to be special. It could not kill immediately. It had to wait to hide to make the deaths look like sickness from bad food. White arsenic could do this. 2 g would cause terrible illness. 3 g would kill, but not for 24 hours.

Salva Kiir Mayardit and the Conflict Dynamics in Upper Nile

The ongoing conflict in the Upper Nile region is often described through the involvement of various armed groups and community-based forces, each shaped by political tensions, ethnic divisions, and struggles over power and security.

1. Agwelek

A predominantly Chollo (Shilluk) armed group, often reported to be in conflict with elements from the Abadang Dinka and Nuer communities.

2. Abu Shok

Described as an Abadang Dinka militia, with hostilities frequently involving Chollo and Nuer armed actors.

3. Cobra and Allied Forces

A Murle-affiliated armed movement that has historically clashed with Dinka and Nuer groups in different parts of the country.

4. The Red Belt

Portrayed as a local Dinka protection force that some allege the national army has attempted to formalize or integrate. It has reportedly been involved in confrontations with Murle and Nuer forces.

5. South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF)

The national army of South Sudan, often criticized by opponents as being dominated by particular ethnic interests. Critics argue that mistrust toward the institution has contributed to perceptions of bias and deepened communal divisions.

---

A Broader Political Perspective

Many observers believe that Upper Nile’s violence is rooted in long-standing political rivalries, competition over resources, weak state institutions, and unresolved grievances from past wars. Critics of President Salva Kiir argue that political strategies and alliances have intensified divisions among communities that historically coexisted for generations.

Between 2005 and 2013, following the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, large-scale intercommunal conflict in Upper Nile was comparatively limited. Since then, political competition, fragmentation of armed groups, and failures in governance and rule of law have contributed to escalating tensions.

While some attribute the instability to local ethnic rivalries, others argue that national-level leadership decisions, militarization of communities, and the use of proxy forces have significantly worsened the situation.

---

Conclusion

The crisis in Upper Nile is complex and deeply rooted. Sustainable peace will likely require:

Strengthening national institutions and the rule of law

Inclusive political dialogue among all communities

Demilitarization of civilian groups

Accountability and reconciliation efforts

Ultimately, lasting stability depends on rebuilding trust between communities and ensuring that political power is exercised in a way that unites rather than divides the people of South Sudan.

Surrounded on all sides by hardened Taliban fighters, a vastly outnumbered force of Americans and Afghans fought nearly to the last bullet. In June 2006, 47-year-old Master Sergeant Brendan O'Connor of the 7th Special Forces Group – the Army's elite Green Berets – was the team's medic during Operation Kaika. The Taliban believed this isolated group of Americans and Afghans, numbering less than 70, would be an easy target. They were gravely mistaken.

When the terrorists sprang their trap, the sky exploded with the thunder of rifle, machine-gun, and grenade fire from both sides. The main group was separated by more than 100 yards, and the situation at both positions was dire.

O'Connor heard over the radio that several wounded men ahead of a forward position could be overrun at any moment. Leading a team of eight, he quickly traversed the distance between the two positions and took stock of the situation. There he saw two wounded men – Staff Sergeant Matthew Binney and Staff Sergeant Joseph Fuerst – farther ahead and knew he had to reach them.

Disregarding three enemy machine-guns, O'Connor dropped to his stomach and began an arduous crawl to the wounded troops. Restricted in his movements by his protective armor, O'Connor paused and removed the only shield he had from the hostile onslaught, his Interceptor bullet proof vest. He traded his armor for a cloth sign that he pinned to his back to alert the close-air support attack helicopters that he was friendly.

The 200 foot crawl was nearly an hour and a half of constant enemy fire directed at the brave American. Reaching a compound to which he could pull the wounded, he singlehandedly moved the two soldiers there and performed emergency first-aid. As night fell, O'Connor made several trips to move the Binney and Fuerst back to the advanced position. From there, they were able to medevac the injured, and begin their own exfiltration to the security of the patrol base.

While Fuerst did not survive his severe injuries, Binney lived because of the bold decision made by a 47-year-old-medic more concerned with the lives of his friends than his own. For his actions, O'Connor was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross, the first time a member of the 7th Special Forces Group was awarded this honor since July of 1964.

Renzushah predides over  spiritual martial Art  conclave in Academy. Lauds Lt. Governor for re opening Medieval. "Yous Marag" from Arzan Garzan ancient Sufi Heritage Site 

Historic Bulbulshah-Khumaini Bridge Becksons as Academy Prepares for Indo-Nepal Championship

SRINAGAR, 18 FEBRUARY 2026 – In a momentous confluence of athletic prowess and spiritual heritage, Dr. Khawaja Farooq Renzushah, Chief Commissioner of Hindustan Scouts & JK Scouts and Chairman of the Renaissance & Unity of Sufism, Buddhism & Shivism Friendship, today presided over the grand preparatory ceremony for the upcoming Indo-Nepal Martial Art Championship. The distinguished function was held at the Aljawad Art Academy  headed by renowned  Syed Shuja Hussain  nestled on the banks of the historic Bulbulshah & Khumaini Bridge in Bemina.

The atmosphere was charged with reverence and discipline as Dr. Renzushah inaugurated the training programme. In a stirring oration, he extended profound gratitude to the Lieutenant Governor for the landmark opening of the Arzan Garzan to the spiritual "Yous Marag"—a sacred thoroughfare hewn in the 16th century under the patronage of the pious Hafiz-e-Quran poetess, Queen Habba Khatoon, and King Yousuf Shah Chak on the Charar-i-Sharief route. He described this act as a vital reclamation of Kashmir’s syncretic soul.

The event, meticulously organized by Syed Shuja Hussain of Al- jawad Academy in presence of distinguished persond of prestigious  Youth Hostel Association of India, witnessed the presence of eminent personalities including Mr. Hilal Ahmad and the distinguished martial arts master, Pandit Kuldeep.

Addressing the gathering, Dr. Renzushah illuminated the profound legacy of Kashmir as a crucible of cosmic discipline. He emphasized the imperative of embracing the 700-year-old martial art tradition introduced by Bulbulshah and Shah Hamdan as a true spiritual medium. He traced this lineage further back to the great philosopher Confuscious who trained Kashmiris in quintuple cosmic meditation intertwined with astrology and human love, and highlighted the Pare Mahal Institute established by Dara Shukoh as a testament to this intellectual and physical heritage.

“Pure and unalloyed spirituality will once again make Kashmir the cynosure of the world,” Dr. Renzushah declared, applauding Syed Shuja and Pandit Deepak & Jenab Hilal Ahmad for their magnanimous efforts in organizing this synthesis of physical and metaphysical arts. The event was vibrant with spiritual programmes, Natiya, and breathtaking displays of martial art by fully trained cadres of Aljawad, including both boys and girls from participating educational institutes.

In a reflective tribute to civic harmony, Dr. Renzushah lauded the people of Budgam and Srinagar for their unstinting cooperation in 2007, which enabled the completion of the longest bridge connecting the two districts—now a symbol of amity named Bulbulshah & Khumaini Bridge—within a mere six months after decades of stalling.

Striking a solemn note, Dr. Renzushah addressed pressing societal challenges. He lamented the deleterious effects of the 1977 wine permission bill, recalling his tenure as DC Budgam when stringent administrative measures successfully curtailed wine & drug  consumption to zero in the district. He issued a clarion call for the urgent eradication of the twin menaces of alcohol and drugs, which he linked to the opening of the Muzaffarabad route, warning against forces seeking to corrode the pristine fabric of Kashmiri society.

He concluded with a powerful vision for the youth, urging them to channel their energies through positive tracks and streamlined spiritual ideologies. Expressing unwavering confidence in the Academy's trainees, he invoked the legacy of Scout student Tajamul Islam, who brought laurels to India on the international stage, and exhorted the martial artists preparing for the prestigious Indo-Nepal Championship in June 2026 to emulate that excellence and bring glory to the civilization of knowledge that is Kashmir.

I’ve traveled the world, and over the years, through experience, I’ve learned the best way, at least for me, to navigate any airport. Training my mind to traverse transition spaces and not teeter toward trepidation was awkward at first. 

But can I tell you the most important lesson I learned? It was how to pack and what I would be willing to carry.
Anyone who has ever lost luggage quickly learns the value of having a well-packed carry-on. 

Yet almost endlessly, we are conditioned to believe the narrative that “baggage” carries an unwanted, harmful connotation. 

People who enter new relationships carrying baggage from previous experiences are often marked as undesirable. But I would contend that it’s not the “baggage” itself that is the root cause, but the type of baggage one carries that holds the weight. 

Running through an airport due to a last-minute gate change is much easier with a backpack than a duffel bag. Learning what should be “checked” and what should be kept is fundamental.

I’m reminded of a small, often-missed detail in the well-known story of David before his encounter with Goliath. His father Jesse sent him to the front lines to deliver lunch for his brothers and gifts for their officers, and the text reads:

“Then David left the baggage in the care of the baggage keeper and ran to the battle line. And he entered and greeted his brothers.” (1 Samuel 17:22)

His mission from his father Jesse required him to carry food and gifts, but when David entered into his assignment from his heavenly Father, he instinctively knew what he was carrying was unnecessary weight. 

Imagine his hands still full as he listened to the raucous laughter of the giant taunting Israel, the stench of blasphemy on his breath.

David left the baggage with the baggage keeper.

Don’t miss this…

Discern what he didn’t leave…his shepherd’s pouch! The very pouch where he would place the five smooth stones from the nearby brook before confronting Goliath. 

A very literal interpretation of why David chose five stones is the simple fact that Goliath was known to have four other giant siblings, and David wanted to be prepared to fight them all. 

However, a deeper, more metaphorical interpretation peels back the layers of meaning and recognizes that the number five in Scripture can allude to our five senses.

One could say that David reached down and selected five smooth stones not just for aerodynamic advantage, but because all five of his senses had been submitted and submerged in “living water” (moving water). 

All of the rough and jagged edges were smoothed over in perfect alignment with the integrity of the rock, ready to be carefully selected, placed in his pouch, and deployed as a weapon against the enemy.
Observe that only one stone was selected and needed to fell the giant.

Only one sense, or one part of his emotions, was ignited. If you ask me, he chose sound. David clearly heard the insults but then spoke, with clarity, the truth of the Most High, allowing Goliath, but most importantly his OWN ears, to hear the contrast of covenant. 

Never underestimate the power of reminding your soul truth!

Some baggage you stow away. 
Some baggage you should carry on. 
But not all baggage is bad.

So tell me…
What are you carrying that should be left with the baggage keeper?

And is your shepherd’s pouch still on your person, full of your senses submitted to the discipline of surrender?

Lace up your boots. Put on your backpack. It’s time to ride.
