On January 9, 1918, in the harsh desert west of Nogales, Arizona, Captain Frederick "Blondy" Ryder and his Troop E, 10th Cavalry Buffalo Soldiers engaged a band of thirty Yaqui fighters in what would become the final armed clash between U.S. Army forces and Native Americans. The Yaquis, driven north by their ongoing war for independence against Mexico, had been using Arizona as a sanctuary to purchase weapons and ammunition before returning south to continue their resistance. When a local rancher reported butchered livestock and suspicious activity, Ryder's men spotted the armed band crossing a ridge and moved to intercept them near the international border.

The battle erupted when Ryder's dismounted troopers pursued the Yaquis up a canyon, only to receive fire from concealed positions among boulders and brush. The engagement evolved into a classic frontier skirmish, with both sides using natural cover while the Yaquis fell back systematically. During the thirty-minute firefight, one bullet struck a Yaqui fighter's ammunition belt, causing a cartridge to explode in a flash of fire—yet the wounded man continued fighting. He was the band's chief, and though mortally wounded with his stomach torn open, he never groaned as soldiers patched him and mounted him on a horse. When ten Yaquis finally surrendered to protect their retreating companions, the Americans discovered an eleven-year-old boy among them, firing a rifle nearly as tall as himself.

The captured Yaquis revealed they had only opened fire because they mistook the Buffalo Soldiers for Mexican troops. All ten prisoners, including the boy, volunteered to enlist in the U.S. Army, but were instead sent to federal court in Tucson. Charged with illegally exporting weapons to Mexico, they pleaded guilty and Judge William Henry Sawtelle sentenced them to just thirty days in jail—the boy's charges were dismissed entirely. The light sentence reflected both judicial mercy and pragmatic reality: deportation to Mexico meant certain execution as rebels. The wounded chief died the day after reaching the Army hospital in Nogales.

While the soldiers recovered a dozen rifles, German Mausers, Winchester carbines, ammunition, and bullet molds, they found no other casualties—the Yaquis had successfully carried their wounded away as they retreated. Captain Ryder later wrote that these fighters were "just as good fighting men as any Apache," acknowledging the courage of the ten who formed a rear guard to save their companions. Though merely a minor skirmish by military standards, Bear Valley holds unique historical significance as the final official battle of the American Indian Wars, closing a chapter of conflict that had defined the American frontier for over 130 years.

Parou de comer peixe depois de ver um homem cortando um que ainda movia a cauda em um pesque-pague. Achou que o peixe estivesse morto. Será que o homem achou a mesma coisa? É por isso que muitos cortam a cauda antes?, questionou-se. Mesmo na ausência de relação, a cauda estar ali e ter se movido reafirmava o que era a vida que ali havia, porém não prevalecia.

Quando parou de olhar para a cauda, concentrou-se na boca do peixe. Parecia gritar, um grito sem som, pior do que se tivesse som. Não é o grito mudo mais desesperador que o grito barulhento? Faz a mente ir longe. Pode ser dimensionado de acordo com os limites da nossa interpretação e consideração.

É horrível essa expressão, monologou baixo. Não é uma impotência aterradora? Olhou em volta e percebeu que estava sozinho nesse incômodo, que ninguém se importaria com isso. Se dissesse alguma coisa, ririam ou ignorariam. Estavam ali por um estranho e tão comum paradoxo – ao mesmo tempo que estavam ali pelo peixe não estavam pelo peixe.

Por que tantos risos e sorrisos? A faca que afundava na carne do peixe quase encostava na madeira da mesa. A ligação entre corpo e cabeça mantinha-se por uma fina tira de pele. Até que foi arrancada e jogada no lixo.

Circulou pela mesa e observou a cabeça no lixo, a mesma expressão agora desconectada do corpo. Tudo que via se resumia agora a uma palavra – desespero. Havia outras cabeças que repetiam a mesma agonia. Se morrem da mesma forma, é no mínimo algo a ser notado, comentou.

Depois pensou em como ele mesmo poderia não ter se importado com nada disso se a cauda não tivesse se movido sobre a mesa. Lembrou-se de que ouviu em algum lugar que mesmo fora d’água muitos peixes demoram pra morrer. Por que não tinha lembrado disso antes, só agora?

Concluiu que a vontade e a disposição humana podem empurrar lembranças incômodas para um quarto escuro da consciência, para não ameaçarem interesses que queremos preservar. Olhou em volta e teve certeza de que tudo que pensava agora era naquele lugar uma conclusão solitária. Se não fosse assim, estaria com os outros, vendo o peixe sem vê-lo, rindo ou sorrindo.

Foto: Unparalleled Suffering

I was traveling end of November from Calgary to Kelowna and had a walker due to a recent back surgery.  Because I purchased a ticket that didn't include a carry on when checking in for my flight, the Air Canada app made me put a credit card on file in case I brought a bag to the gate. When I got to the gate I got a tag from the counter for my walker. As soon as I went to sit down I received an email receipt that I was charged for checking in a bag. I went back to the counter and the lady told me she made a mistake and refunded it, but to watch my credit card in the coming days in case the charge went through I would have to apply for a refund online, but she would make a note on my file. In the coming days my credit card was charged. I made a request online explaining the situation and 3 weeks later Air Canada accessibility department emailed me and denied my refund. I'm a single mom of 2 kids on medical EI at Christmas and they refused to refund a charge for something I didn't do. I sent another email explaining again that I didnt bring a bag and included a picture of my walker and asked for them to show me their policy where they are allowed to charge for a disability aid. I did not hear back. I followed up after 30 days requesting a response and have still not heard anything.  I made a refund request through my credit card and it is still pending. The longer this goes on the more upset I am for being charged for having a disability. It keeps me up many nights just replaying everything in my head. I flew this same ticket with Westjet and they never charged my walker as baggage. I have made a complaint with the CTA, but I want Air Canada to acknowledge this wrongdoing and take appropriate steps so it doesn't happen to someone else. It appears I wont be able to get their attention on my own. Does anyone have any suggestions for any other steps I can take?

It is crucial to acknowledge contributions from all groups involved in our struggle for independence; credit must be given where it is due.

Currently, the truth exists mostly in oral tradition, which is vulnerable to distortion and offers limited influence on national attitudes. We need a written record that can withstand manipulation and foster a more inclusive understanding of our history.

Before the appointment of governor Rin Tueny, the Agar and Ciec Manyiel used to raid from each other despite being Muonyjang or being people of Lakes State.

 Pakam of Rumbek north and Luanjang Aguer Adel of Tonj East raid from each other and they're not only Muonyjang but all from Bahr el gazal region. The same happens between the Bul of mayom and their other Nuers like the Dok of Leer County. 
Raiding has been a practice among the Nilotics and it's independent of tribal hatred. It has something to do with our values, pride, dominance, bravery and sectional hegemony.  Therefore, I don't agree with those who want history to be altered for the sake of emotional regulation. 

Slavery and slave trade is taught to us in secondary schools today but there's no point in time we ever complained and suggested editing the historical facts in it. The only problem with the book is narrowing cattle raiding to the Nuer alone when it's a normal practice among the Nilotics. If there's something that should be added in the second edition, It is that the Dinka too raid from the Nuer and from among themselves and so do the Nuer among themselves because it's not the Dinka alone they raid.

This brother sister combo both weighing above 175 kgs came from Tanzania to take a life defining step in their fight against Obesity. They opted for Bariatric surgery and were ready to take control of their health.

In a short while , the change has been significant, not only in their weight, but in stamina, movement and overall health parameters.

Bariatric surgery isn’t some magic. It works by altering the stomach’s capacity and bypassing parts of the small intestine to induce hormonal responses that influence hunger, alter gut microbiome, food preferences and hence have an effect on metabolism and bring about blood sugar control. It’s a time tested scientifically proven tool, more like a stepping stone toward long-term metabolic health. The real transformation happens when surgery is combined with commitment and structured lifestyle change.

Both are true fighters and I’m happy to see the progress they’ve made so far, my team and I will continue to provide close aftercare and guidance every step of the way.

The journey doesn’t end in the operating room, that’s where it begins.

Our Existence Is Giving Them Nightmares.

By Tut Kuany Kok 

The only thing we agreed on with the Nuer who sold their souls to the devil—Salva Kiir's totalitarian government—is that Nuer are dehumanized in that high school textbook, where the author of the book said, "Nuer are cattle raiders who raided Dinka's cattle," and he further mentioned that Nuer didn't participate in Sudan’s longest civil war and that when the Dinka were fighting for independence, Nuer were busy protecting their areas. But the question to Nuer Wew in Juba is, how do you feel about this—after agreeing that the description in the book doesn't fit us, and if it does, it shouldn't be written in a national book? Isn't this enough for you to understand that that government doesn't mean well for you, but for the Dinka's interest? How could the whole Ministry of Education allow such to be taught in high school?

Before the Rwandan genocide that left 800,000 Tutsi dead, the term "cockroaches" (inyenzi) was used as a dehumanizing slur against the Tutsi minority by Hutu extremists during the 1994 Rwandan genocide. Broadcast by Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, this propaganda aimed to justify the mass extermination of Tutsis, and indeed the Hutu adopted this slur from their leaders—in which young Hutu men axed to death their Tutsi friends because "how can you share a bed with a cockroach?" they asked themselves.

Similarly, the same dehumanization was used during the training of Mathiang Anynor, Dutku Beny, and Gelweng before the 2013 Nuer genocide. They were told by their Dinka generals, including Agel Machar, that Nuer "are our intergenerational enemies—they're killers, they are cattle raiders, they are inhumane. They deserve to be wiped out if we want to rule South Sudan forever." Because of these slurs, 24,000 innocent Nuer died in 2013, and many are still dying. To me, this has been the objective and purpose for which Salva Kiir is in power—to fulfill the Dinka's long plan—"exterminate the Nuer up to their third generation."

If the country is being viewed by one tribe—the Dinka—as rightfully belonging to them, how do you expect stability, equality, pluralism, and equal wealth sharing? And do you expect the children being born and raised in South Sudan to see each other as brothers and sisters from the same country when one tribe is making sure that Nuer history is being taught in high school to dehumanize them?

In 2013, when Nuer survivors were running into hiding and UNMISS, Equatorians were laughing at us—saying a lot of bad things; the things falsely told to them by the Dinka about us. But they later realized that the Nuer man is not the problem, but the Dinka is the enemy of the country. This was how Equatorians viewed us before the Dinka showed them their true colors—grabbing their lands and bedding their girls in an undignified manner.

For us to change all this madness, we should start by rewriting the literature itself—for in all the books written by Dinka authors, they distorted the chronicles—the history in which South Sudan came into existence. In all their writings, Dinka are the ones who fought for the country. But a Dinka with a pure mind would say the truth. For example, in one of his interviews, the late Dr. John Garang admitted that the Nuer man was the first person to wage war against the Arabs, and the rest joined later.

However, for this humiliation to end, we as the Nuer community need to ask ourselves: if this is the kind of situation we will always find ourselves in from people who hate our existence and don't appreciate the fact that without us, South Sudan wouldn't have been an independent country, how long will they continue with their hateful speeches, writings, and gossip while we don't respond in a way they would find painful and regrettable?

As much as we hate someone who tries to subject us to all manners of dehumanization, mistreatment, and slavery, it's time for us to collectively put our minds together and deal with the enemy head-on, but without facing the perennial threat to our very dear lives, we will continue being divided, killed, insulted, degraded, and more. For we understand the motive of this government, we don't have to ask ourselves why Salva Kiir and his tribal confidants are doing everything to make sure our people are killed, displaced, and their lands invaded, because this has been their plan before independence.

Now, our son—Dr. Riek Machar, whom they see as a threat, has been put under house arrest because they don't want him—they want to send him into forced retirement from politics. If this is not a humiliation against the entire Nuer community, how can you describe it? 

Again, they are using our own sons to implement their evil agenda of "we have to make sure we deprive any Nuer man of rising to the political peak—the presidency." They are sending all Nuer generals to fight their own brothers in Jonglei, Upper Nile, and Unity State. Worst of all, they are using the money from the oil mined from our own land to kill us. Isn't this something we need to look into with clear mind?

Lastly, I'm calling on Nuer sons and daughters to come together to face this intergenerational threat that has been planned to make sure we don't exist in South Sudan. It's time to think beyond hate, misunderstanding, and disunity among ourselves. It's time to understand that the enemy is doing everything to divide us, and through this division, he is succeeding in killing us and displacing us.

The other day, I found myself standing in the middle of my living room, holding a single, chipped coffee mug emblazoned with a cartoon cat that had clearly seen better decades. I didn’t like the mug. I didn’t even drink coffee. But as I went to toss it in the donation box, a familiar, icy hand gripped my heart. But what if I need it for a guest? What if it was a gift? What if I’m throwing away a perfectly good memory?

It was in that moment of absurd, mug-induced paralysis that a friend pressed a dog-eared copy of Messie Condo’s "Nobody Wants Your Sh*t" into my free hand. "Just read the first chapter," she said. I did. And then I read the rest in one sitting, because it felt like the author had secretly installed a camera in my childhood home and was now gently but firmly calling me out for the emotional baggage I was storing in my garage.

This isn't just a book about decluttering; it’s a masterclass in unburdening your soul, one hideous vase at a time. With wit as sharp as a freshly organized knife block and a compassion that feels like a warm hug from a friend holding a trash bag, Messie Condo dismantles the hoarder mentality we all harbor, arguing that our homes have become haunted by the ghosts of guilt, obligation, and "someday."

Here are five profound, life-altering lessons I learned from "Nobody Wants Your Sh*t":

1. The "Someday" Lie is Keeping You Hostage.
Condo brilliantly identifies the "Someday" fallacy—the belief that we are merely temporary custodians of objects waiting for their "one day" purpose. Someday I’ll wear that size 2 dress. Someday I’ll learn to play that dusty guitar. Someday I’ll have a formal dinner party for 20 and need those 17 mismatched champagne flutes. She argues that "someday" is a fantasy that steals the peace of today. By holding onto the props for a life we aren't living, we are suffocating the life we actually have.

2. Your Stuff is Not Your Resume.
We keep things because they represent who we were—the trophies from high school, the textbooks from a degree we never used, the business cards from a past life. Condo writes that this turns our homes into museums of our former selves. The lesson is that your identity isn't in the objects, but in the experiences. You don't need the ski trophy to prove you were once adventurous; the adventurous spirit is still in you, or it's not. Holding onto the trophy doesn't bring it back.

3. Guilt is a Terrible Interior Designer.
Perhaps the most freeing lesson is about the items we keep out of obligation: the gift from a well-meaning aunt, the heirloom china we hate, the expensive candle we never lit. Condo reframes this, reminding us that the giving of the gift was the act of love. By holding onto something we dislike, we are not honoring the giver; we are simply creating a daily monument to guilt. A truly grateful recipient, she argues, would pass it on to someone who would actually love it.

4. The "Sunk Cost" Fallacy Applies to More Than Money.
We’ve all done it: bought expensive hiking boots, used them once, and now they sit in the closet for a decade because we can’t bear to admit we wasted the money. Condo calls this the "closet of shame." She teaches that the money is already gone. That was the cost of the lesson that you don't like hiking. Now, keeping the boots is just costing you closet space and daily pangs of regret. Get rid of them and let the lesson be the only remnant.

5. Space is a Verb, Not a Noun.
This was the most poetic takeaway. Condo explains that we think of space as a static, empty area to be filled. But she posits that space is an active energy—it's room to breathe, to move, to think, to create. Every time we get rid of something we don't need, we aren't just creating an empty corner; we are creating the potential for something new to enter our lives, whether it’s a new hobby, a calmer mind, or just the ability to do a cartwheel in the living room.

By the time I finished the book, I looked back at the chipped cat mug. I didn't see a memory anymore. I saw a dusty, unwanted object holding my future hostage. I smiled, thanked it for its service, and dropped it in the bin. My living room didn't just feel cleaner. It felt lighter. And honestly, so did I. "Nobody Wants Your Sh*t" isn't just a book you read; it's a permission slip you give yourself to finally, peacefully, let go.
